The other Post Office scandal: how organised crime launders money on the high street
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
04:00:49 UTC
13:00:49 KST

Leicestershire police won’t say who first told them about Jigar Gheewala, but you can see why, once they had heard of him, they decided to find out more. Gheewala was unemployed, had no apparent income, yet lived in a £1.3m house and sent his three children to private school. “He was a declared bankrupt, with a bank account that was absolutely not reflective of what it should be,” said financial crime supervisor Laura Panter of Leicestershire police’s economic crime team. “That was our starting point.”
Over the course of 2020, despite being on benefits, Gheewala’s bank account received more than £880,000 in cash in 200 different deposits. He was, it turned out, a money launderer, but not the kind you’ll see in the movies. Gheewala’s deposits had been made not in Liechtenstein or on Grand Cayman, but at various post office branches in Leicester, one thick wodge of banknotes after another.
As banks have closed branches all over Britain, post offices have quietly become central to how we move our money. In 2017, post offices began to accept deposits on behalf of banks, and those deposits now exceed £30bn a year. The way it works is straightforward. A customer hands over banknotes to be counted, then inserts a bank card and enters the pin, like a cashpoint in reverse. The post office system then credits the value of the cash to the account linked to the card.
It is a simple system, which Post Office Ltd, the state-owned company that controls the branches, says provides a crucial service to businesses and individuals otherwise cut off from banking services. But the simplicity comes at a cost. It has eliminated many of the checks that previously stopped criminals from laundering their cash. In the same way you can use someone else’s card to take money from a cashpoint, provided you know the pin, you can use any bank card to make a deposit at the post office. The process is deliberately streamlined and, unlike at a bank, the post office operative (often referred to as postmaster or subpostmaster) has no way to access any of the account details, and thus no way to check if the person with the card is its holder, or whether this transaction is part of a suspicious pattern.
Law enforcement agencies estimate that, alongside ordinary businesses’ takings, hundreds of millions of pounds of dirty money are being paid into the post office each year. This allows drug dealers and other criminals to bank their illicit wealth, and profit from their crimes, and to do so with the absolute minimum of effort. “The number of places where cash can come into the economy is vast now but, as bank branches continue to close, the number of places to pay it back in has necessarily become more restricted. You’ve got this sort of reverse funnel effect going on,” said a former Post Office employee with knowledge of how it organises financial services. “The bad guys are genuinely targeting post offices as one of the few places left where they can actually go to put money in.”
Leicestershire police used Gheewala’s transactions to reconstruct how he operated. On a typical day, he might make his first cash deposit in the east of the city, at a post-office counter hosted by a convenience store; then it would be a five-minute drive to another store, with boxes of veg out the front, its windows obscured by decals of soft drinks and spirits, offering post office services alongside the scratchcards. A few minutes away was another branch, between a chemist and a fried chicken shop, before another short drive would bring him to a retail centre where the post office sat next to a bakery on a prosperous-looking residential street. A final drive north would take him to a convenience store among red-brick detached houses, and that was a morning’s work done: thousands of pounds deposited in an hour or so, bundles of criminal cash being paid into the most ordinary of locations.
“When we started looking at this, we were then able to see other individuals in Leicestershire that were mimicking exactly the same activity,” said Panter. “What we were finding was there was quite a consistent pattern in terms of the deposit activity around post offices.”
Panter and her colleagues’ investigation became Operation Kilo, which began in 2021 and culminated in December 2025 with Gheewala being sentenced to almost 12 years in prison, along with six co-conspirators. And this was not just a Leicester-based operation. Officers watched as couriers came to Leicester with bags full of cash earned by criminals from London and Yorkshire, stashing them in shops for Gheewala’s people to pick up. Each day’s haul would be distributed among a network of underlings, who trekked around the city’s post offices, paying rubber-band-bound stacks of banknotes into as many as 10 different accounts at each stop, using cards with the pins written on the back.
The bank accounts into which the money was deposited belonged to ordinary people – “mules” in police jargon – who received small payments for renting them out, or to companies in Leicester’s garment business, where managers faked invoices to make the payments look legitimate. (Gheewala promised the mules £50 per £10,000 laundered, but in reality he often seems to have paid them less than that.) Gheewala controlled the whole operation from a laptop kept in an otherwise empty house, with all the account details and their passwords written down in a notebook. As soon as the money appeared online he would, using cryptocurrency exchanges, disperse it around the world.
In two years, Gheewala’s group moved an astonishing £53m, allowing organised criminals to legitimise their earnings on an industrial scale. It’s not clear how much exactly Gheewala was charging for the service, although to judge by the lifestyle he was living, he was doing well out of it.
His operation might have been big, but it wasn’t unique. Just a month after Gheewala’s conviction, two men were jailed in Birmingham for an almost-identical scheme, in which they paid in up to £200,000 a day as they travelled between 10 post offices in the east of the city. In April, a man from Cheltenham was jailed for six years and eight months for controlling a network of mules paying millions of pounds of cash into post offices in Bristol and Gloucestershire.
And this has been going on for a while. Two men were jailed at Southwark crown court in 2024 for paying £26m into post offices in London and Manchester before their arrests in 2017. Students have been jailed in Scotland for paying criminal money into post offices, and there are other ongoing cases in which similar crimes are alleged.
If it wasn’t for what has been going on elsewhere in the Post Office, this would be a major story. Instead, it has been largely ignored.
The Post Office Horizon scandal burst into the public consciousness thanks to 2024’s ITV drama Mr Bates vs the Post Office, but by that stage it had been dragging on for two decades. Post Office Ltd wrongly prosecuted hundreds of its post office operatives, despite senior figures knowing that the computer program that supposedly showed they had been committing fraud was faulty. Ex-post office operative Alan Bates’s landmark victory against his former employers in 2019 forced the government to overturn his and others’ convictions, and to promise to pay hundreds of millions of pounds in compensation.
The scandal is one of Britain’s worst miscarriages of justice. One of its unfortunate side effects is that it has impeded investigations into how much money is being laundered via post office branches. Even if police officers are themselves confident that figures originating in Post Office Ltd’s Horizon software (a version of which is still being used) are reliable, they are aware that many jury members will – for understandable reasons – be intensely sceptical. Documents released by the inquiry into the Horizon scandal show that, in 2024, just a few weeks after the ITV drama was first aired, a detective constable from Blackburn police station decided to halt an investigation into “large-scale money laundering, and possibly other fraud offences” via post office branches in Lancashire out of concern that defence lawyers would find it too easy to discredit evidence originating from the computer system.
“After the Mr Bates TV show, it became a real hot potato and nobody wanted to get hold of it,” said one officer, who asked to remain anonymous. “For every case that’s brought, there are many more in the background. There is no real appetite to do anything unless it’s a slam dunk, because the public is on the side of the post office operatives.” So the problem remains. “It’s the way that you can pay money into the post office without checks, that’s the problem. It’s huge.”
If you look at the raw numbers, you can see his point. In October 2020, cash deposits at post-office branches across the UK totalled £1.9bn. That is £1.9bn for that single month, not the whole year. The following October, the sum was £2.2bn. That number kept rising each year until, by October 2025, it came to £2.9bn – an increase of 50% in just five years. Although Post Office Ltd then stopped publishing such detailed figures, the trend has continued. It boasted of a 10% increase in deposits in the first quarter of this year, meaning they have now almost certainly passed £3bn a month.
What makes these numbers so astounding is that over the same period, cash usage among the general public has dropped sharply. Cash now accounts for fewer than one in 10 transactions in the UK. Yet cash deposits at the post office have gone sharply in the opposite direction.
According to Post Office Ltd, the reason it stopped publishing monthly cash totals last year was because its post office operatives did not want to alert criminals to the amount of money they had on the premises. Branches are vulnerable to theft for the same reason they are wide open to money laundering. They are often just ordinary shops offering post-office services over the counter, and they lack the specialised equipment that would allow them to track who is on the premises, or to keep their employees safe.
Back when Post Office Ltd was still publishing its monthly cash figures, it would accompany them with upbeat quotes about how much it was helping small businesses by providing banking services. While much of the increase is certainly being driven by the closure of bank branches, a senior police officer would regularly forward the figures to me, accompanied with a single emoji: 👀.
Concerns about being seen to further victimise post office operatives has discouraged police officers from going on the record about the scale of the problem that they’re seeing. “I’m sure you appreciate that anything quotable is going to have to be suitably vanilla,” another senior officer told me. “It would need to be, you know, ‘we work in partnership’, ‘there are many perspectives’-type stuff.”
The sensitivity is understandable, but it comes with dangers. By making it possible for organised criminals – drug dealers, human traffickers, thieves, fraudsters and others – to launder their earnings, and thus to keep their profits, the post office risks creating an entirely different scandal.
The trial of Giuseppe Sangiovanni and seven of his alleged co-conspirators was due to start in May 2025 at Bristol crown court, and to run for several days. Sangiovanni was accused of running a scheme that laundered £2.2m via post office branches in Bristol and Gloucestershire over a few months of 2021. His alleged co-conspirators were accused of letting him move money through their bank accounts in return for small payments.
On the first morning of the trial, however, Sangiovanni changed his plea to guilty and left the courtroom to await a fresh hearing, leaving his co-defendants behind. It quickly became clear that they were not criminal masterminds. I had only just arrived in Bristol and knew only the bare outlines of the case, but even I could tell their chances of escaping conviction were now close to nonexistent. If the prosecutors had all the transaction details, and the ringleader was admitting the charges, then the owners of the bank accounts through which the money had passed would find it all but impossible to convince a jury that nothing untoward had occurred.
Technically, a trial was still scheduled, but it was so obviously not going to happen that the jury never even entered the courtroom. The two prosecution lawyers, far from wargaming the new reality, were using the break to discuss holiday destinations for their unexpected spell of spare time. The only people present who appeared not to realise the consequences of Sangiovanni’s decision were his co-defendants, who continued to sit in the dock like baby birds in smart casual, with only the haziest of ideas what was going on.
The judge tried to help, encouraging them to discuss things with their lawyers. They whispered among themselves, until one at a time – over the course of many hours, and after many hearings were convened, suspended and convened again – they changed their pleas to guilty too. (They were not masterminds, as I say, and mostly received suspended sentences.)
“They’re just run-of-the-mill local criminals. A couple of them weren’t really criminals at all. One that we didn’t charge was a single mum and, to a degree, was exploited,” said Detective Inspector Peter Highway of the south west regional organised crime unit. It was only while being interviewed by police that one defendant discovered that Sangiovanni had laundered more than £1m through his bank account. “He was a bit surprised by that number,” said Highway, “because he hadn’t done the deposits himself.”
Money laundering was criminalised in the UK in 1988 as part of a global effort to close loopholes in the financial system that were allowing criminals to keep their profits. Previously, it had been easy for criminals to walk into a bank and pay in cash, no questions asked, but the new laws obliged bankers to report suspicious transactions to law enforcement agencies. The theory was that, with bankers sending in a steady stream of suspicious activity reports, police officers would be able to see money being laundered in real time, freeze it and arrest its owners.
The world has moved on since then and the most sophisticated crime, such as fraud, involves electronic money stolen from people’s bank accounts and moved in a bewildering variety of ways, involving shell companies, cryptocurrencies, secrecy jurisdictions and more. This requires equally advanced countermeasures from banks, which use AI-powered tools to spot the signs of criminal behaviour.
At the street level, however, not much has changed: criminals still use cash, and the National Crime Agency estimates that they launder about £12bn worth of banknotes in the UK each year, largely by presenting the money as the fruits of legitimate businesses. This is where branches of the post office come in.
From the criminals’ point of view, post offices are quick and easy places to launder dodgy money. “There’s no requirement for ID verification, there’s no requirement for any kind of enhanced screening, there’s no centralised CCTV,” said the second senior police officer. We put a higher bar on buying alcohol than we do on money laundering via the post office.
This is why Gheewala’s mules were able to go into a branch with a pocket full of bank cards, and pay bundles of cash into multiple accounts, one after another. “You definitely don’t want, in a post office that has already got queues out the door, to have a complicated financial transaction going on. So everything that the post office does for banking is done with simplicity in mind,” said the former Post Office employee.
The trouble then is, as happened in Leicester, that criminals move money onwards as soon as it arrives in a bank account. Any reports that post office employees do make about the transaction will come too late for the bank to be able to freeze it. This defangs the UK’s entire anti-money-laundering strategy, which has always relied on being able to block suspicious transactions while officers investigate them.
The criminal possibilities opened up by Post Office Ltd’s foray into banking were quickly obvious. In July 2020, the Post Office’s compliance committee noted £7m of questionable deposits had gone into 45 branches. In November that year, it discussed how £5-7m a week was being deposited at just two branches in east London, and said it was discussing with the banks what action to take.
Sangiovanni and his co-defendants fell foul of this kind of scrutiny, after bank compliance officers spotted what amounted to millions of pounds of suspicious cash transactions at 27 post offices around Gloucestershire, and alerted the police who brought in first the mules, then Sangiovanni, for questioning. “He gave an account that he would go to a car park at Asda, and someone would give him a carrier bag full of cash, and he would then take it away, and then send them some crypto,” said Highway. “He didn’t feel that was suspicious. We did.”
By the time officers from the south west organised crime unit moved in, however, the money was long gone. So, although they caught Sangiovanni, the criminals whose cash he was laundering got to enjoy the freshly laundered money. “Millions of pounds into the laundering, that’s a bit late in the day,” said Highway.
It looks obvious how to close this gap in our defences against dirty cash. If the Post Office is going to act like a bank, it should collect the same kind of information as a bank, make the same kind of reports as a bank, and freeze transactions in the same way that banks do. In 2023, the regulators at the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) took a small step in this direction, by imposing limits on how much cash could be deposited at the post office at any one time. It was a logical step to take, but it ran into immediate controversy.
The fact that two-thirds of bank branches have closed in the UK in the past decade has left businesses and individuals who still rely on cash heavily dependent on post-office branches to pay in their takings. Post Office Ltd used this fact to push back against the FCA’s deposit limits by saying they were penalising hard-pressed businesses that were just trying to stay afloat. “They are hurting legitimate customers and businesses who need support,” said Ross Borkett, Post Office Ltd’s then-head of banking, after the FCA’s changes were announced. Cash-intensive businesses, via the British Independent Retailers Association and the Independent Retail Consortium, mobilised a lobbying operation, writing to their MPs, who in turn held debates in parliament to highlight how few bank branches were left in their constituencies.
As a result, ministers promised to ensure that businesses and individuals still reliant on banknotes and coins would always be able to use them. In other words, the FCA’s cash limit is likely to be the last intervention to make payments at post offices harder.
At a time when an increasingly large proportion of the population can’t access a physical bank branch, the 11,500 post-office branches in the UK will become ever-more central to a strategy of ensuring everyone can still use banknotes. Moving, securing and accepting cash is expensive though, which is one reason why the banks don’t much want to do it any more. Post offices don’t charge their customers for making deposits, however, so who is going to pay for it?
The answer to that question is tied up in the legacy of the Horizon scandal. Post Office Ltd was already in significant financial difficulties before it began having to pay compensation to the hundreds of post office operatives that it had unfairly prosecuted. It has now had to distribute more than £1bn, pushing it into a deep annual loss.
That is already a significant challenge for its long-term viability, but it is only half of the problem it faces. Post-office branches operate as independent businesses, but the amount of money operatives earned from providing post office services fell by almost 5% in the decade to 2023, in part thanks to fewer people sending letters. Meanwhile, post office operatives’ expenses have increased. So Post Office Ltd not only needs to find the money to pay compensation to the post office operatives it has wronged, but it must also simultaneously find a sustainable business model if it wants people to be post office operatives at all. And that is where banking comes in.
Banks pay Post Office Ltd for providing services on their behalf, which helped it to post revenues of £309m from “banking and ATMs” in its 2024-5 accounts. That was more than a third of its revenues for that year, and only slightly less than it earned from handling the mail. In fact, Post Office Ltd may already be making more money from deposits and withdrawals than it does from its traditional business. As the former insider joked: “We should start calling it the Bank Office.”
This isn’t just important for Post Office Ltd, but also for individual post office operatives, who earn a fee for every cash deposit they accept. “The post office operatives will be remunerated on the transactions that they have through their branch, so they will get a transaction fee,” Ben Woollard, the new head of banking at Post Office Ltd, told me. “As with any product, the more a post office operative or any business will deliver, then they will earn more income out of that.”
Woollard argues that post-office branches are no different from any other business in being vulnerable to money laundering. He pointed out to me that anyone offering banking services receives annual training in how to recognise and tackle money laundering, and that the head office sends out alerts to branches in areas that appear to have a large number of suspicious transactions.
But although any business that handles cash could be exploited by criminals, it is also true that few businesses handle banknotes in the volumes that routinely pass through post-office branches, making them more vulnerable to abuse than most. Post office operatives are also running a system that we know is already wide open to dirty money, and are rewarded proportionally to the raw total of money they put through it, so the temptation to look the other way or even to provide financial services to criminals must be ever-present.
We have no idea how many insiders have given in to this temptation, and it looks likely that we will remain in the dark. The disastrous legacy of the Horizon scandal means there has been little appetite to investigate. With such a deeply flawed system, the best that police officers can hope for is to prosecute the more egregious offenders.
So despite the success of Operation Kilo, Leicestershire police’s Detective Constable Catherine Richards wasn’t exactly optimistic that Gheewala’s conviction would change anything: “Crime is continuing,” she told me. “Money needs to be laundered. And, yeah, somebody else fills those boots, don’t they?”

NHS England to offer women ‘gamechanging’ free home testing kits for cervical cancer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
04:00:48 UTC
13:00:48 KST

Millions of women in England who have missed cervical screening appointments will be offered free home testing kits on the NHS.
The move comes amid concerns that only two-thirds of women attend in-person cervical screening appointments when asked to do so, leaving as many as 4 million women not up to date.
The rollout is being described as a “gamechanger”, offering a “discreet and convenient option” to encourage more women to get screened.
The kits contain a swab to collect a sample from the vagina. This is then posted back to the NHS free, where it is tested in labs for high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV).
If high-risk HPV is detected, patients will then be asked to attend a cervical screening appointment with a clinician.
HPV is a group of viruses that can be passed on through sexual contact and cause no symptoms. About 13 high-risk types of the virus are known to cause 99.7% of cervical cancers.
Starting on Tuesday, eligible women between 30 and 65 who have not attended screening appointments will be sent invitations via the NHS app, text message, email or letter.
They will then be able to order a kit through the app or website. The scheme is part of the NHS’s target of eliminating cervical cancer by 2040.
Dr Sue Mann, national clinical director for women’s health at NHS England, said: “Screening saves thousands of lives each year by preventing cancers and catching them earlier, but only around two-thirds of women are attending cervical screening appointments when invited by the NHS.
“Offering millions of women an alternative test they can do from the comfort of their own homes will be a gamechanger – making it easier than ever for them to get tested for HPV.”
Women aged between 24 and 64 are invited for cervical screening every five years, or more often if HPV is detected.
The latest figures from NHS England show 68.8% of eligible women are up to date with cervical screening, below the 80% target. It means about 4 million women are not up to date, according to NHS estimates.
“There are lots of reasons that may stop women from getting their cervical screening – embarrassment, lack of time, or worries about discomfort – and these kits provide a discreet and convenient option we hope will encourage more women to take up the life-saving test,” said Mann.
“So, if you’re invited to take part, please order a test – it’s a simple swab you can do at home in minutes.”
Athena Lamnisos, chief executive of the Eve Appeal, welcomed the move, saying that self-testing at home would be a “step-change” for many women.
Michelle Mitchell, chief executive of Cancer Research UK, said: “Cervical screening is a powerful tool that saves lives – it can prevent cervical cancer or spot it at an earlier stage when treatment is more likely to be successful.
“While it’s best for cervical screening to be done by a nurse or doctor, there are barriers that make it challenging for some people to attend. At-home HPV self-testing kits will help more people take part in a way that works for them.”
Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, said the aim was to make it as easy and convenient as possible for women to keep up with their screening. She said: “This is the future NHS we are building – there for all of us when we need it, and acting as early as possible to stop preventable deaths.”

From Malaysia to the Philippines, residents have begun resisting power-hungry AI projects planned next to their homes
Instead, they learned that Petaling Jaya City Council (MBPJ) had received an application for two three-storey data centre blocks – part of the vast physical infrastructure now being built across Southeast Asia to support cloud computing and artificial intelligence.

Debate star and physicist Guo Yanliang leaves a top European quantum lab for China
Renmin University recruit aims to probe complex quantum matter using ultracold atomic sandbox with lasers
Guo Yanliang, a champion debater who honed his argumentation skills in international contests and on online variety shows, has left one of Europe’s top quantum laboratories to set up his own research group in Beijing.
Guo, 33, says he sees scientific research as a debate between different opinions, which made him more compatible with China than Europe.
This year, he returned to China to take a position as associate professor at Renmin University of China where he is building an ultracold atom experiment platform.
While he has had papers published in Science and Nature and secured a spot on MIT Technology Review’s “Innovators Under 35 China” list, the physicist says he returned because China offered better support for his long‑term research goals.
“The research environment here is more in line with my research characteristics,” he told DeepTech, the Chinese branch of MIT Technology Review, last month.

Morning Briefing: Aug. 25, 2026

Diyar Guldogan
25 August 2026•Update: 25 August 2026
Here’s a rundown of all the news you need to start your Tuesday, including the US State Department's removal of Syria from its State Sponsor of Terrorism list and the US launch of Operation Economic Outcast to sever Iran's financial 'lifelines.’
TOP STORIES
- US removes Syria from state sponsor of terrorism list
The US State Department removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism, fulfilling President Donald Trump's commitment to provide sanctions relief to the post-Assad government.
Syria is no longer subject to prohibitions under the Terrorism List Governments Sanctions Regulations, according to the Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control. Washington revoked the designation of the al-Nusrah Front, also known as Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham, as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist Organization.
The Treasury's office also removed Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham from the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List.
- US launches Operation Economic Outcast to sever Iran's financial 'lifelines'
The US launched Operation Economic Outcast, a sweeping campaign intended to completely isolate Iran from the global financial system, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced.
“Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone,” Bessent told reporters.
Directed by US President Donald Trump, the “unprecedented” sanctions target Iran’s "most vital lifelines," including aviation, shipping, gold, technology and digital assets, he said.
NEWS IN BRIEF
- French President Emmanuel Macron and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman opposed imposing any direct or indirect fees on navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, according to a joint statement.
- The UN condemned the killing of two peacekeepers during an ambush in South Sudan's Jonglei State.
- The Israeli army ordered the evacuation of a residential area north of the Al-Shati refugee camp in northwestern Gaza City, witnesses told Anadolu.
- Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and his Brazilian counterpart Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva discussed ties between their countries as well as regional and global issues, Türkiye’s Communications Directorate said.
- French President Emmanuel Macron said he is enacting a law banning cellphones in high schools starting with the new school year.
- Threats against Iran’s infrastructure will be met with “heavy strikes” on US energy chokepoints and vital interests, an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) spokesman said.
- Syria hailed its removal from the US list of state sponsors of terrorism as the “result of the transformation brought about by the Syrian people,” saying the decision reflects the new Syrian state’s commitment to international peace and security.
- Russia delivered a confrontational message to the UN Security Council, asserting that Moscow will reject any peace settlement that compromises its core security interests as the conflict in Ukraine reaches the 4 1/2-year mark.
- Israeli forces carried out incursions into southern Syria, entering villages in Daraa and Quneitra provinces and conducting searches a day after Damascus and Tel Aviv held talks aimed at reducing tensions.
- A picture taken by a Palestinian photographer was removed from a sports photography festival in the French coastal city of Deauville after organizers got requests from unnamed sources, reports said.
- Türkiye and Qatar aim to increase their bilateral trade volume to $5 billion, Turkish Trade Minister Omer Bolat said.
- The Ukraine war must be made painful to push Russia to peace talks, Ukraine’s president urged.

BUSINESS & ECONOMY
- US set to raise tariffs on Canadian autos, steel to 50% starting Jan. 1
US President Donald Trump escalated a major trade dispute by announcing that Washington will impose a 50% tariff on all Canadian cars, trucks, automotive parts and steel starting next Jan. 1.
“Canada has been ripping off the United States of America for years,” Trump wrote on his social media platform Truth Social.
He claimed that “ridiculously high” Canadian duties on American agricultural goods have made life “impossible” for US farmers and resulted in a $60 billion annual trade deficit.

====================================================================================================

Moving to the countryside for a home: young people flee city housing costs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
03:56:41 UTC
12:56:41 KST

13% of would-be homebuyers plan to move to towns under 10,000 residents. Often single 35-year-olds on average incomes, they see depopulated Spain as their only escape from a housing market that has shut them out.
Spain has a housing problem that has been getting worse for years and has already changed the way its young people think about their future. Buying a flat in Madrid, Barcelona or Málaga is, for most people under 40, a mission impossible. Renting on your own is no more viable: those who move out alone devote on average 98.7% of their salary to housing.
The result is a generation that feels trapped: only 14.5% of young people aged 16 to 29 have managed to move out, and the average age for leaving the parental home has risen to 30, compared with 26 in the European Union. According to data from the National Statistics Institute (INE), 44.3% of young people aged 26 to 34 were still living in the family home in 2025.
The previous generation was able to buy flats, cars and even second homes on an average wage. Today that is a pipe dream. With a shortage of housing and strong demand, purchase prices rose by 14.7% year on year in the past 12 months and rents by 10.9%, according to Bankinter, while wages for under-35s have barely grown in real terms.
On top of this comes the overcrowding of cities, which have become urban spaces hosting more people than they can cope with, with high levels of pollution and where it is impossible to find the rest and disconnection that still exist in the countryside. For all these reasons, more and more young people are swapping cities for depopulated villages where buying a home has not yet become an unattainable luxury.
The village as a solution
In Spain it has always been a summer tradition to go back to the village. Every child had a village to go to, and those who did not went with friends to their grandparents' village. The youngest enjoyed those communities, far from the hustle and bustle of the city, during their holidays: afternoons swimming in the river, a sandwich with sliced luncheon meat for tea, laughter and games with cousins.
Those children are now adults who see buying a home in a big city as hugely complicated, so they are starting an exodus in reverse to that of their grandparents and parents, heading back to small municipalities where buying a house does not mean an Herculean effort.
In this context, some of the generation who should now be buying their first flat in the city have started to look elsewhere. According to a Fotocasa Research study carried out in the first half of 2026, 13% of people looking for a home in Spain plan to move in the coming months to a municipality with fewer than 10,000 inhabitants. They are not retirees seeking peace and quiet. They are young people, in the middle of their working lives, with a life project still to build.
The study draws a clear profile: they are on average 35 years old, with incomes of between 1,000 and 3,000 euros a month, and in many cases they still live with their parents.
Most of them come from Catalonia (22%), Andalusia (19%) and Madrid (18%), and the most revealing point is that the majority are not from major capitals but from medium-sized cities: 44% currently live in municipalities with more than 50,000 inhabitants that are not provincial capitals. They are people who have already taken a step back from the big city and are now ready to take another.
A generational shift, not a fad
"The traditional image of rural repopulation is changing. Today the people who want to settle in a village are mainly young, of working age and with a life project still to build," says María Matos, head of research and spokesperson for Fotocasa.
Matos says this trend shows that rural areas are starting to establish themselves as a real residential alternative, although she warns that "for this opportunity to translate into a genuine demographic recovery, it will be essential to go on boosting employment, services, connectivity and infrastructure that can attract and retain people on a stable basis."
The age factor says it all: the youngest, aged 18 to 24, make up 23% of those planning to move to a rural area, while those aged 25 to 34 account for 38%. These are age groups that in the past would have been the first to look for a flat in the city. Today they are the first to give up on that option.
The most common living arrangements among those planning this move are to live with a partner and children (31%) or with their parents (30%), which reinforces the idea that many of these moves are not a purely vocational choice but also a response to the impossibility of accessing decent housing in urban environments.
"Empty Spain" as a safety valve
What for decades was a problem – rural depopulation, the exodus of young people to the cities – is now, paradoxically, turning into an opportunity. Villages have homes available and at affordable prices.
What they often do not offer is stable employment, quality healthcare, schools, high-speed internet or public transport, because as depopulated areas they have seen few improvements in these basic services. That is the knot that has to be untied if the neo-rural phenomenon is to move from being a statistical trend to becoming a real solution to Spain's housing crisis.
For now, the figures suggest there is a generation willing to give it a try. A generation battered by constant crises that is not asking for luxuries: it is asking to be able to live in a decent and independent way, to have a roof of its own and build a future. And it has reached the conclusion that, in Spain in 2026, that may be easier in a village in Teruel or Cuenca than in any neighbourhood in the big cities.

January – 7,511;

April – 11,028;

July – 19,969;

Ground drones carried out the most missions in July.

WELLINGTON, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- The New Zealand government will cap annual council rates increases at an initial target range of 2 to 4 percent under proposed legislation aimed at keeping local taxes affordable for households and businesses, a senior official said on Tuesday.
Ratepayers nationwide have been hit with median increases of 14.2 percent and 9.2 percent over the past two years, respectively, adding pressure to household budgets, Local Government Minister Simon Watts said in a statement.
Under the proposed system, councils would be required to keep annual rates increases within the target range, which would be reviewed every six years to reflect costs outside councils' control.
Limited, time-bound exemptions would be available in exceptional circumstances, such as recovering from natural disasters, or where councils could demonstrate prudent financial management and a justified need to operate outside the range, he said.
Water services would be excluded from the system and regulated separately, the statement said.
The legislation would also establish an independent regulator to monitor compliance, assess exemption applications and advise on future target ranges, it said.
Councils will need to consider the target range from July 1, 2027, when preparing their long-term plans, with the caps to take full effect from July 1, 2029. ■

CANBERRA, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- Electricity demand to power data centers in Australia is forecast to increase by almost sevenfold over the next decade, according to the energy market operator.
The Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO) on Tuesday released its annual electricity statement of opportunities report for 2026, revealing that there are 225 known data center projects around the country.
The report projected that data center usage in the national electricity market (NEM) will increase from around five terawatt-hours (TWh) currently to 34 TWh by 2035-36.
With that growth, it said data center usage would increase from three percent of power supplied through the NEM currently to 13 percent over the next decade.
Electricity consumption and peak demand are forecast to grow significantly as businesses and households electrify and data centers emerge, the report said.
Despite the looming increase in peak demand for electricity, the report found that the reliability outlook for future supply has improved, with record levels of new generation offsetting the loss of retiring coal and gas-fired power plants.
The report was released ahead of Prime Minister Anthony Albanese meeting with state and territory leaders on Wednesday to discuss the federal government's proposed national controls for data centers.
Under the federal government's proposed obligations for data centers, new developments will be required to include clean energy generation or storage to offset demand and to pay for electricity transmission and distribution infrastructure. ■

National University of Singapore, STMicroelectronics launch lab on edge AI

SINGAPORE, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- National University of Singapore and Switzerland-based semiconductor firm STMicroelectronics have launched a four-year research lab to develop next-generation edge artificial intelligence (AI) technologies.
The lab will "enable new generative and embodied AI use cases at the edge through system-to-silicon innovation," the university said in a statement on Monday.
Edge AI processes data directly within or close to a device rather than relying exclusively on remote cloud infrastructure, it said, adding that this enables faster response times, stronger data privacy, improved energy efficiency, and greater resilience in environments with limited or intermittent connectivity.
Embodied AI, where intelligence is built directly into a physical form, such as a robot, humanoid, or drone, is a key frontier within this space, it noted.
"Delivering that intelligence efficiently, on compact and power-constrained hardware" is the challenge the lab is built to address.
The lab brings together a multidisciplinary research ecosystem spanning AI algorithms, accelerator architectures, low-power memory systems, circuit design, silicon technologies, and application development. ■

US Postal Service implements new rule for mail-in ballots ahead of midterm elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
03:49:19 UTC
12:49:19 KST

Darren Lyn
25 August 2026•Update: 25 August 2026
The United States Postal Service (USPS) implemented a new rule Monday, adding identification verification requirements to all mail-in ballots ahead of November midterm elections.
The rule, however, falls short of President Donald Trump's demands for stricter verification standards, which are currently tied up in court with multiple lawsuits and injunctions pending.
"To ensure the faithful execution of federal law in connection with federal elections, this rule has an immediate effective date," the USPS said in a statement. "Delaying the effective date would jeopardize implementation of this rule in time for the 2026 general election, which will be held on November 3, 2026."
Under the new requirement, states would be mandated to collect and report basic voter information such as a voter's name and home address. In addition, a unique barcode would be attached to every mail-in ballot distributed to all American citizens, regardless of the state in which they reside.
There is currently no standardized requirement or method for states to track this information, instead letting each state independently decide how its mail-in voting system operates. Under the new USPS rule, state election authorities would be required to input voter information into a "federal ballot mail portal" before the ballot is accepted into the mail stream.
The USPS said it would not deliver ballots to any state not in compliance with these changes and that publication of the system of records which collects the voter information will take effect immediately.
"The terms 'mail-in ballot' and 'absentee ballot' are synonymous and interchangeable for the purposes of this rule," said USPS officials. "These terms include any ballot sent through the US Mail, irrespective of state law terminology."
Under Trump's executive order, which is pending before the US Supreme Court, mail-in ballots would have established statewide voter citizenship lists from Social Security or immigration databases as well as established uniform ballots. In addition, the United States Postal Service would "coordinate with the USPS Office of Inspector General and the Department of Justice for investigation of suspected unlawful use of the mail involving Federal election materials."
The new USPS rule generally adheres to Trump's guidelines, "ultimately creating a system that would track eligible voters by name and address, but keep citizenship largely out of it."
"No other voter information, such as birthdate, social security number, or other voter registration details, will be uploaded to the Portal," the USPS continued. "The Postal Service will not play any role in determining voter eligibility, maintaining voter rolls, or counting ballots."
The USPS also emphasized that this is “not a mail-in ballot ban, nor does it include the military, disability, illness, and travel exceptions requested by the president.”

Woman follows ‘bigu,’ a Taoist fasting technique based on the belief that it can lead to transcendence and immortality

The 31-year-old woman from Henan province, who wishes to remain anonymous, was recently reported by local media to have developed walking difficulties and memory deterioration after consuming nothing but water for 15 consecutive days.
Standing at 160 cm tall, the woman, previously weighing 70kg, managed to shed 20kg in mere weeks due to her extreme diet.

Trump administration plans to revoke 200,000 visas of asylum seekers

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
03:38:06 UTC
12:38:06 KST

The move is the latest in the Trump administration's crackdown on immigration. If it happens, the move would mark the largest single mass revocation of visas in US history.
The Trump administration said on Monday it is planning to revoke business and tourism visas of 200,000 foreigners who have applied for or are currently seeking asylum in the United States.
Unless challenges or revised, the move would mark the largest single mass revocation of visas in US history.
“We are coordinating with DHS to identify and revoke the nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently,” State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said.
He did not comment on the exact number of visas that would be revoked, claiming that "the number of revocations remains dynamic and will be done on a rolling basis".
In the coming weeks, the State Department is expected to announce the revocation of B1 and B2 visas issued between 2016 and 2026 for those that have sought or are currently seeking asylum, according to documents obtained by press agency The Associated Press and two US officials that spoke on condition of anonymity.
B1 visas are typically issued for business trips and B2 visas for tourism, family visits and medical care. Current applicants for both categories are asked to confirm that they are not seeking asylum in the US and provide proof that they intend to return to their home countries.
The revocation of the visa would not immediately result in the deportation of the individual, the officials clarified, but those with pending asylum cases would lose their status as business or tourism travellers.
The move is the latest in the Trump administration’s broader immigration crackdown, which has intensified since President Donald Trump returned to office for his second term.
The administration has already tightened restrictions on visa applicants, including requiring applicants to provide their social media histories, imposing expensive bonds before visas can be processed, and complete visa bans on citizens of certain countries.
On Friday, a judge struck down a Trump administration policy implemented earlier this year that suspended the visa issuance of immigrant visas from 75 countries.
US District Judge Jeannette Vargas, who was appointed by former President Joe Biden, said the policy was "contrary to law and in excess of statutory authority," arguing that it undermines Congress's requirement that consular officers are at the forefront of making visa decisions.

Highest-ever ocean temperature measured as super El Nino forms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
03:35:00 UTC
12:35:00 KST

Highest-ever ocean temperature measured as super El Nino forms
BRUSSELS - Scientists have recorded the highest temperature ever measured in the world’s oceans, as climate change combines with a powerful El Nino in the tropical Pacific.
The global average sea-surface temperature hit a record 21.1 deg C on Aug 22, according to Europe’s Earth observation agency Copernicus, which has been tracking the metric daily since 1979.
The previous single-day record of 21.09 deg C was measured in March 2024.
“El Nino is adding heat to the system, but it is doing so on top of decades of human-driven warming,” said Samantha Burgess, strategic lead for climate at Copernicus’ European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts.
“As ocean temperatures continue to rise, the risks to marine ecosystems and coastal communities also increase,” she said.
Higher ocean temperatures contribute to sea level rise and increase the chance of extreme weather events, as warmer water transfers more heat and moisture to the atmosphere, intensifying storms and heat on land. Warmer oceans also have a reduced capacity to absorb carbon dioxide.
Record temperatures have already been measured in isolated areas of the world’s oceans including the western Mediterranean Sea as well as at the Earth’s poles, driven mainly by man-made climate change.
Copernicus expects the trend to continue, with ocean temperatures now being supercharged by El Nino.
The August record is particularly worrying because global ocean temperatures are typically highest in March and April, after the Austral summer, Copernicus said. BLOOMBERG

Six months into Iran war, Hormuz traffic way down, sailors stranded
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
03:35:00 UTC
12:35:00 KST

Six months into Iran war, Hormuz traffic way down, sailors stranded
- The Strait of Hormuz remains largely closed six months into the Iran war, with daily vessel transits dropping from 95 to as low as 10 and thousands of sailors stranded.
- Two main shipping routes now exist, one approved by Iran and a riskier southern route, with many ships using unconfirmed "dark" routes due to disabled tracking systems.
- At least 20 sailors and dockworkers have died in regional attacks, and efforts to evacuate stranded seafarers have stalled amid ongoing security concerns and conflict escalation.
AI generated
PARIS – Six months since the start of the Middle East war, the strategic Strait of Hormuz remains largely paralysed, with thousands of sailors still stranded in the Gulf and commodity carrier traffic way below its normal level.
Only a few transits per day
Before Iran blocked the strait in response to joint US-Israeli strikes in February, around one fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas exports passed through the waterway.
Iran’s Guards have also warned of a “danger zone” covering 1,400 sq km where mines may be present.
After Iran closed the strait on March 1, commodity carrier traffic plummeted to an average of 10 transits per day, compared with a daily average of 95 in February, according to an AFP analysis of data from maritime tracker Kpler.
An agreement signed by the United States and Iran in June led to a temporary rebound to 36 transits per day, before they dropped back to an average of 15 between the resumption of hostilities on July 8 and Aug 22.
New routes, “dark” transits
Before the war, vessels crossed the strait freely via a route through the centre of the waterway adopted by the International Maritime Organization (IMO).
There are now two distinct routes: one to the north, near the Iranian coast – the only one approved by Tehran – and another to the south, between the Omani coast and potentially mined areas.
During the relatively calm period between June 17 and July 7, an average of nine ships per day used the Iranian route and eight for the Omani one. The rest transited via unidentified routes or the traditional IMO corridor.
Ever since the ceasefire collapsed on July 8, two-thirds of transits have become “dark”, or unknown, compared with less than one per cent before the war, according to Kpler.
These transits involve vessels whose exact route cannot be confirmed due to insufficient data stemming from disabled transponders, jammed signals or missing satellite imagery.
Thousands of sailors stranded
Some 6,000 sailors and 500 ships have remained stuck in the Gulf since the beginning of the conflict, the IMO told AFP.
The organisation said there were “ongoing discussions” to ensure a secure maritime route, adding that their outcome “depends on de-escalation in the region”.
The IMO had begun an initiative in June to evacuate more than 11,000 seafarers stuck in the Gulf, but the effort was soon suspended following an attack on a vessel.
Over the past six months, at least 20 sailors and dockworkers have been killed in incidents or attacks in the region, according to the IMO. AFP

Ukraine’s allies agreed in Kyiv on Monday to urgently strengthen the country’s air defenses, increase military support, tighten sanctions on Russia and continue preparations for a multinational force that could deploy after a ceasefire.
The Coalition of the Willing gathered in Kyiv and by video conference as Ukraine marked the 35th anniversary of the restoration of its independence.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz chaired the meeting alongside President Volodymyr Zelensky.
The leaders reaffirmed their support for Ukraine’s fight to defend its “sovereignty, freedom and territorial integrity” and condemned Russia’s escalating attacks on Ukrainian cities, civilians and critical infrastructure.
They also condemned Russian strikes on Ukraine’s cultural heritage, including the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra.
The coalition reaffirmed Ukraine’s inherent right to defend itself against Russia’s war of aggression under international law and Article 51 of the UN Charter.
The leaders also made clear that threats from Moscow would not deter continued military support for Kyiv.
Air defense an ‘urgent priority’
Strengthening Ukraine’s air defenses emerged as one of the clearest immediate commitments.
The leaders agreed to increase military support and strengthen Ukraine’s air defense “as a matter of urgent priority.”
Ukraine Allies Defy Moscow Threats, Pledge Air Defense Boost and Missile Production
They also pledged deeper cooperation with Ukraine’s defense industry and the sharing of relevant military technologies, including through the Anti-Ballistic Missile Coalition.
The commitment comes as Russia intensifies ballistic missile and drone attacks on Ukrainian cities and Ukraine seeks additional interceptor missiles from its partners.
Tougher sanctions on Russia’s war machine
The coalition also agreed to “ratchet up” sanctions against Russia’s military-industrial complex and those helping sustain it.
Leaders pledged to further constrain Moscow’s ability to finance the invasion through sanctions and wider economic measures, while stepping up action against sanctions circumvention and Russia’s Shadow Fleet.
According to the joint statement, measures taken by Ukraine’s partners since February 2022 have deprived Russia’s war chest of at least $495 billion.
The coalition also welcomed efforts in the US Senate to apply further economic pressure on Moscow.
Leaders committed to working closely with Washington in the coming months on coordinated measures aimed at draining Russia’s ability to continue its war against Ukraine.
Winter energy support
Ukraine’s allies also agreed that support for the country’s energy system must be delivered urgently ahead of winter.
The coalition pledged immediate assistance through the Ukraine Energy Support Fund as well as specialist equipment needed to strengthen and repair Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
Russia has repeatedly targeted Ukraine’s power and energy infrastructure throughout the full-scale invasion.
The leaders also committed to supporting Ukraine’s wider economic resilience amid intensified Russian efforts to renew pressure on Ukraine’s maritime trade and ports.
Multinational force after ceasefire
The coalition reaffirmed one of its most significant long-term security plans – preparation of a Multinational Force Ukraine.
The force would be ready to deploy once a “credible cessation of hostilities” is in place.
According to the statement, it would form part of a broader package of “robust politically and legally binding security guarantees” intended to secure Ukraine after a ceasefire.
The commitment means coalition planning extends beyond supplying Ukraine during the current phase of the war to creating a security structure designed to protect the country after hostilities end.
Ceasefire from the line of contact
Coalition leaders praised Zelensky’s readiness to enter meaningful peace negotiations aimed at achieving a “comprehensive, just and lasting peace.”
At the same time, they repeated their demand that Russia agree to a “full, immediate and unconditional ceasefire” beginning from the current line of contact.
The leaders ended the meeting by reaffirming their commitment to Ukraine’s independence and describing the country’s security as part of the wider peace and security of Europe.
They pledged their solidarity with Ukraine “for as long as it takes.”

Hong Kong needs clearer framework for handling high heat on work sites
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

LettersHong Kong needs clearer framework for handling high heat on work sites
Readers discuss work supervisors’ dilemma on extremely hot days, and Hongkong Post’s financial woes
Regardless of which methodology ultimately prevails, the debate has exposed a gap between contractual requirements and operational reality. What should site managers do when local conditions appear unsafe but the official warning framework does not respond accordingly?
The latest generation of construction contracts increasingly recognises extreme heat as a potential ground for extension of time claims. However, such relief is linked to the Labour Department’s Heat Stress at Work Warning system.
That helps explain why the heat on August 9 raised concern. Despite temperatures reaching 39.8 degrees Celsius (103.6 Fahrenheit) in Sheung Shui, the Heat Stress at Work Warning remained at amber, the lowest level. Site managers who believed stronger precautions were warranted could have found themselves without the higher-level official trigger on which contractual protections depend.
The core issue the Labour Department needs to address is what happens when a site manager believes conditions on the ground warrant stronger precautions, but the official trigger on which contractual protections depend is absent.

Villafranca-Trejo is at least the seventh spouse or parent of an active-duty U.S. military service member to be deported under the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown, according to an Associated Press tally.
The Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency, which is part of DHS and has been the face of President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown and deportation drive, arrested her on July 11 after conducting what the DHS called a "targeted immigration enforcement operation." The DHS said she received due process.
Turcios Juarez previously said ICE officers detained his wife outside a Walmart in July as their daughter watched. He said his wife left Honduras in 2016 due to violent crime in the country. The DHS alleged that she illegally entered the United States.
Turcios Juarez joined the military and became a U.S. citizen in 2024 after a nine-month deployment to the Middle East, according to ABC News. He said he began pursuing citizenship for his wife, hoping his service would help expedite her naturalization process.
Over the weekend, the immigrant father of a U.S. sailor on board the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier, which was deployed in the Middle East during the Iran war, was taken into federal immigration custody and remains in detention.
Trump has pursued an immigration crackdown that includes revocations of visas and green cards and an aggressive deportation drive. He says the crackdown aims to improve domestic security.
Rights groups say the crackdown has violated free speech and due process rights and created an unsafe environment, particularly for ethnic minorities, who have raised concerns about racial profiling.

The Nanzih District station recorded 567 millimeters of rain over 24 hours and 913 mm over three days, with both totals breaking records, according to Chen. He said the overall rainfall was greater than levels recorded during Typhoon Morakot in 2009, per CNA.
The heavy rain caused flooding in coastal and low-lying areas of Kaohsiung and power outages in Shizi Township in Pingtung County. In Tainan, authorities reported cumulative pumping of about 54.55 million tonnes of water from Friday through the morning of Monday, exceeding Wushantou Reservoir's effective capacity of about 50.5 million tonnes.
Chen chaired a meeting at the city's disaster response center Monday afternoon before briefing reporters on the flood situation. He said the city would implement mandatory evacuations in mountainous areas when a yellow debris-flow warning is issued. As of Monday, 2,649 people had been evacuated as a precaution, per a city government press release.
Kaohsiung's 26 flood retention ponds had stored about five million tonnes of water, with authorities pre-emptively releasing water when rainfall eased to reduce pressure on storm drains and downstream drainage systems. The city had also deployed 137 mobile pumps in low-lying areas. Together with fixed pumping equipment, 352 pumps were operating to accelerate floodwater removal.
Chen urged employers to prioritize worker safety during the extreme weather. Under Taiwan's labor regulations, workers cannot be treated as absent without authorization in certain circumstances, including when their workplace has been ordered closed or when flooding or other natural disasters block transportation and prevent them from reaching work. The rules also cover cases in which the worker's residence or normal commuting route is in an area subject to a closure order.
Chen also inspected the Erren River in Tainan, where pumping capacity had been increased from 1.8 cubic meters per second to 2.7 cubic meters per second. The city government also raised the embankment in the area, according to CNA.
Although heavy rain early Monday pushed river levels near the overflow point, easing rainfall and faster pumping helped prevent more serious flooding. Chen said damage was significantly less than in previous years.
Chen said the most critical flood-control problem along the Erren River is a bottleneck near Chongde Bridge, where the river channel narrows and can cause water to back up toward nearby low-lying areas. He thanked the Water Resources Agency for its support for flood-control improvements in the area, including work related to the Chongde Bridge bottleneck.
The latest rainfall highlights the increasing challenge posed by extreme rainfall events in southern Taiwan, with authorities continuing to rely on evacuations, retention ponds, pumping capacity, and river improvements to reduce flood risks.

Singapore reports rise in home thefts, shoplifting and molestation
Total physical crime fell in the first half, but a 25 per cent spike in home thefts pushed key offences higher
There were 459 thefts in dwelling cases at residential premises in the first six months of the year, up 25.1 per cent from 367 cases over the same period in 2025, according to the Singapore police’s midyear crime brief for 2026.
Theft in dwelling cases across all types of premises rose just slightly, by 0.6 per cent, from 726 cases in the first half of 2025 to 730 in the same period this year. Such cases accounted for about 7.1 per cent of all physical crime cases.
“Theft in dwelling cases typically occurred in premises where belongings were left unsecured or unattended, creating opportunities for theft,” the police said.
The increase was largely driven by incidents at residential premises involving people who had access to, or were familiar with, the premises. In light of this, they advised residents, co-tenants and property occupiers to store their personal belongings securely and to refrain from leaving valuables unattended in common spaces and shared facilities.
From January to June, the number of physical crime cases in Singapore fell 0.4 per cent to 10,287, from 10,325 over the same period last year. Police described the physical crime situation as “stable”, with robbery and snatch theft recording 12 and nine cases respectively.

====================================================================================================

Israel must remember the danger carried by Gaza kites, Hamas dictating tempo at border - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
03:04:53 UTC
12:04:53 KST

For the past week or so, residents of Israel’s Gaza border communities must have seen the sight of kites crossing from the enclave and thought, “Here we go again.”
Years before October 7, incendiary kites and balloons (including the bizarre incident of an incendiary condom) became one of Hamas’s favored methods of harassing southern Israel. Fields were burned, fires became routine, and what began as a seemingly crude tactic developed into an organized campaign that Israel struggled for years to contain.
That is why the appearance of kites over the border again cannot simply be treated as a curiosity while the IDF waits to establish whether they constitute a broader phenomenon.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz were therefore right on Sunday to warn Hamas that continued launches would bring an increased Israeli response. Katz went further, insisting that Israel would not return to the reality that existed before October 7.
That promise must be backed up with concrete action.
At least six kites crossed from Gaza into Israel over the past week, with other reports putting the number higher. None of those recovered so far carried explosives, and no Israelis were endangered. The IDF said it believes Palestinian youth, some only 12 or 13 years old, are being used to launch them, likely at the direction of Hamas terrorists.
The most troubling comment to emerge over the weekend came from a military official who said the IDF was taking the incidents seriously but needed to “wait and see if this becomes a trend.”
Israel must stop the trend before it becomes an even greater threat
Israel has already seen this trend before, and it must nip the issue in the bud this time.
In 2018, incendiary kites and balloons began appearing over the Gaza border. What initially looked primitive became an organized method of attack. Fields, forests, and nature reserves across southern Israel burned, and thousands of acres were destroyed. Explosives were attached to some of the airborne devices, and Israelis living near Gaza became accustomed to another form of terrorism that Hamas could calibrate according to its needs.
The IDF did respond at times, including by striking Hamas positions and squads preparing incendiary devices. Yet the pattern became painfully familiar during the years before October 7. Hamas would push, Israel would assess whether the latest provocation justified escalation, and life along the border would absorb another deterioration in what was considered normal.
Residents of the Gaza border communities have every right to be alarmed by language suggesting that Israel should again wait to determine whether something is a trend.
Uri Epstein, head of the Sha’ar HaNegev Regional Council, put the concern well. The issue is not whether a particular kite turns out to contain explosives. By the time soldiers discover that it does, the question has already been answered too late. Residents should certainly not be the people discovering unidentified objects from Gaza and then informing the military.
That does not mean Israel should launch a major military operation because a kite crosses the border. Proportionality and judgment remain necessary, but what has to disappear is the idea that Hamas is entitled to a certain number of provocations while Israel gathers evidence that a pattern has developed.
A border is either defended, or it is not. If Hamas permits organized launch sites to operate, it should understand there will be a price. The IDF should also have clear procedures for detecting, intercepting, and handling anything that crosses from Gaza before residents stumble across it.
Hamas adaptations to Israel's threat classifications
Israel spent years drawing distinctions between rockets, incendiary balloons, border riots, and other forms of harassment emanating from Gaza. Hamas understood those distinctions and learned how to operate within them. It could apply pressure without necessarily provoking a response large enough to threaten its rule.
October 7 exposed the disastrous consequences of allowing Hamas to determine the tempo along the border.
Katz’s declaration that “a balloon is treated like a kite, and a kite is treated like a drone” therefore carries importance beyond the latest incidents. Hamas must understand that the old rules no longer exist.
Israel has paid far too high a price to relearn this lesson. The kites crossing the border today may contain nothing, but the next ones may not. We should not wait and see.

Trial for alleged builder of bomb in 1988 Lockerbie attack postponed by US judge days before start
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
03:04:40 UTC
12:04:40 KST

A federal judge on Monday postponed the trial of the man authorities allege built the bomb that blew New York-bound Pan Am flight 103 out of the sky over Lockerbie, Scotland, killing 270 people in 1988.
Jury selection had been scheduled to begin on Wednesday in the trial of Abu Agila Mohammad Mas'ud Kheir Al-Marimi, a Libyan intelligence operative who prosecutors allege once confessed to his role in the 1988 bombing.
In the decision to postpone the trial, US District Judge Dabney Friedrich cited the discovery of new evidence that defense attorneys want to examine.
The judge said "the newly discovered evidence, as well as evidence located in other countries" and "the need for the defense to determine how best to defend this case" made her reach the decision.
Friedrich did not schedule a new trial date but set a court hearing on September 1 to discuss next steps.
Mas'ud rejects allegations that he built the Lockerbie bomb
Mas'ud, now in his mid-70s, has pleaded not guilty to two criminal charges related to the destruction of the aircraft resulting in death and faces a maximum of life in prison if convicted.
The Boeing 747 exploded minutes after takeoff from London on December 21, 1988, killing all 259 people on board, including 190 Americans, and 11 people on the ground in Scotland.
The bombing made former Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi, whose government accepted responsibility for the attack in 2003, an international pariah.
Mas'ud has denied wrongdoing and his lawyers have challenged the credibility of evidence gathered by prosecutors, including Mas'ud's alleged confession to a Libyan police officer in 2012, a year after rebel forces toppled Gaddafi's government.
Mas'ud's trial in Washington, DC federal court has been delayed by years of legal wrangling over the alleged confession and other issues that have exposed the complexities of a US prosecution over a decades-old attack in Britain with crucial evidence gathered in Libya.
Mas'ud, who was arrested in Libya and brought to the US in 2022, is accused of building a time-delayed bomb that was packed into a suitcase and placed in checked baggage in Malta. The explosive-laden suitcase eventually made its way to London Heathrow Airport, where it was stored in the hold of Pan Am flight 103.

'Get it out': ARIA to ban AI-generated music from Australian charts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
03:03:31 UTC
12:03:31 KST

In brief
- ARIA will ban fully AI-generated music from featuring on its charts from Friday.
- Australian artists like Peking Duk's Adam Hyde have welcomed the move.
Music will need to be "substantially human-made" in order to qualify for Australia's main music chart, in an industry bid to stamp out AI-generated tracks.
Songs wholly generated using artificial intelligence will no longer be eligible for the ARIA charts from Friday, in an update to The Australian Recording Industry Association's (ARIA) code of practice.
ARIA chief executive Annabelle Herd said a chart that rewards unlicensed AI output would "undercut the very basis of the recorded music we exist to present".
"The ARIA charts are about tracking consumption and sales of music in Australia, but they're also about celebrating human artistry and success," Herd told ABC radio.
"We're not particularly interested in including AI-generated music as part of that process, particularly when it's taking up a spot from an Australian artist in the chart."
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
AI-assisted songs will still feature on the charts, but they must be substantially human-made and raise no stream or chart manipulation concerns.
"I'm sure that there are a lot of artists that are using AI tools to enhance creativity, to do really cool, new, exciting things," Herd said.
"Artists have always been at the forefront of new tech ... it's made some of the best music ever created, and no doubt AI will create some really exciting evolution of that."
Songs on the ARIA charts that use AI include Gold Coast-based DJ and producer Josh Fawaz's dance track Like a Prayer, which is fourth on the ARIA's top 20 Australian singles after peaking at number two in May.
A dance cover of Madonna's 1989 hit, generative AI is credited for the drums and vocals on the track, according to Spotify.
Australian electronic band Peking Duk supported the association's call to outlaw generative AI from the charts, claiming it was "removing the human experience from life".
"AI is using our stuff. It's using a lot of our peers' stuff, you know, people we know," band member Adam Hyde told Channel Nine's Today show.
"There is so much good art in Australia and something like AI coming along and kind of sweeping the charts and all that jazz, it's like, get it out."
ARIA's decision heeds global AI principles drawn up by the record industry's peak body, The International Federation of the Phonographic Industry, in July.
The federation said the guidelines would be rolled out to official charts in Latin America, the Middle East, Africa and Southeast Asia and advocated to more than 20 other official chart programs in Europe and the Pacific, including the ARIAs.
