US state probes OpenAI over rogue AI hack
WASHINGTON – ChatGPT-maker OpenAI faces an investigation by the US state of Alabama after the company revealed in July that its models went rogue and hacked an artificial intelligence (AI) platform during testing.
In mid-July, two OpenAI models escaped their confined testing environment and gained access to the internet, where they found and attacked Hugging Face, a site AI developers use to store and share models and data sets.
The incident raised alarm about the dangers of AI systems acting autonomously and breaking guardrails set by human programmers to prevent safety violations.
In a 14-page order, the office of Alabama Attorney-General Steve Marshall demanded OpenAI hand over internal records about the July incident, along with a long list of other material, including the identity of every employee involved in the intrusion or in the testing that led to it.
The investigation comes in response to “the company’s complete lack of oversight and adequate safeguards”, Marshall’s office alleged in a statement.
It is the first known state investigation into whether an AI system attacking another company’s infrastructure amounts to a violation of consumer protection law – a finding that would expose the company to major litigation across the US.
On Aug 3, Alabama and 14 other states wrote to OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman asking the company to preserve records on the incident and halt any internal cybersecurity evaluations of its models.
OpenAI has not responded to that August request, a spokesperson for the Alabama attorney-general’s office told AFP.
OpenAI did not immediately respond to an AFP request for comment.
However, OpenAI said in a statement to the tech news site TechCrunch that it was “conducting a thorough review along with external advisers”.
“Once the review is complete, we will share a technical report with relevant government authorities and publish our findings publicly,” it added. AFP

'Rushed effort'
In June, Judge Indira Talwani ruled that the president lacked the authority to order changes in how states administer federal elections, noting that under the US Constitution, states have the role of determining voter-eligibility requirements.
The judge also noted that federal agencies lack the ability to compile accurate lists of citizens for each state.
The states contend that their claims are not hypothetical and that the administration's "rushed effort to change the rules of mail voting on the eve of the November midterms risks disenfranchising a substantial number of voters."
The judge rejected the administration's arguments, finding that the suit was not filed too soon and that the states had legal standing because they would face election administration disruption, compliance costs and a credible threat of criminal prosecution.

Viral false claims about quakes, Hiroshima expose Japan’s online conspiracy problem
Claims that a deadly quake was artificial and Hiroshima was not hit by an atomic bomb have alarmed experts tracking Japan’s online spaces
In the aftermath of the July 28 earthquake in Kumamoto prefecture in southern Japan, a social media user claimed that seismic data from the National Research Institute for Earth Science and Disaster Resilience showed the tremor was “not an earthquake but an artificial explosion waveform”.
The post, published about 30 minutes after the magnitude 7.1 quake, was later listed by Yahoo Japan’s real-time search as a popular post, with more than 2,100 reposts and 6,300 likes. Other posts pushed a related claim that the quake had been triggered by HAARP, a research facility in Alaska that has long been a target of disaster-related conspiracy theories.
Days later, as Japan marked the August anniversaries of the Hiroshima and Nagasaki bombings and the end of World War II, NHK reported that false claims denying the atomic attacks were gaining traction online, with some posts on X and TikTok drawing more than 1 million views and one YouTube video claiming the bombing was a lie attracting more than 300,000 views.
“Both the theory that the earthquake was artificially triggered and the denial of the atomic bombings lack scientific basis, but the contexts in which these conspiracy theories take root differ,” said Yuzuru Kido, a former J-CAST News deputy editor and internet media researcher who tracks Japanese social media discourse.

US State Dept. sanctions Iranian military activities, fuel export in Operation Economic Outcast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
00:10:21 UTC
09:10:21 KST

The US State Department implemented sanctions against Iranian military activities, cyber threats, and illicit oil trade, according to a statement from US State Department Spokesperson Tommy Pigott on Monday evening.
"Today, the United States took sweeping action against multiple entities, individuals, and vessels enabling the Iranian regime’s destabilizing activities," Pigott said.
"The measures target Iranian military officials responsible for procuring weapons and directing attacks against US servicemembers and regional partners, Iran-based entities that gathered intelligence for targeting US forces and allies, and a procurement ring supplying Iran’s military and missile programs," he added.
"The US will continue to disrupt, expose, and dismantle Iran’s military and proliferation activities, procurement schemes, malicious cyber operations, and illicit oil trade that sustains the regime’s malign behavior."
Sanctions target groups for supporting Iranian military actions
The sanctions targeted two Iran-based groups that were involved in procuring images used to attacks US forces and bases located across the Middle East.
DadeNegar Startup Studio and the Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Cyber-Electronic Command (IRGC-CEC) were named in the sanctions package.
DadeNegar was sanctioned for supporting the "targeting of US and partner facilities in the Middle East for the Iranian military during Operation Epic Fury." The State Department said DadeNegar used commercial Chinese satellite imagery to support Iran's military in its efforts to target and damage US forces and bases in the region.
The IRGC-CEC was sanctioned due to obtaining information about US forces and bases that was used to support Iran’s targeting of US assets during the conflict.
Both groups were designated "for having engaged, or attempted to engage, in any activity that materially contributes to, or poses a risk of materially contributing to, the proliferation of arms or related materiel or items intended for military end-uses or military end-users, including any efforts to manufacture, acquire, possess, develop, transport, transfer, or use such items, by the Government of Iran."
Individuals also sanctioned by US State Department
Monday's announcement also targeted seven individuals responsible for directing the use of conventional weapons against US forces.
Sanctions targeted members of Iran's Supreme National Council, several commanders of various military branches of the IRGC, the country's deputy defense minister, and the spokesperson for Iran's Defense Ministry.
Former Secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, was targeted for having "an active role advocating for Iran’s continued support of its so-called Axis of Resistance."
Zolghadr "was designated by the UN Security Council in Annex I of UN Security Council resolution (UNSCR) 1747 (2007), reimposed on September 27, 2025, in response to Iran’s 'significant non-performance' of its nuclear commitments," the statement added.
Ahmad Vahidi, Commander-in-Chief of the IRGC, and Ali Abdollahi, Commander of the Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters, the Iranian government branch responsible for wartime operations were sanctioned for their roles in driving military decisions made by Iran during Operation Epic Fury.
Sanctions also targeted Commander of the IRGC Aerospace Force Sayyid Hossein Mousavi Eftekhari, and Amir Hatami, Commander Iran's conventional military. Both were sanctioned due to their responsibility for Iran’s ballistic missile and drone programs.
Deputy Defense Minister for Industrial and Research Affairs Seyyed Mahdi Farahi was sanctioned by the US for "directing the procurement of arms and related materiel and has demonstrated in-depth knowledge of various missile systems, including those that Iran has reportedly used against US forces and allies."
Reza Talaei-Nik, spokesperson for Iran's main defense ministry body was sanctioned for "engaging in activity that materially contributes to the supply, sale, or transfer, directly or indirectly, to or from Iran, or for the use in or benefit of Iran, of arms or related materiel, including spare parts."
US sanctions also target fuel exports, shadow fleet
The Department of State also sanctioned companies that "engaged in the illicit trade of Iranian petroleum and petrochemical products, activities that have generated millions of dollars in revenue for the Iranian regime," the statement said.
"These Iranian petroleum, petroleum products, and petrochemical cargos," the statement added, "are frequently transported by shadow fleet operators, including vessel management companies that regularly engage in dark activity and other deceptive shipping practices, endangering other vessels and trade flows."
Sanctions targeted both Iranian and international companies that facilitated the trade of petroleum and petrochemical products with Iran.
Implications of the sanctions
The sanctions coming following US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's announcement of the start of Operation Economic Outcast and the implementation of an "economic D-Day" against Iran.
Monday's sanctions mark the start of US action aimed "to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone," said Bessent.
"We are no longer managing the Iranian threat," he emphasized. "We are ending it."
Iran promised to retaliate to sanctions
Before the announcement, Iran threatened both a possible military response and further reduction in oil exports from the Gulf in response to any US economic measures. Afterward, Iranian Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh said, "We are fully prepared for the US sanctions."
"Naturally, the enemies intend to launch an economic terrorist attack on us, but we also have our own tools and know how to play the game. Our defense is no longer so defensive; the enemies should wait for an attack," Madanizadeh told state television.
He also said neither China nor Russia had "accepted" the US measures, and predicted other countries would resist them.
Brigadier General Hossein Mohebbi, a spokesperson for Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, vowed heavy blows to US vital interests and energy chokepoints if Iran's infrastructure is threatened, Press TV reported.

In March, the Trump administration launched an investigation into more than a dozen major trading partners under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 over excess capacity concerns. It was one of two probes that the President’s team used to replace his prior tariffs with more durable ones.
September summit
Administration officials hope to publish the results of the excess capacity inquiry before Trump and Xi are due to meet in Washington on Sept 24. The details of the overcapacity report have proven legally challenging, according to sources familiar with the matter.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told Bloomberg Television in July that the excess capacity investigation would take longer than another on forced labour because of its complexity and that the delay had nothing to do with efforts to maintain the truce with Beijing.
Asked about the tariff plans, a White House official said any announcements will come directly from the administration and that any reporting or discussion of them should be considered baseless speculation. The Office of the US Trade Representative did not immediately respond to a request for comment. China’s Ministry of Commerce did not respond to a fax for comment.
The Trump administration’s approach to China, its foremost geopolitical rival, stands in stark contrast to its stance towards some of the US’ biggest traditional allies.
While the President has been keen not to upset his tariff truce with China, his administration applied a 50 per cent levy on billions of dollars of Canadian products and has mused about tearing up the North American trade agreement he renegotiated during his first term.
Trump is rebuilding a tariff wall that was struck down when the Supreme Court in February ruled that his global levies, issued under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, violated the US Constitution. The President’s temporary 10 per cent global tariffs expired in July and were also deemed illegal by a trade court.
The administration is justifying its new global duties under the findings of its investigations into forced labour and industrial overcapacity in the economies of dozens of trading partners.
As part of that campaign, the Trump administration in July imposed a 12.5 per cent tariff on Chinese goods, citing inadequate efforts to address forced labour practices. While Beijing criticised the move, it stopped short of announcing retaliatory measures, instead saying Washington had agreed to cap any additional duties on Chinese exports at 20 per cent. That clarified earlier comments that referenced tariff ceilings discussed during trade talks in 2025.
Malaysia deal
“We hope that the US will honour its commitments, ensuring that regardless of the reasons given for imposing or replacing tariffs on China in the future, US tariffs on China will not exceed the levels outlined in the Kuala Lumpur trade consultations,” China’s Ministry of Commerce said in a May statement.
Section 301 allows the US Trade Representative, under the direction of the President, to impose tariffs in response to other nations’ trade measures that it deems discriminatory to American businesses or in violation of US rights under international trade agreements. But efforts to implement the levies have already come up against legal challenges.
A coalition of 25 states, including New York, California and Illinois, filed a lawsuit earlier in August at the US Court of International Trade, adding to similar proceedings by small businesses that claim the levies are illegal. The states allege Trump unlawfully invoked Section 301 to replace tariffs struck down by the Supreme Court, using the forced-labour rationale as a pretext.
The Trump administration has said the duties under Section 301 are legally sound and that the provision has been supported by previous court rulings. BLOOMBERG

Judge postpones U.S. trial for man accused in deadly 1988 Lockerbie bombing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
00:08:50 UTC
09:08:50 KST

Judge postpones U.S. trial for Libyan man accused in deadly 1988 Lockerbie bombing, citing new evidence
A federal judge on Monday postponed a trial in the United States for a former Libyan intelligence official charged in the 1988 bombing of Pan Am Flight 103 over Lockerbie, Scotland, citing the discovery of new evidence that defense attorneys want to examine in the nearly 40-year-old case.
Abu Agila Mohammad Mas'ud Kheir Al-Marimi is charged in the U.S. with making the bomb that downed the airplane, killing 270 people, most of them Americans. Jury selection was scheduled to begin Wednesday for his federal trial in Washington, D.C. — the first trial in the U.S. for the Dec. 21, 1988, bombing.
U.S. District Judge Dabney Friedrich's order didn't specify the nature of the newly discovered evidence.
Al-Marimi's lawyers say prosecutors disclosed the new evidence to them on Saturday and added that their "constitutional and ethical obligations require the defense to investigate this development." Defense attorney Laura Koenig, an assistant federal public defender, declined to elaborate in response to an Associated Press inquiry.
The judge scheduled a Sept. 1 hearing in Washington to discuss the status of the case. Friedrich's brief order cited the complex nature of the case, the newly discovered evidence and "the need for the defense to determine how best to defend this case" as reasons to postpone the trial.
Flight 103 was 31,000 feet over Lockerbie when a bomb in the plane's forward cargo area exploded 38 minutes after takeoff from London Heathrow Airport. The flight was bound for John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York.
The blast killed all 259 passengers and crew members and 11 people on the ground in Lockerbie, where the wreckage destroyed an entire city block. Citizens of 21 countries were killed, including 190 Americans and 43 from the United Kingdom. The passengers included 35 Syracuse University students returning home from a semester abroad.
The FBI says that, prior to 9/11, the Pan Am Flight 103 bombing "was one of the world's most lethal acts of air terrorism and one of the largest and most complex acts of international terrorism ever investigated" by the agency.
Kara Weipz, board president of the nonprofit Victims of Pan Am Flight 103, said her organization had received no details about the new evidence that prompted the trial delay. Weipz's brother, Richard Monetti, was among the Syracuse students killed.
She called the delay a shock and noted that some victims' relatives were already packing to head to the trial.
"At the same time, for almost 38 years we've been seeking the truth of what happened," Weipz said. "If that's what this is, then that's a good thing, and this delay is worth it. ... It's important to hear all the facts."
Prosecutors allege Al-Marimi and others carried out the bombing at the direction of Libyan leader Muammar Qaddafi, who was ousted and killed during a 2011 civil war.
Al-Marimi, now in his mid-70s, is charged with two counts of destruction of an aircraft resulting in death. He faces a maximum penalty of life in prison if convicted. In February 2023, public defender Whitney Minter entered a not guilty plea on his behalf in the U.S. District Court in Washington, D.C.
Two other Libyan intelligence agents were tried by a panel of Scottish judges on a former U.S. military base in the Netherlands in 2000. The tribunal convicted one official and acquitted the other, but the bombmaker's possible identity remained a mystery for years.
According to prosecutors, Al-Marimi worked for the Libyan intelligence service as an explosives expert from approximately 1973 to 2011, rising to the rank of colonel, and had ties to Libya and Tunisia.
Prosecutors believe he brought a suitcase containing a bomb to an airport in Malta and gave it to co-conspirators for a flight to Frankfurt, Germany. The suitcase traveled from Frankfurt to London, where it was loaded onto Flight 103, according to investigators.
Al-Marimi was first charged in 2020 and later indicted in December 2022 before he was transferred to U.S. custody.

‘Honest leaders are the first step to a better future’: Cockroach hunger striker targets India’s political class
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
00:00:42 UTC
09:00:42 KST

For 26 days, India watched as Sonam Wangchuk wasted away. His hunger strike, held in solidarity with India’s “Cockroach” youth protest movement, would prove to be one of the most politically consequential fasts held in the country’s modern history.
Many in the country view the gruelling fast, which began on 28 June, as the crucial spark that helped propel the Cockroach movement into one of the most formidable challenges to the government of prime minister, Narendra Modi, in more than a decade.
Abhijit Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach movement, said Wangchuk had “awakened the conscience of an entire nation” through his sacrifice.
The Cockroach movement was launched in May, following the cancellation of a key nationwide exam to enter medical college after a paper was leaked. The cancellation was devastating for the 2 million students who had already sat the exam, a dozen of whom reportedly took their lives.
The movement took its name from comments made by India’s chief justice, Surya Kant, who had compared some unemployed young people to cockroaches and parasites in a court hearing.
Dipke’s demand for education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, to show accountability for the leak by resigning struck a nerve, and anger that had been seething below the surface surged out on to the streets.
The protest ballooned into a nationwide movement. For weeks, deadlock prevailed between the government and Dipke, backed by thousands who flocked to his sit-in protest in Delhi. Eventually, after an unprecedented police crackdown which further influenced public opinion in its favour, the protesters triumphed and Pradhan resigned on 25 July.
The victory was not a foregone conclusion and Dipke has acknowledged the importance of Wangchuck’s fast in determining the outcome. Unlike the students, Wangchuck was a well known and respected figure, recognised for his decades-long efforts to secure educational reforms and environmental protection. Last year, he was arrested in Ladakh on charges of inciting anti-government protests.
The timing was also key: crowds at the Delhi protest site had been thinning before he started his fast on a stage there on 28 June, injecting new energy and momentum into the movement.
Wangchuk had declared he would not end his strike until the government had listened to the demands of India’s protesting youth. He lay outdoors at the Cockroach protest site in the heart of Delhi, day and night, enduring rain, torturous heat and mosquitoes. Already a lean and slight figure, he lost 11kg over the 26 days.
“I felt confined, trapped … like a prison,” he told the Guardian. “The heat and humidity were awful.”
In the aftermath, Wangchuk, a softly-spoken engineer, environmentalist and educationist, remains humble about his role. “I was a known entity and that helped,” he said. His reverence is reserved for the hundreds of thousands of young people in the Cockroach movement, which he says has changed Indian politics for good.
Wangchuk is adamant that the Cockroach movement’s success is far bigger than a single resignation. In an era where dissent is routinely criminalised, young people, he said, had seized back the power of political protest.
“They have stripped away the curtain of fear that existed,” he said. “They are now engaged. They have tasted success in getting results and I expect them to continue.”
The 60-year-old admits the hunger strike took a gruelling toll. By the time he broke his fast on 24 July, he had pushed his body to the limit and was perilously close to organ failure. But as thousands of young people and politicians flocked to his side, his spirit remained unbroken throughout.
The greatest test, he says, came when he was forcibly removed by police from the protest site and taken to hospital against his will. Videos of his frail body being dragged away by burly police went viral and Wangchuk was hailed by young people online as a national hero. When mass protests erupted the following day, Wangchuk’s name was chanted and held aloft on placards.
Wangchuk was not always an obvious figure of anti-government resistance. Born in Ladakh, he rose to international prominence as an engineer and environmentalist, best known for inventing the ice stupor, a unique technique for water storage in human-made glaciers. He became a prominent champion of the rights of Ladakhis and set up his own school and cultural and environmental institution.
He had been a vocal supporter of several prominent policies of Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) but it soon turned to resistance as he accused the BJP of failing the people of Ladakh. Last year, as protests in Ladakh escalated, he was imprisoned by the government for almost six months under draconian anti-terrorist laws.
While his focus has been on rebuilding his body in recent weeks, regaining about 60% of his previous weight, Wangchuk has also continued his call for political reform, albeit without any overt criticism of the Modi government.
In a video message posted before India’s independence day in August, Wangchuk called for a “second independence movement” and urged Indians to choose men and women of “character and substance” to lead the country.
He has urged people to share the names of individuals of integrity who can be trusted and once he has a list, he plans to meet them in Mumbai and Delhi to discuss how elections can be cleansed of those with a criminal background.
“Indians have to trust those at the top,” he said. “At the moment, there is no trust in anything, not in elections, not in exams, not in civil servants. Clean and honest leaders are the first step to a better future.”
He expressed his support for the decision by the Cockroach movement to resist calls to become a political party and instead focus on being a pressure group, championing issues of education. “When we used to talk during the long days of the fast, I used to advise them that being a pressure group is the best way to keep clean and neutral,” he said.
For now, he is back living quietly in Ladakh, finally able to enjoy the one food that lingered on his mind during his hunger strike. “I did dream of apricots,” he said, “but that was just because I was wondering if mine back home had ripened.”

Britain said it will help Kyiv build Storm Shadow missiles in Ukraine. Hours later, the Kremlin announced that Russian forces are already working to find the production sites.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
23:57:48 UTC
08:57:48 KST

Britain said it will help Kyiv build Storm Shadow missiles in Ukraine. Hours later, the Kremlin announced that Russian forces are already working to find the production sites.
Ukraine marked the 35th anniversary of its independence on August 24. The leaders of Latvia, Lithuania, Estonia, Finland, Romania, Moldova, and Luxembourg traveled to Kyiv for the occasion, as did Britain’s new prime minister, Andy Burnham, on his first official visit to Ukraine.
During the visit, Britain’s Defense Ministry announced that it would give Ukraine the technology to produce long-range Storm Shadow missiles — the same missiles as France’s SCALP — on Ukrainian soil.
A day earlier, the British government said it had authorized the defense company MBDA to share classified information about the SCALP missile’s British components, since Kyiv and Paris hope to set up local assembly lines for the missiles in Ukraine. France announced back in mid-July that it would license Kyiv to produce them.
Commentary from Meduza’s Explainers desk:
The move looks like an act of symbolic support. France had already pledged in July to license Ukraine to produce SCALP missiles — literally the same weapon as Britain’s Storm Shadow (the two were developed jointly). The key point is that missiles this complex can’t be thrown together at the kind of small, dispersed, camouflaged sites where Ukraine builds its drones. They require full-scale factories capable of manufacturing jet engines, rocket fuel, and guidance systems.
Ukraine has received licenses for complex weapons before, along with promises to build the factories to produce them. But the plants were never completed, and most were destroyed in Russian attacks. A series of strikes, for instance, destroyed a plant under construction in Kyiv that was meant to build Turkish Bayraktar strike drones under license.
Of course, some or even all of the components could be made abroad, but that would defeat the purpose of the license: Europe already builds Storm Shadow/SCALP missiles and has struggled to scale up production. Transferring the license is meant to solve that problem precisely: Europe can’t build enough missiles for Ukraine. Building plants in Europe specifically for Ukraine’s missile program also faces organizational and financial challenges. For instance, the completion of a plant in Denmark that will produce solid rocket fuel for Ukraine was recently postponed.
Producing complex licensed weapons inside Ukraine will be possible only after the war, and only if the money can be found. That applies not just to Storm Shadow/SCALP but also to interceptors for the French-Italian SAMP/T air defense system, which can shoot down Russian ballistic missiles.
Burnham released a message to the Ukrainian people on the eve of his trip to Kyiv, congratulating them on the 35th anniversary of independence:
On Ukraine’s 35th anniversary of independence, the Ukrainian people should be in no doubt: the UK is behind you today and for as long as it takes.
I am proud of the contribution our country has made to Ukraine, and I want the Ukrainian people to hear it directly from me that our support will not waver. After all, Ukraine’s security is our security.
The friendship between our two countries will long outlast Russia’s illegal war. In both the fight and in the rebuilding to come, we will stand with Ukraine and deliver opportunities for people across both our countries.
Russia should be in no doubt of our resolve. We will not back down until there is a just and lasting peace.
The Kremlin said it views London’s plans to give Kyiv the technology to produce SCALP missiles “extremely negatively.” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Britain “is taking part in this war on the side of the Kyiv regime.” Russia’s armed forces, he said, “are doing the relevant work to identify missile production sites.”
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky also addressed Ukrainians on the 35th anniversary of independence. In a 20-minute video he said, among other things, that Ukraine’s long-range strikes on targets deep inside Russia “are cutting into logistics and revenues.” Zelensky also mentioned Ukraine’s FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles, which he said “should not be a rare species, but a common bird” and “should winter in Russia.”
Putin is stuck in the past. He still sees an old-model Ukraine — the one that will keep quiet, swallow it, and endure. That Ukraine exists nowhere but in his little folders of briefing papers. Our country became something else long ago — not an observer but a player, not a victim but a fighter. […] Russia doesn’t want peace, it wants mobilization.
Separately, Zelensky addressed China, saying it “should no longer stay silent.” “When someone dresses up in a sailor suit and garrison cap and, mispronouncing some words, talks about a nuclear strike, China should cool that enthusiasm,” Zelensky said. “China should prove its ambition to be one of the world’s leaders — not only economically and technologically, but also as a civilization — by making clear that no dictators should threaten the planet with their old warheads.”

AI generated
MONTREAL – The trade war between the United States and Canada has taken on the flavour of a culture war after the collapse of negotiations last week.
According to Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, the dispute with the nation’s largest trading partner was not just about tariff demands but what he called unacceptable “threats” to the French language and “Quebec culture”.
Those are not typical sticking points in trade negotiations, but emotive ones in Canada, particularly in the French-speaking eastern province of Quebec, which has long sought to preserve its distinct identity.
Carney said Canadian subsidies for Francophone culture, the role of Francophone online media and bilingual labeling of products sold in Canada were among the issues at stake.
He described these as “fundamental rights” and said there was “a huge gap between Canadian and American perspectives”.
The Prime Minister also contended that the US wanted to destroy Canada’s automotive, steel and aluminum industries, and restrict Canadian trade deals with other countries.
After the breakdown of talks, Canada now faces additional tariffs on some US$20 billion (S$25.4 billion) worth of its US exports and double tariffs on Canadian vehicles, while Carney has vowed to match the US tariffs “dollar for dollar”.
In Quebec, Carney’s decision to break off negotiations was widely supported.
A poll published on Aug 23 by the Angus Reid Institute found that 85 per cent of Quebecers supported the move – the highest approval rate among the 10 Canadian provinces.
“Our identity is not negotiable,” Quebec Premier Christine Frechette wrote on Aug 23 in a social media post.
She faces a re-election battle in October and is currently trailing in polls to the leader of a Quebec separatist party.
According to the Canadian media, Frechette said Washington wanted concessions on Quebec’s rules for appliances and instruction manuals, as well as its law promoting French-language cultural content.
Recent legislation by Quebec allows it to regulate how much French-language content digital platforms offer and how prominently it appears, which can add to the cost of doing business for US companies, the Montreal Gazette reported.
In an interview on Aug 24, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer played down the language issue in the trade talks as a “funny fake story”.
“What we don’t like is a situation where Canada, the federal government, forces American tech companies to take their earnings and give a percentage to their competitors in Canada,” Greer told CNBC.
“But I understand why the Quebecois want to have French language content and all of that. And we think that’s a really valuable thing.” AFP

U.S. Supreme Court lifts lower court ruling that blocks Trump's order to restrict mail-in voting
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
07:45:17 CST
08:45:17 KST

WASHINGTON, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday lifted a lower court's ruling that blocked part of U.S. President Donald Trump's executive order to restrict mail-in voting, but it remains to be seen whether such measures would be implemented before the November midterm election.
"The Court's disposition of this application does not mean that any measure taken by the Government to implement the Order will necessarily be lawful. On that score, time will tell," the nation's highest court said in a ruling.
"But the Order itself does not harm the States, so the District Court lacked jurisdiction to bar the Government from trying to implement it. And for the reasons discussed, that injunction is likely to irreparably harm the Government if it remains in place while the appellate process runs its course," the court continued.
The ruling marks the latest court action in the legal fight over Trump's order rolled out in March, which calls for the Department of Homeland Security to develop state lists of adult U.S. citizens and for the United States Postal Service to obtain lists of eligible mail voters from states.
U.S. media believe that it remains to be seen whether such measures would be implemented before the November midterm election.
CNN report noted that additional legal challenges could hinder implementation of Trump's plan before the midterm elections.
"It remains unclear what impact the high court's order will actually have on eligible mail-in voters," according to a report from NPR.
"The legal fight is far from over, with a separate set of lawsuits led by Democrats and voting rights groups continuing to play out as this fall's election draws closer," the NPR report said. ■

Calls grow for US to deny visa to RSS chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
23:38:12 UTC
08:38:12 KST

More than 1,000 people across the US have written to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, calling on the State Department to deny or revoke a US visa for Mohan Bhagwat, the head of India’s right-wing Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, or RSS.
The letters, collected by the Indian American Muslim Council (IAMC) alongside allied organisations, call on Washington to cancel Bhagwat's scheduled August 29, appearance at Madison Square Garden in New York City amid widespread public opposition.
"Mohan Bhagwat does not represent Indian Americans, and Madison Square Garden should not present him as though he does. The State Department has the authority to deny him a visa, and a federal commission has already recommended it. They must act before August 29," said Mohammed Jawad, President of the IAMC.
Sanctions calls
In March, the US Commission on International Religious Freedom (USCIRF) recommended targeted sanctions against the RSS, including asset freezes and visa restrictions on its leadership, citing its involvement in "acts of extreme violence and intolerance against members of minority groups for decades."
The Congressional Research Service classifies the RSS as a "hardline Hindu nationalist" organisation.
Human Rights Watch has identified the RSS and its affiliates as "most responsible" for violence against Christians and "directly responsible" for the 2002 anti-Muslim violence in Gujarat.
International watchdogs, including Genocide Watch and the US Holocaust Memorial Museum's Early Warning Project, have repeatedly raised alarms over state-tolerated mob violence, bulldozer demolitions of Muslim properties, and the systemic disenfranchisement of India's religious minorities.
Global pushback
The US petition follows actions in Canada, where more than 40 civil society, human rights, and faith groups urged Ottawa to bar Bhagwat, and Canadian MPs called for a ban on the RSS.
The RSS, founded in 1925, serves as the ideological parent organisation of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
Amid mounting scrutiny, senior RSS leaders, including General Secretary Dattatreya Hosabale, have recently conducted outreach tours across the US, Britain, and Germany to counter international criticism and oppose calls for Global Magnitsky sanctions.
IAMC has urged Madison Square Garden management to cancel the event and has called on New York officials to condemn the platforming of the RSS leadership.

Ukraine and Syria planning to expand agricultural cooperation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
23:35:00 UTC
08:35:00 KST

Ukraine and Syria planning to expand agricultural cooperation
The issues were discussed during an online meeting between Ukraine’s Minister of Agrarian Policy and Food Taras Vysotskyi and Syria’s Minister of Agriculture Basel Hafez al-Suwaidan, Ukrinform reported, citing the ministry.
“Our agricultural sectors face similar challenges, so it is important to exchange experience and seek practical solutions together. A separate priority is the swift restoration of safe navigation. Ukraine is working on this with international partners, as stable maritime logistics is essential for bilateral trade with Syria,” Vysotskyi said.
The sides paid particular attention to food support for Syria. Under the Food from Ukraine program, Ukraine has already delivered 15,662 tonnes of wheat flour to the country.
Vysotskyi stressed Ukraine’s readiness to share modern agrotechnologies, engage in joint research and trials, and supply specialized seed material adapted to local climatic conditions.
Following the meeting, the parties will continue preparations for an official visit by a Ukrainian delegation to Syria, during which the memorandum of cooperation is expected to be signed. The document will define further areas of interaction in agriculture and lay the foundation for long‑term partnership between the two countries.
As reported, Ukraine terminated trade and economic agreements with Syria in May 2023 due to the Assad regime’s support for Russian aggression. After the change of government in Syria at the end of 2024, the countries resumed contacts: Ukraine began supplying humanitarian grain and flour under the Grain from Ukraine program, later moving to restore diplomatic relations and agricultural trade.

German court convicts siblings over looted Egyptian artefacts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24

Breadcrumb
German court convicts siblings over looted Egyptian artefacts
A German court on Monday convicted two siblings of money laundering over the illegal sale of ancient Egyptian artefacts, and ordered the confiscation of 32 million euros ($37 million).
The brother and sister, who were not identified, were also hit with hefty fines in the case related to the objects, which allegedly came from illegal excavations in Egypt.
The artefacts, which were sold for millions of euros to museums, included a bust of Cleopatra, a stone slab associated with King Tutankhamun and items from a princess's grave.
Sentencing the pair, a judge at a regional court in the northern city of Hamburg said "unique cultural treasures" were involved in what was a "highly complex legal case".
The man and woman were accused of acting with other suspects, who are being prosecuted separately. The pair are the children of one of the main alleged perpetrators, reportedly an archaeologist from Hamburg.
The male defendant is said to have been involved in illegally trading the artefacts since 2013, according to prosecutors.
He was accused of bringing several sarcophagi from the princess's grave to Germany, having them restored and then reselling them to a museum in the United Arab Emirates, concealing their origins.
A few years later, he was involved in the illegal sale of the bust of Cleopatra, Egypt's last pharaoh, and the Tutankhamun slab to museums in the UAE.
The court ordered the confiscation of 26 million euros from the male suspect, and that he pay a fine of more than 90,000 euros.
He was however cleared of the more serious charge of working with a gang to deal in stolen goods, because of insufficient evidence.
Some of the sale proceeds flowed through the account of the female defendant.
The court ordered that six million euros be confiscated from her, and fined her 30,000 euros.

Minnesota’s kicking competition muddied by NCAA eligibility court ruling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
23:23:02 UTC
08:23:02 KST

Minnesota’s kicking competition muddied by NCAA eligibility court ruling
MINNEAPOLIS (AP) — The eligibility chaos across college football has seeped into depth charts for several programs with the regular season fast approaching.
The competition at Minnesota for the place kicking job has sure become complicated.
Brady Denaburg handled that job last year for the Gophers after spending his first three college seasons at Syracuse, and he was out of the picture until a federal judge in Denver ruled on July 31 that athletes from the 2022 high school class were eligible for a fifth year.
The NCAA had previously excluded that class from the new “five-for-five” rule that was designed to add clarity and fairness to college sports in the wild era of the transfer portal, revenue sharing and name, image and likeness earnings.
The Denver ruling was then temporarily halted on Friday by an appeals court injunction, putting thousands of athletes nationwide, like Denaburg, back in the lurch.
“Playing’s in limbo,” Gophers coach P.J. Fleck said after practice on Monday, just 10 days before his team’s opener against Eastern Illinois. “I do hope that we come to some resolution at some point about what we’re going to do with all these players, because at the end of the day, if all we say is it’s about the student-athlete, then we have to make the decisions for them. Right, wrong or indifferent, legal cases, all those things, let’s get some direction of exactly what they’re going to be able to do. Because it’s lawsuit after lawsuit, just a ping-pong match that goes back and forth.”
The confusion also has spilled into Indiana’s national championship title defense.
Following the initial ruling, sixth-ranked Indiana welcomed back two starting defensive linemen — Stephen Daley, who was the Big Ten’s co-leader in tackles for loss (19) last season despite getting injured during the conference championship game celebration, and Kellan Wyatt, who missed the final nine games last season with a knee injury in mid-October.
Daley and Wyatt were practicing, for now, and Indiana coach Curt Cignetti threw his full support behind them on Monday.
“I think in their case, you’re creating opportunities,” Cignetti said. “You look at Wyatt, he started less than half the games last year and got hurt. Then, Daley started six out of 16 games, got hurt. Both had pro potential, but because of injury didn’t end up in NFL camp. We’d have to make no roster cuts if they’re eligible to play. We’re going to support them in their quest to be eligible to play.”
For the Gophers, it’s even more nuanced than that.
The federal ruling from Denver was clarified three days later to exclude athletes who’d already signed professional contracts, which prompted a countersuit filed in Louisiana state court that gained a temporary restraining order on Wednesday. Former New Mexico kicker Luke Drzewiecki, who was in rookie minicamp with the Baltimore Ravens this spring, was in that group.
Drzewiecki entered the transfer portal and picked Minnesota, following special teams coordinator Daniel Da Prato, who’d jumped from the Lobos to Gophers this offseason.
With sophomore Daniel Jackson and Michigan transfer Beckham Sunderland, who has begun his third college season, the Gophers now have four kickers in the mix in practice. Anywhere between two and four of them will be eligible to play in the opener, which has obviously complicated the decision for Fleck and Da Prato.
“It kind of reminds you of the 2020 season with COVID. You didn’t know who was going to play. You didn’t know who passed the test right before the game or who wouldn’t pass the test,” Fleck said. “You’d have no idea, so you had to prepare for all of it. In that small scale, it’s kind of a little bit what we’re preparing for.”
With four kickers rotating, the Gophers have spent more time on field goal drills in fall camp than they have in the past. Sunderland also had Da Prato as a special teams coordinator at Texas State in 2024. He has never attempted a kick in a college game, only kickoffs. Jackson took two extra points and three kickoffs last season.
Denaburg was 33 for 33 on extra points last year and 14 for 21 on field goals, missing three of five attempts from 40-plus yards. Drzewiecki sparkled for New Mexico during his senior season, making 36 of 36 extra points and 18 of 19 field goals.
“We don’t know what will happen and who will be eligible and who won’t be eligible. You’d love some answers as soon as possible,” Fleck said. “We’re preparing for some of those guys to be eligible and we’re also preparing for everybody to be eligible, and that’s why this kicking competition continues to go through all the way.”

AP Sports Writer Mike Marot in Indianapolis contributed to this report.

Mexico resumes limited cattle exports to US after screwworm pause, relieving ranchers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
23:23:02 UTC
08:23:02 KST

Mexico resumes limited cattle exports to US after screwworm pause, relieving ranchers
AGUA PRIETA, Mexico (AP) — Mexico resumed live cattle exports to the United States on Monday after they were halted for nearly two years by restrictions imposed by the Trump administration following a screwworm outbreak.
Even under strict limitations, the reopening of the trade channel brought relief to Mexico’s ranching industry, which was dealt an economic blow by the controls. The flesh-eating worm is now present on both sides of the border.
In the sprawling desert mountains along the U.S.-Mexico border, hundreds of cattle began to cross from the Mexican town of Agua Prieta in the state of Sonora to the Arizona town of Douglas at around 3 p.m.
The process began after several hours of inspections by Mexican and U.S. authorities, who used dogs to inspect each animal and determine that they were not infected with screwworm.
The larvae come from the Cochliomyia hominivorax fly, which invades open wounds or the mucous membranes of body openings in any warm-blooded animal, including humans, and devours tissue, causing the wounds to become increasingly deep and painful.
The pest arrived in Mexico in November 2024 and is now present in 30 of the country’s 32 states, including the northern state of Sonora. In the United States, the first cases began to be reported in June in the states of Texas and New Mexico.
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum celebrated the reopening on Monday morning, and her administration outlined precautions to beat back the outbreak. That included strengthening cattle tracing systems and continuing to disperse sterile flies in border states like Sonora and Chihuahua, the largest exporters of cattle to the U.S. Mexico currently has 1,937 active screwworm cases.
To resume exports from Mexico on Monday, the U.S. approved a new protocol that included placing radio-frequency identification tags in the cows’ ears and installing scanners to detect the tags.
Cattle crossings into Arizona were also limited to 700 head per day, increasing to 900 per day next week and 1,300 per day the following week.
While Mexico has hundreds of cattle ready for export, the Trump administration controls will slow recovery of the industry, leaving herds in the U.S. with the lowest cattle counts in 75 years, and a shortfall of about 1.2 million cows, which has led to a surge in beef prices.

Some homes and businesses in Gary, Indiana, still without power 13 days after storms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
23:23:02 UTC
08:23:02 KST

Some homes and businesses in Gary, Indiana, still without power 13 days after storms
GARY, Ind. (AP) — Things became all-too familiar for Kimya Williams after storms rumbled through Gary, Indiana, earlier this month leaving big chunks of the mostly-Black city in the dark for two weeks.
The power outage reminded the 50-year-old of what she experienced in New Orleans in 2005 when Hurricane Katrina knocked out electricity to many.
Williams’ home was one of more than 38,300 homes and businesses in Gary to lose power from the Aug. 11 storms. She initially tried to stick it out and stay put, but the darkness got the best of her and Williams’ left for Indianapolis to stay with her children.
“It was too triggering. It was too dark,” Williams told The Associated Press Monday.
On Monday, one of the poorest and blackest cities in America still had no power. The day before, Gary Mayor Eddie Melton called the pace of restoration “unacceptable.”
“We’re at day 12 and 12 days is too long for families to be without power, 12 days is too long for parents to worry about their children and for businesses to lose revenue,” Melton said in an update to the community.
Northern Indiana Public Service Co., the area’s electricity provider, said Monday that more than 370,000 customers lost power and that more than 364,000 have had their service restored. The remaining customers should have power back by Tuesday.
“Our teams are assigned to outages large and small, and we remain committed to reaching every affected customer in all of our communities,” the company said. “No outage is being overlooked, and no customer will be left behind as we continue this restoration effort.”
As the Indiana residents awaited restoration of their service, roughly 34,000 customers in the majority Black city of Memphis were still without power as of late Monday afternoon, after storms swept through the city on Saturday, according to information on Memphis Light, Gas and Water’s website. The utility said that figure represents less than 8% of its customers.
Some residents were comparing the situation to Gary.
Lawsuit filed after long outages
A resident in neighboring Porter County filed a lawsuit in state court last week accusing NIPSCO of negligence and requesting a class action for residents of Indiana who have suffered as a result. The complaint said the utility company failed to maintain trees and other vegetation hazards growing near its power lines, a failure that “predictably” resulted in the recent outage and others after storms caused the vegetation to fall on the lines.
In a written statement, NIPSCO strongly disagrees with the characterization of their vegetation management practices and will “vigorously defend” itself in court, the company said in a statement. The vegetation management process is overseen by the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission.
Indiana Gov. Mike Braun on Monday said he has directed the state consumer advocate to petition for an investigation into NIPSCO’s preparation for, and response to, recent prolonged power outages caused by severe weather.
The investigation also is to look into whether the utility “adequately maintained vegetation and cleared rights-of-way to protect its infrastructure and whether funding approved by state regulators for infrastructure and reliability improvements was spent as promised,” Braun said.
Decades of disinvestment worsen weather impacts
Experts have noted that in cases of severe weather, natural disasters and especially extreme heat, the poor are most vulnerable.
Gary, like many northern rust-belt cities, has suffered for decades from disinvestment following the loss of population and industries. About 55,000 of the city’s 69,000 residents are Black, with more than 29% of the population living in poverty, according to the Census’ 2024 American Community Survey.
The poverty rate for Indiana is about 12%.
Gary’s estimated median household income of about $40,752 was far below the $71,959 for the rest of the state.
The more well-off a person is financially, the more options they have when faced with severe weather and natural disasters, said Stephen Pantano, senior vice president of market transformation for the Urban Land Institute’s Impact Lab.
“Some people don’t have the luxury of owning a car to drive somewhere else or having access to a place to go that’s outside of their immediate community where there might still be power,” he said.
The problems likely are to increase as climate risks grow.
“It’s a matter of where the lightning strikes on any given day as to which specific community is hit,” Pantano said. “Gary’s number came up this time, but it’s going to be another city next time. And the problem with aging infrastructure and disinvestment tends to accentuate the impacts when they hit communities that have been experiencing those problems for a long time.”
Residents, white and Black, await improvements
Williams, who is Black and describes herself as low-income, did what she could to save the food in her home.
“I used my car battery as a generator,” she said. “I plugged my refrigerator into an inverter. I learned that from Katrina.”
That was a last gasp effort. Williams, who returned from Indianapolis after learning her power was back on Sunday, said the food still went bad.
“My house smells like mold and mildew,” she said.
Gary’s troubles didn’t start with the storms and run much deeper than the outages, said Erin Carreon, who is pursuing a doctorate in social work at the University of Chicago.
She said white flight and the scaling back of jobs and closures of steel factories contributed to decades of disinvestment in Gary.
“I grew up in Gary and social inequality was very evident to me,” she said Monday. “Seeing how the city has been neglected over the years has been very central to my life.”
Carreon, 40, is white and lives in the city. She also has been without power since the storms hit.

Colombian president orders immigration raids, vows deportations of migrants without legal status

Colombian president orders immigration raids, vows deportations of migrants without legal status
BOGOTA, Colombia (AP) — Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella has promised to deport thousands of migrants who are in the country without residence permits, mainly Venezuelans, as he attempts to make significant changes to the nation’s immigration policies that he says will reduce crime.
De la Espriella, who was sworn into office three weeks ago, said that he would order the country’s national immigration service to conduct raids with Colombian police as early as this week. He announced the new policy in a video released on Sunday night in his X account where he spoke of multiple measures to reduce crime and confront criminal groups.
The ultra conservative leader, who is closely aligned with the U.S. President Donald Trump, said that law enforcement will first target migrants who are “committing crimes” and then, those who are living in the country without regular status.
“I will not accept any illegal immigrants, wherever they come from,” de la Espriella said in the video. “They will have to leave and be deported. It is a political decision I am taking responsibility for.”
Most migrants living in Colombia come from neighboring Venezuela, a nation that lost about a fifth of its population over the past decade as Venezuelans fled a repressive regime that oversaw years of economic turmoil, and a 75% contraction in the nation’s GDP.
Around 2.8 million Venezuelans were living in Colombia as of August, according to the United Nations, making it the largest Venezuelan diaspora. In July, Colombia’s national immigration service said that it had granted temporary residence permits to about 2.3 million Venezuelans under a scheme rolled out in 2021 by then President Ivan Duque during the peak of Venezuela’s immigration crisis.
De la Espriella’s effort to deport migrants who have no regular status marks a major shift for Colombia, which had long worked to protect incoming Venezuelans and grant them a pathway towards permanent residency.
Ana Karina García, director of Juntos Se Puede, an organization that helps Venezuelan migrants in Colombia, said that the Colombian government stopped handing out new temporary residency permits three years ago. She said that de la Espriella’s incoming administration should expand pathways to legal residency, instead of punishing people who cannot obtain residency permits.
“We understand that the president wants to protect Colombians,” she said. “But there is no need to protect them from migrants. It has been proven that foreigners do not commit crimes at greater rates” than the local population.
Arles Pereda, the president of an association that represents Venezuelans in Bogota, said the announcement worried him, because new groups of Venezuelans displaced by the twin earthquakes that rocked the country in June have been arriving in Colombia to seek opportunities.
“The doors seem to be closing,” Pereda said. “Not just in Colombia, but also in Chile, Peru and Ecuador,” where conservative leaders have also made it harder for Venezuelan migrants to get residency permits.
In a text message, Colombia’s national immigration department, Migracion Colombia, said that the agency is currently without a director. The agency said it will only implement the new policies outlined by Colombia’s incoming government once a new director is appointed and installed. ___

Inside the IDF’s high-risk missions: Documenting rescue efforts around the world
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
23:21:22 UTC
08:21:22 KST

A still camera, a video lens and an M4 rifle. This is the main equipment carried by IDF documentation soldiers as they head into some of the most complex locations, from combat zones in the Gaza Strip, Lebanon and Syria to areas devastated by disaster and destruction on the other side of the world.
Recently, IDF documentation soldiers took part in two international aid missions: the “Reim Alliance” mission to Colombia following the country’s powerful earthquake and a rescue mission to assist those affected by the earthquake in Venezuela. Through their lenses, they documented not only rescue and engineering operations but also captured the human drama, quiet diplomacy and encounters between soldiers in green uniforms and local civilians.
In Colombia, Sgt. H. and Sgt. Y. found themselves at the heart of search and rescue efforts in the city of Cali. The delegation, which included about 80 search and rescue, engineering and technology specialists from the Home Front Command, along with representatives of the Defense and Foreign ministries, worked alongside local forces.
“Getting off the plane as a regular-service soldier alongside reservists and senior officers for a mission like this is a historic event,” Sgt. Y. recalls. “I was attached to the commander of the National Search and Rescue Unit. We moved between the sites. At one of them, where a building had collapsed near a hospital, I photographed the overall situation over the commander’s shoulder. You could see the destruction, but also dozens of local residents who pitched in to help clear the site.”
For Sgt. H., who was stationed at the main site at a multistory residential building where most of the search efforts were concentrated, the human angle was the most important.
“Our goal is to document the forces, but what struck me was the residents’ willingness to help,” she says. “The rescue teams and population officers met with the families and learned their names. Every time someone missing was found, we knew exactly who was being rescued. These are moving moments that are etched in the photographs.”
Alongside the direct assistance in locating 29 missing people and surveying more than 100 buildings, the visual documentation also captured the breaking down of barriers.
“At one of the sites, a local family came over to us, smiled and gave us high-fives,” Sgt. Y. says. “It stood out especially against the backdrop of pro-Palestinian demonstrations that had taken place in the area earlier. The connection formed on the ground was purely a human gesture of solidarity, and it was expressed through the most genuine hugs.”
'Enormous support on the ground'
As the role of the documentation soldier continues to evolve, the team produced more than 1,000 photographs and video clips during 12 days of activity in Colombia, including training in vertical photography tailored to digital platforms and social media.
“Beyond the operational importance, our photographs are also meant for the families back home,” H. says. “These soldiers left home in mid-August to save lives on the other side of the world. The photographs show their loved ones the magnitude of what they are doing.”
For Sgt. First Class S. (22), who recently completed his military service, the mission to Venezuela was part of a chain of operational events in which he had taken part since November 2023. The delegation to Venezuela was sent to assess the situation and provide advice following two earthquakes, with the goal of developing an engineering plan to rehabilitate buildings.
“We arrived in a country with no official diplomatic relations with Israel, but on the ground we encountered enormous support,” says S., who was attached to the delegation commander. “The role of a documentation soldier is to be on the front line and tell the story. I documented high-level meetings with the local government, but also the engineering work of assessing buildings.”
One of S.’s most significant photographs captured the moment when the local infrastructure minister informed a family that its home was uninhabitable and would have to be demolished.
“You see all the emotion and human turmoil of a family losing its home, and on the other side, IDF soldiers coming over and embracing them. It is the most human encounter there can be.”
S. represents a new generation of operational documentation soldiers who, alongside international missions, operate deep inside enemy territory. During his service, he documented operations in Gaza, Syria and Lebanon, culminating in the moment he documented the return of live hostages in one of the releases.
“Going from the Gaza Strip and Syria to a civilian aid mission is a conceptual shift,” S. says. “In combat zones, soldiers are happy to see the camera. It boosts morale and captures the visual side of the fighting, along with the jokes about equipment and food in the evening. When I saw my photographs appear on the front pages of newspapers in Israel and around the world, or when I documented the hostages returning home, I realized that this was history unfolding in real time. The camera is not just a reporting tool. It is the lasting testimony to the IDF’s work.”

First Ladies, Gentlemen meet in Kyiv to create 'shared language of resilience' amid crisis
Ukraine's First Lady, Olena Zelenska, led the sixth Summit of First Ladies and Gentlemen in Kyiv on Aug. 24, focusing on creating an international "language of resilience" to help navigate global challenges.
The summit, established by Zelenska in 2021, featured first ladies and gentlemen from 14 countries, as well as other global leaders. The event was held as part of Ukraine's 35th Independence Day celebrations.
This year's summit introduced a Global Vocabulary of Resilience program, aiming to bring together concepts that different societies use to withstand crises. Such concepts included "civic volunteerism" from the U.S. and the British idiom "keep calm and carry on."
The Ukrainian concept of sophiynist, a philosophy of resilience that involves "the capacity to perceive reality with both mind and heart" and turn that understanding into action, was also highlighted.
"Coming in person, seeing, feeling, understanding — it is the fastest way to find an answer to a question I often hear: 'How do you Ukrainians endure this?'" Zelenska said in the opening of the summit about Ukrainian resilience during the war.
"This dissonance between war and life continuing is surprising only to those who have never been to Ukraine."
The vocabulary project is part of Zelenska's "How Are U?" mental health initiative, a program launched to address the war's impact on Ukrainians' mental wellbeing.
read also
The different resilience frameworks have been compiled into a public online dictionary that allows users to search by country or concept. A print version of core vocabulary entries will also be published. 
Attending the summit in person were Lithuanian First Lady Diana Nausediene, Estonian First Lady Sirje Karis, Finland's First Lady Suzanne Innes-Stubb, Serbian First Lady Tamara Vucic, Romanian First Lady Mirabela Gradinaru, and Slovenia's First Gentleman Ales Musar.
First ladies and gentlemen from Germany, Belize, Israel, the Czech Republic, Turkey, Guatemala, Georgia, and Panama joined the conference virtually.
Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda, Estonian President Alar Karis, and Finnish President Alexander Stubb also spoke at the summit and shared their own language of resilience. 
"The Estonian phenomenon of Tiigrihupe (tiger leap) proves that resilience can be built long before crisis hits," Karis said, celebrating the early adoption of digital technologies in Estonia.
Energy Minister and former Prime Minister  Denys Shmyhal also  lauded the resilience of Ukraine's energy infrastructure against Russian attacks.
"Our energy workers and engineers have created a unique engineering and technical protection, which helps to protect energy facilities even after the arrival of ballistic missiles," Shmyhal said. "Damage is repaired in a week, not in a month."
President Volodymyr Zelensky delivered the summit's closing address, speaking about finding stability in times of great crisis. 
"All previous summits, and this one, of First Ladies and Gentlemen demonstrate that humanitarian diplomacy is not an addition to major politics, but one of its pillars," Zelenksy said. "And may this pillar of ours be strong and always resilient. May we be resilient. May Ukraine be strong – in our community with you."

====================================================================================================

Literacy Owns AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
23:15:16 UTC
08:15:16 KST

Despite recent hiccups and doomsday warnings, AI will continue to develop and become part of our everyday lives in much the same way that the internet has since the dotcom bubble burst over 20 years ago. Fears that widespread use of AI will make many job functions obsolete are well founded, but it will also create many opportunities for people skilled in its operation, especially those who can clearly communicate instructions and break down ideas into text. These skills are more than AI literacy, they are skills that we acquire through reading, listening, writing, and speaking—advanced literacy skills.
We need to recognize what AI is good at and what makes it work best for us—how it can automate mundane tasks and streamline processes, but not replace perspective or lateral or critical thought.
AI won’t replace communication or critical thinking, but it is replacing many entry-level jobs.
To make the most of AI, language and critical thinking are prerequisites. You can’t construct prompts to give AI instructions without using precise language. Nor can you check output without careful and critical review. So, if we are to provide our next generation of AI natives with the skills they need for success, we should focus on developing advanced literacy in middle and high school and then increase our attention on humanities like English, World Languages, Linguistics, and Philosophy.
Courses combining AI and philosophy are surging in popularity in China, Hong Kong, and the Philippines, driven by the demand from employers for graduates who can understand and use generative technologies as well as critically evaluate them.
In France, philosophy is strictly compulsory for all students in their final year (Terminale) across general academic tracks, and university applicants must take a philosophy exam to pass the baccalauréat.
Just a few weeks ago, The Economist reported that AI companies are hiring philosophers in large numbers, as philosophy plays a key role in improving the reasoning ability, safety, and ethical judgment of AI models. According to data released by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York earlier this year, the unemployment rate for computer science majors in the US was 7% as of 2024, but for philosophy majors it stood at just 5.1%.
This is not to say that all students need to focus on philosophy. Studying language and literature is another, more practical, route to acquiring many of the same valuable skills—comprehension, reasoning, argument, and communication.
While we must continue to focus on helping ALL children achieve basic literacy in the early grades, we also need to recognize the importance of developing ALL students’ literacy skills as they advance through their schooling and make the most of their linguistic assets.
To work effectively with the latest technological tools in their learning and their work, today’s students need to articulate complex ideas, concepts, and functions; understand detail and nuance; and produce output that speaks to our increasingly multilingual and multicultural society. Our educational policymakers need to react to a world where AI is the ubiquitous tool by encouraging students developing their communication and literacy skills throughout their elementary, high school, college, and work careers.
Daniel Ward

Vice President J.D. Vance on Monday called Canada a “state,” before claiming it was an accident.
“We have to remember, Canada is a state—sorry, Freudian slip,” Vance said during a political event in Maine, after being asked about the recent heated trade talks between the U.S. and its northern neighbor. “That was actually an accident.”
He went on to say that “Canada is a country that has underinvested in its military that quite literally would get invaded by a foreign country were it not for the umbrella of protection provided by the United States of America.”
Vance’s slip-up comes after President Donald Trump has hurled a number of barbs at Canada and its political leaders since he took office for a second term. The President has repeatedly referred to Canada as the “51st state,” suggesting that the U.S. should annex its northern neighbor. In March, Trump called Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney the “future Governor of Canada.”
Carney has repeatedly and firmly pushed back on Trump’s comments; last year, the Canadian Prime Minister said of the suggestion of annexing Canada: “As I’ve said to anyone who’s raised this issue in private or in public, including the President, it will never happen.”
When TIME asked Trump last year whether he was “trolling a little bit” when he speaks about making Canada a U.S. state, Trump replied, “Actually, no, I’m not.”
Trump: ‘Without the United States, Canada couldn’t survive’
In a Truth Social post on Monday afternoon, Trump continued to fling digs at Canada.
“America has been carrying Canada for decades, but no longer!” Trump said in his post. “The U.S.A. will always be far bigger, richer, and stronger than Canada. Without the United States, Canada couldn’t survive — It’s where they get all of their money and, because of their current bad leadership, primarily Governor Carney, and his Flunky, Ford, they will not be allowed to keep taking advantage of the United States — Their key to survival.”
Trump referred to Ontario Premier Doug Ford, who has been a vocal critic of the tariffs that the Trump Administration has imposed or threatened to impose on Canadian goods. In addition to calling Ford Carney’s “Flunky,” Trump said the Premier was “the less charismatic, intelligent, and overall unimpressive brother of the late, great, Rob Ford,” a former mayor of Ontario’s capital, Toronto.
Tensions between the allied countries have escalated in recent days. Trump claimed earlier last week that, “subject to the finalization of documents,” the two nations had reached a deal, but trade negotiations between the two broke down on Friday, and both sides have pointed the finger at the other.
In a statement shared late on Friday, Carney said that “progress has not been enough to meet our objectives for Canadians” and so he “decided to suspend trade negotiations with the U.S.” He accused the U.S. of proposing “last-minute changes” that he called “unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal."
On Monday, Trump said that he plans to raise automobile tariffs on Canada to 50% starting on Jan. 1, 2027. His 50% tariffs on about $20 billion worth of goods imported into the U.S. from Canada went into effect over the weekend, and Carney said that Canada would respond with retaliatory tariffs on U.S. goods that will take effect on Sept. 8.
At a press conference on Monday, Carney said that Canada was still open to trade talks, but that any deal would have to “be one that respects Canada’s sovereignty.”
“When the Americans go to the negotiation table first with the right attitude towards our industries and a true partnership, of course we’ll come to the negotiating table,” he said.
“An attitude at the negotiation table that Canada is a subsidiary of the United States,” he continued, “that’s not something we’re going to accept.”

Tens of Thousands of Nevadans Evacuated in Latest Wildfire of Record-Breaking Year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
23:01:47 UTC
08:01:47 KST

The ongoing “Hawk” fire outside the city of Reno, Nevada, has prompted the evacuation of tens of thousands of people in yet another devastating blaze contributing to one of the worst U.S. wildfire seasons in recent history.
Roughly 42,000 people have been evacuated around Reno, while an additional 45,000 were warned that they may also have to flee. The evacuation is among the largest prompted by a U.S. wildfire this year, following the fires around Spokane, Washington, in early August during which roughly 60,000 people were evacuated.
The Reno evacuations mark another flashpoint of a record-breaking fire season. The fire is dwarfed in acreage by larger blazes from this year, at roughly 15,000 acres burned so far, but its direct effect on civilians is one of the largest in recent years, and demonstrates the potential risk that worsening wildfires may have on people and their communities in years to come.
Here’s how fires around the U.S. have set new records, and why they have been so bad this year.
More acres burned and more entrapments
Compared to the past 10 years, more acres have been burned this year in the U.S. to date.
The National Interagency Fire Center (NIFC) posted on Monday that firefighters have responded to 50,784 wildfires that have scorched over 7.8 million acres this year: 168% of the 10-year average for acres burned, and 129% of the average for total fires.
Around the same time last year, roughly 4 million acres had been burned, around 50% of the current acreage for 2026 so far, according to NIFC tracking.
The U.S. has also been at the highest level of “fire preparedness” for 38 days, since July 18th, at a five out of five, which means that federal resources are strained and may not be available to address every new fire.
The 10-year average for fire preparedness in August is four. The last time the fire preparedness level was at a five for the entire month of August was in 2021.
Meanwhile the 10-year annual average for days spent at level four and five combined is 48 days, and so far, the U.S. has already spent 57 days within that range, after reaching level four in late June.
There has also been a 20-year high of firefighter entrapments, life-threatening situations in which firefighters’ safety zones and escape routes are compromised. According to a Reuters report, there had been 12 entrapments in 2026 as of Aug. 13, more than the year-total average of nine in the last 20 years. This year’s entrapments also marked the highest year-to-date figure since 2006.
Six out of 13 firefighter deaths have involved entrapments, the report shows. An average of 17 firefighter fatalities occur each year from wildfires.
Hotter, drier, and windier conditions
Wildfire trackers often use the “30-30-30” rule to identify conditions that can lead to extreme wildfires. The rule refers to when the temperature is at least 30 degrees Celsius (86 Fahrenheit), humidity is at 30% or lower, and wind speeds are at 30 kilometers per hour or more (roughly 19 miles per hour). When combined, these hot, dry, and windy conditions can produce extremely large and destructive fires, as they have this year.
Reno has experienced an average daily high temperature of 92.8 degrees Fahrenheit (33.7 Celsius), 27% humidity, and 18 miles per hour (29 kilometers per hour) daily maximum wind speed over the last 10 days, including the week before the “Hawk” fires began on Saturday and the three days since as the blaze continues.
Although the 30-30-30 rule is a metric for local weather conditions’ effect on wildfires, increases have been exhibited this year compared to past years across the U.S. in each of its categories—temperature, dryness, and wind speed.
When it came to temperature, the average in the contiguous U.S. from January through July was the second warmest in 132 years, at 4.2 degrees Celsius (55.5 Fahrenheit), according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).
July in particular was the hottest month on record in the U.S., with an average of 76.9 degrees Fahrenheit (24.9 Celsius). Nevada specifically had one of its warmest July’s on record, according to NOAA.
Wind speeds generally fluctuate the most by region, but from January through June of this year, they averaged 0.5% above the 20-year average during 2005-2024, according to an S&P Global analysis.
These hotter, drier, and windier conditions have set the stage for an active wildfire season.
One underlying explanation for increasingly fire-prone conditions is climate change, which has contributed to longer-lasting fire seasons, now lasting for six to eight months in some areas, compared to what used to be roughly four months in past decades.
“Generally we're having drier summers and higher winds,” Peter Sunderland, professor of fire protection engineering at the University of Maryland, previously told TIME. “We are seeing more and more climate extremes.”
