Ukraine got independence as a gift in 1991. Now we pay in blood
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
18:49:18 UTC
03:49:18 KST

In 1991, Ukraine did not shed a drop of blood. It was a transition of power. We raised a flag, we declared ourselves independent, and we received our independence as a gift.
Now we are shedding rivers of blood for real independence.
That is the difference between this Independence Day and the ones before it, and I do not think we have absorbed it yet.
Colonial theory has a name for what happened to us thirty-five years ago. It is called flag independence. You raise the flag, you declare the state, and for a while you believe that was it—that this was the end, and now we simply continue as an independent nation.
In theory it was believed to be like that. In practice, every decolonized nation eventually discovered the same thing: it is not the end. It is the beginning.
The nations that gathered at Bandung in Indonesia in 1955 worked this out before us. They had their flags. They also had the former metropolis still holding the strings—to their economies, their cultures, their political classes. They named it: neocolonialism.
And they understood that real independence would take something longer and harder than a declaration. Not only liberation with arms, but liberation of the mind from the colonial legacy. Not erasing the colonial memory—reworking it, synthesizing it into something new.
So here is the shape of it. Before 1991, Ukrainians waged a struggle for independence without statehood. After 1991, we have been waging a struggle for independence within statehood. The struggle did not end. It changed its conditions.
What was gathered into the Act of Independence
The declaration was a beginning, but it was also a result—of generations.
It begins in the nineteenth century, with people like Taras Shevchenko, who essentially invented a Ukrainian identity. It was a construction. It was not, as Putin claims, the invention of Vladimir Lenin. It was the invention of Ukrainian intellectuals, writers, and religious leaders, who constructed this nation on the basis of what came before—the Cossack Republic, Kyivan Rus, the long stretch from the Middle Ages through early modernity.
Then the dissidents of the Soviet period. Then the Ukrainian Insurgent Army, which fought on two fronts against three colonizers: the Germans, the Poles, and the Soviets. Their struggle was clearly anti-colonial. Brutal, but anti-colonial. I do not justify everything they did. I am applying postcolonial theory in order to make sense of what they did, or tried to do. They were defeated. Their ideas resurfaced in 1991 and were gathered into the Act of Independence.
And that Act, while it closed a long period of Ukrainian struggle without a state, opened a new one.
Today, more independence than colonialism
Before 2013, I would say, there was more neocolonialism than independence.
This is a description, not a figure of speech. The former metropolis re-established the strings. Russian capital came into the economy under the presidencies of Leonid Kuchma and Viktor Yanukovych, and Russian corruption came with it.
Proxy parties were planted—the Party of Regions and its various clones. Russian pop music was everywhere, which sounds like a small thing and is not: in postcolonial studies, literature and popular culture are considered among the most effective vehicles of neocolonial control.
Today it is the other way around. Neocolonialism has not evaporated, but the proportion has changed. There is now more independence than neocolonialism—and that itself is what thirty-five years of struggle have achieved.
And corruption was a neocolonial instrument. This is the part Ukrainians resist, so let me put it plainly: our fight against corruption is effectively an anti-colonial fight. In Ukraine people sometimes present this as a dilemma—either we fight corruption or we fight the Russians, we cannot do both. From the perspective of postcolonial studies the dilemma does not exist. Both are anti-colonial efforts. They go hand in hand.
Empires have always travelled with religion on their shoulders, and religion has always helped establish imperial rule in the colonies. In the Ukrainian case it was first the Greek Catholic Church, established in 1596 an instrument of Polish colonization, although this is not the case anymore. But that is how it began.
And presently Russia’s instrument of recolonization is the Moscow Patriarchate, still present in Ukraine as the Ukrainian Orthodox Church under the Moscow Patriarchate (UOC MP).
Anatomy of treason: how the Ukrainian Orthodox Church sold its soul to the “Russian world”
Here I have to say something uncomfortable for many Ukrainians.
Nations that decolonize very often produce new subalterns. In post-colonial language, these are parts of the population that are subdued, oppressed by the dominant power. But we may be producing such subalterns as an effect of pushing back against Russian colonization: groups of Ukrainians belonging to the UOC MP being marginalized, subalternized, by our own struggle. It is a very difficult dilemma how to deal with this subalternization, and I do not have a resolution for it.
Two revolutions against the ratio
Both of Ukraine’s major “Maidan” protests were anti-neocolonial revolutions.
In the Orange Revolution of 2004 and again during the Euromaidan Revolution in 2013, Ukrainians protested because they had decided there was not enough independence—that what we had was more neocolonial than independent, more fake than real, and that the proportion had to be corrected. That is what a Maidan is. A public consensus that the ratio is wrong.
In February 2022, independence very nearly ended. People gave our statehood three days—and not only Russians. That was the opinion of most observers. It did not end. We survived it. But our statehood is still not secured, and it is being secured every day, including today.
What Ukraine contributed to the empire, and how
There is an argument against everything I have said so far, and Ukrainians make it as often as anyone. They object: look, we have contributed to the Russian Empire and to the Soviet one. We have basically built them.
Which is true.
Ukraine helped build the Russian empire. Now it stands in the way of its resurrection – Serhii Plokhii
But Ukrainians were never permitted to contribute as independent agents. They were allowed to contribute exactly as long as they lost their identity—as long as they denounced their own agency. They were contributors without their will and without their identity.
Corsica is my example. It had its own culture, its own identity, its own language, still spoken in pockets. Go into a good Corsican restaurant in Corsica and they may speak Corsican to you; I have had this experience. But it is not a language widely spoken anymore. It has been completely subsumed by French, and France holds Corsica tightly today. And what is France? To a great extent, it is the creature of a great Corsican named Napoleon Bonaparte, who built the French Empire. Nobody concludes from this that Corsica was not a colony.
It is remarkable to me that Putin still does this. He puts people with Ukrainian backgrounds into key positions—in the military, in propaganda, in negotiations.
- Vladimir Medinsky, one of his chief propagandists and now his negotiator, was born in Smila, in Cherkasy Oblast, my own small motherland.
- Valentina Matviyenko, third in the official hierarchy, comes from Shepetivka in Khmelnytskyi Oblast.
- Kirill Dmitriev, who negotiates with the Americans, was born in Kyiv to a family of Ukrainian biologists.
It was Medinsky, incidentally, who announced in a 2012 interview that the Russian people has one extra chromosome—his explanation for how Russia survived the catastrophes of the twentieth century when other nations, the Scythians and Sarmatians among them, broke and vanished. Russians mocked him for it, since an extra chromosome is the marker of Down syndrome.
As a claim, though, it is a race claim. Made by a man born in Cherkasy Oblast, about a people he was not born into.
They contribute to the Russian neo-empire. They contribute to it not as Ukrainians but as those who denounced Ukrainian identity. This is how empire functions. It absorbs the representatives of subaltern nations who willingly denounce their own will. It was so under the Romanovs. It was so in the Soviet empire. It is so in Putin's quasi-empire now.
Ukrainians were, and still are, a subaltern nation.
Papua, and Scotland
There are worse outcomes than ours and there are better ones.
The Papuans of West Papua tried. They fought for independence, failed, and many of them were killed. They are still oppressed. That is the bad end of the range, and it is not hypothetical.
The better scenario would be the Scots. They had statehood, and it was strong—kings and queens, pride, history, narratives, everything a full and self-sufficient nation possesses. Then they lost it. They are not being killed. They do not suffer the way the Papuans suffer. And yet many of them remain deeply dissatisfied with what they are. We support the United Kingdom, of course, but we are also mindful of the peoples who constitute it—Scots, Irish, Welsh. They have their pride, their nation, their language, their history, their self-consciousness, their identity.
They cannot fully live any of it without independence.
That would be a much better scenario for us than the Papuan one. From where we are now, I still do not think it would be enough.
Colonies taken by neighbors
Timor-Leste has stayed with me. One of the newest countries in the world, independent since 2002, and before that a genocide. Up to a third of its population died. Its capital, Dili, was destroyed in 1999.
Our own Baturyn, the capital of the Cossack Hetmanate, was destroyed by Peter I's army in 1708 in the same way.
And Timor is not an overseas colony. That is the other thing. There is the colonization conducted across an ocean—the Dutch in the Malay Archipelago, to which Timor belongs—and there is the colonization conducted by a neighbor. Indonesia, having been a Dutch colony itself, became independent, developed a colonial attitude within thirty years, and invaded Timor.
Ukraine was taken by neighbors too. First Poland, then the Russian Empire. Both committed atrocities here. We always resisted, and always with some violence—there has never been an anti-colonial struggle that was not violent, and ours is not an exception. I wish it were an exception. It was not.
The first colonization, and the first decolonization
The Polish colonization is the one Ukrainians forget, and it matters for a reason that has nothing to do with Poland.
It ended. And the decolonization from it was successful: we regained our ground, re-established Ukrainian identity on our territory, our own way of living. And there was a process of reconciliation that worked, at least to some extent. That is the first decolonization Ukrainians ever accomplished, and it is the paradigm I hold onto when I think about what happens with Russia.
Which does not mean it is finished. Some of the reactions coming from the Polish side now are, to me, surprising and incomprehensible, and I can explain them only through this lens: post-colonial phantom pain. They lost a limb and they still feel it. Russia feels the same phantom pain about what it calls the Russian World, and reacts far more violently, because Russia is historically far more violent. But the pain is the same kind of pain.
One white nation killing another
Much of the world does not accept that any of this is decolonization. In the Global South the response is: one white nation is killing another white nation, why should we care.
They should care, because our struggle is the same as theirs was. If ours is meaningless, then theirs was meaningless too.
They are working with a black and white colonial paradigm—sometimes literally—which skims over the surface. There is a name for what we are: a South within the North. Inside the Global North pockets of land and people exist whose experience and self-perception are closer to the peoples of the Global South than to their neighbors. Ukraine is one of those pockets. Our vision of ourselves may be nearer to the Global South than to Europe.
Race is the real difference, and I will not pretend otherwise. Though even there the resemblance is closer than people assume. When we were a Polish colony, the Poles developed the idea that we were an inferior people—chłopy—while they were Sarmatians, a superior nation. Not race as skin color. Race as ethnic origin, which does the same work.
By my own study, something like 90% of the criteria that apply to other colonies apply to Ukraine. Perhaps 10% do not.
But before the world can see this, we Ukrainians have to see it.
Why the blood
Fanon believed that violence is embedded in colonialism—that it is intrinsic, that you cannot be a colonial power without being violent, without being prepared to kill the subalterns. He also believed that anticolonial struggle is inevitably violent. Sartre, who wrote the preface to him, believed it too. Maybe that is right, and it would be a good and easy explanation.
But our struggle is particularly bloody for a particular reason, and it is Russian. Russia has adopted most of its ideas from the West, and has almost always put them into practice through violence exceeding anything done in the place the idea came from. Marxist ideas about the counter-revolutionary nature of the peasantry produced the Holodomor; American culture wars are producing this one.
Our resistance is violent because their aggression is. It is a reaction, and it does not exceed the action. If anything it is disproportionate in the other direction. They kill our civilians in daylight and destroy hospitals and residential buildings. We destroy their oil plants and the warehouses of their online marketplaces.
From the standpoint of genocide studies, what is being done to us is a classical genocide. Not a rhetorical trope—a scientifically provable case. What is unprecedented is not the death toll but the intensity: the quantity of weaponry and ammunition involved in this anti-colonial war has no precedent among anti-colonial wars.
Agency
This is what Ukraine has to contribute to postcolonial theory, and I think it is the important thing.
The victims are not powerless and they are not will-less. They have their own volition. They have their own agency. And the purpose of an anti-colonial struggle is to regain agency—not merely independence, not merely economic freedom, not merely the cutting of ties with international capital or with the old and new empires. Agency.
Our struggle is a struggle for and through our agency. And it is a path that other peoples still living with the residues of colonialism could follow.
The neocolonialism that is not Russian
The Russian form is the most obvious available to us. It is not the only one.
The newest arrived with the Trump administration, which tried to exchange support for our resources—rare earth elements and so forth—essentially requiring us to give them up in return for help. This is a classical neocolonial attitude. It is what happens when a neocolonial power is being established.
I want to be careful here, because this is the policy of the White House and not of Americans. Most Americans who come to Ukraine come as volunteers, prepared to sacrifice their lives, because they understand that global democracy depends on what happens here. The neocolonial attitude belongs to a minority. Unfortunately, that minority currently holds power.
It is a new situation for us, but it is not unique for the world. Still, we can survive it if we understand what it is.
Russia is the last European colonial empire, but the West looks away. Expert explains why
Whether it is worth it
It is not for us to answer that.
Our generation has decided that it is worth it. But we should remember that we have also decided for the next generation. The Ukrainian Sich Riflemen, a volunteer legion of students and intelligentsia raised in Lviv in 1914, decided in their time that it was worth sacrificing themselves for Ukrainian independence, and we now judge that they were right. The UPA, fighting into the 1950s, decided the same. They were defeated.
We do not know how the next generation will judge us. Because there will be millions of Ukrainians who will not have been born as a result of this war. They will not decide whether we were right or wrong. They will not exist.
Those who do exist will make the judgment.
Edited by Alya Shandra

US revokes Syria’s designation as State Sponsor of Terrorism — Treasury Department
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
18:49:06 UTC
03:49:06 KST

WASHINGTON, August 24. /TASS/. The United States has officially revoked Syria’s designation as a State Sponsor of Terrorism and the designation of Syria’s Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham (HTS, outlawed in Russia) as a terrorist organization, the press service of the US Department of the Treasury said.
"In line with President [Donald] Trump’s promise to deliver sanctions relief to Syria, the U.S. Department of State today rescinded Syria’s designation as a State Sponsor of Terrorism, and revoked the designation of al-Nusrah Front, also known as Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist (SDGT) organization. Concurrently, the U.S. Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) removed HTS from the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List ("SDN List")," it said.
Concurrently, it imposed sanctions against two former HTS affiliates who continue to support al-Qaeda (outlawed in Russia).
The U.S. Department of the Treasury may take action against legal entities, individuals, and countries that engage in trade with countries on the list of state sponsors of terrorism. Currently, the list includes Iran, North Korea, and Cuba.

US unveils ‘economic onslaught’ against Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
18:48:59 UTC
03:48:59 KST

US unveils ‘economic onslaught’ against Iran
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has announced new sanctions against Iran, and threatened to boot any country dealing financially with Tehran out of the US dollar system, in a bid to make Iran an “economic outcast.”
The new sanctions target nearly 60 entities, individuals, and vessels in multiple jurisdictions that allegedly trade in “illicit nuclear and missile technology” with Iran, aid Iran’s “cyber operations,” and move Iranian oil, the US Treasury Department said in a statement on Monday. More than a third of the sanctioned entities and individuals – 21 – are based in China.
The Treasury also said it had identified digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping as areas for potential secondary sanctions.
Speaking at a press conference later on Monday, Bessent went further, announcing the beginning of “Operation Economic Outcast,” which he described as “an economic onslaught against Iran’s financial connections around the globe.”
In the Second World War, D-Day marked the historic beginning of a campaign with our allies to target and drive the enemy from its positions, including those in third countries. Today, in that same spirit, we are launching an economic onslaught against Iran’s financial connections… pic.twitter.com/1fLyobUucu
— Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent (@SecScottBessent) August 24, 2026
Bessent explained that the US would penalize any country refusing to sever its economic ties with Tehran. “Any entity that facilitates money laundering on behalf of Iran will be removed from the US dollar system,” he said, adding “the clock just started ticking.”
Iran exports goods to 147 countries, and imports from 114, according to the most recent data from the World Bank. Asked how the US intends to force three quarters of the world’s nations to cease trade with Iran, Bessent said that US President Donald Trump phoned multiple world leaders over the weekend “with specific requests to cease their interactions” with Iran, and that every country had been given “a defined timeline” to comply with his demands.
Bessent refused to share any more details, telling reporters that “we’re not going to name names,” nor was he “going to set timelines.” Pressed on whether Washington expected China – which is Iran’s largest trading partner – to abide by the sanctions regime, Bessent did not give a definitive answer.
“We find that the best way to engage with countries is through quiet diplomacy. And we are level-setting with every country to tell them our expectations. We know who they are. They know who they are,” he replied, adding “no-one is above the reach of US sanctions.”
Bessent’s threats were shrugged off in Tehran. “Americans know that no one buys their bombast,” senior Iranian negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf wrote on X after the treasury secretary's press conference.
“The United States is not in an economic position to further restrict its relations with other countries,”he explained. “Iran’s trading partners, both in the media and through messages sent to us, have made it clear that they don’t take these statements into account anywhere.”
Mohsen Rezaei, the head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, warned on Sunday that “not a single drop of oil will leave the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz” if the Gulf states join the US’ economic pressure campaign. If US President Donald Trump “wants to do something, we will retaliate in a seismic manner,” Rezaei added.
Last week, Trump threatened to inflict what he called “Economic D-Day” on Iran, after a 60-day window for negotiating peace with Tehran expired with no breakthrough. Trump ruled out a return to negotiations, but Pakistani Chief of Defense Forces Asim Munir arrived in Tehran on Monday in an attempt to revive the talks.

Breaking Down the Ending of Spooky in Love
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
18:48:32 UTC
03:48:32 KST

Extraordinary Attorney Woo’s Park Eun-bin and Doona!’s Yang Se-jong star as ghost-whispering hotel heiress Cheon Yeo-ri and ace prosecutor Ma Gang-uk, respectively, in the supernatural romance series Spooky in Love. In the Korean drama, which broadcast domestically on tvN and was distributed globally by Netflix, Yeo-ri and Gang-uk are initially brought together by their shared desire for justice. For Yeo-ri, this takes the form of helping the ghosts she alone can see. For Gang-uk, it means doing a good, by-the-book job as an investigator. But when Gang-uk learns Yeo-ri’s secret, the two grow closer.
While Spooky in Love starts out with a strong, ghost-of-the-week format, the second half of the drama leans more into corporate in-fighting and family drama as context for Yeo-ri and Gang-uk’s romance. When Chairwoman Baek insists that Yeo-ri get engaged in order to secure a more stable future for the hotel and resort company, Yeo-ri side-steps the advances of family friend and fellow chaebol Kang Min-hwan (Ong Seong-wu) to announce she is engaged to Gang-uk. What starts as a fake relationship to keep Yeo-ri’s grandmother off of her back soon develops into the real thing. But can Yeo-ri and Gang-uk’s love survive Min-hwan’s machinations to take control of both Yeo-ri and her company? Here’s everything that happens in the Spooky in Love finale.
Yeo-ri’s supernatural powers, explained
Yeo-ri wasn’t born with the ability to see ghosts. She developed it 12 years prior to the start of the series, when she nearly died in the mysterious yacht accident that killed her boyfriend and Min-hwan’s little brother, Kang Ji-hwan (Kim Min-chul). The condition has ghosts constantly nagging Yeo-ri for help, and also keeps her isolated from the land of the living. If she touches hands with someone else, they will temporarily gain the ability to see ghosts for a month. As a result, she wears gloves constantly, and keeps a physical distance from her friends, family, and co-workers.
The stakes of Yeo-ri’s secret are intensified due to the power her family holds. Yeo-ri is the heir to the Reina Group, a corporate hotel chain that wields immense wealth. Yeo-ri’s grandmother, Baek Kyung-ja (Ye Soo-jung), plans to pass the baton to Yeo-ri—rather than step-daughter Ok Gye-hui (Baek Ji-won) or her adult children, Ha-ri (Cho Hye-joo) and Don-jun (Lee Dal). However, if Chairwoman Baek, or the larger public, finds out that Yeo-ri is haunted by ghosts, it could call her ability to run the family corporation into question.
Still, Yeo-ri’s sense of justice runs deep. In Spooky in Love’s early episodes, Yeo-ri is visited by the ghost of Jang Eun-ju (Yoon Hye-rim), a young woman who was murdered by her boyfriend, Park Seung-jae (Kim Do-wan), after she becomes pregnant with their child. Seung-jae is well-connected. Not only is he a rich pro golfer, but his father is one of the leading contenders in the next presidential race. When he is initially tried for murder, with Gang-uk acting as prosecutor, he is acquitted due to his father’s immense influence. It is only when Gang-uk and Yeo-ri team up that they are able to gather more evidence, and definitively pin the murder on Seung-jae.
What happened on the yacht?
Yeo-ri grew up close to Kang Ji-hwan and Kang Min-hwan, brothers poised to inherit ownership of CL Raymond Group. Though both brothers had feelings for Yeo-ri, Ji-hwan was the first to ask her out. For Min-hwan, this intensified the jealousy he had long felt of his little brother. Jin-hwan, who looked up to his brother, didn’t realize that he was often treated better by some members of the family compared to Min-hwan, who was adopted. When Jin-hwan started dating Yeo-ri, it was the final straw for Min-hwan.
On the day of the accident, the brothers are out on a yacht with their friends, including Yeo-ri and fellow rich kid Park Seung-jae. We learn in the penultimate episode that when the yacht hit a rock and Jin-hwan was thrown over the side, Min-hwan had the chance to pull his brother back onboard, but let the pleading Jin-hwan fall into the water below instead. Jin-hwan dies, and Yeo-ri, who also went overboard in the accident, is rescued from the water. She is wearing a protective pendant gifted to Jin-hwan by his grandmother. He asked her to wear it while they were on the boat, joking that, if something should happen, she should live and he will die.
Later, Yeo-ri and Gang-uk seek out the shaman who made the pendant. The original maker is dead, but her daughter informs them that the power of the pendant changed Yeo-ri and Jin-hwan’s fates. That power, paired with Yeo-ri’s inability to let Jin-hwan move on in the immediate aftermath of the accident, led to Yeo-ri’s ability to see ghosts. The shaman tells Gang-uk and Yeo-ri that, in order for Yeo-ri to stop seeing ghosts, she owes the afterlife a life.
Gang-uk’s connection to Jin-hwan
Gang-uk, who was raised by his grandmother, did not grow up in the same social circles as Yeo-ri, Min-hwan, and the other members of the chaebol class. However, he shares a unique connection to Jin-hwan. When Jin-hwan died, a sick Gang-uk was given Jin-hwan’s heart. The transplant allowed him to live on. Ever since, Jin-hwan and Min-hwan’s mother, Song Hee-won (Kim Seo-ra) has kept tabs on Gang-uk through his grandmother. Though she lost one of her sons, it makes her happy to see Gang-uk doing well.
Min-hwan’s crimes escalate
This truth of Jin-hwan’s death is known only by Min-hwan for more than a decade. Yeo-ri doesn’t remember what happened during the accident and, even if she did, she didn’t witness what occurred between the brothers that day. However, when Seung-jae temporarily gets out of jail to attend his father’s funeral, he happens to stumble upon a camcorder memory card with footage of Min-hwan choosing not to save Jin-hwan. Seung-jae attempts to blackmail Min-hwan with the evidence. When the two meet up in an abandoned warehouse, Min-hwan kills him for it.
Gang-uk finds Min-hwan’s cufflink at the scene of the crime, but Min-hwan counters. He hires someone to hit Gang-uk with a truck. Yeo-ri pushes the man she loves out of the way at the last second, saving his life and putting her own in grave danger. She is hit by the truck, and ends up in a coma. As Yeo-ri’s life hangs in the balance, we see her traverse a beautiful kind of purgatory. The ghosts she has helped in the past 12 years, including Eun-ju, are waiting for her there. They lend her some of their warmth to keep her from crossing to the other side.
Yeo-ri and Jin-hwan balance the scales
Still, Yeo-ri finally does make it to a Styx-like river, a boundary between the world of the living and the world of the dead. Before she can step onto the boat that would bring her across, the ghost of Jin-hwan appears to take her place. The two share a teary conversation in which they process Jin-hwan’s death. Yeo-ri apologizes for living instead of him, but Jin-hwan doesn’t see it that way. He says she still has so much to live for, and that the ghosts she has helped are rooting for her. When Yeo-ri wakes back up, she no longer has the power to see ghosts. Jin-hwan has crossed to the other side; the afterlife has been given the soul it was robbed of 12 years prior.
Min-hwan is brought to justice
Unbeknownst to Min-hwan, Seung-jae has hidden the memory card in a hollow golf ball at the warehouse. When Yeo-ri and Gang-uk are investigating, they find the card and have the evidence to take Min-hwan down. In the most dramatic way possible, Yeo-ri reveals the evidence to Min-hwan’s mother and the other people gathered at Jin-hwan’s memorial service. More than losing his power or going to jail, Min-hwan seems most distraught at the idea of his mother discovering his betrayal. A year later, when she visits her remorseful son in jail, she tells him that after he has finished serving his time, she will be waiting for him. Min-hwan, who always thought his mother’s love for her biological son diminished her love for her adopted son, can perhaps finally see otherwise.
Does Spooky in Love have a happy ending?
Spooky in Love has the happiest of endings. A year following the main events of the series finale, Yeo-ri is announced as the new chairwoman of Reina. Yeo-ri and Gang-uk are happily together. Gang-uk, who had been transferred out of Seoul after reporting internal corruption at the prosecutor’s office, has just received a promotion back in the capital city where Yeo-ri lives. The two visit Siena Hall, the Reina wedding property that symbolizes Yeo-ri’s late parents’ love for one another, and walk together, hand in hand.
When the two first started falling for one another, Yeo-ri had said that her greatest wish was to walk hand-in-hand with the person she liked. Then, she was too afraid to touch anyone, burdened by the certainty she would pass her curse onto them. Now, she does so, unafraid. The simple scene doesn’t just demonstrate the love between Yeo-ri and Gang-uk; it demonstrates the intimacy and warmth Yeo-ri is able to let into her life more broadly. She is no longer alone, and Gang-uk is only one part of that reality.

UN demands accountability after deadly attack on peacekeepers in South Sudan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
18:48:13 UTC
03:48:13 KST

The UN has condemned the killing of two peacekeepers in an ambush in South Sudan’s Jonglei State.
“The Secretary-General (Antonio Guterres) strongly condemns this attack in no uncertain terms,” spokesperson Stephane Dujarric told reporters on Monday.
He confirmed that the two peacekeepers killed were Ethiopian nationals. Seven others were injured, including three UN peacekeepers, two South Sudanese police officers and two civilian staff members.
Guterres extended his condolences to the families of the fallen peacekeepers and to the people and government of Ethiopia, Dujarric said, adding that the UN chief wished all those injured a speedy recovery.
Dujarric did not specify who was responsible for the attack but said “armed gunmen” attacked the unit while it was conducting a regular patrol to address local insecurity.
Asked about the nature of the incident, Dujarric said available information indicated that the peacekeepers appeared to have been intentionally targeted.
He noted that the incident brought the number of peacekeepers killed in “malicious acts” since January 1 to nine.
The UN mission deployed a quick reaction force to secure the area and assist in the emergency response.
Dujarric emphasised that attacks on UN personnel may constitute war crimes under international law.
Anita Kiki Gbeho, head of the UN peacekeeping mission in South Sudan (UNMISS), called for a prompt investigation to ensure that the perpetrators are brought to justice.
“Such deadly violence targeting UNMISS personnel who are serving to support peace in South Sudan is unacceptable,” she said.

Germany’s far-right AfD pushes headscarf ban for Muslim girls under 14
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
18:47:00 UTC
03:47:00 KST

Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) renewed its push Monday to restrict Muslim headscarves in schools, calling for a ban for girls under the age of 14.
The AfD parliamentary group said Germany should follow neighboring Austria, where a new regulation taking effect next month bans Islamic head coverings in schools for girls under 14.
AfD lawmaker Kerstin Przygodda described reports that some Muslim communities in Austria plan to defy the ban as "alarming.” She argued that Germany needs a similar measure to defend "Western values.”
"While Germany’s established parties - intoxicated by migration - shamelessly abandon the affected girls to their fate, the AfD parliamentary group calls for the introduction in Germany of the Austrian model banning headscarves for children in public educational institutions,” Przygodda said.
An AfD attempt earlier this year to introduce a similar ban sparked a heated debate in parliament.
The proposal drew strong criticism from Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s center-right Christian Democratic Union, its Social Democratic coalition partner and the opposition Greens.
Critics accused the AfD of distorting facts to fuel anti-Muslim sentiment and using the issue as a campaign tool ahead of state elections in Saxony-Anhalt on Sept. 6 and in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania on Sept. 20.
They said the AfD’s claims of widespread forced veiling in Muslim communities in Germany lack solid evidence.
Critics said most young girls who wear headscarves do so as a cultural practice, family tradition or personal choice rather than under coercion.

Trump administration seeks to formalise H-1B fee of more than $100,000
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
18:46:09 UTC
03:46:09 KST

Trump administration seeks to formalise H-1B fee of more than $100,000
The new proposal would charge $103,265 for H-1B visas, and attempts to make permanent a temporary rule challenged by the US courts.
The administration of United States President Donald Trump has proposed a rule to formalise a controversial fee for H-1B work visas to the US and charge $103,265 for these visa applications going forward.
The proposed fee for highly skilled foreign workers was published in the US Federal Register on Monday, and will now be subject to a 30-day public comment period, after which it could be finalised and put into practice by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). It would dramatically increase the cost of visas that are in high use in recruiting workers in the tech, education and research sectors.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3First lawsuit filed challenging Trump’s $100,000 H-1B visa fee
- list 2 of 3Trump suspends immigrant visas for 75 countries: Who’s affected?
- list 3 of 3US judge strikes down Trump’s $100,000 H1-B visa fee
Last year, Trump temporarily imposed a fee of $100,000 for the visa programme, which was then blocked by court rulings. The temporary proclamation is due to expire in September, and the new DHS proposal would replace it and make the fee permanent.
In June, a federal judge ruled the fee was illegal and barred the Trump administration from collecting it. A Boston-based appeals court is reviewing that decision, while a different court considers whether a judge in Washington, DC properly rejected a challenge to the fee by a major business group.
The H-1B programme allows US employers to hire foreign workers with training in specialty fields and offers 65,000 visas annually, with another 20,000 for workers with advanced degrees, approved for three to six years.
The order Trump issued last year sharply increased the cost of obtaining some H-1B visas, which had typically come with about $2,000 to $5,000 in fees, depending on various factors.
The increase in fees has discouraged H-1B visa requests, according to court filings. As of February 15, US Citizenship and Immigration Services had received from 70 employers just 85 payments of the $100,000 fee, the administration said in a March filing.
Debate over visa programme
Trump, a Republican, and other critics of the H-1B programme say it is abused by many companies who replace US workers with cheaper foreign labour.
But business groups and many individual companies have said the visa programme is needed to address a lack of qualified American workers for some jobs and to allow US businesses to recruit top talent.
In imposing the fee, Trump invoked the president’s power under federal immigration law to restrict the entry of certain foreign nationals who would be detrimental to US interests.
The fee is being challenged by the US Chamber of Commerce, the largest US business lobbying group, Democratic-led states, and a coalition of unions and employers. Those lawsuits could be amended to challenge the rule proposed this week once it is finalised.
Legal challenges mount
The lawsuits claim that Trump’s power to restrict entry does not allow him to override the law that created the H-1B visa programme. The states and groups that sued also say that DHS cannot impose fees, taxes or other means to generate revenue for the US without permission from Congress.
The Trump administration has maintained that the fee is not a traditional tax and that courts have little power to question the president’s authority to restrict entry into the country.
Amid Trump’s broader immigration crackdown, employers last year registered for about 344,000 H-1B visas, down more than 25 percent from 2024, and fewer than half of the 794,000 visas sought in 2023, according to data from US Citizenship and Immigration Services.
The Trump administration has also ordered enhanced vetting of H-1B applicants and proposed a new visa selection process that would favour higher-skilled and better-paid workers. Earlier in August, the Department of Homeland Security, in a separate rule, added fees of up to $4,500 to applications to extend the stay of H-1B workers or to transfer employees based in other countries to the US.

How a 17th-century Irish law is shielding Big Tech from class actions in Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
18:45:47 UTC
03:45:47 KST

DUBLIN — An obscure 400-year-old Irish law is holding back collective legal action against Big Tech firms in Europe.
For decades, consumers in the United States have been banding together to sue companies for billions of dollars in compensation for harm caused by everything from tobacco and oil to online shopping. Five years ago, Europeans got similar rights to file continent-wide consumer class-action cases against corporations, prompted by the "Dieselgate" emissions scandal that forced German carmaker Volkswagen into a settlement of more than $9.5 billion with U.S. consumers.
But many of the world's largest tech giants, with millions of users, deep pockets and a track record of breaking EU rules, have so far been spared from major class action challenges. That's because in Ireland, where many of these firms have their EU headquarters, it is illegal for a funder to finance a legal case unless it is directly involved or has a legitimate interest.
Advertisement
At the same time, the EU's landmark 2020 Representative Actions Directive that enabled class action across Europe stipulates that these cases can only be filed by non-profits, who tend to rely on outside funding to cover the huge costs of taking on Big Tech.
Ireland is the only EU country with such a restriction — a rule rooted in legal concepts dating back to the Middle Ages that were written into Irish law in 1634. And it is holding back rights activists from raising funds to mount new, big cases against tech giants.
Five non-profits are registered in Ireland to take class actions under the new directive, three of which (the Irish Council for Civil Liberties, Noyb and Digital Rights Ireland) have a track record of taking on Big Tech.
So far, only one class-action case has been lodged: the Irish Council for Civil Liberties filed the first such case in Ireland last year against Microsoft over its online advertising system. They were able to fund it through their general budget, which comes from donations and philanthropic grants.
“To take complex litigation like this in Ireland costs at least €1 million in the first instance. We cannot take multiple cases unless the State allows us to raise the necessary funds,” said Johnny Ryan, director of the Irish Council for Civil Liberties' enforcement unit, pointing out the organization doesn't have the resources to launch more challenges.
He characterized the EU's requirement that non-profits lead class action cases and the Irish law's ban on raising outside funding as the “fatal contradiction” for Europeans seeking compensation from Big Tech.
Advertisement
Fundraising Big Tech cases
“To bring a case against a Big Tech company, it just costs an awful lot of money,” said Gerard Rudden, an Irish lawyer who helped notorious privacy campaigner Max Schrems bring two landmark legal cases involving Facebook through the Irish courts.
“They obviously have unlimited resources to put into litigation," Rudden said of the tech firms. "It takes a lot of time, a lot of effort, a lot of bodies and it costs a lot of money to do it. This has ramifications across Europe, because if funding was permitted, you could have a European-wide collective redress case against Meta, Google, Microsoft or whoever in Ireland. But at the moment it’s just impossible because it would cost too much.”
The ban's origin comes from Ireland having inherited two legal concepts from English law, called “maintenance” and “champerty.” The concepts date back to medieval times; the Irish 17th century law enacting them is still in effect today.
The Irish Council for Civil Liberties filed the first scase under the new directive in Ireland last year against Microsoft over its online advertising system. | Nicolas Tucat/AFP via Getty Images
Maintenance is where an individual funds or supports a lawsuit without a direct interest, while champerty is a form of maintenance whereby the funder is given a share of potential winnings in return for financing the case.
While England abolished the two offenses in 1967, Ireland’s courts have upheld the ban on third-party funding. There are a few exceptions, such as when a case is funded by charitable donations from people who don't expect a share of any payout.
Up for review
A spokesperson for Ireland’s Department of Enterprise, Trade and Employment, who declined to be named, pointed out that Ireland’s independent Law Reform Commission is due to publish a report later this year on whether the rules should be reformed. Changing the law would be a decision for the government’s justice department, they added.
Advertisement
Irish Justice Minister Jim O'Callaghan has said he is "very hesitant" to introduce third-party funding in Ireland, since there is a risk of "commodifying justice," which could result in lawyers or other financial backers taking a big chunk of payouts. That dynamic has long been criticized as prompting an overload of U.S. class action suits.
When it transposed the EU directive into national law, the Irish government also capped the entry fee for individual consumers to join a class action suit at €25.
Johannes Caspar, the former head of Hamburg’s privacy regulator who has been on the front lines of the EU’s battle to rein in Big Tech, said "collective redress" allows the bundling of compensation claims that individuals would never have the means to bring on their own. "They are time-consuming and there is a high cost before even getting before a court,” he said in an interview.
The Irish enterprise department spokesperson said that the way the directive is written into Irish law aims to “strengthen consumer protection by providing accessible and effective redress mechanisms for mass harm,” and the €25 cap is to meet requirements that fees are “modest and do not deter a consumer from requesting to be represented in a representative action.”
In the “coming weeks,” the Irish government is expected to begin waiving High Court fees (typically in the low hundreds of euros depending on the type and number of filings) for qualified non-profits taking collective redress cases, the spokesperson said.
The European Commission is in “close contact with all Member States, including Ireland” and is “assessing” how the class action directive is being rolled out, it said in response to POLITICO's questions. “Under the Representative Actions Directive, when Member States prohibit third-party litigation funding, they need to ensure that costs of proceedings do not constitute an obstacle for qualified entities to exercise their rights to seek collective action,” they said.

Putin signs decree allowing state takeover of Russian infrastructure whose owners fail to protect it from drone attacks
Russian President Vladimir Putin has signed a decree allowing the authorities to place critical infrastructure facilities under temporary management when their owners fail to protect them from security threats, including Ukrainian drone attacks.
The decree defines “critical infrastructure facilities” as sites in the fuel and energy sector, electric power, industry, and communications, as well as utility, transportation, and logistics infrastructure. The definition also covers “other facilities of especially high importance to Russia’s security and economic stability.”
External management will be imposed if the owners of a facility have:
- failed to take steps to ensure its security
- violated the security requirements set by the authorities
- created a threat to the facility’s security and normal operation, including by taking ineffective measures against drone attacks
- failed to restore the facility after an attack
The temporary administrator, according to the decree, will be Rosimushchestvo — Russia’s federal property management agency — or “another party” to be designated by the government. The authorities will be able to grant the administrator rights to the facility owner’s real estate, securities, and other property. The property’s upkeep will be funded by revenue generated from its use.
The decree is now in effect.
Putin issued the decree amid repeated Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil industry sites and on logistics centers belonging to the online marketplaces Wildberries and Ozon.

Data centres to use nearly as much power as every NSW and Victorian home by 2036
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
18:41:58 UTC
03:41:58 KST

Data centres to consume nearly as much power as every home in NSW and Victoria by 2036
In short:
Data centres are expected to draw as much power from the grid by 2036 as all homes in NSW and Victoria do today, the energy market operator has forecast.
The energy market operator says the number of data centres in development since last year has more than doubled from 97 to 225.
What's next?
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese will detail more of his proposed energy rules for data centres at a Business Council dinner today, with the rules expected to be settled at national cabinet on Wednesday.
The rush of data centres coming to Australia will consume almost as much power from the electricity grid in a decade as all households in New South Wales and Victoria do today, the latest energy market forecast has found.
The Australian Energy Market Operator considered the expected energy demands of 225 known projects at various stages of development that want to hook up to the national electricity market, saying even with high uncertainty over how many proceed, it now expects a surge in power demand far larger than its estimates even a year ago.
There are 165 data centres already in operation across the national electricity market, which covers all states and territories except Western Australia and the Northern Territory.
Those data centres are consuming about 3 per cent of electricity supplied to the grid, but in just 10 years AEMO expects energy-hungry data centres to consume 13 per cent of power demand — even after accounting for the high cancellation rate of projects in the pipeline.
That amounts to 34TWh (terawatt-hours) of electricity from the grid by 2036, almost as much as the 38TWh consumed by every home in NSW and Victoria today.
Just a year ago, AEMO forecast that data centres would not consume that much power until some time after 2050, and even under its "accelerated transition" forecast, estimated data centres would consume about 24TWh by mid-2035.
While the outlook is uncertain, particularly after 2030, AEMO has documented a data centre rush over the past 12 months, with the number of known data centres in development more than doubling since last year from 97 to 225.
The vast majority of that data centre growth is expected in NSW and Victoria, with South Australia the next-largest in the national electricity market.
Rules to require data centres to bring renewables with them
The federal government has expressed its concern that the data centre rush, which promises as much as $150 billion in new investment to Australia, would also strain the grid and increase power prices without intervention.
At a Business Council dinner this evening, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese will tell business leaders that AI's success depends on ensuring it does not drive up energy bills.
"Australia is in a strong position to attract investment in data centres, but maintaining social licence will be essential," Mr Albanese will say.
"That means ensuring energy bills do not rise, water security is maintained, and locations are appropriate."
The Albanese government expects to settle new rules at a national cabinet meeting on Wednesday that would require data centres to guarantee new renewables supply to cover their energy use, to counteract the forecasted surge in electricity demand.
Data centres would have to strike power purchase agreements with new renewables projects — which would also enable those projects to secure financing, a roadblock currently holding up several renewables projects in the development pipeline that have been unable to prove customer demand when trying to get a loan.
The Coalition has criticised that approach, saying the federal government is tying an enormous economic opportunity to the renewables transition, which could weaken investment in Australia.
The Queensland government has also opposed the proposal for a renewables guarantee, meaning the federal government will have to legislate "guarantee of origin" laws to override Queensland's refusal to tie data centres to renewables.
Those rules are proposed to apply when data centres seek to connect to the grid.
Resources Minister Madeleine King said there had been "some really troubling views around data centres" globally, and that the government wanted data centres here to have an "Australian flavour".
"If these data centres don't have the social licence and acceptance of the community ... we'll find this a very short-term boom where no-one's really happy with it at all," she told ABC's Radio National.
She said energy was at the forefront of people's minds, as well as location and water usage.
Dan Tehan, Shadow Minister for Energy and Emissions Reduction, was critical of what he described as the government's "ideologically-driven renewables only approach" and said each state should be able to decide their energy mix for powering data centres.
"There are states like Queensland that want to use all their abundant energy. They should be allowed to do that to attract data centres to their state, and we should be encouraging all states to do that," he said.
Mr Tehan said the Coalition was open to working with the government on data centre principles, pointing to recent cooperation on the NDIS bill and changes to gambling advertising.
"Where there's legislation before us, whether it be with regards to data centres, whether it be with regards to a gas reservation scheme, we will make sure that we will always work in the national interest."
Conditions for AI on copyright, safety and security
Wednesday's agreement will also ask states and territories to minimise community impacts, avoiding major developments in "inappropriate locations" near homes, schools and prime land that could be used for housing.
Data centres will also have to use more efficient technologies to minimise water use and meet their own water infrastructure costs.
Alongside the renewables and water requirements, Mr Albanese has said the legislation to be introduced next year will set conditions for AI on copyright, security, safety, and skills development, developed under a single framework within the prime minister's department.
"We must establish conditions to attract investment in frontier AI training, ensuring AI is developed safely, securely, and in ways that respect copyright and provide control and payment to the creative sector," Mr Albanese said.
"Getting this right can ensure Australia is the infrastructure partner for our region, aided by our status as a Five Eyes Partner. It will advance our national sovereignty."
While the government will hope to legislate that quickly so rules are in place in all states and territories, the Greens have indicated they will not simply wave through data centre laws.
"Of course data centres should be using more renewables — but sky-high energy and water usage is just one part of why people are growing increasingly worried about the massive roll-out of AI data centres across our communities," Greens leader Larissa Water said.
"We don't need to roll out the red carpet for tech bros. The government should put a pause on data centres until we get the rules right."
AEMO said the grid's reliability was not yet under threat, but warned that it depended on new supply being delivered "on time" to cover retiring coal facilities and growing electricity demand.

As cases surge can Australia eliminate diphtheria again?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
18:39:12 UTC
03:39:12 KST

More than 500 diphtheria cases recorded, but experts warn real numbers likely higher
In short:
There have been 538 cases of diphtheria in 2026 across Australia as part of the largest outbreak of the disease since records began.
However public health experts warn a drop in testing means actual numbers could be higher.
What's next?
The federal government says it is delivering a $13 million package to support affected jurisdictions responding to the outbreak.
There have been almost 540 cases of diphtheria across the country so far this year, as experts caution a drop in testing could mean actual numbers of a disease once considered eliminated are much higher.
Federal and state governments continue to work to mitigate the largest outbreak of diphtheria since records began in 1991, with 538 cases recorded primarily in the Northern Territory and Western Australia, as well as in South Australia and Queensland.
That is more than 17 times the previous peak in 2022, when 31 cases were recorded.
The latest report from the Australian Centre for Disease Control (CDC) notes cases peaked between late May and early June this year, and have since declined across affected jurisdictions.
The CDC told the ABC that in the last fortnight 26 cases of diphtheria were reported, compared to almost 80 at the height of the outbreak.
However, Megan Campbell, a public health physician and medical adviser at the National Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Organisation (NACCHO), said while the lower case numbers were encouraging, testing rates had not been consistently high across affected areas.
"We're just a little bit cautious about how we interpret that data when we're hearing that testing is quite low in some parts of Australia," Dr Campbell said.
"So we do worry with that drop in numbers that part of that may be due to a lack of testing in some areas."
What is diphtheria?
Diphtheria is a highly contagious and dangerous bacterial infection that can affect the nose, throat, airways or the skin.
It is treated with antibiotics, and vaccination is considered the primary line of defence against the disease.
Diphtheria spreads through respiratory droplets from coughing or sneezing, or direct contact with infected wounds.
Most of the cases this year have spread through skin lesions, with the vast majority among Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in outer regional and remote areas.
Professor of epidemiology at Adelaide University, Adrian Esterman, said while the type of diphtheria which mainly affected the skin was generally milder, that could mean it sometimes went undetected or could be mistaken for something else.
"Unfortunately Aboriginal children and adults are prone to skin lesions, especially in crowded housing."
Loading...
He said if people had scabies or insect bites, that could increase the risk of diphtheria spreading.
Dr Campbell urged people in affected regions to remain vigilant and proactive in being tested.
"We still really want people to be coming in early for testing if they've got skin infections or skin sores or a sore throat," she said.
"Serious illness can occur from diphtheria, and the hospitalisation rate for this outbreak has been around 20 per cent … we really do want people to keep thinking about diphtheria and keep talking to their health professionals and coming in to get their vaccination."
How did this outbreak occur?
Once a leading cause of childhood deaths and historically known as the "strangling angel", diphtheria has been considered largely eliminated in Australia since the 1950s, on the back of routine vaccination use.
Governments and public health experts have attributed this outbreak to a complex cluster of factors, such as waning immunity and housing conditions.
The CDC report said a high proportion of people with diphtheria in 2026 had received at least three valid vaccine doses.
However, CDC epidemiologist Stephanie Williams said vaccine immunity wanes over time and urged people to stay up to date with vaccines and boosters.
"Whilst those antibody levels generally do decline over time, they are still providing some protection [and] when we look at the cases in this outbreak, we have seen mostly mild disease," Dr Williams said.
Experts note the outbreak has disproportionately affected people in lower socio-economic areas, where poor housing conditions and crowding have meant the disease has spread easily.
"What I'm talking about is overcrowded housing, housing that's not been designed or maintained for large families and where there's inadequate health hardware in the home," Dr Campbell said.
"So that's making sure there's enough space, enough beds and bedding, enough towels, consistent water, soap and so on so that people can maintain a healthy living situation."
Can diphtheria be eliminated again?
As the outbreak peaked in May, the federal government announced a multi-million-dollar package to build a surge workforce to administer booster vaccinations and treatments, as well as to procure additional vaccines and antibiotics.
A health department spokesperson said that package now totalled $13 million.
Professor Esterman said he believes Australia can stamp out diphtheria once again but only if meaningful improvements to Aboriginal housing are made.
"We can vaccinate until the cows come home, but it won't help unless they do something about housing and sanitation," he said.
Dr Campbell agreed improving living conditions needed to be a priority.
She said while there were "proactive partnerships" between governments and the community-controlled health sector to respond to the outbreak, more investment was needed in environmental health programs.
A Health Department spokesperson said the government's $13 million package was supporting affected jurisdictions to respond to the outbreak, and included $3 million for NACCHO to deliver community liaison and on-the-ground health supports.
A CDC spokesperson said the public health response was focusing on identifying and treating cases, tracing contacts and providing vaccination and treatment.
"Maintaining strong immunisation uptake remains the best way to prevent severe cases of diphtheria," they said.
"We encourage people in affected areas to continue to follow advice from their local public health authorities and Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Services."

For the first time, Russia has purchased a shipment of gasoline from Turkey, analytics firm S&P Global Commodities at Sea (CAS) reports. A batch of 200,000 barrels will be delivered by the tanker Wendrix (IMO: 9299886), which departed from the port of Mersin on Turkey's Mediterranean coast. The gasoline’s manufacturer is unknown.
According to data from Starboard Maritime Intelligence, the Wendrix left Mersin on July 31 and as of Aug. 23 is in the Gulf of Finland, reportedly heading for the Primorsk marine oil terminal in Leningrad Region. The tanker, which sails under the flag of Equatorial Guinea, is part of the “shadow fleet.” The Wendrix (formerly known as the Jasper) is on the sanctions lists of the EU, the United Kingdom, Ukraine, and Switzerland.
The delivery marks the fifth known gasoline shipment to Russia since the start of July. According to CAS and Kpler data, Russia has already received three tankers carrying gasoline originally loaded at a refinery in Vadinar, India, and delivered to Russia after transshipment in Egypt. Another batch came from Morocco (a country that has no operational oil refineries). Analysts estimate the total volume of seaborne gasoline deliveries to Russia during this period at more than 1 million barrels.
On Aug. 22, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told a United Russia congress that gasoline supplies to the domestic market are expected to increase. He said that several oil refineries have completed maintenance and resumed production. However, in order to cover the shortfall, Novak identified imports and the production of gasoline of environmental classes K2, K3 and K4 — which are of lower quality than the Euro-5 standard.
Russia’s fuel crisis, which began in May, saw another rise in intensity earlier this month. Between Aug. 10 and 15, at least six Russian regions reinstated or tightened restrictions on gasoline sales, and the Novosibirsk Region signed the country’s first agreement capping the retail markup on fuel. In July, officials declared that the crisis was easing — but a new wave of strikes on oil processing facilities, including the complete shutdown of the Orsk refinery, largely reversed that progress.

How does H5N1 bird flu spread to humans and what are the health risks?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
18:37:03 UTC
03:37:03 KST

How does H5N1 bird flu spread to humans and what are the health risks?
The detection of a deadly strain of bird flu in seals in Australia may have you wondering about the risk to humans.
Although H5N1 has previously spread to mammals elsewhere in the world, the chance of people catching it is considered low by Australia's Centre for Disease Control (CDC).
Since a dominant new clade, H5N1 2.3.4.4b, emerged in Europe six years ago, there have been just 141 reported cases of H5N1 globally, including 24 deaths.
CDC director-general Zoe Wainer said bird flu was rarely transmitted from animals to people and spreading between people was also very rare.
While the current risk of being infected is low, with no human cases in Australia, scientists are studying the potential of the virus to mutate and cause a human pandemic in the future.
Raina MacIntyre, the head of the biosecurity program at the Kirby Institute, said flu viruses mutated rapidly and the H5N1 strain had already changed a lot since it emerged.
That's because the virus has been hopping around a lot of different species beyond birds.
"There's much greater opportunities for mixing between humans and infected birds or animals," Professor MacIntyre said.
So how can you catch H5N1, what are the symptoms and how can you help protect yourself if it takes hold in Australia?
How do humans get bird flu from animals?
So far, most infections have come from close contact with farm animals.
Seventy-one of the H5N1 cases in humans in the past six years have been in the US and mostly among poultry and dairy farm workers.
Only a handful of people in the US have been infected from contact with wild animals or unknown sources.
Professor MacIntyre said there were a couple of ways people could get bird flu from poultry.
"The virus can be transmitted from infected poultry by direct contact or aerosolisation of any poultry components including faeces, respiratory secretions, and contaminated dust in coops, as well," she said.
The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (US CDC) warns human infection may happen when someone touches the virus and then touches their eyes, nose or mouth.
Raw milk from infected dairy cows is also thought to be a key transmission risk if workers come into contact with contaminated milk and touch their face or it splashes their eyes.
Veterinary epidemiologist Jason Lombard, from Colorado State University, said how exactly the virus moved from cow-to-cow or to people remained unknown.
"Milk, which has the highest concentration of the virus, is believed to be a key component of disease transmission but studies evaluating transmission of disease during milking has not been able to replicate disease transmission," he said.
"Other routes of exposure, including aerosol exposure, has been documented but none of the possible modes of transmission has risen to the top as the most likely route."
Human-to-human transmission of bird flu viruses is rare.
But Professor MacIntyre said there was a report from Indonesia of this happening with a different clade of H5N1 in 2006.
"This occurred in Sumatra in a remote area, where a family cluster of eight cases occurred," she said.
"It was possibly because of the remote location that it died out."
Can you get bird flu from eggs or milk?
There have been no reported cases in the world of humans getting infected with H5N1 from consuming eggs or milk.
Australian CDC advice says it is safe to eat properly handled and cooked meat or eggs.
According to the US CDC, it could be possible to get infected by eating uncooked or undercooked poultry and eggs.
Loading...
But the watchdog also noted pasteurisation killed bacteria and viruses, including bird flu, in milk.
Although there aren't any examples of people getting bird flu from consuming eggs or milk, there is some evidence animals can be infected.
ViroEpiVet veterinary virologist and epidemiologist Robyn Hall said raw milk consumed by cats appeared to give them the virus.
"What we've seen in the US, where a lot of cats on dairies were dying, is often the virus goes to the brain in cats and there's a very high mortality in that species," she said.
What are the symptoms of bird flu in people?
Professor MacIntyre said many people in the US infected with bird flu had conjunctivitis (eye inflammation).
The Australian CDC highlighted several other symptoms, which usually start within one to 10 days of being infected, to watch out for:
- fever
- coughing
- sore throat
- runny nose
- muscle aches and pains
- headache
- fatigue
- nausea and vomiting
Diarrhoea is a less-common potential symptom.
Some people who are infected with bird flu could also be asymptomatic and show no obvious signs of infection.
How deadly is bird flu in humans?
Professor MacIntyre said the fatality rate of the 2.3.4.4b clade was much lower than other H5N1 clades in the past.
Out of the 71 cases of H5N1 in the US, there has been one death. A second US bird flu death in November was from a different strain, H5N5.
Most of the human cases in the US contracted from poultry and dairy herds have been from two different types of H5N1 2.3.4.4b known as D1.1 and B3.13.
The type of bird flu detected in Australia is known as B3.2 and entered Australia via Antarctic islands.
Are there treatments if you get bird flu?
The US CDC recommends people are treated with an antiviral drug, like baloxavir and oseltamivir, as soon as possible if they show flu symptoms after being exposed to infected birds or animals.
Antivirals are thought to work best within the first two days of symptoms and can reduce some complications from flu.
A study published in Nature Communications this year found mice infected with H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b didn't die when given a dose of baloxavir.
The researchers recommended baloxavir be considered in pandemic planning as a potential frontline therapeutic approach to treatment of humans.
Professor Wainer said Australia had access to antivirals and pandemic influenza vaccines through the National Medical Stockpile as part of preparedness planning.
What should you do about bird flu?
There are a few ways you can keep yourself safe while authorities continue to investigate.
The CDC recommends:
- Washing your hands thoroughly before and immediately after handling any bird, even if they are healthy.
- Staying away from sick or dead birds and their surroundings, droppings, body fluids, feathers and eggs.
- Not allowing pets to touch or eat sick and dead birds.
- Thoroughly cooking meat and eggs before eating.
There is currently no bird flu vaccine for the general public, but Professor MacIntyre urges people to stay up to date with their seasonal flu jab.
That's because it can reduce the chance of someone getting human and bird flus at the same time.
Could bird flu turn into a human pandemic?
The virus would need to mutate further for this bird flu outbreak to turn into a pandemic.
Professor MacIntyre said there were certain mutations in the different types of H5N1, associated with adaptation to mammals, that researchers were looking out for.
A particular mutation linked with mammal-to-mammal spread in the US is not present in the strain we know has arrived on Australian shores so far.
Loading...
The strain detected in Australia, the B3.2 genotype, is most closely related to an outbreak on Heard Island and McDonald Islands where thousands of birds and mammals, like southern elephant seals, were killed.
But this genotype, according to a pre-print study on bioRxiv, had several mutations that increased disease severity or aided virus replication in mammals.
Professor Wainer said the risk of a pandemic could increase if someone got both bird flu and seasonal human flu at the same time.
"The viruses could exchange genetic material and this may create a new strain that more easily infects humans," she said.
This is when you could get a pandemic, according to Professor MacIntyre.
"A flu pandemic, if it starts, will start quite suddenly and could start anywhere in the world," she said.
"It's not necessarily going to start in Australia."
Professor Wainer said there were currently no human cases of bird flu in Australia.
"Public health authorities are identifying and monitoring any individuals who may have had close contact with infected birds," she said.
If you find a sick or dead bird take photos or video, if possible, and report it to the Emergency Animal Disease Hotline on 1800 675 888.

Second Russian MiG-29 in two days: Ukraine’s drones worked over Millerovo airbase

2026-08-24
18:36:11 UTC
03:36:11 KST

Ukrainian drones worked over dozens of Russian military and industrial sites overnight on 24 August, reaching from occupied Ukraine and the Black Sea to southern Russia, the commander of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces (SBS) reported. The night's targets included a fighter jet at a Russian airbase, air-defense radars, fuel and propellant facilities, and vessels of Russia's sanctions-evading shadow fleet. A fuller breakdown released later in the day named the site of each strike and the unit that carried it out. Footage released with the breakdown shows the strikes.
Ukraine has been running mid-range strikes across the belt from occupied Crimea to Rostov Oblast for months, taking out the radars, missile batteries, and the aircraft that fly air-defense patrols over it — a rolling effort to thin the cover that meets every deeper Ukrainian strike.
A fighter jet and a decoy at the same airbase
Robert Brovdi, callsign Madyar, said his crews hit 66 targets in the operational depth of the Russian rear. Among them was a MiG-29 at Dolotinka, on the grounds of the Millerovo airbase in Rostov Oblast. The 1st Separate Center of the SBS carried out that strike.
The same unit hit a mockup of a Ka-52 Alligator attack helicopter at the same location. Russia uses such decoys to draw drones away from real aircraft.
Ukraine’s drones hit two Russian fighters and a spy drone—and blinded radars from occupied Crimea to Rostov
It was the third Russian fighter jet Ukrainian drones reached in two days. Crews struck another MiG-29, a jet SBS identified as a Su-33 and Militarnyi assessed as a Su-30SM, and an Orion strike-reconnaissance drone at Vityazevo in Krasnodar Krai on 23 August. Ukrainian drones have caught a MiG-29 on a Russian airfield before, at Kursk in July.
Four radars, from Rostov Oblast to occupied Crimea
Crews hit four radar systems overnight. Two Kasta-2E2 sets went down at Geraskin and Karaichev in Rostov Oblast, and a Nebo-SV at Gukovo in the same oblast. All three fell to the 1st Separate Center.
The fourth, an ST-68, stood at Rozdolne in occupied Crimea. The 9th Kairos battalion of the 414th Madyar's Birds brigade struck it.
The radar work is part of a campaign against Russian sensors and launchers that has run for months without a pause.
Rocket propellant, fuel, and two ships
The 1st Separate Center struck the Kamensky Combine at Kamensk-Shakhtinsky in Rostov Oblast, a plant producing solid rocket fuel, according to SBS. The 9th Kairos battalion hit a fuel tank at Yeysk in Krasnodar Krai. In occupied Luhansk Oblast, the 20th K-2 brigade struck a fuel depot belonging to the 106th material support brigade of Russia's 41st Army at Dovzhansk.
Brovdi also said his crews hit and destroyed two shadow-fleet vessels, a tanker and a bulk carrier, in the Black Sea. No independent account of either loss has appeared.
A drone school, relays, and a base in occupied Kherson Oblast
In occupied Kherson Oblast, Ukrainian crews destroyed the quarters of a Russian National Guard rapid-response unit and hit two relay stations for Geran attack drones, according to the SBS breakdown.
They also struck a shelter for a Zala reconnaissance drone crew in occupied Crimea, a drone school in occupied Zaporizhzhia Oblast, and a drone laboratory in occupied Donetsk Oblast.
Brovdi also reported 11 Russian rear deployment points burning across occupied Zaporizhzhia, Donetsk, and Luhansk oblasts, along with strikes on energy nodes in occupied territory.
