Trump slaps 50% tariffs on Canadian cars
US President Donald Trump has announced a 50% tariff on Canadian cars, trucks and auto parts starting next year, escalating a bitter trade war with Ottawa after negotiations collapsed last week.
In a post on Truth Social on Monday, Trump accused Canada of “ripping off the United States of America for years” and imposing excessive tariffs on American farmers. He claimed that bilateral trade has left the US with a “$60 billion deficit.”
“Not sustainable, and NOT ANYMORE! On January First, 2027, Tariffs on all Cars, Trucks, both large and small, Automotive Parts, and Steel, will be increased to 50%,” Trump announced. The move will double the current 25% tariff on Canadian auto imports.
“Build in the U.S. and there are ZERO TARIFFS,” Trump added, saying Canada would no longer be treated “like a State” and calling it “among the worst nations in the world to deal with.”
“WE DON’T NEED CANADA, THEY NEED US!” he wrote.
The announcement comes just two days after a separate package of 50% US tariffs took effect on around $20 billion worth of Canadian imports, including wine, cement, plywood, clothing and hockey equipment.
Last week, the two sides spent three days trying to wrap up months of heated trade negotiations and avoid mutual tariffs spiraling into an all-out trade war. However, the talks broke down on Friday as both sides accused the other of making last-minute changes to a proposed agreement.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney called the US terms “unfair” and “uneconomic” and pledged to match Washington’s tariffs “dollar for dollar” to protect Canadian workers and businesses.
Ottawa’s retaliatory measures, which are set to take effect on September 8, will target US goods including steel, dairy products, appliances, and electronics.
Trade tensions between Washington and Ottawa, which date back to Trump’s first term, reignited after he returned to office last year and launched a sweeping tariff campaign against major US trade partners. These include Canada, Mexico, China, the EU, and Japan, who Trump has accused of unfairly benefiting from access to the US market.

Ukraine Lands Rare Hit on Mobile Iskander Launcher Used for Ballistic Missile Strikes

Ukraine Lands Rare Hit on Mobile Iskander Launcher Used for Ballistic Missile Strikes
Ukrainian forces struck a Russian Iskander ballistic missile launcher near the border in a rare and potentially significant operation aimed at destroying Moscow’s missile systems before they can fire, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, Ukrinform reported on August 23.
The strike comes at a particularly critical moment for Ukraine as supplies of interceptor missiles for its Patriot air defense systems remain under severe pressure.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russia has increasingly relied on ballistic missiles to attack Ukrainian cities, and the threat is becoming more acute as another winter approaches. Patriot remains one of Ukraine’s most important defenses against such weapons, which descend toward their targets at extremely high speeds and are far harder to intercept than conventional cruise missiles or drones.
With interceptor stocks limited, however, Ukraine is increasingly seeking another solution: destroying the launchers themselves.
“Today we have another success. We can’t give many details due to the sensitivity of the operation, but a fact is a fact,” Zelenskyy told journalists.
“We hit an Iskander launcher near our borders. I’m grateful to our soldiers who carry this out. This is our operation of hunting their systems that are positioned nearby,” he added.
The strike represents an important success precisely because Russian Iskander launchers are exceptionally difficult targets.
The Iskander is a road-mobile system capable of firing short-range ballistic missiles. Unlike fixed launch sites, its launchers can rapidly move into position, fire and leave before Ukrainian forces have time to locate and attack them.
Serhiy Beskrestnov, an adviser to Zelenskyy, said that mobility significantly complicates efforts to hunt the systems.
According to Beskrestnov, Russia generally positions the launchers more than 100 miles behind the front line, helping keep them beyond the reach of Ukrainian HIMARS strikes.
“Catching an Iskander on the move, or near the position where it’s deploying, is difficult,” he said.
Previously, reports emerged that Russia is maintaining a vast missile arsenal while its defense industry can produce more than 200 cruise and ballistic missiles every month.
As of August 5, Russia had approximately 130 9M723 ballistic missiles for the Iskander-M system allocated to its military grouping.
As of July, Moscow additionally possessed around 50 Kinzhal air-launched ballistic missiles and approximately the same number of North Korean KN-23, KN-24, and KN-30 ballistic missiles.

Irish police chief Justin Kelly commented that “what makes this reckless behaviour even more appalling is that in some cases it is being done for social media”.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Aug 24 – while visiting Kyiv – that “anybody who glorifies dangerous driving is doing something that’s truly reprehensible and unacceptable”.
Downing Street said the government had “raised the issue of this appalling content with social media companies”, including TikTok.
Britain’s communications regulator Ofcom in July launched an investigation into whether TikTok, owned by Chinese company ByteDance, is doing enough under UK law to protect children from harmful content, focusing on its age checks.
According to TikTok, it strictly prohibits content that could cause significant physical harm including dangerous driving and proactively removes such content.
Ofcom said in a statement sent to AFP on Aug 24 that under the Online Safety Act, “platforms must minimise children’s exposure to violent material and content promoting dangerous challenges”.
The watchdog said it had shown it would “take action if evidence suggests companies are falling short”.
National Highways for England told AFP that there were 947 reports of wrong-way driving in the year ending May 2026, slightly down on the previous year.
Irish police told AFP there have been 62 such incidents so far this year with no marked recent increase. AFP

What the renewed Black Sea blockade means for Ukraine’s farmers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
17:41:42 UTC
02:41:42 KST

What the renewed Black Sea blockade means for Ukraine’s farmers
As Ukraine and Russia hammer each other’s Black Sea ports, the amount of grain being shipped through the crucial waterway has slowed to a crawl. For Ukraine’s farmers, the Black Sea blockade could hardly have come at a worse time.
The fields are white for harvest, but the way through the Black Sea is shut.
Faced with a grinding Russian advance towards the last cities in the Donbas left under Kyiv’s control, Ukraine’s state security services in June launched what Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called a “40-day campaign” of mid-to-long-range drone strikes deep into Russian territory.
The aim of these strikes, he said, was to put pressure on Moscow by targeting infrastructure vital for the country’s economic life – first and foremost, the oil refineries needed to sustain Russia’s lucrative fossil fuel exports and keep Russian consumers able to fill up at the pump. Kyiv has also carried out deadly air strikes against online retailers’ warehouses that many Russian small businesses rely on to reach their customers.
Read moreLive: Zelensky calls on allies to cover €27 billion gap for Ukraine’s air defence needs
Since July, Ukraine has also targeted Russian ships transporting grain through the Black Sea and hammered rail and port infrastructure around the neighbouring Sea of Azov. Earlier this month, grain terminals at the major port of Novorossiysk – where the remnants of Russia’s Black Sea fleet have taken shelter – came under heavy drone fire from Ukraine.
In response, Russia has stepped up its own strikes on Ukraine’s critical infrastructure, raining down drones and missiles on the grain silos and port facilities around the Black Sea city of Odesa and shelling any ship that tries to dock.
For weeks now, Kyiv and Moscow have both struck commercial container ships and grain export terminals in and around each other’s Black Sea ports, effectively cutting off both nations’ ability to ship grain – or anything else – through the crucial sea route.
In a state media interview published Saturday, Russian President Vladimir Putin accused Ukraine of having “opened … Pandora’s box” and pledged to pummel the embattled nation’s “most sensitive economic sectors”.
Agriculture certainly qualifies. Ukraine’s farmers are among the world’s leading producers of wheat, barley, sunflower seeds and corn, and 90 percent of those exports reach the world through the Black Sea. In peacetime, the country’s thriving agriculture sector made up a full fifth of Ukraine’s economy, and almost half of its exports.
So perhaps it’s no surprise that Zelensky on Sunday said that Russia had rejected Kyiv’s efforts, through third parties, to establish a Black Sea truce that would allow civilian vessels to move through the waters unmolested by either side.
Instead, he alleged, Moscow had insisted that any such deal would only be struck if Kyiv called off its campaign against Russian energy infrastructure, which has triggered worsening fuel shortages across the country. Russia, for its part, has devastated Ukraine’s energy infrastructure throughout the war, trying to starve the country of heat and light as each winter draws near.
Aysmmetric warfare
Oleh Nivievskyi, an associate professor at the Kyiv School of Economics, said that the consequences of the Black Sea blockade weighed far heavier on Ukraine than on Russia.
“For Russia, this is an asymmetric issue, because yes, they export a lot of grain, predominantly wheat,” he said. “But for the economic powerhouse, agriculture is not as important as the energy sector. So on paper it might look the same – Ukraine does not export, and Russia does not export – but it's really asymmetric, because for Ukraine, sea routes are more important economically in terms of the share of exports and in terms of the share of the overall economy.”
Between them, Russia and Ukraine account for more than a quarter of the world’s agricultural exports, most of which feeds people in North Africa and the Middle East. Despite this, Russia’s agricultural exports last year made up less than 10 percent of its total export revenues.
In some ways, we’ve been here before. Tens of millions of metric tonnes of grain remained grounded in Ukraine’s Black Sea ports in the first months of Russia’s February 2022 invasion as Russian ships blockaded the waterway.
Making a deal
As global food prices surged and analysts began to warn of the very real threat of famine in the countries relying upon Black Sea grain, Ukraine, Russia, Turkey and the UN signed the Black Sea Grain Initiative in July 2022 to carve out a safe passage for ships transporting food and fertiliser through to the Bosphorus Strait.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Moscow pulled out of the deal almost a year to the day later, alleging that Western sanctions continued to interfere with Russia’s own food and fertiliser exports. Despite this, both countries have largely continued to move their agricultural exports through the Black Sea – until now.
Nivievskyi said that the renewed blockade could prove far harsher than that of 2022.
“If you look at this from all angles, the situation is much worse,” he said. “The timing now is to plant winter crops, and winter crops are very important for Ukraine – winter wheat makes up the majority of the wheat that Ukraine produces.”
August is the height of Ukraine’s wheat harvest, and farmers would normally begin harvesting the country’s corn crop next month. If farmers can’t sell this year’s harvests, Nivievskyi said, many will struggle to raise the money they need to plant next year’s crops.
“For this, farmers they would need the liquidity, the working capital, to buy the seeds – and it’s not available right now,” he said. “Usually, around 50 percent of the harvest that’s sold in Ukraine is to purchase the materials for the autumn planting season, and this is now difficult to get because the prices are much lower, and volume-wise we cannot really sell as much as last season. And that’s going to be difficult.”
Storage pressures
With Ukraine’s grain exports down by some 75 percent year-on-year the first two weeks of August, the question of where exactly producers are going to store all the grain they can’t shift is becoming critical. Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotsky said the country’s grain storage shortfall could reach as much as 11 million metric tonnes.
All-Ukrainian Agrarian Council deputy chairman Denys Marchuk told DW last week that Ukrainian farmers have already harvested more than 28 million tonnes of grains and pulses – and the corn harvest, estimated at some 33 million metric tonnes, hasn’t even begun.
“The capacities to store the exportable surpluses that Ukraine cannot really export right now are also limited -- and the major harvest is still in the fields,” Nivievskyi said. “So that's also going to create additional pressure on Ukrainian farmers, because they have to store the stuff somewhere.”
As local grain piles up, he added, domestic prices have only fallen further.
“Domestic prices in Ukraine now are quite low compared to the world market prices, and compared to the production costs,” he said. “There are messages and interviews of farmers saying that domestic prices are not at the level of production costs. So they will have to decide whether it’s worthwhile to bring the harvest in – or to keep it in the field.”
And while Russia is trying to reroute its grain shipments through the Caspian and Baltic Seas, Ukraine may struggle to find its own alternatives. The Danube River that has long served as Ukraine’s other major grain route has fallen to historically low levels as droughts wrack Europe, and the ports along its banks come under regular attack from Russian drones and missiles.
Nor can the country’s railways pick up the slack. Ukrainian authorities in July said Russia had damaged more than 200 locomotives in 2026 alone as Moscow systematically targets the country’s rolling stock. According to the agriculture minister, river and rails between them can carry just a third of what used to flow through Ukraine’s Black Sea ports.
Logistics aside, the political landscape has also changed considerably since the opening months of the full-scale war. Where the European Union once liberalised agricultural trade with the beleaguered country, suspending all import duties and quotas to help farmers move their produce west, the resulting influx of Ukrainian wheat and falling prices sparked fierce farmers’ protests across eastern and central Europe. Poland, Slovakia and Hungary all maintain bans on specific Ukrainian agricultural goods in the name of safeguarding their own farmers’ livelihoods.
"The willingness of European partners to help Ukraine out is also not there as it was in 2022," Nivievskyi said.

Ukrainian Defense Forces Strike Astrakhan Gas Processing Plant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
17:39:25 UTC
02:39:25 KST

Satellite imagery shows that Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck Astrakhan Gas Processing Plant on August 24, 2026, approximately 800 kilometers from the front line.
The ‘Absolutely Reliable Source’ Telegram channel published the satellite images.
According to the channel’s analysts, the strike hit gas separation units 1.U-272 and 2.U-272. The extent of the damage is not yet known. The images show burn marks on protective structures, with several fire trucks visible nearby.
Astrakhan Gas Processing Plant is located near the settlement of Aksarayskoye in Russia’s Astrakhan region and is part of Gazprom’s processing division.
Astrakhan Gas Processing Plant produces commercial natural gas, sulfur, stabilized gas condensate, gasoline, diesel fuel, fuel oil, liquefied petroleum gases, and a broad fraction of light hydrocarbons.
Its sulfur production is particularly important for Russia. Under normal operating conditions, the plant produces around 3.5–3.8 million tonnes of sulfur annually, accounting for roughly 60–63% of Russia’s total sulfur output.
The plant’s contribution to Russia’s motor fuel production is much smaller. In 2023, it accounted for about 1.6% of the country’s gasoline production, 0.6% of diesel fuel, and 0.7% of fuel oil.
The field is notable for the extremely complex composition of its gas. The reservoir mixture contains approximately 25% toxic hydrogen sulfide and 15% carbon dioxide.
Without deep purification, this gas cannot be processed further or transported through main gas pipelines. Together, units 1.U-272 and 2.U-272 can process up to 3 billion cubic meters of gas to remove hydrogen sulfide and carbon dioxide, accounting for about a quarter of the plant’s total designed capacity.
Astrakhan Gas Processing Plant has been targeted in strikes several times before. The first known attack took place on February 3, 2025, causing a fire and a prolonged shutdown of fuel production. A second attack followed on March 17, 2025. The plant was struck again on September 22, 2025, after which condensate processing was suspended once more. On December 15, 2025, a major fire broke out at the facility.
So far in 2026, the plant has been attacked once, on May 13. The attack halted motor fuel production, while industry sources reported damage to equipment used to process stabilized condensate and hydrogen sulfide and to produce sulfur.
Following the attacks in 2025, Russia’s production of industrial sulfur fell to 4.38 million tonnes, down 21.7% from approximately 5.6 million tonnes in 2024.
The decline continued in 2026. From January through May, Russia produced 1.75 million tonnes of industrial sulfur, 19% less than during the same period in 2025.
The attacks have had a major impact on Russia’s sulfur trade. The country went from being the world’s third-largest sulfur exporter, an important raw material for the chemical industry, to becoming a net importer.
With domestic production falling, the Russian government extended its ban on sulfur exports through December 31, 2026.

Companies that help Iran launder money will be excluded from the U.S. dollar system - Bessent
Kyiv • UNN
The U.S. will target organizations that help Iran launder money or circumvent sanctions. Bessent announced sanctions against a financial institution.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is threatening to exclude groups that help Iran launder money from the American financial system, which underpins the global economy, UNN reports, citing CNN.
"Let me be clear: any organization that facilitates money laundering on behalf of Iran will be excluded from the U.S. dollar system. The clock has just started ticking," Bessent said in his prepared remarks on Monday.

Asked whether Chinese banks could face secondary sanctions for their alleged role in helping Iran, Bessent said that the best approach was "quiet diplomacy," but added that "no one is above U.S. sanctions."
"We are leveling the playing field with all countries to inform them of our expectations," he said. We know who they are. They know who they are. So when the U.S. Treasury's measures come crashing down on them, they will have only themselves to blame."
Bessent said a major announcement on sanctions against an unnamed financial institution should be expected by the end of this week.

What are Iran's options to escalate further in face of US economic threats? - explainer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
17:37:52 UTC
02:37:52 KST

US threats to impose "the toughest sanctions in history" to force Iran to buckle to its demands after nearly six months of war have raised the prospect of a new round of escalation in the Gulf.
How could Iran respond to the economic pressure?
Can Iran stop more oil from leaving the Middle East?
Mohsen Rezaei, the former Revolutionary Guards chief and secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, has already threatened to shut down oil exports — one of Tehran's main strategic approaches since the war began on February 28.
"If the economic war continues, not a single drop of oil will be exported, neither through the Strait of Hormuz nor from anywhere in the Persian Gulf," he said.
Iranian attacks and threats to shipping have already stopped most traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, largely shutting down a waterway that carried around a fifth of global energy before the conflict.
Although some oil tankers have been moving through the strait in recent weeks, volumes remain very low and on Sunday Iran blacklisted 45 tankers it says failed to comply with the rules it wants to impose on Hormuz shipping.
Missile, drone or speedboat attacks on tankers trying to leave the Gulf have repeatedly pushed up oil prices during the six months of the conflict.
Meanwhile, Tehran's Houthi allies have restricted Red Sea shipping with attacks and threats to blockade all Saudi Arabian shipping, which carries crude to Asia through the Bab el-Mandeb strait past the group's Yemeni stronghold.
While the attacks initially stopped only some vessels, with more than half still getting through in mid-August, the situation is difficult for shippers, and Chinese shipping companies are now rerouting away from Bab el-Mandeb, according to industry sources.
Further attacks, such as the one that targeted a vessel off the main Saudi Red Sea oil terminal at Yanbu on Monday or a drone strike near the Suez Canal in early August, could raise oil market anxiety levels and crude oil prices.
Are Gulf states still at risk of an Iranian attack?
Iran has threatened to retaliate against any neighbors who take part in US efforts to strangle the country's economy with "earthquake" force.
It has targeted Gulf states and Jordan repeatedly during the war, mostly focusing on US bases but also hitting energy infrastructure and other targets.
Any intensified attacks on upstream oil or gas facilities could further drive up energy prices in ways that inflict political damage on the Trump administration and may be harder to reverse than attacks on shipping.
Targeting power and water desalination plants in the hot, parched region would also pose a major risk to US-aligned Gulf monarchies that function as significant financial hubs for the global economy.
Can Iran attack Western countries directly?
While Western countries are beyond the range of Iran's main munitions, the Revolutionary Guards have historically been willing to find alternative ways of attack.
On Monday, Britain said Iran-linked hackers had shut down a small electricity station, while US officials have said Tehran was likely behind cyberattacks on water plants in Minnesota. Iran has not commented on those allegations.
Western security services have also accused Iran of recruiting local people to stage attacks or attempt assassinations in the West. Iran has denied that.

Israel must repair its strategic triangle with the US and American Jewry - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
17:37:20 UTC
02:37:20 KST

At the heart of the national security equation of Israel and the Jewish people lies a strategic triangle of immense value. One side is the relationship between Israel and the United States; the second, the relationship between American Jewry and the US administration; the third, the relationship between Israel and American Jewry.
For years, Israeli governments understood the dynamics among these three sides and what those dynamics required, including preserving bipartisan support for Israel and nurturing solidarity with American Jewry in all its diversity.
After many years in which this strategic triangle proved to be a vital force multiplier, troubling cracks are now appearing and deepening.
Every Israeli government must keep one fact firmly in mind: Israel has no great-power ally other than the United States.
Our great advantage is that the United States is home to a remarkable, prosperous and influential Jewish community.
Its influence is far greater than its small share of the American population would suggest. American Jews play prominent roles in government, academia, business, the media, law and culture. They are well organized and leave a significant imprint on policy, public narratives and social norms.
In today’s polarized America, preserving bipartisan support has become increasingly difficult. Yet Netanyahu, rather than navigating sensitively between the two political camps, chose to align himself with the Republican camp, helping turn Israel from a consensual issue into a partisan one, while alienating the majority of American Jews, who hold liberal views.
Three illusions weakening Israel’s strategic relationships
To rebuild the triangle, we must first rid ourselves of three illusions.
The illusion of Hasbara (Public Diplomacy). Campaigns portraying Israel as a “strategic asset”, a “front-line outpost against radical Islam”, or the “Start-Up Nation” are searching for the coin under the streetlamp.
The coin, however, was lost elsewhere, at the substantive points of friction. Israel’s government is increasingly perceived as undermining democratic norms, offering no political horizon on the Palestinian issue, and widening the values gap with liberal and younger Americans, Jewish and non-Jewish alike.
The illusion of symmetry. There is no symmetry in the Israel-US relationship. We are the ones existentially dependent on the United States for weapons, diplomatic vetoes, legal backing, and economic support.
Arrogant conduct, bypassing the administration, and publicly confronting American presidents are perceived in Washington as impudence, and they accelerate the erosion of support for Israel.
The illusion that “nobody understands America like Bibi”. While bipartisan support for Israel has collapsed, one need look no further than the test of recent events: Kushner, the son-in-law of Bibi’s loyal friend Donald Trump, was sent to Cairo to negotiate with... Hamas. So much for “understanding America”.
The next government must rebuild the triangle
If the coming elections produce a responsible government that is not hostage to the political blackmail of the far right and the ultra-Orthodox parties, a historic window of opportunity will open to rescue the strategic triangle.
Netanyahu’s departure alone would remove much of the personal baggage that has weakened it, but that would not be enough. The next government must take substantive initiatives.
First, it must demonstrate a willingness to chart a path toward resolving the Palestinian issue. The absence of any route toward ending the occupation is turning support for Israel into a political and moral burden, even for some of our closest friends.
Second, it must embrace the values of Israel’s Declaration of Independence: protection of the rule of law, separation of powers, judicial independence, individual and minority rights, and a constitution anchoring the rules of the democratic game.
Third, it must recognize Jewish pluralism as a component of national security, by implementing the Western Wall compromise and recognizing conversion and personal-status arrangements conducted by all streams of Judaism.
Beyond the intrinsic importance of these measures, why should we assume they would also strengthen support for Israel? Few organizations are as attuned to the American political pulse as AIPAC.
On its website, the lobby itself emphasizes precisely these attributes of Israel: democracy, equality before the law, human rights, pluralism, and even... the pursuit of a two-state solution. (Here is another example of why hasbara is doomed to fail: how can hasbara persuade when policy itself moves in the opposite direction?)
Repair requires policy change, not better PR
The next government must make repairing the triangle a top priority. It must recognize that this cannot be achieved through public relations or the supposed magic of more sophisticated hasbara. Repair does not depend on packaging but on substance - on a change of direction in Israel's domestic and foreign policy.
If Israel changes in substance, not merely in its PR image, its standing will change as well, and the strategic triangle’s resilience will be restored.
The writer is a former director-general of the Foreign Ministry. His latest book, The Leviathan Option: A Deep State Story, is available on Amazon

The Vatican wants a seat at the Ukraine peace table. Here’s why
The head of the Vatican’s diplomatic service, Archbishop Paul Richard Gallagher, is visiting Moscow from August 24-28. This visit is part of the Holy See’s diplomatic efforts on humanitarian issues and the discussion of ways to resolve the Ukraine conflict. This is reflected in the fact that the Vatican, together with the authorities of several states, including Bulgaria, Hungary, and Italy recently contributed to keeping Patriarch Kirill off the latest EU sanctions list.
The visit is clearly necessary to revitalize communication between the Vatican and Moscow, as the formal diplomatic channels – though fully operational – have recently lost the historical depth and back-channel confidentiality previously maintained through the Russian Orthodox Church’s external relations. Below, we examine the true operational motives behind the Holy See’s urgent mission within the broader context of its geopolitical and financial survival in Central and Eastern Europe.
American Pope
Pope Leo XIV has been in power for a year, allowing us to draw certain conclusions about his leadership style. We see a tough, sovereign politician who skillfully uses conservative symbols to promote the Church’s internal stability, but on the world stage, he advocates a center-left, global agenda that criticizes both rigid state borders and the power of algorithms.
For example, the Vatican has returned to the use of traditional ornate vestments, which had been shelved under Francis XII. The public appearance was also received extremely favorably by conservative critics of the use of 'gender ideology' in schools and the promotion of non-traditional lifestyles. At the same time, the Pope is promoting ideas for decentralizing Vatican authority and proposing synodal reform, the essence of which is aimed at collegial governance of the Church, where decisions are made collectively by a large number of bishops and laypeople.
Most notable, however, have been his public disputes with various factions of his compatriots on the right; he has publicly criticized the immigration policies of US President Donald Trump’s administration and US Vice President J.D. Vance. In his first encyclical, Leo XIV harshly criticized artificial intelligence, calling for the “disarmament” of technology, a ban on its use for military purposes, and an end to the IT corporations’ proverbial race to the bottom, arguing that it could result in mass unemployment and that people could use it to escape into an “illusory world.”
Importantly, his statements provoked a counterattack from Silicon Valley leaders; Marc Andreessen and Peter Thiel were among those who reacted negatively.
Overall, this paints him as a representative of the systemic wing of the Catholic Church – a supranational sovereign structure that thinks in terms of centuries, not electoral cycles. His accession to the throne signaled the Roman Curia’s intention to establish a strict leader from the New World, free from parochial European caste disputes.
The Institute for the Works of Religion, aka the Vatican Bank: Personnel Changes and Conservatism
It’s logical that Pope Leo XIV began his sovereign expansion on the throne not with abstract peace declarations, but with an immediate, surgical reformatting of the Holy See’s entire financial vertical. His very first significant document was the Apostolic Letter ‘Coniuncta Cura’ (Joint Care), which dealt a crushing blow to the former monopoly over the Institute for the Affairs of Religion (IOR). The Pontiff officially rescinded Francis’s harsh decree, which had previously forcibly locked 100% of the liquidity of all Vatican departments and orders within the Vatican Bank.
Why did Leo XIV make this sensitive issue his very first priority? The answer is cynical: the previous centralization of accounts in the IOR had completely paralyzed the Vatican’s operational para-diplomacy, and most importantly, blocked the influx of capital from the New World. Conservative US Catholic foundations and Wall Street heavyweights – with Cardinal Timothy Dolan serving as the bridge – were ready to resume multi-billion-dollar donations but flatly refused to place them under the total control of the old IOR bureaucracy.
With the issuance of the ‘Coniuncta cura’ decree, Leo XIV restored the right of dicasteries and external bodies to legally move and place assets in major international commercial banks and foreign investment platforms. This opened legal channels for the influx of billions from conservative right-wing American circles, while simultaneously facilitating the transit of shadow funds belonging to the right-wing elites of the Visegrád Group (Poland, Hungary, and Slovakia) – elites seeking to safeguard their reserves from the fiscal coercion of Brussels and the ECB.
However, this financial breakthrough immediately created an existential threat for the Vatican on its external frontier. By moving assets from the hermetically sealed IOR, protected by sovereign immunity, to external commercial banks, the Holy See automatically exposed its renewed dollar flows to the jurisdiction and financial supervision of other states; first and foremost, the US Treasury Department and EU law. Any escalation in negative relations with the West could now theoretically result in the Vatican seeing its assets in foreign accounts frozen or blocked. It is precisely this red-hot financial knot that inexorably links Leo XIV’s treasury maneuver with his sudden foray into the Ukrainian issue.
The mechanism of this combination is simple: as long as the Vatican is outside the official peace track, US financial authorities retain leverage over IOR transactions. But as soon as the Vatican is officially recognized by Moscow and Washington as an international arbiter (and the Pontiff has repeatedly stated that the Vatican is ready to play such a role) its bank automatically receives the status of peace process infrastructure. Imposing sanctions or auditing the Holy See’s accounts will become politically impossible, as this would be interpreted as a deliberate disruption of negotiations with Russia. Mediation in Ukraine is a legal shield shielding the Vatican’s assets from American and European regulators.
Moreover, the influx of hundreds of millions of dollars from conservative New World billionaires demands reciprocal political steps from the Pope. Ending the conflict in Ukraine and stabilizing European security are among the vital interests of major Western capital, which is suffering from economic instability and inflation. By becoming a participant in the peace settlement, Leo XIV is proving to his American donors that the Vatican is not just a 'church', but a highly effective instrument of global influence, in which it is profitable to invest money.
At the same time, Leo XIV’s policy is more subtle than it seems. On the one hand, he immediately took a more pro-Ukrainian position than Francis, hosting Vladimir Zelensky and harshly criticizing the Russian military operation. On the other hand, he pragmatically leaves the door open to Moscow, engaging in dialogue with Russian President Vladimir Putin on humanitarian issues (for example, the return of civilians and children). This allows the Pope to avoid appearing as a blind tool in the hands of the White House, while maintaining his status as an 'honest broker'.
Why does the Vatican need Ukraine?
Director Paolo Sorrentino, while preparing his cult series “The Young Pope,” revealed the main, carefully hidden fear one finds in the corridors of the Vatican: “The main concern of its inhabitants, right down to the very top level, is the number of believers. How many believers do we have? How many are we losing? How many can we bring back?” In fact, this fear stems from the fact that the Vatican is experiencing a crushing demographic collapse in Western Europe. Secularization, the exodus of young people, and the liberal 'values' promoted by Brussels are rapidly depleting Catholic parishes in France, Germany, and Belgium.
Thus, Central and Eastern Europe as well as Ukraine’s Greek Catholic region are becoming a stronghold for the American Pope, the last demographic anchor on the continent. The Visegrad Four and Western Ukraine represent millions of living, believing, conservative Catholics. Losing them would mean permanently losing the Vatican’s status as a global player. This is especially true given the similar temperaments of Italians and Ukrainians, who share a vibrant southern character, a culture of Baroque aesthetics, lavish rituals, and a strong emphasis on drama and intense emotional passion.
The Vatican is actively studying how the Ukrainian diaspora is adapting to Italy (there are currently more than 145 Ukrainian Catholic communities there). Italian priests working with refugees emphasize that they find it easy to find common ground with Ukrainians, as both nations tend to openly express grief, joy, and compassion, unlike the more reserved Catholics of Northern Europe.
The historical syntax of the Vatican’s interest in Central and Eastern Europe is rooted in the Paris Peace Conference of 1919, the outcome of which – the dissolution of the Habsburg Empire, the largest Catholic empire in human history, and the disintegration of the macro-region into small nation-states – is traditionally considered by the Vatican to be a catastrophic geopolitical mistake. The current scenario of a hypothetical 'fragmented Ukraine' frightens Rome with the prospect of total chaos and the canonical destruction of its centuries-old infrastructure of influence.
Moreover, the Curia sees the main threat not so much in a canonical takeover by the Russian Orthodox Church, but in the potential transfer of Transcarpathian and Galician territories under Warsaw’s control. If such a scenario materializes, the aggressive Polish Roman Catholic Church will inevitably eliminate the autonomy of the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church, forcibly converting millions of believers to the Latin Rite and forever cutting off the Vatican’s unique gateway to the 'Eastern Rite' for soft expansion into the Orthodox world.
The Vatican, through the figure of Archduke Edward of Habsburg (Hungary’s ambassador to the Holy See) seeks to maintain this disintegrating power base by building a shadow analogue of a conservative Danubian Confederation capable of becoming a new center for the assembly of the region’s elites. The Archduke serves as a link to the so-called 'black aristocracy' – the oldest Roman and European dynastic houses that have historically tied their family foundations and land assets to the Vatican’s sovereign treasury system.
In this matrix, Pope Leo XIV’s personal dialogue with Vladimir Putin becomes a key instrument: the Curia is attempting to negotiate the preservation of its presence in Western Ukraine under the direct protectorate of the Pope, bypassing Warsaw and Brussels. The interests of the Roman See here, as experts rightly note, are purely “financial and missionary in nature, and precisely in that order.”
The Vatican is proposing to Moscow to transform the IOR Bank into an external, secure gateway for Russia’s cross-border transactions with conservative Europe in exchange for security guarantees for its flock. Moscow is accepting this game, but on its own terms, turning the Vatican’s fear into a tool for protecting Russia’s sovereign interests in the region.
Diplomatic vacuum and the 'Kirill paradox'
The main hidden marker of the depth of informal ties between the Holy See and Moscow remains an unprecedented fact: Patriarch Kirill has never been included in the official sanctions list of the European Union. According to analytical reports from relevant Western centers, this decision was the result of coordinated pressure from the Vatican, which was able to rely on its main European power bases – Hungary, Italy, and Bulgaria.
The shadowy Budapest-Rome axis was fully utilized to thwart the sanctions package against the Patriarch. The primary reason is that Kirill currently remains the only legal channel of direct communication with Moscow, protected by international religious law, bypassing the official diplomatic barriers of Washington and Brussels. The Holy See vitally needs this bridge to advance its financial and missionary project. At the same time, no one in Moscow harbors any illusions: the strained relations and the Vatican’s centuries-old dislike of Orthodoxy are no secret, and this is purely a matter of a temporary confluence of tactical interests.
However, by the time the Vatican representatives visit Russia later in August, the previous architecture of contacts between the Russian Orthodox Church and the Roman Catholic leadership will have been completely abandoned. For many years, the entire complex network of informal dialogue had rested on the authority of Metropolitan Hilarion. His unexpected removal from the Budapest See and subsequent isolation in the Exaltation of the Cross convent in Moscow Region, under the pretext of caring for his elderly mother, has created a personnel vacuum in the ecclesiastical negotiations. Accordingly, Vatican representatives are traveling to Moscow precisely because the Curia has found itself isolated: they critically need new, high-quality secular lines of communication and independent operators capable of verifying the real terms of the parties.
The subtle threat of the Vatican’s scheme is that the resources offered by the papacy are de facto tied to conservative circles within the American 'deep state'. At the same time, the Holy See is attempting to legitimize a permanent ideological foothold and cordon sanitaire in the 'fragments of Ukraine' under the shadowy control of representatives of the European 'black aristocracy'. Given that the Russian Orthodox Church lacks sufficient room to maneuver under severe sanctions pressure, Rome is convinced that Moscow will lose this order’s bargaining game through subtle psychological maneuvering due to the lack of personnel figures of comparable intellectual caliber.

Regarding Nesrine Malik’s article (Here is the news from the US: Woke 1.0 is over. I grew up in a divided society in which it was crystal clear, at least to my community, that we were second-class citizens. Nothing ever seemed to change and in the end we fought a war over it. Today attitudes are a lot different, but new truths are universally embedded.
What we learned was that the self-evident truth of “first-class” citizens was that their position was one established long ago by right and might. Against that sense of rightness, you cannot appeal to another truth that is diametrically opposed. I raised boys and girls in a progressive, liberal home. It was some surprise to me that my boys were not onboard with Woke 1.0. Their truth was Jordan Peterson’s “equality of access, not equality of outcome”, and a belief that their own privilege as middle-class, intelligent white males was good luck to be defended.
Phrases such as “toxic masculinity” and “check your privilege” were heard as an attack, and qualifiers like “not all men” and “I don’t mean you” as insincere.
It is not all doom and gloom. We chip away, parents and siblings, and even in the pushback in defence of Woke 1.0 at home, we feel the softening. I think that is where the hope lies in the next phase of progressiveness – the changing of minds in the home and among friends, one self-evident truth at a time. That is not to deny the need for the public political 2.0 movement that will inevitably arise, but to acknowledge that its roots will be in smaller truths and smaller conversations. So you can start now, and with hope.

Something like “community policing” would resonate with most Americans and pique curiosity in how police and citizens can work together.
This is only one example of how liberals snatch defeat from the jaws of victory. We need to forget ideological purity and instead formulate simple, easily understood positions that point towards positive solutions to real problems. We have to be more than “not them”.
Bert Love
Shrub Oak, New York state, US

We need public records on the delivery of social housing | Letter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
17:32:53 UTC
02:32:53 KST

Your editorial on London’s social housing (16 August) makes a persuasive case for treating social housing as economic infrastructure. However, infrastructure is normally monitored and social housing is not, either when it is delivered or across the years in which it is meant to remain affordable. A home is counted as affordable on the day that planning permission is granted and is rarely examined again, through completion, tenure change and the service charges that can make it unaffordable within months of occupation, as your reporting on shared ownership has shown.
Southwark, like almost every local authority, publishes every pound of the financial contributions developers pay, yet offers no scheme-level account of whether the promised social rented homes were built. The consequences showed at Elephant and Castle, where residents needed three years of freedom of information battles to force out the viability evidence behind an affordable housing commitment that ended at 82 social rented homes in place of more than a thousand. By the time it came out, the estate was gone, and a record that arrives after demolition can only count the losses. On the Old Kent Road, where the council plans around 20,000 new homes and only a few thousand are yet built or under way, the record could still be kept in time to shape what is delivered.
You close with Nye Bevan’s idea of housing as an essential service like the NHS, and the comparison is instructive. The NHS publishes waiting lists and inspection results, and is held to them, whereas housing has no equivalent, whoever the landlord is. If social homes are economic infrastructure, they deserve public, dated records of what was promised, what arrived and what it costs to live in them.
Marco Scalvini
London

24 August 2026•Update: 24 August 2026
 The US on Monday launched Operation Economic Outcast, a sweeping campaign intended to completely isolate Iran from the global financial system, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced.
“Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone,” Bessent told reporters. 
The US is "no longer managing the Iranian threat" but rather "ending it,” Bessent said, adding that the "strength of America's economy" enabled Washington to conduct such a financial offensive alongside military operations.
Directed by US President Donald Trump, the “unprecedented” sanctions target Iran’s "most vital lifelines," including aviation, shipping, gold, technology, and digital assets, he said.

'No one is above the reach of US sanctions'

Iran-linked hackers took U.K. power plant offline for first time, reports say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
17:30:35 UTC
02:30:35 KST

Iran-linked hackers blamed for taking down U.K. power plant for first time, reports say
London - Iranian-affiliated hackers successfully but temporarily took a power plant offline in the United Kingdom, according to multiple British media outlets.
The Telegraph and Financial Times reported the attack, which they say happened in July but is only now being reported, is believed to be the first time Iranian-linked hackers managed to shut down such a facility in the country.
Of further concern, the breach also happened the same month Iranian-linked hackers are believed to have targeted the water systems of a dozen states including New Jersey, Minnesota, Georgia and South Dakota, locking out operators and causing pressure loss and flooding.
CBS News reached out to the U.K.'s cybersecurity agency, the National Cyber Security Centre, but it neither confirmed nor denied any hacking had occurred.
In both attacks, computers called "programmable logic controllers" were targeted, according to U.S. officials and people familiar with the matter in the U.K. Also known as PLCs, these are the brains of automated industrial systems found around the world that in large part span energy, water and manufacturing. But they are also used ubiquitously in hospitals to help supply power in blackouts, in chemical plants to control temperature and pressure to avoid explosions and in elevators and trains to control speed. PLCs are also employed to control prison security gates, in the timing of traffic light systems and in the activation of fire suppression systems.
Industry estimates on how many PLCs are in use worldwide vary widely, from roughly 12 million to more than 70 million, according to market research firms. The first model was manufactured in the late 1960s — and many older units still in use today were never designed with 21st century cybersecurity challenges in mind.
Yet, security researchers say the methods hackers use to breach PLCs are not sophisticated.
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has reported Iranian-linked actors are using simple techniques that include scanning for exposed devices and exploiting default credentials — default passwords that have not been changed — rather than deploying sophisticated exploits of holes that companies may not know exist. The strategy is more akin to looking for unlocked doors versus high-tech hacking.
CISA has also said the responsibility for securing this equipment has largely fallen on individual plant operators - often small utilities with few to no dedicated cybersecurity staff - for devices that were never built with security as a priority in the first place. One 2024 scan by cybersecurity researchers found thousands of PLCs sitting exposed and searchable on the open internet.
In the attack on the British power plant, that system was offline for four days as employees worked to restore control, reports said. British officials and industrial executives have not disclosed which plant was hit, but it is understood the attack targeted a small-scale facility and did not impact the U.K.'s overall power supply. No organization has claimed responsibility, but security experts say it is possible these attacks may be proof-of-concept attempts — testing how to navigate the systems of more vulnerable targets before attempting to reach more sensitive, high-value ones in the future.
For years, the U.K. has warned of Iranian-linked cyber activity. In 2022, officials condemned Iran for a cyberattack that crippled Albania's government services. But the warnings sharply intensified early this year, triggered by the U.S.-Israel war against Iran and the killing of Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
In June, the head of the U.K.'s National Cyber Security Centre, Dr. Richard Horne, disclosed it had "managed" more than 200 cyberattacks against UK critical infrastructure in the past year, with roughly 75% of the attacks linked to hostile states including Russia, China and Iran.

The eastern approach
Ukrainian military observer Kostiantyn Mashovets reported that Russian forward units are advancing across several tactical areas at once in the Sloviansk direction. He said the command of Russia's 3rd Combined Arms Army rushes assault infantry forward right after each successful infiltration. Russian troops reached the southeastern edge of Pyskunivka, east of Sloviansk, from the east and northeast, moving off positions they had seized on the southern bank of the Siverskyi Donets, Mashovets said. Zakitne lies northeast of Pyskunivka and Kryva Luka southeast of it, and ISW read the advance as evidence Russia has consolidated positions in both.
They also infiltrated the southern and southeastern outskirts of Mykolaivka from western Rai-Oleksandrivka. ISW assessed that Russia is running a dual effort to connect its units near Kryva Luka with those at Rai-Oleksandrivka, so it can assault Mykolaivka from dominant terrain to the east and south at once. Mashovets added that other Russian groups slipped through three settlements along the E-40 Bakhmut-Sloviansk highway, trying to hold the western bank of the Siverskyi Donets-Donbas Canal and reach the river just east of the city.
ISW observed reports on 23 August that Ukrainian forces repelled a Russian infiltration attempt in Mykolaivka.
Oleksandr Borodin, spokesperson for Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps, said the Lyman direction falls in his corps' zone and that Russia's goal there is to half-encircle the Sloviansk-Kramatorsk agglomeration from the flank—first securing bridgeheads across the rivers, then cutting logistics. He called those plans unrealistic:
"We have quite serious defensive positions there and have been preparing for a long time. The capabilities they currently have to try to accomplish this task are insufficient even to come close to achieving such a goal."
Why Moscow switched directions
Russia prioritized attacking Sloviansk from the northeast through Lyman when it opened its spring-summer 2026 offensive, but that effort has largely stalled. The Siverskyi Donets River, which loops north and northeast of the city, together with a web of canals, handed Ukrainian defenders a natural moat. So Russian commanders now treat Mykolaivka as a key prize. Taking it would let them strike west toward Sloviansk from the east, skirting the water obstacles that blocked the northeastern route.
Ukrainian intelligence units will not help: Analyst warns that once Russia breaks into Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, reinforcing them only delays inevitable
A slow road into the Fortress Belt
Sloviansk anchors the northern end of Ukraine's Fortress Belt, a chain of fortified cities that has blunted Russian advances in Donetsk Oblast since 2014. ISW cautioned that Russian forces are extremely unlikely to make fast gains west of Mykolaivka, since they still need to seize several more settlements first.
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 23 August that Putin has ordered his army to seize all of Donetsk Oblast by 31 December. By ISW's count, it is the 15th such deadline since 2022, and Russia has missed every one that has come due.
Zelenskyy put Russia's frontline casualties this year at around 267,000, including about 155,000 killed, and said 70% to 80% of them fall in the Kostiantynivka direction. Russia holds about 79.89% of Donetsk Oblast, by ISW's count, and Zelenskyy said the Kremlin is preparing to mobilize around 300,000 men after the 18–20 September State Duma elections, partly to reinforce Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts.

The US will not recognize the occupied Ukrainian territories as Russian — Kellogg
Kyiv • UNN
Keith Kellogg said that the US would not recognize Crimea and the occupied areas as Russian. According to him, these territories will eventually return to Ukraine.
Former U.S. special envoy for Ukraine, retired Lieutenant General Keith Kellogg, said that the United States would not recognize the occupied Ukrainian territories as Russian, adding that Ukraine would reclaim them. Kellogg made the statement in an interview with "Naspravdi MAХ", reports UNN.
"The United States has a doctrine called the Welles Doctrine. It means that we do not recognize the conquest of territories that become part of another state. I’ll give you an example. Instead of Ukraine, as with the Baltic countries during World War II, the Soviet Union occupied the Baltics, but we never recognized them as part of the Soviet Union. They still remained a separate occupied country," Kellogg said.
He noted that the United States has this view regarding the occupied territories.
"Are they physically occupied? Yes. But do we legally recognize that this is now their territory? No. Do we recognize Crimea as Russian territory? No. The same applies to Donbas, Luhansk or Donetsk, Kherson or Zaporizhzhia. They are simply occupied, that’s all. We recognize this," Kellogg added.
Kellogg stressed that "over time, perhaps not tomorrow or the day after tomorrow, but they will return to Ukraine".

How the No. 2 pencil became a uniquely American school supply staple
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
17:23:02 UTC
02:23:02 KST

How the No. 2 pencil became a uniquely American school supply staple
For generations of Americans, a sharpened No. 2 pencil has represented childhood and coming of age. Still a fixture of back-to-school shopping lists, it outlines a child’s first letters, erases their mistakes and lets them doodle in the margins when they daydream.
For decades, sweaty hands clutched the ridged yellow wood on test day. “Bring two sharp No. 2 pencils,” generations of Americans were told, as they prepared to fill in bubbles on the SATs and other standardized tests that might shape their futures. Whether it’s true that Scantron machines could only read No. 2 scribbles is up for debate, but those were the rules.
The pencil itself was not invented in the United States. But American industry and innovation made it iconic.
“The idea of painting a pencil yellow and putting an eraser on top is specifically American,” says Caroline Weaver, a pencil historian and author of “The Pencil Perfect: The Untold Story of a Cultural Icon.” Until the mid-1800s, pencils in America had no eraser, and the eraserless pencil is still standard in the rest of the world.
One of America’s early pencilmakers was John Thoreau, father of Henry David Thoreau. The writer worked for his dad’s Massachusetts pencil company in the mid-1800s before moving to a cabin in the woods and composing “Walden.”
The young Thoreau is credited with pioneering the concept of grading pencils on a scale of 1 to 4, with No. 2 striking a balance of graphite and clay that is dark enough, yet not too smudgy for writing. (“Pencils have never contained lead. This is a myth!” says Weaver.)
The rest of the world uses a similar scale to grade pencils, known as “HB,” measuring hardness and blackness.
The other end of the pencil contains another American invention. The ferrule is a metal piece that has held the eraser for more than a century — except during World War II, when rationing forced a shift to plastic and even cardboard.
In an increasingly digital world, pencils are less commonplace. Most school testing has moved online. Students use laptops and touch screens as early as kindergarten.
But all this tech has produced a backlash. In the age of AI, many schools and colleges are requiring handwritten exams and paper tests to safeguard against cheating — or just to give kids a break from screens.
And so many will pick up a No. 2 — like generations before. In that way, Weaver says, the pencil represents democracy itself. No matter who you are or where you live, you have written with a No. 2, sharpened its point or possibly, in moments of stress or boredom, chewed on one.
Part of a recurring series, “American Objects,” marking the 250th anniversary of the United States. For more American objects, click here. For more stories on the anniversary, click here.

Britain tells TikTok and other platforms to remove videos glorifying dangerous driving after deaths
LONDON (AP) — Britain’s government Monday urged TikTok and other social media companies to take down viral videos “celebrating” dangerous driving, after two police officers and five young men were killed in a crash when a car was driven down the wrong side of the road.
Officers Matthew Blades and Tom Clough were killed Saturday when a Volkswagen was driven the wrong way along a road in northeastern England and hit their vehicle. Five people in the car — three boys who were 17 and 18 years old and two men, both 23 — were also pronounced dead at the scene.
The collision took place as concerns grow over social media videos showing people driving dangerously on purpose, posted by the drivers themselves or others inside the vehicles at the time.
British media reports suggest that one of the people who died in the Volkswagen on Saturday may have previously posted such a video.
U.K. Defense Minister Luke Pollard said the government has told TikTok and similar platforms to “step up” and remove such “awful content.”
“We’ve communicated to those social media platforms that have been hosting content that celebrates this type of dangerous behavior on our roads to take down that content,” he told the BBC.
“It’s one of the reasons they’ve argued against some of the regulations, saying they can police themselves,” Pollard added. “This is the perfect opportunity to demonstrate it. Remove the content that celebrates dangerous behavior on our roads.”
Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s office said “the glorification of dangerous driving for clips and entertainment is utterly disgraceful.”
It said the U.K. media regulator has the government’s full backing to take tough action against platforms that fail in their legal duties.
TikTok did not comment but said its policies strictly prohibit content that could cause significant physical harm.
Police said that the car in the fatal crash had a cloned number plate to avoid detection. They said 12 people were arrested Monday in connection with suspected criminal activity, including possessing a firearm, before the crash.
Separately, four people, including a child, were seriously injured last week in County Kildare, Ireland after their car was struck by another vehicle going the wrong way down a highway. Five teenagers in the other car died in the crash.
An Irish parliamentary committee invited TikTok to discuss how it deals with content that “glorifies illegal activity” following that crash, but the social media company declined to attend.

Colombia’s armed groups recruit children and train them in drone warfare, rights group says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
17:23:02 UTC
02:23:02 KST

Colombia’s armed groups recruit children and train them in drone warfare, rights group says
BOGOTA, Colombia (AP) — Drug gangs and rebel groups in Colombia are increasingly recruiting children and using them to perform potentially lethal tasks that include piloting explosives-laden drones, Human Rights Watch said in a report published Monday.
The international watchdog said criminal organizations in the South American country often use social media to recruit children as they try to assert control over rural areas where they profit from the drug trade, extortion and illegal mining.
“Armed groups in Colombia are recruiting children with impunity,” said Juanita Goebertus, Americas director at Human Rights Watch. “Protection systems are failing, and social media platforms have become a more effective recruiting ground.”
Child recruitment is on the rise again
According to Colombia’s Human Rights Defenders’ Office, at least 1,500 children have been recruited by armed groups since 2021, with 625 cases reported in 2024.
In 1999, during the peak of the conflict between Colombia’s military and the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, or FARC, an estimated 1,320 children were recruited into the fighting, according to a report by a national truth commission.
A 2016 peace deal between Colombia’s government and the FARC rebels reduced violence in many parts of the country and slowed the recruitment of children by armed groups.
But child recruitment is picking up again as smaller rebel groups and other criminal organizations fight over control of rural areas abandoned by FARC guerrillas following the peace deal, where law enforcement and social services continue to be weak.
In Colombia, rebel groups have long used children to perform tasks that include serving as messengers, gathering intelligence, cooking or engaging with the enemy — while girls are sometimes forced into sexual acts with commanders.
The Human Rights Watch report says children are now also being trained in drone warfare, as rebel groups increasingly use drones outfitted with explosives to strike at rival groups or launch attacks on police and army bases.
Human Rights Watch verified videos published on social media that show children using explosives-laden drones, and interviewed family protection officers who work with children who have escaped from armed groups or have been allowed to demobilize.
“Released children who report having operated drones say that armed groups describe the activity as a game rather than as participation in armed fighting,” the report said.
Colombia’s Human Rights Defenders’ office said in a separate report published Monday that armed groups conducted 121 attacks with drones in the first five months of this year, in which 21 people were killed and 145 were injured.
Social media accounts ‘glorify’ life with rebels
Human Rights Watch identified dozens of social media accounts that “glorify” life in rebel groups, echoing a concern previously voiced by the United Nations.
The watchdog group said in some cases, the algorithms of platforms like Meta and TikTok “appear to have actively promoted” such content that encourages children to join rebel groups.
Meta and TikTok replied to Human Rights Watch saying they prohibit content that promotes violence, and that they had taken down accounts flagged by the organization.
Human Rights Watch also said a FARC holdout group led by a commander known as Ivan Mordisco is involved in most cases of child recruitment and is recruiting heavily in Colombia’s Cauca region.
Nearly half of all recruiting cases reported by Colombian authorities since 2021 involved Indigenous children, according to data analysis by Human Rights Watch, despite Indigenous people making up just 4% of the population.
The watchdog group also said girls made up 40% of all recruited children.
Human Rights Watch called on the Colombian government to devote more resources to prosecuting members of armed groups who recruit children, while stepping up efforts to prevent recruitment in rural areas.
There was no immediate government response to the report.
The organization also called on social media platforms to establish channels where users can easily report content that’s related to the recruitment of children, and preserve evidence that can be made available to prosecutors.

Source: a joint statement by the leaders of the Coalition of the Willing posted on the UK government website, as reported by European Pravda
Details: The statement says the leaders condemn Russia's systematic and intensifying attacks on Ukrainian cities, critical infrastructure, civilian facilities and cultural heritage sites, which have recently caused the highest civilian casualties since the beginning of the full-scale war.

They stressed the need to support Ukraine's economic resilience amid Russia's attempts to block exports through Black Sea ports.
The leaders agreed to continue efforts to restrict Russia's financial resources for waging the war through sanctions and measures to combat sanctions circumvention, including action against Russia's shadow fleet.
According to their estimates, joint measures in this area have prevented Russia from earning around US$495 billion throughout the full-scale war.
They welcomed the US Senate's decision on steps to increase economic pressure on Russia and committed to working closely with the United States in the near future on coordinated measures.
Quote: "The leaders commended President Zelenskyy's continued readiness to enter into meaningful peace talks, in order to bring about a comprehensive, just and lasting peace, and reiterated their call for Russia to agree to a full, immediate and unconditional ceasefire starting from the line of contact.
The Coalition would continue to prepare the Multinational-Force Ukraine to deploy once a credible cessation of hostilities was in place, as part of a wider set of robust politically and legally binding security guarantees to ensure Ukraine's future security and prosperity once a ceasefire enters into force."

- Following the Coalition of the Willing meeting, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported that Kyiv's international partners have pledged support for Ukraine through "military and energy aid packages".

Nvidia says Groq racks will be online this year following $20 billion purchase
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
17:19:34 UTC
02:19:34 KST

Nvidia announced Monday that its Groq 3 LPX rack is in full production, marking the commercialization of technology from the company's largest acquisition on record.
The Groq rack will be deployed alongside Vera central processors and Rubin graphics processors at neocloud Nebius, and will be online later this year, Nvidia senior director Dion Harris told reporters.
Nvidia's race to manufacture Groq's chip and make it available to customers highlights the growing importance of low-latency inference that's needed to make artificial intelligence agents feel responsive without long lags for users, especially for coding. Cloud companies can charge more for these kinds of tokens, Nvidia says.
"For folks who are serving tokens, it unlocks the ability to offer premium tiers of service for those users and those customers who actually demand the most latency-sensitive" service agreements, Harris said.
In December, Nvidia bought assets from chip startup Groq for $20 billion, the company's largest purchase.
The Groq architecture includes 500 megabytes of speedy SRAM on the chip's die itself to reduce memory-related bottlenecks. Groq chips are manufactured by Samsung, while Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. makes Nvidia's GPUs.
Nvidia packages 256 individual Groq 3 chips into its LPX racks. Nvidia said its Groq 3 LPX rack can deliver 3,400 tokens per second, citing a benchmark from Artificial Analysis.
It's a competitive space. Smaller GPU maker Advanced Micro Devices announced earlier this year it would integrate its rack-scale systems with chips from Cerebras, which recently went public, focusing on low-latency inference. OpenAI's newly announced Ultrafast mode currently promises 750 tokens per second, and is "powered by Cerebras."
Low-latency chips don't replace the GPU, the workhorse of AI chips, which can do training as well as inference and are flexible enough to adapt to new technologies and models. Low-latency chips like Groq mainly focus on a part of serving models called the "decode" phase.
"This isn't about replacing GPUs," Harris said. "It's about using the right price, right processor for the right part of the workload."
Nvidia is currently ramping up shipments of its Vera Rubin systems, which started production earlier this year. At the Vera Rubin and Groq 3 LPX unveiling in March, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang projected $1 trillion in cumulative sales between the current-generation Blackwell chips and the new Vera Rubin systems, through 2027.
Huang said at the time he would allocate a quarter of data center space intended for coding applications to Groq chips.
"The rest of my data center is all 100% Vera Rubin," Huang said.
Nvidia is scheduled to report earnings on Wednesday.

Homa Theater hosting adaptation of Jean Teulé’s book
TEHRAN – The play “The Suicide Shop,” based on the book of the same name by French novelist Jean Teulé, is on stage at Homa Theater in Tehran.
Hossein Nasiri has directed this loose adaptation, which has Davoud Geravand, Arezou Sarraf Rezaei, Yeganeh Vaqefi, Elnaz Shakeri, Shahrzad Alimohammadi, Ali Khatibi, Arshia Hosseini, Asal Zendegani, and Mojdeh Mokhtari in the cast, among others.
“The Suicide Shop” is a black comedy novel, published in 2006. Set in a near-apocalyptic city grappling with the severe consequences of climate change, the narrative unfolds in a world where pervasive sadness reigns, reflecting the grim atmosphere surrounding its characters.
At the core of this novel is the Tuvache family, whose name draws inspiration from three renowned suicides: the father, nicknamed Mishima, pays homage to the Japanese author Yukio Mishima; the eldest son, Vincent, takes his name from the troubled artist Vincent van Gogh; and their daughter, Marilyn, mirrors the iconic actress, Marilyn Monroe. Their younger son, Alain, named after the brilliant mathematician Alan Turing, stands out as the sole ray of hope in a family entrenched in despair.
The Tuvaches run a shop specializing in suicide paraphernalia, offering grim products and instructions to customers aiming to end their lives amid an environment characterized by hopelessness.
However, Alain is born with an unwelcome spark of optimism that disrupts the family's embrace of melancholy. His siblings, Vincent and Marilyn—each grappling with their own existential issues—struggle to thwart Alain's positivity. Vincent is an emaciated figure, consumed by his creativity in designing the shop's morose inventory, while Marilyn battles obesity and loathing for her existence.
As the story unfolds, Alain's intrinsic joy gradually transforms the family dynamics, challenging the pervasive gloom that envelops them. The family's attempts to pull Alain back into their cynical worldview ultimately fail.
In a surprising twist, over time, the Suicide Shop evolves into a novelty store, shedding its morbid roots and finding unexpected vitality. Paradoxically, despite his uplifting influence on the family, Alain's journey culminates in tragedy; he decides to take his own life, recognizing that he provided a purpose for others to reject despair and embrace life.
The novel's unique premise also inspired an animated adaptation directed by Patrice Leconte. Critics have praised Teulé's work, noting its careful balance of humor and somber themes.
Jean Teulé (1953-2022) was an illustrator, filmmaker, and television presenter. He is also the prize-winning author of over 20 books.
“The Suicide Shop” will remain on stage until September 4 at the Homa Theater, located at Ziba Dead-End, Nofel Loshato St., Hafez St.

Turkish Radio and Television Supreme Council, Cinema Museum of Iran discuss mutual cooperation
TEHRAN – In an effort to develop cultural and cinematic cooperation between the Islamic Republic of Iran and Turkey, a delegation from the Turkish Radio and Television Supreme Council (RTUK) visited the Cinema Museum of Iran in Tehran on Saturday.
During the visit, the Turkish delegation met with Fatemeh Mohammadi Sijani, Director General of the Museum, to discuss potential avenues for cooperation in cinema, research, education, and co-productions, ILNA reported.
The Turkish delegation included Feyza Gizligider, head of the Strategy Development Department at RTUK, along with Fatma Güleç, deputy of the Strategy Development Department of the RTUK.
During the visit, the Turkish delegation toured various sections of the museum and examined a collection of historical artifacts, documents, equipment, and items significant to Iranian cinema history. They were also provided with presentations regarding the origins of cinema in Iran and the evolution of film technology within the country.
Expressing her admiration for the history of Iranian cinema, Feyza Gizligider noted that the arrival of cinema cameras in Iran—only five years after their invention—was a particularly fascinating aspect. Highlighting the documentation activities and existing capacities in both nations, she emphasized the importance of expanding cultural and academic collaborations.
While noting that Turkey also possesses a cinema museum, she described the Cinema Museum of Iran as a comprehensive and significant collection. She expressed hope for the development of academic ties between the Iran Cinema Museum and Turkish universities.
For her part, Mohammadi detailed the museum’s diverse capabilities, stating that its activities extend far beyond the mere preservation and display of cinematic equipment. The museum also houses cinematic literature from around the world and various film scripts.
Highlighting the museum’s research institute and its established links with Iranian film universities, Mohammadi expressed readiness to establish similar connections and partnerships with Turkish film universities.
In another segment of the meeting, the Turkish delegation emphasized the importance of providing “media literacy” training to filmmakers, noting that such specialized training has a more profound impact compared to general public education.
The establishment of film analysis sessions involving film students from both countries was also proposed as a key area for cooperation. It was suggested that Turkish film students travel to Iran to participate in these sessions, while Iranian students would conversely attend similar programs in Turkey. Based on this vision, direct dialogue and the exchange of cinematic perspectives between students are expected to lead to effective and sustainable scientific and cultural engagement.
Furthermore, the proposal to establish a “Kiarostami School” was raised as a potential pillar of educational and cultural cooperation.
The meeting underscored vast opportunities for bilateral cooperation across various cinematic fields, including co-production, educational programs, student exchange, research collaboration, film analysis, and the exchange of expertise in media policy and content monitoring.
Gizligider noted the Council’s responsibility regarding the monitoring of film and media content in Turkey. She highlighted the cultural sensitivities and shared values existing between the two countries in this regard.
Mohammadi referenced successful cultural collaborations among member states of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO), including the idea of producing a joint film. She suggested exploring a similar initiative among the member states of the Economic Cooperation Organization (ECO).
She proposed that, with the participation of ECO member states, a joint cinematic project could be produced to facilitate cooperation among filmmakers and showcase the cultural and artistic capacities of these nations. Mohammadi noted that such a project could serve as an effective cultural tool to better introduce the ECO organization and strengthen cultural ties, moving toward implementation upon further review and agreement.
In conclusion, both parties emphasized the readiness and potential for expanding cultural, cinematic, research, and educational cooperation, expressing hope that continued engagement will pave the way for joint projects and the exchange of expertise between the cinematic and academic centers of Iran and Turkey.

Attacks on U.N. personnel are rare but not unprecedented in South Sudan, where U.N. patrols operate in volatile areas affected by intercommunal fighting, armed youth mobilizations and clashes involving government forces.
