Survey shows attitudes on oil scandal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:43:44 UTC
01:43:44 KST

A public survey on food safety related to the Central Union Oil Corp (CUOC) soybean oil scandal released yesterday showed that 61 percent of the respondents have no confidence in the government’s food safety inspection mechanism and 63 percent are against allowing sales of processed food products containing less than 20 percent of CUOC’s problem oil.
CUOC, which was jointly established by Taisun Enterprise Co (泰山企業), Fwusow Industry Co (福壽實業) and Formosa Oilseed Processing Co (福懋油脂), was ultimately found to have seven noncompliant batches of soybean oil; the first was reported to regulators on June 30.
Yen Yung-shen (顏永森), the Grassroots Influence Foundation’s convenor of polling, said the foundation commissioned TVBS Poll Center to conduct a computer-assisted telephone interviewing survey from Aug. 7 to 13.
Photo: CNA
It collected a total of 1,147 responses from people aged 18 or older, with a margin of error of 2.9 percentage points, Yen said.
The survey showed 69 percent of the respondents were worried that they would consume the benzopyrene-tainted cooking oil when eating out, while 26 percent were not concerned.
Fifty-two percent of respondents said they were unsatisfied with the government’s response speed in conducting inspections, seizures and removal of products, while 29 percent were satisfied; and 63 percent were against allowing sales of oil products containing less than 20 percent of CUOC’s problem oil, while 21 percent supported the policy, the survey showed.
Regarding the government’s food safety management ability, 61 percent of the respondents have no confidence in the inspection mechanism, while 30 percent were confident; and 54 percent were unsatisfied with the government’s handling of the scandal, while 33 percent were satisfied.
Asked if they agree that heavy penalties and fines should be imposed on CUOC and its responsible managers, 87 percent of the respondents agreed, while only 4 percent disagreed.
The survey also showed that 43 percent of the respondents did not think Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) needs to resign over this scandal, while 41 percent thought he should, and 16 percent had no opinion.
The survey showed that people’s attitudes toward food safety do not entirely align with their political party affiliation, Former Health Promotion Administration director-general Chiou Shu-ti (邱淑媞) said.
“Even for people with obvious political stances, their body is honest,” she said, adding that even supporters of the ruling party were concerned about the possibility of consuming contaminated oil, showing that food safety is a livelihood issue transcending political lines.
The survey shows that about 70 percent of people are concerned about consuming contaminated oil when eating out — an anxiety shared across political parties, National Taipei University Department of Public Administration and Policy professor Liu Jia-wei (劉嘉薇) said.
Meanwhile, 63 percent do not support allowing oil products containing less than 20 percent of the tainted oil on store shelves, indicating that food safety concerns have not subsided following the incident, so the government should re-evaluate its decisions, she said.
The poll showed that 73 percent agree with a “zero-detection” policy for carcinogens, so the government should adopt the strictest standards for carcinogens in food products to alleviate public concerns at the source, the foundation said.
While 87 percent agreed that the companies and responsible people should face severe penalties, it also suggested the government should uphold the principle of strict enforcement, conduct speedy trials, and impose heavy penalties to deter companies not reporting abnormalities, and restoring public trust in food safety and the rule of law, it said.

China’s latest meme is a complete load of bull
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:43:43 UTC
01:43:43 KST

Frustrated stock investors in China are finding dark humor from a crude, low-budget film that has become a box office hit.
Niu Lai (牛來), which translates as “Here Comes the Bull,” is an 86-minute animation about a newborn calf that follows a skylark into an abstract dream sequence. In it, the calf, Niu Lai, encounters a mysterious cobra, befriends a young leopard and fights against a pack of wolves. He learns life lessons from his mother who sacrifices herself, so her son has a chance to escape the predators. When Niu Lai wakes up, he finds the strength to stand up and live a full life.
The film grossed just 7,700 yuan (US$1,145) in the first 10 days after its release on Aug. 5, but online discussions of how bad it is, especially the “hand-crafted” animation in the era of artificial intelligence (AI), has turned it into a meme not just for young audiences, but for retail investors. It has now generated more than 25 million yuan at the box office, the biggest dark horse — er, wrong species — of this summer’s movie season.
It was good timing. Having just emerged from a nasty wipeout last month, individual investors are turning the young bull’s personal growth story into a reflection of the brutal reality of being preyed on in China’s US$15 trillion stock market. They tend to chase after momentum stocks, and last month, this investment style had its worst drawdown in history.
The parallels came naturally. The mysterious cobra is perceived to be the shape-shifting K-line chart that millions of mom-and-pop investors use to read market psychology. However, just like Niu Lai, who gets bitten by the snake and becomes scared of it, over-reliance on technical analyses has not panned out, causing many to lose faith in their validity.
Over the last decade, good candlestick patterns, which many believe foretell upward market trends, are followed by negative 20-day returns 55 percent of the time, data compiled by Bloomberg Opinion showed. Clusters of strong technical indicators and poor returns tend to overlap with negative macro backdrops. Examples are 2022’s COVID-19 pandemic lockdowns, or in 2023, when China’s reopening failed to revive the economy, and in late 2024 after Beijing did not undertake the massive stimulus it had vaguely promised.
The young leopard, whom Niu Lai befriends, is uncannily called Bao La (豹拉). Its name can be translated as a sharp spike up. The brave Bao La tries to fend off a pack of wolves with little success — just like the many dead-cat bounces that Chinese traders are all too familiar with.
Niu Lai’s name is eerily called out many times during the movie, as the herd panics over predators and migrates across arid land with little food or water, hoping to get to a safer landing. Is this not the experience of a typical retail trader? There is no slow and steady bull; the benchmark CSI 300 Index is a perpetual manifestation of booms and busts, with less-informed investors caught out by brokerage hype. By comparison, average Americans are faring much better. They have come to rule the market, notching impressive gains by buying the dip.
With the aid of AI, the Internet is creating parodies with clever word plays. My favorite is a video that borrows from a scene in the movie, in which Niu Lai comes to his mother crying after tripping over a big stone. “Silly child, that’s semiconductors. Even dogs won’t touch them,” the mother says.
The benchmark index of Shanghai’s STAR board, which hosts chip companies that the exchange claims to align with “national strategies,” is down as much as 30 percent from its late June peak.
To be sure, the animation is poor quality, but watching the movie through an investor’s lens, it is full of symbolism and dark humor that bring knowing laughter. Here Comes the Bull is an ironic name in a nation that is perpetually waiting for one. It has become a meme for good reason.
Shuli Ren is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering Asian markets. A former investment banker, she was a markets reporter for Barron’s. She is a CFA charterholder. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

These conflicts are demonstrating that a less conventionally powerful state, by leveraging asymmetric capabilities, can impose major costs on an aggressor and fundamentally reshape the outcome of conflict. Taiwan is not only drawing lessons from those conflicts, but also translating them into practice. Far from seeking to match China ship for ship, missile for missile or aircraft for aircraft, Taiwan needs to make Chinese aggression so costly, problematic and uncertain that Beijing is deterred from launching an attack. Work harassment survivor fights for right to know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:43:42 UTC
01:43:42 KST

Kept in the dark after reporting her boss for harassment, South Korean advocate Baek Song-yi is now campaigning for survivors’ right to know how their bullies were disciplined.
Baek, 40, experienced first-hand a troubling paradigm in South Korea’s workplace harassment response, with victims often expected to keep silent while employers have no clear legal duty to tell them how their cases ended.
At her former company, a US firm with offices overseas, Baek said she was verbally harassed by her boss, an older man.
Photo: AFP
When she reported him, the company asked her to accept a confidentiality agreement warning she could be fired for disclosing information discussed during the process.
“I was just so stunned,” Baek said, adding that she had believed her employer encouraged victims to come forward.
Baek refused to accept the agreement and the investigation went ahead anyway, ultimately upholding her complaint.
The company still declined to disclose what disciplinary action had been taken, citing the need to “align with a privacy protection law” in South Korea, Baek said.
An investigator told her only that the harasser would be “monitored.”
Baek, who has since left the company, never learned whether her request to bar him from the firm’s South Korean office had been granted.
‘NO CLOSURE’
“I just felt like victims are left with no closure, no sense of justice and no way of knowing,” she said.
She is now campaigning for legislation asimilar to California’s Silenced No More Act, which restricts non-disclosure agreements in workplace harassment cases, and for a clear legal right for victims to be informed of disciplinary measures.
South Korea introduced a workplace anti-bullying law seven years ago, but critics say it fails to guarantee adequate protections.
A study last year by workplace abuse support group Gapjil 119 found that just 15.3 percent of victims reported harassment.
Nearly half of respondents said they believed action would change nothing, and about one-third feared career repercussions.
Experts say the law requires employers to act against confirmed harassers, but stops there, often leaving victims in the dark while shielding perpetrators and their reputation.
“Employers have full discretion over whether to disclose disciplinary action, as there is no provision requiring them to inform the victim,” labor attorney Kim Yu-kyung said.
A woman identified only by her surname Yoo spent about 10 months pursuing a complaint, only to face a Kafkaesque process to learn how it ended.
Her former employer, a South Korean firm, cited “privacy concerns,” saying only that action had been taken under “company rules.”
The Ministry of Employment and Labor, which upheld her complaint, later intervened, allowing Yoo to inspect the company rules — but only in person, without taking any photos or making notes.
Yoo discovered that the rules contained no provisions on workplace harassment, she said.
She was then told that her harasser had merely been asked to submit a written account of what happened.
Yoo, who quit over the harassment and waited until leaving to report it for fear of retaliation, said she suffered insomnia and panic attacks.
“I wondered what I had put myself through more than 10 months of stress and fighting for,” she said.
“It all felt a bit pointless,” she said.
RIGHT TO KNOW
In Baek’s case, she turned to Seoul’s regional labour office, hoping to find out what action had been taken.
Instead, she was told the company had complied with the law.
“There is no provision in the law requiring disclosure of what measures the perpetrator received,” a labor official said in a recorded call reviewed by Agence France-Presse.
The company was required only to ask Baek what measures she wanted before deciding what action to take, the official said.
Withholding the outcome to protect a perpetrator’s privacy is a “distorted interpretation,” labor attorney Kim said, adding that seeking victims’ views should also mean informing them of the decision.
Baek said that her former employer was “just using ambiguous law” to protect victims “in the most minimal way possible.”
“Victims should not be silenced, victims should be able to speak about their experiences” for their own safety and that of others, she said.
The labor ministry said it revised its workplace harassment guidelines last month, “recommending” employers share with victims the outcome of investigations and the basis for their conclusions.
However, it said mandating such disclosure would “require careful consideration,” weighing the involved parties’ privacy and individual rights.
Baek said she reached out to several South Korean lawmakers proposing restrictions on confidentiality agreements and a requirement that employers disclose disciplinary measures to victims.
None responded.

‘Taiwan Grapevine’: An expat time capsule from the end of martial law
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:43:40 UTC
01:43:40 KST

During the Martial Law era, newspapers and magazines were strictly controlled by the government. But from 1985 to 1990 — a period that straddled the lifting of martial law in 1987 — a free monthly expat magazine emerged as one of the first published and edited by foreigners. It was also perhaps the first to express a uniquely local expatriate voice.
Taiwan Grapevine’s articles were irreverent, politically incorrect and plagued by typos. Neither editors nor writers were named in the magazine, and those bylines that appeared were obvious pseudonyms like Archibald Hellbender.
Yet the magazine achieved nationwide distribution. And while its circulation is not known, similar publications that followed on its heels printed 15,000 to 20,000 issues per month.
In concept, Taiwan Grapevine plied the route of American ad-driven community magazines. In voice, it took inspiration from alternative US newspapers like Village Voice and the bawdy, gonzo reportage found in the likes of the Bangkok Post’s legendary bar column, “Night Owl.”
One article from Jan 1989, which loosely described a visit to Taipei Adventist Hospital, opened as follows:
“I had been nursing a bad liver for some time. I had found that I couldn’t take the grind of trade reports, market surveys, public relations consultations and so forth without drinking heavily. I was desperately casting about for something to do. I probably should have known better than to enter a den of Christians, but I randomly decided to check out the Seventh-Day Adventist Hospital’s five-day quit-smoking clinic. There might be an article there, I thought.”
Photo: David Frazier
Mainly, however, Taiwan Grapevine was a vehicle for community news. Dubbing itself “a publication for the Taiwan expatriate community,” it reported on changing flight routes, holidays and festivals and the goings-on of international clubs and associations, including a number of veterans’ organizations that no longer exist. Advertising came from major expat watering holes of the day.
“There was really no other place to get information at that time in English,” said Trace Gomez, a 66-year-old American who served as Taiwan Grapevine’s final managing editor.
Describing the magazine as a “time capsule,” Gomez pointed to articles on having to apply to the phone company to hook up a modem or answering machine, the launch of Wellcome supermarkets, and the explosion of pubs and discos that accelerated during the 1980s.
“This was martial law-era news for foreigners,” he said.
GOING DIGITAL
Only around 50 issues of Taiwan Grapevine were ever published, and until recently the magazine was almost completely forgotten. I first learned of its existence around three years ago from Gomez, who showed me a large but deteriorating stack he’d kept stored in his basement.
Since then I’ve asked numerous Taiwan old-timers about it, but only a few had vague recollections.
Gomez, who built his career in manufacturing, says he inherited the magazine in late 1989 from its final editor and publisher Dennis Keagan, who died mysteriously in Thailand three years later.
Gomez had arrived in Taipei in 1987 and initially helped the magazine’s editors with layout and graphics. After taking charge, he went on to publish its final few issues before folding the publication around March 1990.
“When [Keagan] left, it fell in my lap totally,” said Gomez. “But I didn’t want to do it because I was already working full time.”
Now four decades later, Gomez — in part at my urging — has digitized the 13 issues of the magazine he can still locate and uploaded them to archive.org for all to access. He says he will continue to search for more issues and add them if possible.
‘GREATEST PUBLICATION’
The magazine was hardly Taiwan’s only English-language publication of its day. Daily newspapers of the time included the China Post and the China News. In 1970, AmCham Taipei also launched a newsletter, Taiwan Business Topics, which by the 1980s had become a magazine.
Taiwan Grapevine’s main competitor was another expatriate-run monthly, This Month in Taiwan. Founded in 1974 by an ex-military man, E. Kirk Henderson, that publication had a strong commercial focus and placed little value on original writing. According to Earl Wieman, an editor working in Taipei since the early 1970s, Henderson referred to everything except his advertisements as “non-revenue paper.”
Taiwan Grapevine set itself apart from this field with its irreverent voice and strong doses of irony. From its letters section, one can see that readers both loved and hated it.
One reader slammed an entire issue as “blatantly insulting to black people, women, and gays.” Another declared the bar column to be “gutter talk.”
But others praised the magazine. “Taiwan Grapevine is the greatest publication to ever hit the Taiwan expatriate community,” declared one reader.
Another opined, “A month without Grapevine is like a month without ketchup. Your efforts are deeply appreciated by those of us who are here by choice, who love Taiwan and its people and who dread the prospect of returning to the quagmire of reality that awaits us on the other side of the Pacific.”
‘GETTING ACQUAINTED’
One of Taiwan Grapevine’s more fascinating columns, “Getting Acquainted,” offered short biographies of long-term expats. These linked the roots of Taiwan’s foreign community to the end of World War II and — in the case of British tea merchant Frank Berger, who’d first arrived during the Japanese colonial era — even earlier.
One of these columns profiled one of ICRT’s first news readers, David G. White. A UK native, White had been present at D-Day in a spotter submarine and also fought for the British army in Burma. He first arrived in Taiwan in 1949 working for Civil Air Transport, a commercial airline that was acquired covertly by the CIA in 1950.
White eventually got into radio in 1955 when he took a job with the BBC in England. He then hopscotched the globe before returning to Taipei and ICRT in 1980 — the radio station’s second year of operation.
A column on American Ed Little offered just as much intrigue, though from a later generation. Little came to Asia as part of a US Marines Corps combat unit and fought in Vietnam from 1968 to 1969. During that tour, he “had the first seed of Buddhist dharma planted in his soul by a Bangkok prostitute.”
It was Buddhism that brought Little to Taiwan in the mid-1970s — to live as a monk at Kaohsiung’s Fo Guang Shan (佛光山寺) monastery. But he only lasted six months, complaining that there was “too much ‘Pureland’ chanting and not enough meditation.” He eventually walked out of the monastery in his orange robes, bought pants and a t-shirt in a Kaohsiung department store and started looking for work as an English teacher.
As Taiwan moved toward liberalization, the magazine also commented on the December 1986 election. An April 1987 column signed “Cyril H.B. Dilling” treated the democratic transition with a mixture of gravitas and barstool irony.
“We live in remarkable times… and are seeing elements of fundamental history played out before our very eyes,” wrote the magazine’s anonymous political columnist. Then, with eyes on the future, the column predicted that Taiwan “will find out that it is as impossible to be a little bit democratic as a little bit pregnant.” Finally, it welcomed Taiwan “on board the often leaky, sometimes badly ballasted Ship of Democracy.”
MYSTERY FOUNDER
It is perhaps impossible to know who wrote most of these articles. Even the identity of Taiwan Grapevine’s founder remains something of a mystery.
As government regulations made it difficult for foreigners to own media businesses, Gomez says the magazine operated under the aegis of publishing companies run by Taiwanese proxies.
As a result, the name of the magazine’s founder does not appear in business registration records, and he further concealed his identity by omitting a masthead. One guest editor noted that the founder, in addition to serving as managing editor, was “also the chief writer, sales executive, delivery boy and all around handyman,” but did not mention his name.
Gomez and former advertisers contacted for this article can only remember that Taiwan Grapevine’s founder was an American man named “Dave.”
Gomez remembers that “Dave” left Taiwan for Thailand around March 1989. At that time the magazine passed to Keagan, who he says wrote the bar column under the pseudonym Durdley Drinkright, before Keagan in turn gave the magazine to Gomez later that same year.
After the magazine folded in early 1990, Taiwan’s publishing landscape continued to liberalize. Later that decade, other publishing ventures sprang up that were ad-fueled and expat-targeted, including Taichung Compass, which began in 1994 and has been published continuously ever since.
According to Taichung Compass co-publisher, Courtney Donovan Smith, who is also a Taipei Times columnist, even into the late 1990s, “publishing magazines was still very much in a grey zone.”
Smith said that in those early years, his magazine was repeatedly targeted by citizen complaints, and the publishers were once called in by the police for questioning. But the magazine was cleared in every instance.
Later on, local governments “gave us positive attention because we were doing a better job than their own tourism bureaus at promoting what to do and where to go. Taichung mayor Jason Hu (胡志強) said as much, both to us personally and publicly in city council,” Smith said.
Taiwan Grapevine perhaps produced too little too early to leave such a lasting impression. But an archive can now be found online at: archive.org/details/taiwangrapevine/

US territories hit out at Trump plan to explore deep sea mining in the Pacific
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:43:40 UTC
01:43:40 KST

A US government plan to lease out millions of hectares of seabed near the Mariana Trench for deep sea exploration has drawn opposition from US territories in the Pacific, as US President Donald Trump’s administration remains locked in a race with China for control of critical ocean minerals.
The Marine Mineral Administration, an agency under the US Department of the Interior, on Tuesday last week released a proposal to auction deep sea mining leases for 28 million hectares of seafloor off the coast of the Northern Mariana Islands and Guam.
The leases would allow companies to explore the seabed and potentially extract deposits of critical minerals — known as polymetallic nodules — that could be used in batteries, electronics and defense technologies. Many environmental groups have opposed deep sea mining, arguing that more research is needed on its effects on marine ecosystems.
Photo: AFP
The Northern Mariana Islands is a self-governing commonwealth of the US, while Guam is an unincorporated territory of the US.
Northern Marianas Governor David Apatang has said his government would approach the Trump administration’s proposal “with extreme caution.”
Apatang, while acknowledging the strategic importance of critical minerals, said it was necessary that “no activity, survey or otherwise, takes place without rigorous scientific baseline studies, complete transparency, and explicit protections for our marine resources.”
He said his administration would “thoroughly examine the proposed terms over the next 60 days to ensure that the ecological integrity of our waters and the long-term wellbeing of the [Northern Marianas] are fully safeguarded.”
The Guardian approached the Marine Mineral Administration for comment.
In an earlier statement, the agency said it had completed an environmental review of proposed commercial leases for critical minerals in the Marianas area. It said it would consider comments from the governor.
A statement from the office of the governor of Guam acknowledged the Trump administration’s focus on national security and strategic needs, but added: “National security cannot mean asking the people of the Pacific to accept environmental risks before those risks are fully understood.
“We’re unequivocally opposed to the deep sea mining efforts in this region,” Guam Lieutenant Governor Joshua Tenorio said.
“The Department of Interior is giving assurances that mining activity is not going to commence with the awarding of these licenses, [but] I think that this is a matter where we can’t really trust that because this has been rapidly evolving,” he said.
The proposed lease notice for deep sea exploration in the Marianas region came just weeks after the initiation of a leasing process for 12.4 million hectares of American Samoa’s seafloor, with plans to award contracts in November.
American Samoa Governor Nikolau Pula said his government remained opposed to deep sea mining, adding that untested extraction processes could harm the territory’s tuna industry, which fuels its economy.
On Wednesday last week, environmental groups in American Samoa and Hawaii launched legal proceedings against the US government to halt the proposed auction of seafloor permits around the islands, alleging that federal agencies failed to evaluate the destructive impact mineral extractions could have on marine ecosystems.
In a Hawaii court, Fa’asao Ameika Samoa and the Conservation Council for Hawaii warned that the extraction machinery “can destroy nearly all life in its path” and “stirs up sediments that can introduce toxic substances into the food web and smother seafloor ecosystems.”
“Even just exploring for seabed minerals introduces extremely loud noise into the marine environment that can harm marine mammals and other wildlife,” the complaint reads.
The Marine Mineral Administration was approached about the concerns over the American Samoa leasing process.

European leaders yesterday joined Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy in Kyiv for celebrations marking the 35th anniversary of Ukraine’s Independence Day as Russia pressed on with its four-year-old invasion of the country.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, on his first overseas trip since taking office last month, joined almost a dozen other European leaders, as well as other dignitaries, including European Council President Antonio Costa, in Kyiv.
Photo: AFP
“For Ukraine, independence is not an abstract idea. We defended it against all odds,” Ukrainian Minister of Foreign Affairs Andrii Sybiha said on social media. “In times like these, nations learn how important it is to have allies by your side.”

Zelenskiy said in a speech at Kyiv’s St Sophia Square that the presence of European leaders reflected continental fears about Russia’s wider ambitions.
Photo: Reuters
“We all understand that in this Russian war against us — against Ukraine — far more is being decided than the future of Ukraine and Eastern Europe,” Zelenskiy said, adding that foreign help was vital.

SCALP is the French version of the UK’s Storm Shadow missile, with both systems incorporating shared French and British technology.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the Kremlin views the plan “extremely negatively.”
He accused the UK of “taking part in this war” on Kyiv’s side.

Both Russia and Ukraine are trying through long-range strikes to inflict economic pain, disrupt military supplies and erode public morale.
Ukraine’s long-range drones have repeatedly hit facilities in Russia’s vital oil industry, causing fuel shortages, and have also engaged in a campaign against Russia’s largest online retailer, Wildberries.

Stubb: Strikes deep inside Russia are a smart strategy for Ukraine
Finnish President Alexander Stubb said this at a press conference following the Coalition of the Willing summit in Kyiv, in response to a question about his view of Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries and online retail networks, according to Ukrinform.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:41:37 UTC
01:41:37 KST

Rupert Lowe, the leader of Restore Britain, is on course to earn as much from the social media platform X as he does from his salary as an MP, after surging income from posts that include demands for mass deportations.
Lowe has earned £932 an hour for his posts on X, formerly Twitter, since the start of the year, according to his own declarations in the register of MPs’ financial interests, which detail how many hours he has spent on X for each payment he received from the platform.
The figure is more than twice the £377 an hour on average he earned last year. His hourly rate rose steeply again this summer, reaching £1,476 since the start of June.
X critics claim it is further evidence that X is favouring and incentivising divisive political content, pulling the UK’s political discourse to the right. Elon Musk, the site’s owner, has repeatedly amplified Lowe’s posts.
Under X’s revenue-sharing scheme, premium subscribers such as Lowe are paid based on the performance of their posts. The scheme resulted in record payouts last year. The platform recently announced forthcoming changes, designed to reward original content and commentary.
Lowe’s total income from X since the 2024 general election has now surpassed £105,000. He earned more than half of that in the first eight months of 2026.
Should his average earnings for 2026 so far continue throughout the year, he would earn just over £93,000 – close to the current MPs’ £98,599 annual salary. He could easily exceed that figure should the higher rate of earnings of recent months persist.
Lowe has previously said he donates his net MP’s salary to charities and worthy causes in his constituency of Great Yarmouth.
The politician’s extraordinary success on X has led to concerns among some campaigners, who fear it is a sign that Musk’s site is effectively funding an MP that reflects the hard-right views of the billionaire.
“We tend to treat a politician’s online reach and their income as two separate stories, but for Rupert Lowe they’re part of the same mechanism,” said Ambrose Pym, a researcher covering the far right and technology who analysed Lowe’s rising X earnings. “The more his content is seen, the more X pays him for it.
“Scrutiny is rightly falling on other sources of foreign money in British politics. However, a US-based billionaire simultaneously paying and boosting an ideologically aligned British politician through his own platform is going strikingly under-reported. X’s financial and reach incentive structure rewards division and is shaping British politics with almost none of the scrutiny it deserves.”
Lowe, who founded Restore Britain after leaving Nigel Farage’s Reform UK, describes his party’s most significant achievement as “dragging mass deportations [of migrants] into mainstream politics”.
Asked about his accelerating X earnings, Lowe told the Guardian: “If I wanted to make money, I would not be in politics. I donate my entire net MP salary to local charities in my constituency – being a politician is the most expensive job I’ve ever had.”
His recent posts on X show the extraordinary amount of engagement the Restore leader secures on the platform. Over the weekend, one of his posts stated: “An illegal migrant could read ten thousand Home Office pamphlets in some woeful attempt to ‘integrate’, I’d still want him deported.
“They broke into our country – they are not welcome here, and they all need to be removed. This is not complicated.” It received 1.3m views, 25,000 likes and 3,000 reposts.
Last week, a post about how the UK should replicate Portugal’s ban on the burqa in many public spaces received almost a million views.
Lowe’s previous posts have included describing diversity policies as a “wicked, malicious, viperous cancer” and have criticised illegal migrants as “unvetted foreign males” loitering “where your daughter walks home”.
The Guardian has contacted X with a request for comment.

The Duke of Sussex has stepped down from the board of a major African wildlife charity that had been at the centre of a human rights controversy.
Prince Harry’s spokesperson confirmed he was no longer a trustee of African Parks, which admitted last year that human rights abuses were committed by its rangers in the Republic of the Congo.
The charity’s admission followed an independent review into allegations made by members of the Baka community.
In a 2024 report published by the Mail on Sunday newspaper, community members accused African Parks rangers of beating, waterboarding and raping locals to stop them from accessing their ancestral forests, which are now in a conservation area.
After the review, African Parks published a statement acknowledging that human rights abuses occurred in the Odzala-Kokoua national park, which it manages. It said that it had improved its safeguarding processes both at the park and institutionally.
A spokesperson for Harry said the duke, who was president of the charity for six years before he became a member of its board of directors in 2023, remained an active and avid supporter of African Parks.
“The duke is proud of his 10 years with African Parks and fully supports the ongoing strengthening of its board,” the spokesperson said.
“His commitment to conservation in Africa continues, and he remains a supporter of African Parks’ mission.”
Survival International, a global human rights charity that campaigns for the rights of Indigenous people, had called on Harry to step down as a member of the board.
Caroline Pearce, the executive director of Survival International, said it was “outrageous that for 10 years Prince Harry has served African Parks” while people working for it had “been responsible for abuse and violence against Indigenous people. His departure doesn’t undo that record — African Parks itself must now be held accountable, and must abandon this model of fortress conservation for good.”
Founded 26 years ago, African Parks manages more than 20m hectares (50m acres) in partnership with 13 African governments and hundreds of local communities.
African Parks expressed “deep gratitude” to the duke on concluding his tenure after his 10-year commitment to the organisation.
“His relationship with the organisation dates back to Malawi in July 2016, when he supported one of the largest elephant translocations in history. He served as president for six years before being appointed a member of the board of directors,” it said.
“Over the years, the duke has brought global attention to the urgent need for biodiversity protection for the benefit of people and wildlife, and has contributed greatly to promoting philanthropy for the cause of conservation in Africa. The duke remains deeply committed to this cause, and remains a strong supporter of African Parks’ work.”
The announcement comes as the Duke and Duchess of Sussex are due to relocate to the UK from California with their children, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five.
Former Suits star Meghan is said to be pursuing an acting role, with reports she has been in talks about a role in the third series of Guy Ritchie’s Netflix hit The Gentlemen, swiftly followed by other reports that the deal was off.
The couple are understood to be planning an “extended stay” in the UK, and their children are already enrolled in school, but it has not been confirmed for how long.

Israeli authorities change name of Jerusalem’s Damascus Gate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:39:33 UTC
01:39:33 KST

Breadcrumb
Israeli authorities change name of Jerusalem’s historic Damascus Gate in unprecedented move
Israeli authorities have changed the name of one of the historic gates leading to the highly revered al-Aqsa mosque in occupied East Jerusalem, triggering major concerns that this is an example of the latest efforts to change the character of the area.
Photographs of roads leading to Al-Aqsa now show signs which refer to the gate as the ‘Ancient Gate’ in Arabic, English and Hebrew.
Fakhri Abu Diab, a member of Al-Aqsa’s board of trustees, told The New Arab that the move to change the signs “is part of Israel’s plans to change the visual identity of areas with Palestinian, Arabic and Islamic symbolism in Jerusalem”.
Abu Diab noted that Israeli authorities started off with one of the most prominent and important gates in the Old City, which is sometimes referred to as “Victory Gate” – a name that emerged after the Second Intifada.
“The gate’s name also has significance in Islamic history, as it is one of the entrances to the Old City and is linked to the narrative of Salahaddin passing through this side during the recapturing of Jerusalem in 1187,” he continued.
Sources who spoke to The New Arab said that the move was clearly motivated to erase Islamic history and significance, as Sultan Suliman the Magnificent street leads to the gate, sending a message that any historical context will be removed. The sources also noted this comes as there has been a surge in Muslim tourists visiting from Turkey.
According to Abu Diab, the choice of the new name – Ancient Gate - has links to Talmudic Jewish narratives.
“These narratives claim there was a gate in this area that was once used to access what they refer to as the Temple. It passes through Silwan and heads towards the Al-Aqsa mosque, passing through what Talmudic narratives refer to as facilities associated to the Temple, such as the Silwan Spring.”
Members of Al-Aqsa’s board of trustees told The New Arab that the change in name was not merely a matter of linguistics but rather is a direct attempt to associate Israeli and Jewish narratives with the site, to allow Israelis to claim that the gate existed during the period described in those accounts, and that it was a path leading to what Israel refers to as the ‘temple’.
Israelis refer to Al-Aqsa as the Temple Mount, based on their belief that two ancient Jewish temples once stood there - the temple built by King Solomon, which was destroyed by the Babylonians, and the Second Temple, destroyed by the Romans.
Israeli extremists have called for Jewish prayer at al-Aqsa, despite this violating a long-held agreement, and some call for the destruction of the mosque and the building of a Jewish temple.
Palestinians have also raised concerns that changing the names and changing signs to make them Hebrew reinforces the Israeli narrative among tourists visiting the city, further stripping it of its heritage.
Far-right Israeli ministers regularly storm al-Aqsa.

Mudra's defense team asking court, journalists to take critical look at prosecution's wording
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
19:39:02 EEST
01:39:02 KST

The defense team for Iryna Mudra, the former deputy head of the President's Office who is suspected of involvement in corruption schemes involving money laundering and corporate raiding, is calling on the High Anti-Corruption Court (HACC) and media representatives to take a critical view of the statements made by the prosecutor in justifying the need to impose a preventive measure in the form of pretrial detention with an alternative bail of UAH 150 million.
Speaking on Monday at the HACC hearing on the selection of a preventive measure for Mudra, the defense specifically pointed out that the phrase from the National Security and Defense Council (NSDC) document regarding "control of corruption" does not actually belong to Mudra, and that the context of the phrase has been altered. The attorney explained that "control of corruption" is an indicator as defined by the World Bank – that is, a metric that measures a country's level of protection against corruption. It was precisely in this context, according to the defense, that this phrase was used.
In other words, as Mudra's defense asserts, the excerpts from the covert investigative actions cited by the prosecutor are incomplete; the prosecutor does not provide full quotes, thereby distorting the meaning of the conversations.
"I ask the court not to rely on subjective interpretations," the attorney urged, adding that he calls on media representatives to do the same.
In general, according to the defense, there is no need to impose a preventive measure as such, since the risks listed by the prosecutor do not exist. According to him, Mudra has not changed her place of residence or traveled abroad at any time, and while covert investigative actions were being conducted, the prosecutor's office never once applied to the court regarding the need to impose a preventive measure.
"A preventive measure is not mandatory… There is no such obligation under the Code of Criminal Procedure. We will ask the court to refuse to impose a preventive measure altogether," the attorney said.

Coalition of Willing reiterates Ukraine's 'inherent right' to defend itself against Russia

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24

Marking the 35th anniversary of Ukraine's independence, the Coalition of the Willing countries have reaffirmed Kiev's "clear and inherent right" to defend itself against Russia.
"They were united in their continued support of Ukraine’s fight to defend its sovereignty, freedom and territorial integrity," a joint statement on Monday said after the leaders of the Coalition of the Willing convened in the capital Kiev and by video conference to commemorate the 35th anniversary of the restoration of Ukraine’s independence, as the erstwhile Soviet Union’s collapse was imminent.
The leaders condemned Russia’s "systematic and escalating" strikes on Ukraine’s cities, critical infrastructure, and civilians during the meeting co-chaired by UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, French President Emmanuel Macron, and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
"Leaders reiterated Ukraine’s clear and inherent right to defend itself against the Russian war of aggression, in full compliance with international law and Article 51 of the UN Charter," said the statement.
They said they would not be deterred from their support for Ukraine by what they called "irresponsible Russian threats".
The statement also condemned Russia’s attacks on Ukraine’s cultural heritage sites, which form an integral part of Ukraine’s national identity, including the Kiev-Pechersk Lavra, a historic monastery.
"The coalition would continue to prepare the multinational force for Ukraine to deploy once a credible cessation of hostilities was in place, as part of a wider set of robust politically and legally binding security guarantees to ensure Ukraine’s future security and prosperity once a ceasefire enters into force," it added.
Immediate assistance
The leaders also agreed on the urgency of providing "immediate assistance" for Ukraine’s energy sector ahead of the coming winter, including through the Ukraine Energy Support Fund and providing specialised equipment.
They voiced determination to increase military support to Ukraine, strengthen its air defence as a matter of urgent priority, enhance cooperation with its defence industry, and share relevant technologies, including through the Anti-Ballistic Missile Coalition.
The statement also stressed the need to continue to support Ukraine’s economic resilience in the face of Russia’s intensified attempts to renew its maritime blockade on Ukraine’s ports.
Telling how joint efforts through sanctions and economic measures have deprived "Russia’s war chest" of at least $495 billion since February 2022, when the war began, the leaders said they welcomed the US Senate’s efforts to apply further economic pressure on Russia.
The statement also commended Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s “continued readiness” to enter into meaningful peace talks to bring about a comprehensive, just, and lasting peace, and reiterated their call for Russia to agree to a full, immediate, and unconditional ceasefire starting from the line of contact.
Concluding, the leaders once again reaffirmed their commitment to support Ukraine’s independence as part of Europe’s wider peace and security.

Earth’s oceans just hit their hottest temperature ever—it’s only going to get worse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:38:53 UTC
01:38:53 KST

Average ocean temperatures hit a record 21.10 degrees Celsius (69.98 degrees Fahrenheit) on August 22, according to the European Union’s Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S).
That’s not as hot as a warm bath, but it is the hottest the world’s oceans have been since C3S started keeping records in 1979.
“As a climate scientist, this is not surprising to me all,” says Zachary Labe, a climate scientist at Climate Central, a climate research nonprofit. “It’s consistent with decades of research showing how our climate is changing as the planet warms. And without reductions in the burning of fossil fuels, this warming will only continue.”
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The previous high, with a temperature of 21.09 degrees C (69.96 degrees F), occurred in March 2024, C3S said in a statement.
The new high also reflects the fact that we are heading into an exceptionally strong El Niño year. This cyclic climate pattern is marked by unusually hot Pacific Ocean temperatures, which can affect the entire planet’s weather.
“This record is another clear signal of an ocean under growing stress,” said Samantha Burgess, strategic lead for climate at the European Center for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF), in the same statement.
Hotter ocean temperatures can worsen sea-level rise, disrupt weather patterns and pose dangers to sea life such as coral reefs, Labe says. “These changes can affect nearly every part of society, including the economy, coastal infrastructure and global security.”
The new record is unlikely to last long, he adds. “This won’t be the last time we say this, and unfortunately, it’s very possible we could break this record again in the coming months,” Labe says.

A massive data center hub is likely heating up a town outside London
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:38:12 UTC
01:38:12 KST

Is a massive data center hub heating up a town outside London?
Slough, England — Residents of the small industrial town of Slough, just west of London, told CBS News the soaring temperatures have been difficult to bear this year as Britain records its hottest summer ever. But emerging research suggests Slough may have had it particularly rough, as it sits next to the second largest data center hub on the planet.
"Slough is very hot. Every year we think this is the hottest, and then the next year it gets hotter than the last," Nabeel Nawaz, who runs a restaurant in the center of the town, told CBS News as he sweltered through a July heatwave with temperatures in the 90s.
The low hum of cooling units on Slough's massive data center hub, less than two miles from the heart of the town, provides a non-stop soundtrack for the surrounding area.
The coolers regulate the temperature of the hundreds of computer servers inside the cavernous buildings, of which there are about 40 in Slough, transferring excess heat from the machines into water or air and then venting or evaporating the heat into the atmosphere outside.
Many of the data centers around the world work this way, and all that excess heat could be creating a "heat island effect," increasing local temperatures by an average of 3.6 degrees Fahrenheit, with extreme localized temperature spikes of up to 16 degrees, according to research published by scientists at the University of Cambridge earlier this year.
"We tried to work at scale. We started to look at data centers we could identify around the world and we found around 11,000 locations," Andrea Marinoni, a co-author of the research paper, told CBS News. "The temperature increase that we found was consistent in different areas of the world."
While the research by Marinoni and his colleagues did not include Slough's data center hub, he told CBS News the sheer scale of the facility raises even bigger questions about the potential impact of a heat island effect for residents in the densely populated area.
"There are more and more situations where these data centers are concentrated in one single plot of land," he said. "So, this is an experiment, in the sense that the compound effect of all of these different facilities very close to each other has not been studied yet."
CBS News compared local weather station data on daily temperatures in and around the data center campus in July to two other nearby towns, Windsor and Uxbridge, and found Slough was just over one degree warmer on average over the course of the month.
"It's really hot. I cannot sit down without a fan here, whereas normally in the morning, 9 a.m., 10 a.m., it should be fine without a fan, so maybe it's to do with that," Khadija, who lives in a neighborhood right next to the data center complex, told CBS News. She declined to give her full name.
A spokesperson for Digital Realty, a real estate company that maintains some of the data centers in Slough and provides services to U.S. tech giants including Amazon and Microsoft, told CBS News that "any large development, whether it's a warehouse, a mall, a parking lot, can contribute to localized warming by replacing natural land cover with pavement and buildings."
"We keep heat output low by operating our facilities efficiently, using light-colored roofing and paving that reflect rather than absorb solar energy, maximizing green space and tree cover, and minimizing paved surface area," the spokesperson said. "The result is a smaller heat footprint than you might expect and significantly better than the industry average."
Experts who spoke with CBS News agree that any concrete structure can increase local temperatures, but some say the infrastructure associated with data centres like the ones in Slough could amplify that effect significantly.
"The part where data centers are a little bit different is they are often a giant block, so as far as built environments go, it's the worst you can imagine for the urban heat island effect," Ladd Keith, an Associate Professor of Planning at the University of Arizona, told CBS News Thursday.
"As we see more data centers of this scale being built around the world, we need more evidence on how much waste heat is being emitted by them in different geographies and different climates," he said. "I think one other really important question is, is this a bubble for data center building, or will it be sustained and continue for a longer time?"

‘We Don’t Need Canada’: Trump Escalates Trade War With Threat of 50% Auto Tariffs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

16:37:53 UTC
01:37:53 KST

President Donald Trump threatened to raise automobile tariffs on Canada to 50% as the trade rift and political slanging match between the neighboring nations escalated.
Trump announced Monday morning that U.S. tariffs on all Canadian cars and trucks, automotive parts, and steel will increase to 50% starting Jan. 1, 2027.
“Build in the U.S. and there are zero tariffs. Canada will be treated like a State no longer! On trade, and in other ways, also, they are among the worst nations in the world to deal with,” he said on social media.
Trump’s comments came after trade talks between the two countries broke down, with each side accusing the other of making eleventh-hour demands that derailed negotiations.
“They feel entitled, and yet, we don’t need Canada, they need us!” the President said, repeating his accusation that “Canada has been ripping off the United States of America for years.”
Trump previously touted the nearly finished deal between the two countries last Tuesday.
However, negotiations broke down on Friday, and the Administration's 50% tariffs on about $20 billion worth of imports into the U.S. from Canada took effect Saturday.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney vowed to match the U.S.’s tariffs “dollar for dollar.”
“We are stronger now than when the United States started this trade war. More unified, more determined, and more ambitious,” Carney said during a press conference Saturday, referring to the year-long trade rift that has come to affect both countries.
“Last spring, I warned that America is trying to break us so that they can own us. And promised: “That will never, ever happen.” We are keeping that promise. Canada is becoming stronger and less dependent on America.”
Both sides have since blamed the other for making unreasonable demands late in the negotiating process.
“While we believed, earlier this week, that we were moving toward a mutually beneficial agreement, in recent days, the U.S. proposed new terms that were uneconomic, unfair, and undermined the net benefits to Canada, calling into question the reliability of any deal,” Carney said on Saturday. “In short, they asked too much and offered too little.”
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, meanwhile, framed the breakdown in negotiations as leaving the U.S. with little choice but to retaliate against Canada.
“We’ve said enough, and so we’ve taken countermeasures. Our interest is in protecting American workers and protecting American supply chains,” he told "Fox & Friends" on Saturday.
Greer said the Republican Administration had offered to cut tariffs on steel, autos, and lumber, “things that are sensitive for them. And they’ve always had the best deal, and they still would have an even better deal, but they didn’t want that.”
As a result, he said, “We’re moving forward with measures that respond to Canadian retaliation.”
The broader 50% tariffs that took effect Saturday were initially announced in July, and would affect around 5% of trade between the U.S.-Canada.
Shortly after the collapse of the talks, Trump took to Truth Social on Sunday and said that Canada “wants the benefits of being a State, without being one” and that it has “also charged our great farmers, for many years, massive amounts of tariffs. No more!!!”
Despite not being clear what the President meant, Trump has repeatedly expressed his desire to annex Canada and make it the 51st U.S. state—an idea Carney has strongly rejected.
Canada retaliates as U.S. lawmakers warn of higher costs
The collapse of the deal and escalating trade tensions between Washington and Ottawa have been met with both praise and criticism on either side of the border.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford praised Carney for standing firm and refusing to accept what he described as a “bad deal.”
“It was a bad deal for Ontario. It was a bad deal for the auto sector, the steel sector and manufacturing sector,” he said. “We never started this fight, but I can assure you we're going to win.”
On the U.S. side, Trump has faced criticism from both sides of the aisle.
Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota said Trump’s tariffs “have created higher costs and chaos.”
“His 50% tariffs on Canadian goods will raise prices. And now Canada is retaliating dollar for dollar, which will hurt Minnesota farmers, businesses, and workers,” she said Monday of the newly announced tariffs.
Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine similarly warned that the “on-again/off-again trade talks between the U.S. and Canada lead to higher costs, risk, and uncertainty for Maine businesses.”
“If the Administration proceeds with these tariffs, they will increase costs for Maine families, as most businesses will have no choice but to pass on the tariffs to their customers through higher prices,” she said Saturday after trade talks broke down, urging “both sides to return to the negotiating table.”
Democratic Gov. Abigail Spanberger of Virginia warned that this latest round of automobile tariffs will have “devastating consequences.”
“President Trump’s new 50% tariffs on Canada will disrupt supply chains and raise costs for Virginia businesses of every size and in every industry, and retaliatory tariffs will hurt Virginians,” she said Monday.

Will China Rewrite the Rules of Global Supply Chains?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:37:00 UTC
01:37:00 KST

Faced with the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act (UFLPA), U.S. legislation that presumes any goods made in Xinjiang involved forced labor, as well as with new European forced labor rules, China has not retreated. Instead, Beijing is building its own corporate responsibility and supply chain standards, limiting how some Western audit and standards systems operate in China, and promoting China-led standards abroad.
China’s Ministry of Commerce recently accused the Responsible Business Alliance (RBA) of assisting U.S. sanctions against China over alleged forced labor in Xinjiang and barred Chinese organizations and individuals from doing business or cooperating with it. The RBA is one of the world’s largest corporate social responsibility initiatives; it has over 600 member companies that together employ more than 21.5 million workers. Its Responsible Minerals Initiative runs the Responsible Minerals Assurance Process (RMAP), the only supply chain due diligence scheme so far formally recognized by the EU under its Conflict Minerals Regulation.
According to the publicly disclosed list of RMAP conformant and active facilities, as of January 31, 2026, 71 out of 196, or 36.2 percent, of the cobalt, tantalum, tin, and tungsten smelters and refiners were located in mainland China.
For years, many Chinese companies and suppliers have participated in RBA-related auditing and compliance systems, even though the Chinese government has never formally recognized the RBA. Now, as China’s economic power and international influence have grown, Beijing is moved to head off any such cooperation. The significance of the RBA sanctions thus goes far beyond corporate compliance – it is part of a broader shift through which China is moving from the position of rule-taker to that of rule-maker in global supply chains.
I have watched this shift develop for several years. In 2023, in New York, I met with a representative of the China Association of Social Workers, a government-linked organization. At the time, the organization was reaching out to China Labor Watch and other overseas groups working on labor and forced labor issues. The Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act had recently taken effect in the United States, and Europe was moving toward its own forced labor rules.
In retrospect, I can see that those contacts appear to have been part of a broader effort to understand the existing international system as Chinese institutions became increasingly active in developing standards of their own.
By 2025, this shift had become much more apparent. At an Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) forum in Paris, Jiang Hui, chairman of the China Chamber of Commerce of Metals, Minerals & Chemicals Importers and Exporters (CCCMC), a large government-linked industry association, said that some Chinese companies would not allow foreign organizations to audit them because of information security concerns. Instead, he urged Western companies to participate in China’s emerging supply chain governance system.
China’s efforts soon gained international recognition. The London Metal Exchange, for instance, has already accepted the CCCMC’s due-diligence guidelines for mineral supply chains as an approved standard. Chinese-led frameworks have also drawn Western firms in directly: The CCCMC’s Responsible Cobalt Initiative, which promotes due diligence across the cobalt supply chain, counts multinationals such as Apple, Tesla, and BMW among its members.
In 2025, a CCCMC draft mining standard included prohibitions on forced labor and requirements for human rights due diligence. The China Enterprise Confederation and the Ministry of Commerce also issued new guidelines on labor compliance and corporate responsibility for Chinese companies operating overseas.
Then, in July 2026, China’s new Regulation on Outbound Investment took effect. It requires Chinese investors abroad to respect workers’ legitimate rights and comply with applicable laws and international practices. More significantly, it goes beyond compliance with existing rules, calling on China to “actively participate in the formulation of international investment rules.”
China is also building platforms to promote its current approach abroad. In 2025, the CCCMC brought governments, companies, NGOs, and international organizations, including independent trade unions from some mineral producing countries, together in Xiamen for its International Forum on Sustainable Mineral Supply Chains.
This expansion of China’s regulatory ambitions comes as Washington has reduced some of its own international labor work. In 2025, the U.S. Department of Labor terminated hundreds of millions of dollars in international programs addressing child labor, forced labor, and trafficking, leaving more space for China to expand its influence over global labor and supply-chain governance.
Beijing’s language on corporate responsibility also stands in stark contrast to Washington’s current position: China now emphasizes shared development and improving local livelihoods, while the United States increasingly focuses on actions that it claims are protecting American workers from unfair competition. China’s message may resonate more strongly in developing countries because it presents its standards as part of their own development.
The West’s greatest weakness is that, after decades of writing and promoting these rules, it still has not ensured that workers worldwide genuinely benefit. That gives China room to promote its own standards and its own narrative. However, Beijing is clearly willing to expand its influence over global rules even without first improving conditions for workers in China itself.
The logic behind the two approaches is increasingly similar: Both governments are tying labor standards to broader national economic interests. The two systems nevertheless differ in important ways.
Western supply chain due diligence systems generally emphasize access to information, external assessment, and risk identification. China’s emerging system also emphasizes labor rights and corporate responsibility, but gives greater weight to oversight by the state, information security, and the role of Chinese institutions in setting and implementing standards.
For now, therefore, the competition is largely about who gets to write the rules for global supply chains.
If those standards strengthen the competitiveness of Chinese companies overseas and give China a greater role in governing those chains, especially in developing and critical mineral producing countries, Beijing has ample reason to promote them. In fact, it already has.
Ultimately, the matter of who writes the rules is less important than whether or not those rules actually improve conditions for workers worldwide. If competition pushes both sides to prove that their standards work, it may not be a bad thing for global workers.

Burnham’s visit to Kyiv marks a renewal of badly needed support for Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:33:22 UTC
01:33:22 KST

Since moving into Downing Street in July, Andy Burnham – a foreign policy neophyte – has expressed strong support for Ukraine. But on Monday he saw the bitter human cost of the war up close for the first time, visiting Kyiv during his first international trip as prime minister.
The occasion was the 35th anniversary of Ukraine’s independence. Volodymyr Zelenskyy gave awards to the families of fallen soldiers. Relatives wept, hugging Ukraine’s president. Photos of young men in their prime were shown on a giant screen.
The setting was St Sophia cathedral in the old heart of the Ukrainian capital. Built in the 11th century, the building predates Moscow and is a symbol of Ukraine’s ancient statehood. Next to it were modern weapons used by Kyiv in its struggle against Russia, including quadcopter drones and unmanned land robots.
In a speech in front of other western leaders, Burnham compared Ukraine’s fight to that waged by Britain during the darkest days of the second world war. “My nation kept the flame of European freedom alive in the 20th century, you hold that flame in the 21st,” he declared.
Like other high-profile visitors, Burnham arrived with a gift. Since 2023 the UK and France have been providing Kyiv with long-range Storm Shadow or Scalp (as the French version is known) cruise missiles, used to knock out Russian naval ships and command centres.
It was now handing over British blueprints for key components, Burnham said, so Ukraine could eventually make its own version with France.
More Storm Shadows could go some way to dealing with Ukraine’s biggest problem: the wave of ballistic missiles fired by Russia that rain down on Kyiv and other cities most nights. As of now, Ukraine has run out of US-made Patriot interceptors capable of shooting them down. The Trump administration is disinclined to provide more.
The British cruise missiles carry a larger payload than the long-range drones favoured by Kyiv. They could be used to destroy enemy ballistic missile launch systems, which can be quickly moved, and are dotted around sites in western Russia. Depending on their range, they could also disable military runways and aerodromes.
But nobody expects production to start soon. In the meantime, the Kremlin has responded with characteristic belligerence. Vladimir Putin’s press spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said Moscow would destroy any Ukrainian Storm Shadow factories, and accused London of taking part in the war and adding “fuel to the fire” though it is France that is helping with building them.
Last week Russia threatened “consequences” over the supply of British drones to Kyiv and withdrew its ambassador from London. It is unclear how Putin might escalate further. He has already sent assassins to poison Russian dissidents on UK territory including the murder in 2006 of Alexander Litvinenko, killed with radioactive tea.
Burnham appears unmoved by what he dubbed “outrageous” Russian threats, an encouraging sign for Kyiv. On Monday he pointed out that it was Putin who “started the fire” with his illegal and unprovoked invasion, and assured Zelenskyy of his “personal commitment” to Kyiv’s existential cause.
Ukraine has warmly welcomed the Storm Shadow initiative. Oleksandr Merezhko, head of the Ukrainian parliament’s foreign affairs committee, told the Guardian he hoped manufacturing could begin in “months, not years”. “We have proved many times we can do impossible things in producing weaponry,” he said, adding that the missile strengthened Kyiv’s position in negotiations with Moscow.
Of Burnham’s visit, he added: “For us, it’s hugely symbolic and important. It illustrates that for the UK Ukraine remains a top priority. You are an important bridge and have rectified the situation whenever we have a crisis in our relations with the US. Your king is a valuable diplomatic tool and puts in a good word for us with Trump.”
The trip also signalled to allies that the UK will continue to play a leading role in the coalition of the willing after the departure of Keir Starmer. Co-hosting a coalition meeting for the first time, Burnham said Europe would do everything it could to source more Patriotic interceptors for Ukraine. Zelenskyy has asked for 300 to help the country survive the coming winter.
Burnham’s speech made clear that he regards Ukraine’s struggle as Britain’s too – at a time when the US has in effect given up on its attempts to broker a peace deal, and has halted direct military aid. “Ukraine has been Europe’s protector, not a drain on our security but the frontline in keeping Europe safe,” he said. “The Ukrainian people deserve not just our continued support but our gratitude and respect.”
Ukrainian leaders and soldiers are grateful for British diplomatic and moral support, though they know that London’s military power is limited. Storm Shadow is deemed to have been one of the UK’s most useful contributions but stockpiles were modest.
Ukraine’s focus has been on developing its own long-range drones and cruise missiles, such as Fire Point’s Flamingo, which have been used to strike refineries and warehouses deep inside Russia. The goal is to attack Russia with 1,000 drones and some missiles a day this year, not when Storm Shadow production lines are ready.
But the deal that Burnham has agreed with Zelenskyy is an important renewal of goodwill. At some point Zelenskyy will probably need the help of European allies whenever the White House re-engages with the peace process. Burnham may become an important interlocutor with Trump, and today’s trip is from Ukraine’s perspective an encouraging start.

Lebanon under pressure to deploy troops to strategic Ali al-Taher ridge as Israel bombs area
The strategic Ali-Al-Taher ridge located in south Lebanon’s Nabatieh district has been subjected to almost daily Israeli shelling, amid reports that Hezbollah is refusing to hand it over despite increased pressure.
Reports on Monday stated that Washington has intervened in the matter, seeking for the ridge to be transferred to the Lebanese Army in exchange for Israel withdrawing from the area.
The Ali al-Taher ridge is an important site, as it overlooks the city of Nabatieh from the east, sits around 600 metres above sea level, and is around five kilometres from Beaufort Castle. The ridge’s location is key, as it would give Israelis a better military viewpoint, providing a commanding view of southern Lebanon, the Galilee Panhandle, and beyond.
Israel has failed to seize the ridge in recent years, despite making efforts to do so.
The renewed shelling in the area comes as Israel claims that Hezbollah members are allegedly holed up underground.
While the Lebanese army has not objected to taking over the hill, it has sought guarantees from the US that Israel would halt its attacks on the ridge and its vicinity, withdrawing completely before the army’s forces enter the area.
Discussions between Lebanon and the US in recent days have centred on Ali al-Taher, and growing fears that the confrontations could result in all-out war.
The fears have also prompted calls for Lebanon and Israel to implement the 14-point framework agreement from 26 June, which aims to end active conflict and ensure a phased Israeli withdrawal from the south of the country as well as the disarmament of Hezbollah.
Lebanon’s President Joseph Aoun has reportedly already engaged in discussions with the US to find a solution to the matter and prevent further escalation.
Aoun has proposed the Lebanese Army enter the area after Hezbollah withdraws, noting that a major concern is Israel occupying the ridge and carrying out large-scale demolitions which would have a knock-on effect on surrounding villages.
However, sources told The New Arab that Hezbollah has so far rejected the proposal because the group does not trust US or Israeli guarantees, citing violations of the ceasefire and what it said was the failure of the 26 June framework agreement.
A source close to Hezbollah also told The New Arab that members of the group are present on the ridge, but declined to give information on how many were there.
The source further said: “The consequences of Israel taking control of the ridge would not be limited to Hezbollah; it would affect Lebanon as a whole. Israel would not stop occupying more hills and expanding into areas beyond the Yellow Line it established and beyond the southern bank of the Litani River.”
“This shows Israel’s desire to violate agreements,” the source added.
The latest developments come as Israel has increased threats to occupy Ali al-Taher, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu increasingly mentioning the hill amid his election campaign.
“It is becoming clear from the Israeli mood that there is a shift toward more extreme positions, in line with the sentiment of the public,” the source told The New Arab.
In recent weeks, the Israeli military has been encircling the hill and has carried out several attempts to seize it.

UN proposes 'confidence-building mechanism' for global trade routes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:29:04 UTC
01:29:04 KST

Muhammed Yasin Güngör
24 August 2026•Update: 24 August 2026
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Monday proposed a UN-led initiative to secure global maritime choke points, warning that regional conflicts are "choking arteries of global trade" and threatening the world's food system.
"Maritime choke points must never become instruments of coercion, and the world's food supply must never become collateral damage of conflict," Guterres told reporters.
He highlighted that transits through the Strait of Hormuz have reached a near standstill, while oil prices have surged by 36% since the war began on Feb. 28. Additionally, global container rates have spiked by 84% over the last year, severely affecting the cost of fertilizers and essential goods, he underlined.
The proposed "confidence-building mechanism," developed by a task force led by the UN Office for Project Services (UNOPS), would serve as a "neutral facilitator" for the registration and verification of vessels. The initiative would focus initially on ships carrying fertilizers and related raw materials, providing an "orderly and predictable" transit process to reduce immediate risks and foster diplomacy with a "deconflicting mechanism" in Oman.
Guterres emphasized that the mechanism would not authorize passage or alter existing international laws. "Sovereign decisions remain entirely with participating member states," the UN chief said, adding that the plan can only proceed if all involved nations agree to the framework. He confirmed that the UN Office for Project Services has maintained intense contact with all parties and that all the parties involved have detailed knowledge of what the mechanism is about.
Guterres stressed that protecting navigational freedoms is a "legal obligation and a humanitarian imperative" as "millions of vulnerable people around the world depend on the collective ability of all parties to uphold it."
He issued an appeal for "full respect for international law," including the law of the sea and humanitarian mandates. Guterres demanded protection for civilian seafarers and infrastructure while calling for the "full restoration and respect of navigational rights and freedoms" in the Strait of Hormuz. He further urged an "immediate end" to attacks against commercial shipping in the Black Sea and the Red Sea, emphasizing that these rights are vital for "international peace and security."

Kenya arrests four in probe into 18 elephant deaths in Amboseli
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:28:01 UTC
01:28:01 KST

Police have arrested four suspects in an investigation into the deaths of 18 elephants in Kenya's Amboseli ecosystem, where authorities also seized assorted substances including chemicals, the Kenyan Tourism and Wildlife Ministry said.
A Kenya Wildlife Service (KWS) spokesperson told Reuters on Monday that the four have since been released on bail.
Preliminary laboratory results point to the probable involvement of a toxic substance, the ministry said in a statement released on Saturday, with earlier indications suggesting cyanide poisoning due to the ingestion of pesticide-contaminated tomatoes from farms bordering Amboseli National Park.
Some wildlife experts have expressed doubt that farm pesticide was responsible for the deaths, citing the absence of reported deaths among other animals in the area.
The ministry said investigators were also pursuing a fifth individual believed to have information relevant to the case. A search in Tikondo in Loitokitok sub-county, about 220 km southeast of Nairobi, led to the discovery of assorted substances, including chemicals believed to have come from a neighboring country, the statement said.
Investigation still ongoing, no criminal convictions yet established
The ministry said the arrests and recovered substances did not in themselves establish criminal culpability and added that investigations were ongoing.
The ministry said the first 15 elephant deaths were recorded between June 24 and July 24. In July, KWS said the deaths occurred in Amboseli National Park, Kimana Sanctuary and the Kuku Ranch area, and that the animals showed symptoms including partial paralysis before dying within one or two days.
The broader Amboseli ecosystem spans the national park and surrounding community land in southern Kenya near the Tanzanian border, providing habitat and movement routes for elephants and other wildlife beneath Mount Kilimanjaro.
The area has a history of human-wildlife conflict, with elephants roaming beyond protected areas into community and agricultural land, trampling crops and angering farmers.
