India's Iran exports set to fall further due to Dubai halt, US sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:27:55 UTC
01:27:55 KST

Planned new US sanctions on Iran and the United Arab Emirates's (UAE) halt on trade with Tehran could severely disrupt Indian exports of rice, tea and pharmaceuticals to Iran, which have been largely routed through Dubai's port in recent years, Indian exporters said on Monday.
India has been among Iran's five largest trading partners, though bilateral trade has fallen by more than 90% from its 2018/19 highs of $17 billion, with exports now limited mostly to goods exempted on humanitarian grounds.
Indian exporters fear US President Donald Trump's proposed "economic D-Day" plan, likely to be unveiled later on Monday, could further squeeze trade weakened by sanctions, banking caution and shipping constraints.
The UAE last week suspended all trade activities, exchanges and financial transactions with Iran until further notice.
"We are already seeing indications that transactions and payment mechanisms traditionally routed through the UAE are exploring alternative jurisdictions," said Dev Garg, vice president of the Indian Rice Exporters Federation, suggesting Turkey as an alternative.
Exporters could face higher freight, other costs
In the first half of 2026, India exported $383.11 million of rice to Iran - the second-largest overseas market for premium rice, including long-grained basmati.
"Any prolonged disruption in this corridor will have a much greater bearing on the basmati industry, especially on millers and exporters in northern India than on India's overall non-basmati rice trade," Garg said.
Until recently, Indian exporters typically received payment through an Indian authorized-dealer bank from a UAE trader's account - in dirhams, dollars or another permitted currency -while the trader separately collected payment from its Iranian customer through legally compliant banking channels.
Indian tea exports to Iran totaled $14.34 million in the first half of 2026. Prabhat Bezboruah, a senior tea planter and former chairman of the state-run Tea Board, said sales to Iran will be affected as a lot of that goes through the UAE.
There was no immediate comment from India's trade and foreign ministries.
A New Delhi-based exporter said direct shipments could rise, but payment problems may worsen.
Ajay Srivastava of the Global Trade Research Initiative said India's Iran trade has already fallen sharply since the previous sanctions.
"We hope food and pharmaceutical products may receive exemptions, although exporters could still face higher freight, insurance and payment costs," he said.
Iran's exports to India were dominated by crude oil, valued at about $707 million, with far smaller shipments of liquefied petroleum gas, apples, dates, almonds and kiwi fruit in the first six months of 2026. Officials have said crude oil imports from Iran were largely enabled by a US exemption granted earlier this year, and may be difficult to sustain.

Netanyahu meets with senior security officials to discuss West Bank violence, Israeli settlement

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu held a situational assessment in the West Bank on Monday, following recent outbreaks of violence in the area at several flashpoints, including Kusra and Gilad Farm near Nablus, as well as Yatta and Sa'ir near Hebron.
Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir warned Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in recent discussions that, given the situation on the ground, “there is a risk of an explosion in the West Bank,” according to two Israeli sources.
Defense Minister Israel Katz, IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir, National Security Council head Shmuel Ben Ezra, Central Command head Maj.-Gen. Avi Bluth, Military Intelligence Chief, Maj.-Gen. Shlomi Binder, IDF Operations Division head, Brig.-Gen. A, Judea and Samaria Division commander, Brig.-Gen. Kobi Heller, and other senior officials attended.
The meeting covered a general assessment of security threats in the region, with a particular focus on terror, as well as the "dramatic increase" in Israeli settlement in the West Bank, Katz said afterward. He also praised the IDF soldiers and other service members who enforce Israel's policies in Judea and Samaria, "including the order we gave to evacuate refugee camps in northern Samaria and destroy terror infrastructure there."
During the briefing, Bluth warned that “there has been a significant decline in the scope of terrorism over the past two years, but there is a match that could set everything on fire in an instant — and that is nationalist crime.”
Bluth’s comments referred to the significant decline in the number of Israelis killed and wounded in Palestinian terror attacks, alongside a substantial increase in incidents of violence by Israelis against Palestinians. However, Central Command has been able to bring about a partial decline in such violent incidents since their peak in March, coinciding with the US-Israeli military campaign against Iran.
The IDF chief also warned during the briefing about the volatility of the situation on the ground, two Israeli sources told The Jerusalem Post.
On Monday evening, members of the Security Cabinet convened for a meeting against the backdrop of recent events in Syria, including the bombing of a Syrian Air Force base shortly before Turkish troops and air-defense systems were deployed there. The ministers were also expected to discuss the situation in the West Bank and hear warnings from the IDF chief and other senior military officials about the volatility on the ground.
Paratroopers to join Israeli security forces in West Bank following three-month Gaza tour
Also on Monday, the IDF announced that members of the Paratroopers Brigade would be transferring to the West Bank following the completion of their previous posting in the Gaza Strip.
Stationed in Gaza since June under the command of the 143rd Gaza Division and the 99th Division, the troops dismantled a total of 13 km of underground tunnels, including part of the tunnel where Lt. Hadar Goldin was held for over a decade.

Maine Jewish summer camp seeks protection order against neighbor after shooting incident
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:27:09 UTC
01:27:09 KST

Camp Modin has filed for an emergency protection order against a neighboring property owner in the wake of a shooting incident that sent the Maine Jewish summer camp into lockdown in early August.
The August 7 incident began with an angry verbal confrontation over a damaged tractor and quickly escalated into gunfire, forcing hundreds of children and staff members to shelter while roughly 20 rounds from a semi-automatic rifle were discharged in various directions, including toward a basketball court at the back of the camp.
According to local reporting from Central Maine reviewing court documents, the emergency protection order would temporarily block 36-year-old Nathan R. Hewett of Belgrade, Maine, from camp premises and from having any contact with camp personnel.
In his request for the order, camp owner and executive director Pascal Cohen stated that Hewett deliberately disrupts the grounds by shining vehicle high beams and launching late-night fireworks, alongside a pattern of discharging firearms nearby that causes distress to campers.
Camp security guards detail escalating confrontation
The court records detail an initial confrontation on the evening of August 7, when Hewett and his father, Raymond, walked up to the property to demand an interaction with a staff member.
According to statements submitted by Joshua Ewing, an armed security guard and former law enforcement officer, the younger Hewett blamed the camp for wrecking his tractor lawn mower after hitting an obstacle.
Ewing recounted that while Raymond engaged calmly and privately expressed concern that his son posed a danger, Nathan Hewett lost his temper, hurling insults and profanities while acting entirely irrational.
Additional testimony in the filings from security guard Timothy Black claimed that tensions had been simmering for weeks, pointing to a July complaint from Hewett regarding the volume of the campers, accompanied by veiled threats about the noise levels.
Black further alleged in the court paperwork that the neighbor regularly crossed to the boundary line to hurl abuse, a behavior exacerbated whenever he drank alcohol.
Minutes after Hewett walked away from the initial verbal clash, both guards reported hearing rounds fired from a powerful rifle, prompting them to immediately lock down the facility.
Deputies seize 23 firearms after shooting
According to the Kennebec County Sheriff’s Office and deputy affidavits, responding deputies found the camp under lockdown while Hewett discharged approximately 20 rounds from a .22-caliber semi-automatic rifle, with shell casings suggesting bullets may have been directed at a basketball court near the back of the camp.
Deputy Tyler Johnson stated in his probable cause affidavit that Hewett was suspected of using alcohol and harboring an antisemitic bias during the incident. Law enforcement officers subsequently seized 23 firearms from Hewett’s property, many of which were semi-automatic.
Hewett faces multiple felony counts – including reckless conduct with a dangerous weapon, criminal threatening with a dangerous weapon, and terrorizing.
While Hewett was initially held on $50,000 bail following his arrest, local court tracking reported by Central Maine confirms he has since been released.
Camp seeks protection order as criminal case continues
The hearing on the camp’s request for a protection order is scheduled for 8:30 a.m. next Monday at the Capital Judicial Center, while Hewett’s next court date on the criminal charges is set for November 10.

DR Congo peace roadmap: Can it end the fighting?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:25:00 UTC
01:25:00 KST

DRC peace roadmap: Will the fighting finally end?
August 24, 2026
Representatives of the Congolese government and the Rwanda-backed M23 rebel group agreed on a roadmap for peace after negotiations in Geneva.
It builds on the US-brokered framework signed in Doha last year, and sets out steps and timelines for negotiations and implementation: a ceasefire monitoring mechanism is also due to receive support from the UN peacekeeping mission, MONUSCO.
The United States, Qatar, the African Union (AU) and Switzerland have all expressed their support for the process as brokers of the push for peace.
However, it is not a full peace plan with bindíng resolutions and terms; rather, many aspects of the push will still need to be fine-tuned.
The new diplomatic initiative could nevertheless be offering fresh hope following years of bloody conflict in eastern DRC; fighting in the region has killed hundreds of civilians and displaced millions since 2022. The M23 rebel group continues to control large parts of North Kivu and South Kivu — two provinces in eastern DRC that are highly coveted for their minerals.
As disagreements remain over key issues, doubts continue to cast a shadow over the prospect of a lasting peace.
From signature to implementation
"There are likely to be many more bumps on the road — disagreements remain over issues including sanctions against M23, the release of detainees and the timing of political reforms. So this remains a very fragile commitment," Alex Vines, Africa program director at the European Council on Foreign Relations, told DW.
Conflict analyst Clifton Chifuwe, executive director of the Centre for Peace Research and Advocacy (CPRA), a local NGO that focuses on conflict management, agrees with that assessment, pointing to the presence of multiple armed groups in the area, the deep level of mistrust between DRC and Rwanda, and competition over eastern Congo's mineral wealth.
He believes that the biggest of the challenges across the board is to turn this roadmap into action.
"Signing it is easier than implementing it on the ground," Chifuweexplains.
Chifuwe told DW that independent monitoring mechanisms and the involvement of all key stakeholders will be essential for any peace to hold.
Rwanda's role in the conflict
Rwanda has repeatedly rejected accusations that it backs M23 rebels — though international groups maintain the view that the small neighboring nation is deeply entrechned in the conflict.
Kigali's relationship with the rebel group therefore remains central to the peace process, says Vines:
"Rwanda's good faith and its relationship with M23 is a really key consideration. Kigali's buy-in to any agreement and influence over M23 is key."
Rwandan President Paul Kagame's comments at a press conference on August 24 further underline the complexity of the issue; Kagame rejects the narrative that Rwanda is responsible for the current conflict, blaming factions within the DRC instead.
He links any Rwandan involvement in the conflict to what he describes as a longstanding security threat from the other side of the border, naming the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR) armed group — which fights against M23 rebels alongside the Congolese military — as his main target.
Kagame said that "if this problem of the FDLR is not resolved," Rwanda would act to protect itself "at any cost."
Mixed messages of hope and skepticism
There also are signs and reasons for cautious optimism: Chifuwe highlights that the roadmap focuses on a sequenced implementation plan, with monitoring initiatives to be put in place to help identify warning signs before any violence resumes.
These international mediators will also have to maintain pressure on the parties while ensuring regional concerns are heard.
In this context, Vines believes that US and Qatari involvement remains important, while stressing that African input through the AU must not be ignored.
All parties involved have signed off on a pledge to "pursue negotiations towards comprehensive peace and conflict resolution" — for now.
What does peace mean for the displaced?
Ultimately, the roadmap will not be measured by the signatories' attitudes but by results for thousands upon thousands of people in the eastern DRC, who remain displaced.
"The real test is ... whether ordinary Congolese people become safer and better off," Chifuwe says emphatically, highlighting also the restoration of state authority and the management of mineral resources as key objectives that need to be achieved.
For Congolese civilians, the diplomatic language carries a personal meaning: One refugee named Linda Kasongo finds herself stuck in Zambia five years into the conflict.
She told DW that she wants to return home, but can't even entertain the thought, since violence on all sides continues to wreck lives and livelihoods in her war-torn home region.
"I hope it works out because I want to go home," Kasongo says. "I want to be with my people. I miss my people. I miss my home."
Edited by: Sertan Sanderson

They were diagnosed with blast injuries, a shoulder fracture, contusions and concussion. One of the victims is in moderate condition.
During another attack on the city, a 16-year-old girl suffered a blast injury and contusion.
Three more men, aged 40, 47 and 50, sustained bodily injuries in Druzhkivka. During the occupiers' artillery shelling of the settlement, the men were outside. The victims, who suffered mine-blast injuries and shrapnel wounds, were provided with medical assistance.
In addition, a 58-year-old civilian in the settlement of Bilenke, part of the Kramatorsk community, suffered a mine-blast injury and a thigh wound.
In the settlements, 24 private houses and 7 apartment buildings were damaged.
Under the procedural guidance of the Sloviansk and Kramatorsk District Prosecutors' Offices, pre-trial investigations have been launched in criminal proceedings concerning war crimes (Part 1 of Article 438 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine).

Chinese President Xi Jinping on Monday said a two-state solution is the “right direction” for resolving the longstanding Palestinian issue, urging the resumption of peace talks between Palestine and Israel.
Xi made the remarks during a meeting with visiting Jordanian King Abdullah II, whose week-long state visit to China concluded Monday after stops in Shanghai, Shenzhen and Beijing.
Xi stressed that the Palestinian question is at the core of the Middle East issue and that efforts to resolve it should be guided by four principles, according to a statement by Chinese Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning on US social media company X.
“We must uphold political settlement, adhere to the two-State solution as the right direction, work for the resumption of peace talks between Palestine and Israel, and realize the early establishment of an independent State of Palestine,” Xi said.
“We must uphold the principle of Palestinians governing Palestine. Palestine is the homeland of all Palestinians. The principle of Palestinians governing Palestine should be followed in advancing the governance of the West Bank and postwar reconstruction of Gaza,” Mao cited Xi as saying.
Calling for upholding humanitarianism, Xi said the international community, particularly the UN Security Council, should truly take up the responsibility to protect civilians, ensure the delivery of humanitarian assistance and put an end to humanitarian disasters.
“We must uphold fairness and justice,” he added.
“We should act on the basis of international rule of law, aim at addressing both the symptoms and root causes, and take practical actions to realize a comprehensive, just and lasting resolution of the Palestinian question at an early date,” Xi said, according to Mao.
On bilateral relations with Jordan, Xi said the two sides should carry forward their longstanding friendship, enhance strategic mutual trust, deepen mutually beneficial cooperation and strengthen multilateral coordination to further advance the China-Jordan strategic partnership and contribute to regional peace, stability and prosperity.
China is Jordan’s largest trading partner, with bilateral trade reaching around $6.7 billion.
King Abdullah paid a week-long state visit to China, his ninth overall and first since 2015. He visited the financial hub of Shanghai and the tech hub of Shenzhen before traveling to Beijing, where he met Chinese Premier Li Qiang, top lawmaker Zhao Leji and business representatives.

Mawlid 2026: Muslims mark Prophet Muhammad’s birthday this week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:18:12 UTC
01:18:12 KST

Breadcrumb
Mawlid 2026: Muslims mark Prophet Muhammad’s birthday this week
Muslims around the world are commemorating the birth of Prophet Muhammad, also known as Mawlid, this week with prayers, gatherings and festivities.
While the exact date traditionally associated with Mawlid is uncertain, the Prophet Muhammad’s birthday is widely believed to fall on the 12th day of Rabi’ al-Awwal, the third month of the Islamic calendar.
The date is recognised across many Muslim-majority countries, particularly in the MENA region, where several states mark the occasion with a national holiday.
However, many Shia Muslim communities observe Mawlid on 17 Rabi al-Awwal.
Some observers have announced that Mawlid will fall on Tuesday, August 25, after the new Islamic month began on August 14 following the sighting of the crescent moon earlier this month.
Following centuries of tradition, Mawlid is set to usher in celebrations across much of the Muslim world, with the occasion taking different forms depending on local religious and cultural practices.
However, some Muslims have historically opposed Mawlid celebrations, arguing that during the Prophet’s lifetime, his birthday was never designated as an annual religious occasion.
They describe the practice as bid’ah (religious innovation), maintaining that practices that develop into recurring religious festivals on a particular date require evidence from the Qur’an or Sunnah.
In the UK, where Islam is the country's second-largest and fastest-growing major faith group, British Muslims spoke to The New Arab about how Mawlid is observed and understood within their communities.
Khadijah, a care worker based in the Midlands, described how Mawlid was widely commemorated during her upbringing in Tanzania.
In East Africa, she said, the occasion is marked by vibrant annual celebrations featuring large street processions, Quran recitations and rhythmic devotional singing, combining established Islamic practices with Swahili and wider regional cultural traditions.
"We grew up with Mawlid and because we were surrounded by those kind of celebrations- I think the concept of reading poems and praising the Prophet is actually a beautiful thing," she told The New Arab.
"For me, I look forward to celebrating Mawlid- especially being with my community where I see nasheeds being sung or poems about Prophet Muhammed being recited. It makes me emotional every time."
Meanwhile, Pakistani-British university student Anika Khan, 20, told The New Arab that her heritage has played an important role in maintaining the tradition of Mawlid al-Nabi.
She said members of her community typically hold gatherings in their homes, where devotional poetry praising the Prophet Muhammad are sung during the day, the Quran is recited, and food and gifts are distributed to those in need in remembrance of the Prophet.
"This day focuses on the Prophet's teachings, good character and forgiving nature," Khan told The New Arab.
"Therefore this day is important to me as it showcases our love, gratitude and remembrance to prophet Mohammad peace be upon him and his teachings."
In the Gulf, where the public holiday marking the Prophet Muhammad's birthday has been confirmed for Friday, August 28, 41-year-old Moe, who is based in the United Arab Emirates, said he does not personally observe the occasion, in accordance with anti-Mawlid scholars who argue that it is not an act of worship.
"The concept of birthdays is alien to Islam," he argued, adding that "Mawlid was never celebrated by the Rasul (Prophet Muhammed)."
He continued: "In my opinion, I believe it's just an innovation and from what I have now learned, the Prophet did not teach us to do this and Islamic teachings state that we must always follow the Quran and the Sunnah. And so the celebration of the Prophet's birthday is not mentioned in any of his teachings."

US strategic oil reserve continues decline, hits lowest level since 1982
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:16:47 UTC
01:16:47 KST

Mücahithan Avcıoğlu
24 August 2026•Update: 24 August 2026
Crude oil stocks in the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) fell below 290 million barrels last week, reaching their lowest level since 1982, official data showed Monday.
The reserve declined by about 3.7 million barrels to 289.7 million barrels as of Aug. 21, down from 293.4 million barrels a week earlier, according to the US Department of Energy.
The latest inventory comprised 98.7 million barrels of sweet crude and 191 million barrels of sour crude.
The reserve is now filled to around 41% of its authorized storage capacity of 714 million barrels.
Historical data from the US Energy Information Administration showed the SPR last held less crude in November 1982, when inventories stood at 288.2 million barrels.
The stockpile has fallen by more than 125 million barrels, or about 30%, since late February, when it contained approximately 415.4 million barrels.
The decline reflects continued releases under an emergency program announced in March in response to Middle East supply disruptions and restrictions on shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.
US President Donald Trump authorized the release of 172 million barrels from the reserve as part of a coordinated International Energy Agency initiative to make 400 million barrels of oil and petroleum products available to global markets.
The Energy Department’s data showed 15.1 million barrels had been released from the SPR so far in August, following drawdowns of 17.4 million barrels in July, 33 million in June and 39.4 million in May.

Costa: Only Ukraine should determine terms of just peace
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
19:15:31 EEST
01:15:31 KST

Only Ukraine should determine the terms of a just and lasting peace, according to European Council President António Costa.
Costa said on Monday during celebrations marking the 35th anniversary of Ukraine's Independence that the European Union could not remain neutral when international law was being violated and that the EU stood with Ukraine. He said the bloc supported all serious initiatives aimed at achieving peace in Ukraine, but stressed that Ukraine alone must determine the terms of a comprehensive, just and lasting peace.
According to Costa, such a peace must affirm Ukraine's independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity, while also guaranteeing its long-term security and ability to defend itself.
He said European solidarity had remained strong and unwavering since the first day of Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine. The EU, he said, had consistently supported Ukraine politically, financially, humanitarianly, militarily and diplomatically, while also helping to build the Coalition of the Willing, which was intended to provide Ukraine with reliable security guarantees after the war and prevent such aggression from happening again.
Costa said the EU would continue to provide Ukraine with as much support as necessary during the war, in future peace negotiations and throughout the reconstruction process.
He also said the EU's vision extended beyond the war and that Ukraine's future membership in the European Union represented the best guarantee of security and long-term democratic stability both for Ukraine and Europe as a whole. According to him, the goal was to integrate Ukraine into the EU's peace project, a union of nations that transcended nationalism, upheld democracy and the rule of law, and worked together for shared prosperity and development.
Costa acknowledged that accession to the EU was a demanding process, but said the challenges involved should not weaken political resolve, which was based on geopolitical necessity and the free and democratic choice of the Ukrainian people.
According to him, Ukraine had already contributed to rebuilding a genuinely geopolitical European Union that took responsibility for its own defence, strengthened its strategic autonomy, firmly upheld international law and multilateralism, developed partnerships around the world and was ready to welcome Ukraine into the bloc.
Costa also expressed confidence that Russia would not win the war against Ukraine. He said international law must prevail and noted that, after more than four years of full-scale war, Russia had failed to achieve its objectives. He added that the human cost had been devastating and the economic consequences catastrophic, while Russia's resources were being increasingly depleted. Costa said the EU's unprecedented sanctions were also having an impact and that pressure on Russia would continue until it stopped the killing and demonstrated a genuine commitment to peace.

Iranian currency plunges as new US ‘economic D-Day’ looms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24

01:14:42 KST

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced new measures Monday evening aimed at further isolating Iran’s economy, in the hope that the sweeping pressure campaign he has described as the “largest economic offensive ever” will force the ayatollahs’ regime to yield and compromise in stalled talks on ending the war. At a special news conference, Bessent unveiled what he called “Operation Economic Outcast” and announced new sanctions intended to “tighten the noose” around Iran.
In practice, for now the move amounts primarily to a threat to countries around the world, demanding that they halt all business and commercial ties with Iran. Bessent said those that fail to do so could themselves face sanctions.
“The clock starts ticking,” he said, calling on world leaders to “make a decision” and choose between Iran and the United States. Bessent added that President Donald Trump is holding phone calls with leaders around the world and demanding that they sever trade ties with Iran, but when asked whether there was a deadline, he said only that U.S. patience “is not unlimited.”
It remains unclear whether Trump actually intends to follow through on the threat against Iran’s closest allies, chief among them China, since imposing sanctions on Beijing could risk reigniting a trade war. Analysts believe he would currently prefer to avoid such a confrontation, especially ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s planned visit to Washington in a month.
“Iran now faces a very clear choice, and there are only two paths open to it: total global isolation and a survival economy, or a return to normalcy with an opportunity to rejoin the global economy,” Bessent said.
“Today we are launching Operation Economic Outcast to block every other option available to the Iranian regime. The Treasury Department has mapped every node, every facilitator and every network Iran has used to smuggle oil and evade sanctions. Beginning today, actions by the Treasury Department and other agencies will tighten the noose and block every potential source of revenue that funds the Revolutionary Guards and the evil Iranian regime. We are enforcing a zero-leakage approach. There will not even be the slightest breathing room for the regime to rebuild its ability to carry out terrorism against America and the world.”
A source familiar with the details told Reuters earlier Monday evening that the measures include an expansion of secondary sanctions that the administration could impose on countries or other entities that violate restrictions on ties with Iran.
The source described the move as a “final warning” to countries to sever their ties with the Islamic Republic, saying that if they fail to do so, their companies or other affiliated entities could risk being cut off from the U.S. dollar-based financial system.
A senior administration official added that the Treasury Department had “mapped Iran’s oil smuggling and sanctions-evasion network,” and that the information would be presented to countries helping Iran circumvent sanctions as part of the warning issued to them.
A source familiar with the matter told Reuters that they will expand the use of secondary sanctions the administration can impose on countries or other entities that violate restrictions on ties with Iran. The source described the move as a “final warning” to countries to sever their ties with the Islamic Republic, adding that failure to do so could result in their companies or other affiliated entities being cut off from the U.S. dollar-based financial system.
The source did not specify which new activities or sectors of Iran’s economy could be targeted, but said that in some Iranian sectors any activity, even in a third country, could also be subject to secondary sanctions. A senior administration official added that the Treasury Department had “mapped Iran’s oil smuggling and sanctions-evasion network,” and that the information would be presented to countries helping Iran circumvent sanctions as part of the warning issued to them.
Trump has shifted strategy in recent weeks following the deadlock in talks with Iran and Tehran’s refusal to allow the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, the “oil artery” of the global economy, unless it receives U.S. recognition of its control over the strategic waterway. Rather than resume the war, Trump chose a policy of a suffocating economic blockade and last week promised to launch what he called an “economic D-Day,” invoking the Allied invasion of Normandy in World War II. He also threatened to punish countries that continue doing business with Iran.
So far, only the United Arab Emirates, which had been an important hub for Tehran’s efforts to evade sanctions, has formally announced that it is cutting all trade ties with Iran. But many analysts doubt whether economic pressure, even if additional countries join the effort, can force Iran into submission quickly.
Iran, which has already shifted to what has been described as a “survival economy” aimed at minimizing the effects of sanctions, has been dealing with them for decades. But its economic crisis has worsened significantly following the two most recent wars.
According to the International Monetary Fund, inflation in Iran is expected to approach 70% this year. Since the latest war, prices of some food products, such as meat, have risen by far more, as much as 150%, while the economy as a whole is expected to contract by a steep 5.4%.
Unemployment has surged, with at least 1 million people losing their jobs since the war broke out in late February. The Iranian currency, the rial, fell to a new record low of 1.9 million to the dollar at the beginning of the month and continued to slide ahead of the expected announcement of the new measures. On Sunday, it crossed the threshold of 2 million to the dollar, and on Monday it fell further to 2.02 million.
Against that backdrop, and just hours before Bessent’s news conference, Trump wrote in a brief post on Truth Social: “IRAN IS COMPLETELY COLLAPSING!!!”
New testimony is also emerging from frustrated Iranian residents who describe growing difficulty affording basic food products.
“We have basically given up on a lot of things,” 52-year-old taxi driver and father of two Ahmad Karimi told The Associated Press. Karimi said he works 15 hours a day to make ends meet. “We give up fruit, we give up protein, we have given up leisure time, and we even work on weekends.”
Karimi said he believes Iran’s leaders will eventually have to act soon to ease the hardship he and many others are experiencing.
“People can't keep living like this,” he said. “We’re just breathing, surviving and trying to get through one day at a time.”
Sadeq Mahmoudi, a 73-year-old Tehran resident, expressed pessimism that a solution could be found that would lead to the lifting of sanctions.
“There is no hope for an agreement and peace,” he told AP while waiting in line to buy U.S. dollars with the last of his savings.
Although senior officials in Tehran repeatedly say they are aware of the severe crisis and the hardship facing citizens, they insist that the Islamic Republic will not surrender and are now threatening renewed escalation, including attacks on countries that join the U.S.-led economic blockade.
Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, warned Sunday: “If the economic war continues, not a single drop of oil will leave the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz. If Trump takes new aggressive steps, we will respond with force. If neighboring countries cooperate with the economic war, we will attack their interests. Any cooperation or support on their part will be interpreted as war."

Nevada sues Trump administration over its Colorado River plan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:12:40 UTC
01:12:40 KST

-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Nevada has filed the first lawsuit challenging the Trump administration’s Colorado River plan, which orders Nevada, Arizona and California to cut water use by about 20% over the next two years and allows for much larger cuts in the future.
- Gov. Joe Lombardo warns the plan would severely harm the Las Vegas area, while four other states upstream avoid any mandatory reductions.
- The lawsuit underscores growing tensions among seven states that depend on the river. Lake Mead and Lake Powell, the river’s largest reservoirs, have fallen to record lows.
In the first salvo of what could become a prolonged court battle over Colorado River water, the state of Nevada has sued the Trump administration over its plan to impose major water cutbacks on Las Vegas.
The state filed the lawsuit three days after the Trump administration released the plan requiring Nevada, Arizona and California to cut water use by about 20% for the next two years. The plan allows for much larger mandatory cuts over the next decade if necessary to prevent the river’s drought-depleted reservoirs from reaching critically low levels.
“Southern Nevada could lose more than 70 percent of its already meager Colorado River allocation,” while four other states — Colorado, Utah, New Mexico and Wyoming — “are not required to contribute a drop,” Nevada Gov. Joe Lombardo, a Republican, said as he announced the lawsuit Monday.
“This isn’t about political posturing,” Lombardo said. “This is a matter of survival for a community that represents about two-thirds of our state’s citizens and the lion’s share of its economy.”
Colorado River reservoirs have dropped dramatically over the last 26 years as global warming has worsened severe drought. The largest, Lake Mead and Lake Powell, have never been lower.
Nevada leaders said that under the plan, the state’s annual allotment of 300,000 acre-feet could be slashed to as little as 86,500, which they said would devastate Las Vegas and surrounding cities.
“That’s simply not a reduction that a major metropolitan area can adjust to,” said John Entsminger, Nevada’s lead negotiator and general manager of the Southern Nevada Water Authority. “It would have catastrophic effects on our ability to provide a safe, reliable water supply.”
The Las Vegas area gets about 90% of its water from the river. It has already reduced its use by about 40% over the last 25 years by eliminating thirsty grass in many areas and outlawing front-yard lawns for new subdivisions.
“We have clearly demonstrated our ability to adapt and do more with less,” Entsminger said. “However, conservation has its limits, and there is just no way to meet even the basic needs of this community with the volume of water Interior has proposed.”
The Colorado River provides water for about 35 million people in cities from Denver to San Diego, as well as 30 Native tribes and 5 million acres of farmland. About three-fourths of the water taken from it flows to farms via canals, producing alfalfa for cattle as well as lettuce, broccoli and other crops.
This year, the Rocky Mountains had the least snow on record, and the lack of snowmelt is sinking reservoir levels lower.
Over the last three years, negotiators repeatedly held talks to try to reach a seven-state agreement, but the three downstream states, California, Arizona and Nevada, deadlocked with the four upstream states.
As part of its plan, the Trump administration accepted an offer by California, Arizona and Nevada to reduce the water they take by 3.2 million acre-feet between now and the end of 2028.
California will cut its Colorado River water use by about 12%, while Arizona will take about 31% less and Nevada 28% less.
The Trump administration is not requiring water cuts for Colorado, Utah, New Mexico and Wyoming.
Andrea Travnicek, the Interior Department’s assistant secretary for water and science, said that’s because the federal government has different “responsibilities and authorities” in the upstream and downstream states.
The Trump administration orders water cuts along the Colorado River, where reservoirs have been dropping dramatically.
In previous agreements, however, all seven states have contributed, Entsminger said, and the federal plan represents a sharp break with that collaborative approach.
“Everybody that uses water from the Colorado River has a stake in using that water more efficiently, so that we can all get by with less,” Entsminger said. “A plan that focuses on a minority of states ultimately has no chance of success.”
Even as the state goes to court, Entsminger stressed that Nevada is open to negotiating.
In the lawsuit, Nevada argues that the Trump administration’s plan violates the National Environmental Policy Act, the Administrative Procedure Act and the “Law of the River,” and asks the court to halt its implementation. It also alleges the Interior Department failed to account for the severe damage drastic water cuts would inflict on southern Nevada’s $180-billion economy.
Arizona’s leaders have raised similar concerns, saying the most draconian cuts under the plan would severely harm their state.
Tom Buschatzke, Arizona’s lead negotiator, said last week that the state is “reserving our right to potentially take legal action.”
The Trump administration’s plan for the water-starved Colorado River is drawing criticism. Arizona warns it could sue.
Arizona faces especially large water cutbacks because the Central Arizona Project, the series of canals that run to the Phoenix and Tucson areas, isn’t nearly as old as other aqueducts, giving it low-priority water rights and putting it among the first in line for reductions. Much or all of the water Arizona gets via the canal could be cut off under the Trump administration plan.
Brenda Burman, general manager of the Central Arizona Project, called the federal plan “flawed” and said “every state that relies on the river should be part of the solution.”
Her agency said in a written statement that after 2028, the federal plan would allow for “disproportionate, unlawful, and intolerable cuts on Arizona.”
Nevada’s case is likely to end up before the U.S. Supreme Court, and the state makes strong claims, though the outcome is hard to predict, said Rhett Larson, a water law professor at Arizona State University.
“The litigation over the Colorado River isn’t just about who gets how much water, but about what the U.S. Constitution says about who does or should have the power to make that decision,” Larson said in an email.
Negotiators for seven states remain deeply divided over how to cut water use along the Colorado River. The chances of a court battle appear to be growing, with the threat of deep cuts in water deliveries to California and other Western states.
The case will probably take years, he said, and if a court blocks the plan, the states could have to figure out what to do in the meantime.
“Litigation is far from an ideal outcome, and carries a lot of costs, risks, and uncertainties that everyone wants to avoid,” Larson said. “But it has its benefits. When parties are not communicating very well ... it’s time for litigation.”
The last time the Supreme Court got involved in a major Colorado River dispute was its landmark 1963 decision in Arizona vs. California.
California uses more Colorado River water than any other state. None of California’s water officials have indicated the state is considering suing.

The conference was set to take place in 2025, a year after the police volunteer program marked 50 years since its founding. In recent days, volunteers in the organization said that their commanders exerted heavy pressure on them to participate in the conference, where singers Moshe Peretz and Ivri Lider are expected to perform. However, due to low ticket purchases by volunteers, the police opened sales to rank-and-file police officers, as well as to relatives and friends of the volunteers.
The state stated in a filing submitted on Sunday that the tender for producing the event concluded only 10 days earlier. This statement contradicts Ben-Gvir's claim that the event's date was set before an election date was determined.
"According to the state's position, Ben-Gvir's participation in the event, including of course delivering remarks, is prohibited," the petitioners argued. "It raises serious concern that it would in practice constitute illegal electioneering and could even color the entire event with electioneering tones. His participation in the event amounts to the use of public resources for electioneering, contrary to the law."

Riyaz ul Khaliq

Malaysia is preparing to launch cloud seeding operations, including in Indonesian airspace, to combat worsening haze as neighboring Indonesia battles widespread forest and land fires, officials said Monday.
Malaysian Natural Resources and Environmental Sustainability Minister Arthur Joseph Kurup discussed the operations with his Indonesian counterpart Jumhur Hidayat, with Jakarta approving Malaysia's use of Indonesian airspace for the effort, according to Malaysian state-run Bernama News.
Cloud seeding involves dispersing substances into clouds to encourage rainfall, which can help reduce haze and assist efforts to contain fires. The two countries are discussing the timing of the operations along their shared border.
The move comes as the intensifying El Nino phenomenon and the Southwest Monsoon increase the risk of severe peatland and forest fires heading into October.
Fires have already affected around 285,000 hectares (704,000 acres) in Indonesia so far this year.
By Monday, 10 areas across four Malaysian states registered Air Pollutant Index readings in the unhealthy range, with the town of Serian approaching the "very unhealthy" threshold.
In neighboring Indonesia, around 3 million people have been exposed to smoke from forest and land fires, Health Minister Budi Gunadi Sadikin said, according to Antara News.
Berton Panjaitan, head of the communications center at Indonesia's National Disaster Management Agency (BNPB), told Anadolu that the country "is currently facing an elevated risk of forest and land fires, particularly in parts of Kalimantan and Sumatra."
“The situation is serious, but it remains under active control. Ground and aerial firefighting operations are being carried out simultaneously, including water bombing, aerial patrols and weather modification operations where conditions allow,” he said in a written statement.
He added that forest and land fires have been reported across several provinces since the beginning of the dry season, with "activity increasing significantly in recent months."
Local authorities have also been investigating 89 fire-related cases across nine provinces, Berton said.
Indonesia's president on Monday ordered the revocation of business permits held by corporations suspected of ordering forest and land fires.
Indonesian police have also named 72 suspects in forest and land fire cases across nine regional jurisdictions as authorities step up efforts to curb the blazes, broadcaster Kompas TV reported.
Police seized evidence including plastic bottles filled with diesel fuel in cases involving suspected deliberate arson, according to the report.

Bessent to speak as Trump administration expected to unveil new Iran sanctions
Unknown

2026-08-24

01:06:11 KST

Bessent announces campaign to create "economic onslaught" against Iran and its partners
Washington — Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday announced Operation Economic Outcast, the Trump administration's ramped-up push to use economic tools to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end the war with Iran.
"Today, at President Trump's direction, the United States Treasury has begun Operation Economic Outcast, an unprecedented campaign against the Islamic Republic of Iran and its enablers," Bessent said. "In the Second World War, D-Day marked the historic beginning of a campaign with our allies to target and drive the enemy from its positions, including those in third countries. Today, in that same spirit, we are launching an economic onslaught against Iran's financial connections around the globe."
The operation expands the categories for secondary sanctions on entities and countries that transact with Tehran and also introduces new sanctions across a variety of vital sectors, including digital assets, gold, aviation, technology and shipping.
Bessent said any entity that facilitates money laundering on behalf of Iran "will be removed from the U.S. dollar system. The clock just started ticking."
Many of the secondary sanctions, he said, won't be immediate.
"We are giving everyone the opportunity to remedy bad behavior," Bessent said. "Why would I want to blow up the global financial system? We believe that it is important to level set and give people a cure period, but they should know that that will move very quickly and that we are serious."
The treasury secretary did say he expects an announcement of a major financial institution being sanctioned by the end of this week.
Bessent said the president is making phone calls to world leaders to cease their interactions with the Iranian regime. Bessent declined to name any names when asked by CBS News, and didn't get into the timeline.
"We do not have infinite patience here," he told CBS News.
Bessent said this economic pressure campaign "will not end until this regime stands alone."
Asked whether Chinese banks that finance Iranian oil imports would be among those hit with the punishing financial measures, Bessent said that "no one is above the reach of U.S. sanctions."
He also criticized countries that engage in trade with Iran — which includes U.S. allies in the Persian Gulf like the United Arab Emirates — as guilty of "appeasement."
Last week, UAE said it has suspended financial and economic transactions with Iran, potentially threatening Tehran's access to a major source of imports and a financial back door to the world.
Bessent also said that Iran's Bank Melli, which has branches across the Gulf "must be shuttered and dark."
But not all think that these actions will cause as much harm as the touted by Bessent and the administration.
"This was not economic D-Day," said Brett Erickson, a Washington-based sanctions expert who runs Obsidian Risk Advisors. "It was something in the middle.The core constraint facing the United States in the Iran War is the global economic timeline. If the United States is unwilling to meaningfully target China, can Washington reasonably justify damaging our international relations and global standing, for a strategy with only a farfetched likelihood of achieving victory?"
The move is part of the Trump administration's effort to apply economic tools to pressure Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and eventually end the war that the administration originally said would last four to six weeks. That war is now in its sixth month.
After months of military operations and failed negotiations, Bessent plans to outline the "single greatest financial offensive ever marshaled against an adversary."
"President Trump has dismantled Iran's military capabilities, destroyed nearly 100 percent of its military factories, and buried its nuclear program," Bessent wrote in the Financial Times on Sunday. "We are now entering the endgame. At dawn begins an economic D-Day — the single greatest financial offensive ever marshaled against an adversary."
"IRAN IS COMPLETELY COLLAPSING!!!" Mr. Trump wrote Monday morning on Truth Social. The president has been insisting Iran has fallen for months.
This will be the latest round of Treasury action that targets Iran's economy. On Aug. 7, the department levied sanctions against a number of companies and individuals that it alleged laundered hundreds of millions of dollars. It was the eighth such action since the start of the second Trump administration.
"Every facilitator that keeps the regime afloat is putting a target on its own back," Bessent said in a statement at the time. "Treasury will continue to expose these networks and cut them off from the U.S. financial system."
Specifically, the department designated Shahr Bank and two Dubai-based exchange houses, Titan Exchange and Alps International, that it says helped Shahr Bank retrieve oil revenue for major Iranian exporters, including the National Iranian Oil Company and Naftiran Intertrade Co.
Several Iranian nationals were also designated, including Shahr Bank employee Saeed Ghasempour, who allegedly coordinated currency conversions with Russia's VTB Bank, and staff members of Iran-based Farab Soroush Afagh Qeshm, who allegedly managed invoices and payments for the scheme. A cluster of shell companies in Hong Kong, Singapore and Dubai — accused of funneling payments through intermediary accounts — was also designated.
Separately, the Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control sanctioned former Fly Baghdad CEO Basheer Abdulkadhim Alwan al-Shabbani for allegedly helping the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps-Qods Force move fighters, weapons, and money to militia groups in the region. Earlier this week, however, OFAC removed Fly Baghdad from its sanctions list.
The U.S. has been imposing sanctions on Iran for decades, although Tehran has often found ways to evade sanctions.

NEW DELHI: India adopted a cautious approach and opted against holding a joint media interaction after Prime Minister Narendra Modi's meeting with US President Donald Trump in France in June amid concerns over the US president's "unpredictable behaviour", government sources told news agency PTI on Monday.The sources said that foreign delegations meeting Trump are often "wary about his unpredictable behaviour as may be seen from his interactions with the presidents of South Africa and Ukraine". "Thus, the cautious approach by India," one of them said, according to PTI.PM Modi and Trump held bilateral talks on June 17 at Evian-les-Bains on the sidelines of the G7 summit. The meeting was seen as an effort to stabilise ties between India and the US after relations had come under strain over the preceding year.The clarification came after US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor said that New Delhi had informed the American side ahead of the meeting that it preferred not to have questions from the media.Gor, speaking at the Economic Times World Leaders Forum on Sunday, had said India wanted media access without a full-fledged press conference. He recalled discussing the matter with Trump before the meeting."We were behind the scenes, behind the stage, and at one point it was just the president and I, and he asked me, he goes, ‘What the Indians are going to raise?’ We went over some topics," Gor said.
"And he (Trump) said, ‘Do they have any asks?’ And the MEA had one ask. He said, and it was, ‘Let’s bring in the media, but let’s not do a full press conference,’" the ambassador added.Gor said he conveyed the preference to Trump. "I told the president, I said, the Indians prefer no questions. He said, 'Sure, no problem'," he recalled.
During the meeting on June 17, Trump also praised PM Modi, saying India would continue to play a major role globally as long as he remained in office. Asked about India's role in West Asia, Trump said: “Yes, I do. I think India plays a big role in everything. As long as he (PM Narendra Modi) is the leader, India is going to play a big role.”Trump also praised PM Modi personally, saying: "So you look at this man. I'll give you a lesson. He's the most beautiful-looking man. He looks so nice. He's like an angel. But actually, he's tough, he's a killer. He's as tough as they come. But he looks so good. So he gets you by surprise," the POTUS said.He added that the US would help India if it came under attack: "If they (India) are attacked and he's (PM Modi) the leader, we would be there to help," Trump said.

Ceasefire verification mission deploys to eastern DR Congo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:04:37 UTC
01:04:37 KST

Ceasefire verification mission deploys to eastern DR Congo
A ceasefire verification mission comprised of representatives from DR Congo's government, the Rwanda-backed AFC/M23 rebel group, and observers from the International Conference on the Great Lakes Region (ICGLR) member nations arrived in South Kivu on Monday. The deployment came a day after the DRC and AFC/M23 agreed on a Switzerland-mediated roadmap for peace talks.
A mission to verify a fragile ceasefire between the Congolese army and Rwanda-backed AFC/M23 armed group was deployed Monday to the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo as the two sides traded accusations of abuses.
The eastern DRC has been riven by decades of conflict with multiple armed groups fighting over its mineral-rich territory, including the M23, which seized further swaths of the region last year.
Peace efforts led by Qatar and the United States last year sought to end the crisis, leading to the signing of two separate accords.
Watch moreUS cracks down on mineral trafficking in DR Congo with new sanctions
The Congolese government and the AFC/M23 signed a commitment towards a ceasefire in Doha in July 2025, while the DRC and Rwanda formalised a US-brokered peace deal in December in Washington.
However, fighting has continued on the ground.
On Sunday, the Swiss government announced in a statement that the DRC and AFC/M23 had agreed on a roadmap for peace talks, following negotiations held in Switzerland.
It also mentioned the upcoming deployment on the ground of a regional body to verify violations of the ceasefire to which the parties have committed.
Read moreDR Congo, AFC/M23 group agree on roadmap for peace negotiations after Swiss talks
The mechanism for verfiying ceasefire violations comprises Congolese government and AFC/M23 representatives as well as observers from member countries of the International Conference on the Great Lakes Region (ICGLR).
The mission, the first of its kind, was deployed on Monday by UN helicopters to Minembwe in South Kivu province, which has seen intense clashes in recent months, according to UN and government sources.
The mission will also travel to the lakeside town of Uvira, from where the AFC/M23 withdrew in January, as well as to the territory of Kalehe, where fighting has been reported in recent weeks, South Kivu governor Jean-Jacques Purusi told AFP.
Neither the DRC nor AFC/M23 authorities have yet reacted to the announcement of the mission.
Alleged abuses
Several international mediation efforts have failed to silence the guns in the eastern DRC, where a myriad of armed groups are active.
In April, the DRC and AFC/M23 agreed to facilitate humanitarian aid and release prisoners following talks in Switzerland.
An initial group of prisoners was handed over to the M23 by the Congolese government earlier this month.
New talks were held behind closed doors from August 17 to August 21 which included representatives from the United States, Qatar, Switzerland, the African Union Commission and Togo, serving as African Union mediator.
The two sides said they had "agreed on the importance of a standardised method for reporting allegations of ceasefire violations", according to the Swiss government statement on Sunday.
They also agreed to establish a "mechanism tasked with reviewing progress and addressing challenges in implementation of obligations and commitments under the Doha Framework Agreement", it added.
The DRC in a statement on Monday condemned alleged "crimes and serious human rights violations" committed by the M23 in the territories under its control and accused the group of killing "more than 300 people" in June and July.
Meanwhile, an AFC/M23 spokesperson on X accused government forces of having launched a "deadly attack" with artillery on a village near Minembwe.
Both sides have regularly accused the other of alleged abuses and ceasefire violations, often unverifiable by independent parties.
The area surrounding Minembwe, which has been fiercely contested for months, has been particularly difficult for international organisations to access.
Reports by NGOs and UN experts have said the AFC/M23 has also silenced dissenting voices, including journalists and human rights activists in areas under its control.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

“That Ukraine exists nowhere anymore, except in his ‘little folders of reports.’ Our state has long been different. Not an observer, but a player. Not a victim, but a fighter.”
The Ukrainian leader said Kyiv would not allow Russia to regain the initiative or convince Ukraine’s partners that territorial concessions could provide a shortcut to peace.
“We will not let them seize the initiative, deceive Europe and the entire world into thinking that they simply need to give up Donbas, and everything will be over soon,” the President said.
Zelenskyy said there were no grounds for trusting such Russian promises and made clear that Ukraine would continue resisting rather than effectively rescuing Moscow from further battlefield losses.
“We have no illusions. We don’t trust them. We are not going to save the Kremlin half a million soldiers,” according to Zelenskyy.
He pointed to Russia’s repeatedly delayed ambitions to capture the entirety of Ukraine’s Donetsk region as evidence that Moscow’s military plans continue to fall short of its own timelines.
“Russia keeps pushing back the dates when they will ‘definitely, any day now, take the entire Donetsk region.’ It will keep pushing those dates back. Ukraine is different, and it does not give away what is its own,” he stated.
Zelenskyy also said Russia was preparing for another wave of mobilization rather than genuinely seeking an end to the war. For Ukraine, he said, the response must be to strengthen its military and ensure frontline troops have the weapons and equipment necessary to maintain the defense.
“We have to strengthen our military, have everything needed to hold our defense. Our warriors must be supplied and equipped with everything so that the replenishment of the enemy army can be turned into fertilizer for our soil.”
Zelenskyy ended his Independence Day address by directly challenging the expectations of Russian leader Vladimir Putin and contrasting Moscow’s original ambitions with the losses Russia has suffered during more than four years of full-scale war.
“Putin hopes that we are tired. But we know that he is mortal. He never understood us. Now he will not have time to. You wanted to take all our Ukraine, all our land; instead, you lost your oil refineries, your fleet, your profits, your entire generation that you sent into the meat grinder. You wanted us erased from the map; now you are absent from the international agenda of the future civilization,” he said.
Zelenskyy also pointed out the image of power the Kremlin has spent decades trying to project.
“For 27 years, the head of Russia has talked about greatness, while Russia is standing in lines for gasoline,” he concluded.
Earlier, reports emerged that fuel availability at Russian gas stations has plunged sharply, with gasoline reportedly available at only 28.1% of stations nationwide as authorities open dozens of antitrust cases against oil companies and independent fuel operators.

Netanyahu vows to raise Altalena wreck as political battle erupts over 1948 legacy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:03:14 UTC
01:03:14 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu vowed Monday to raise the wreckage of the Altalena, the Irgun arms ship shelled during Israel’s 1948 War of Independence, after its remains were located off the Israeli coast nearly eight decades after it sank.
The announcement set off an immediate political battle over credit and memory surrounding one of the most divisive episodes in Israel’s early history.
Netanyahu delivered a separate statement before National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Heritage Minister Amichai Eliyahu held their own news conference about the discovery. Ben-Gvir’s aides described Netanyahu’s intervention as an “embarrassing event,” while Ben-Gvir used his appearance to take a swipe at the prime minister, saying Menachem Begin, the Irgun commander who later became prime minister and a founder of Netanyahu's Likud party, “knew well the taste of persecution — the taste of people not wanting to be photographed with you on the same stage.”
Despite the clash over credit, both Netanyahu and Ben-Gvir used the occasion to warn against internal conflict.
Netanyahu said the Altalena “will be raised from the depths of the sea.”
He recalled then-prime minister David Ben-Gurion’s order to open fire on the ship in June 1948, weeks after the establishment of the state and the creation of the Israel Defense Forces.
“Ben-Gurion decided to open fire on the Altalena,” Netanyahu said. “It rained fire on our fighters during the War of Independence. Haganah forces on the shore opened a deadly barrage that claimed the lives of 16 Irgun fighters and three IDF soldiers.”
Netanyahu said he had attended annual Altalena memorial ceremonies for years and accused political rivals of desecrating them with what he described as incitement against his camp.
He also sought to claim a role in the long search for the ship.
“In 2009, I established the Heritage Department in the Prime Minister’s Office,” Netanyahu said. “A few years later, in 2019, I instructed that the search be renewed with a special budget. Using documentation from the Altalena captain’s logbook, today, finally, after 78 years, we found the ship after it sank into the depths.”
Ben-Gvir: ‘The lesson of Altalena is no civil war’
At his separate news conference, Ben-Gvir said the Altalena affair left a “bleeding wound” in Israeli history.
“They tried to make this wound disappear, to erase the legacy of the fighters who fought,” he said. “That is no coincidence. It is a symbol of the national camp, of its leader and later prime minister.”
Ben-Gvir also described the discovery as personally meaningful. His mother had been an Irgun member as a teenager, he said, distributing leaflets and being arrested.
“I grew up at home on those stories of heroism,” he said. “Every home in Israel, no matter the background or community, no matter who we vote for — there must never be a civil war. That is the lesson of the Altalena.”
Likud Minister Haim Katz, who joined Ben-Gvir’s news conference, credited researcher Roni Sadeh with persistently pursuing the ship’s location and the Heritage Ministry with providing dedicated funding for the search.
Political scramble for credit
The discovery quickly became entangled in election-season politics.
Ben-Gvir moved swiftly to claim credit, releasing a video with Eliyahu in which he declared: “Today is a historic day. We found the Altalena.”
“After so many years of searching, Heritage Minister Amichai Eliyahu and I are happy to announce — the Altalena has been found,” he said. “There is a message in finding the Altalena precisely now. Disagreements are allowed. Differences of opinion are allowed. But there must never be a civil war.”
Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz were initially left outside the announcement. Netanyahu’s office was reportedly surprised by the news of the discovery, despite having known about the search, while the Defense Ministry was apparently not informed.
Netanyahu later joined the public battle over the discovery, unsurprising given the Altalena’s deep association with Begin, whose Herut movement eventually became a central component of Likud.
A ship loaded with immigrants and arms
The Altalena sailed from France to the newly established State of Israel in June 1948 carrying about 930 immigrants, including Holocaust survivors, as well as a large shipment of weapons.
The ship belonged to the Irgun, the pre-state underground militia led by Begin. The crisis erupted just after the IDF was established and the separate Jewish underground organizations were being dismantled and integrated into a single national army.
Begin demanded that some of the weapons aboard the Altalena be allocated to Irgun units in Jerusalem. Ben-Gurion rejected the demand and insisted that all the weapons be handed over to the IDF.
When the dispute escalated, Ben-Gurion ordered military action against the vessel. In the ensuing fighting, 19 people were killed — 16 Irgun members and three IDF soldiers.
Begin, despite coming under fire, ordered his men not to retaliate in a way that could trigger a civil war, a decision that later became central to his political legacy.
Netanyahu promises to raise it — but experts question feasibility
The Altalena remained visible for months off the Tel Aviv coast before Ben-Gurion ordered it removed. Israeli forces later towed it farther out to sea and deliberately sank it.
The ship’s precise location was subsequently lost because records of the operation were incomplete or obscured.
Officials said Monday that the wreckage had been located about 20 kilometers, or 12 miles, off Israel’s coast at a depth of 503 meters, or about 1,650 feet, using sonar technology.
What happens next is less clear.
Netanyahu has promised that the Altalena will be raised, but recovering an entire vessel from that depth would be an extraordinarily difficult engineering operation and may prove impossible.
Among the alternatives being discussed are a floating memorial, a maritime heritage center or the recovery of selected parts of the wreck.
Veteran Yedioth Ahronoth journalist Shlomo Nakdimon, a former Begin adviser and author of a book on the Altalena affair, cast doubt on claims that the ship had been found intact.
“If they are talking about the Altalena as it once was — that does not exist,” Nakdimon said.
He said the lower part was sunk while the upper section had been dismantled and burned.
“Ben-Gvir and Eliyahu announced that they had discovered the Altalena in its entirety. It would take an act of God, because I saw it when it was sunk and it disappeared,” he said. “The lower section was sunk, the upper section was dismantled and set on fire. Irgun archives describe exactly where that section is located.”
The fight over the Altalena narrative
The discovery comes amid a broader political struggle over how the Altalena affair should be remembered.
About a year ago, seven ministers led by Eliyahu asked Defense Minister Israel Katz to remove the artillery piece known as the “holy cannon” — the IDF gun that fired at the Altalena — from the military’s Command and Staff College at Glilot and transfer it to the Menachem Begin Heritage Center in Jerusalem.
The cannon had been displayed at the senior officers’ college as a teaching tool about the tragedy and the importance of national unity.
The ministers argued that displaying it there sent a distorted educational message.
“The message is as though force and gunfire prevented disaster, while the truth is the opposite: restraint and the refusal to return fire saved the nation,” they wrote.
Katz later said he would order the cannon transferred so it could “express the true meaning of the event, out of deep appreciation for the work and legacy of Menachem Begin, who prevented a civil war.”

What is Portugal’s new ‘burqa law' banning face coverings?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:02:54 UTC
01:02:54 KST

Breadcrumb
What is Portugal’s new ‘burqa law’ and what does it mean for Muslim women?
A new law in Portugal banning face coverings in public spaces, believed to particularly target Muslim women who choose to wear the burqa, has sparked controversy and concerns from human rights groups.
The law, which was approved by parliament in July, came into effect after President Antonio Jose Seguro signed it earlier this month.
Local media in Portugal has dubbed the ban on face coverings as the ‘burqa law,’ as the bill originated with the right-wing Chega party.
A statement issued by the President’s office said: “The face must be considered a central element of human identity and communication”.
While the president noted that the issue was one of “great social and cultural sensitivity,” the decision has raised questions over how it will affect Muslim women who choose to wear the burqa, also known as niqab.
Here, The New Arab breaks down what the law says, and what it means for Muslim women.
What does the law state?
The law states that wearing any form of clothing which conceals or obstructs the face is prohibited.
Any violations of the law will incur fines of between150 Euros (£128) and 750 Euros (£641) if it is determined to be a case of negligence.
In cases where intent is proven, fines can range from 400 Euros (£342 GBP) to 3,000 Euros (£2,566).
Anyone found to be coercing another to cover their face on the grounds of religion, gender, origin or race can be jailed for up to three years.
The law clarifies that exemptions will be made for healthcare professionals and artistic, entertainment and advertisement reasons, and does not apply for places of worship, aircraft, diplomatic or consular premises.
How did it come about?
The law banning face coverings dates to October 2025, when parliament approved a first version of a draft bill that was pushed by the far-right Chega party.
The party, which has become a major political force, describes itself as a nationalist party with some of its members disparaging the Roma ethnic group and its founder, Andre Ventura, being accused of Islamophobia after he called for “the drastic reduction of the Islamic presence in the European Union”.
The party cited women’s rights and security concerns, noting it was for the “dignity and respect for women that should guide any state governed by the rule of law”.
Despite backlash from rights groups at the time, the bill on banning face coverings was passed on 17 July, with a two thirds majority in the Portuguese parliament.
Why is it controversial?
Activists and human rights commentators believe the law will unfairly target Muslim women and restrict freedom of expression.
Last month, Amnesty International issued a statement condemning the law.
“This new law is discriminatory and is a threat to human rights. Despite having removed direct references to Islam, which were a part of previous versions of the text, this new law clearly violates the human rights of Muslim women who choose to cover their faces,” the executive director of Amnesty's Portugal branch, Joao Godinho Martins, said.
Martins said the law was a “direct threat to their freedom of expression and freedom of religion,” and said that even though women’s rights were being cited as a justification for the law, the ban will likely have the opposite effect by excluding women who wear the burqa from public life and accessing education, employment and public services.
“The law also has implications for the right to privacy and the right to freedom of peaceful assembly, as it specifically prohibits the concealment of one’s face during demonstrations. This directly contradicts international law, which permits their use to ensure the possibility of participating anonymously and to prevent reprisals,” Martins continued.
Rights groups have called for the law to be reversed while some have noted a rising hostility towards Muslims in Portugal.
Which other countries have face covering bans?
The development comes after several countries in Europe have also adopted similar bans, while activists have raised concerns over polarisation in societies and noting it could pave the way for increased surveillance, unnecessary fines and conflict between communities.
France was one of the first countries to enact a full-face covering law in 2011, also arguing that face coverings prevent people from being identified and designating it as a potential security risk. Belgium also adopted a similar law in 2011, with anyone violating the law facing fines or up to seven days in prison.
Denmark, Austria and Bulgaria, too, have adopted laws against face coverings, restricting face-veils to places of worship and the homes.
Last year, Austria’s parliament approved a law banning the hijab for girls under the age of 14 in schools.
Some parts of Germany have bans in schools and public spaces on face-coverings, while Luxembourg bans them on public transport, schools and other common areas.

What to expect as Iran braces for new US economic measures amid war
