Washington Post ordered to reinstate opinion writer fired over Charlie Kirk posts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
15:42:21 UTC
00:42:21 KST

An independent arbitrator has ordered the Washington Post to rehire the high-profile opinion columnist Karen Attiah, abruptly fired by the news organization last September over comments she made on social media about Charlie Kirk, the then recently killed conservative activist.
On Monday, an arbitrator ruled that the Post had violated her rights as a union-protected employee and ordered the newspaper to reinstate her and compensate her for lost wages.
“This decision confirms what we’ve said from the start: I was doing my job as an opinion journalist, and doing that job is not misconduct,” Attiah said in a statement. “After spending over a decade of my career at the Post as an editor and an opinion columnist focusing on race, gender and global human rights, I’m relieved to finally have that record set straight … I hope that this win sends a message to journalists and media institutions everywhere that freedom of expression is always worth fighting for.”
A Post spokesperson said the company respects the arbitration process but declined to comment further. It’s unclear if the company plans to appeal the reinstatement ruling.
Attiah was backed by the union that represents most Post employees, the Washington-Baltimore News Guild, and Democracy Defenders Fund, a legal advocacy group co-founded by Norm Eisen. In his own statement, Eisen called it a “thunderous win” for Attiah and “a landmark decision for every journalist who refuses to be silenced”.
The Post had argued that Attiah was fired for cause after violating the company’s social media policy, which dictates that employees “must not harm the editorial integrity or journalistic reputation of The Post”.
After Kirk was shot and killed on 10 September 2025, Attiah took to social media and wrote: “Refusing to tear my clothes and smear ashes on my face in performative mourning for a white man that espoused violence is … not the same as violence.” She also posted: “Part of what keeps America so violent is the insistence that people perform care, empty goodness and absolution for white men who espouse hatred and violence.”
According to the arbitrator’s record of the case, Adam O’Neal, the Post’s opinion editor, had emailed the company’s head of human relations the following morning and said that Attiah’s posts were “beyond the pale- completely unacceptable for someone associated with Opinions”, calling for an urgent meeting. A few hours later, the Post’s top brass, including Will Lewis, then the publisher, met and decided that Attiah’s employment should be terminated because of her social media conduct.
O’Neal also testified in the case that Attiah’s posts created security risks for the Post and its journalists. “People were at this intense moment of violence in America, and we didn’t know what was coming next,” he said in a hearing for the case. “And we’re walking into a building that says Washington Post on top of it, and here there’s a columnist at Washington Post on this account that’s making these horrific comments and that was of deep security concern beyond the professional – beyond the publication standards and our policies.”
Attiah was emailed a copy of her termination letter – “for gross misconduct” – later that day on 11 September.
The union representing Attiah charged that she had not engaged in any kind of misconduct, “let alone gross misconduct”, and that her professional mandate included expressing opinions.
The arbitrator, Sarah Miller Espinosa, concluded that it was improper to punish Attiah on the basis of potential security threats to other Post employees.
“In the Arbitrator’s view, the Post’s witnesses’ testimony seems to attempt to hold the Grievant accountable for the actions of bad actors who were posting threats against her and The Post on social media,” she wrote. “To imply that the Grievant’s posts were justifiable provocation for threatened criminal acts or that the Grievant’s employment may be terminated for just cause because bad actors threatened The Post is unsupportable.”
Calling the Post’s termination of Attiah “absolutely disproportional”, she concluded: “The Post’s rushed decision to terminate the Grievant approximately four hours after O’Neal became aware of the Grievant’s posts … is not supported by good and sufficient cause.”

Govt seeks generation data from rooftop solar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
15:41:42 UTC
00:41:42 KST

Rooftop solar (RTS) systems under the PM Surya Ghar scheme. Photo credit : PTI
NEW DELHI: As the number of households installing rooftop solar (RTS) systems under the PM Surya Ghar scheme rises and renewable energy capacity increases, govt has decided to track how much electricity these systems are actually generating, with inverter makers required to share daily generation data with the national portal.The move could give govt, for the first time, a system to monitor the performance of individual RTS installations rather than merely track the capacity added under the scheme.Under new guidelines issued by the ministry of new and renewable energy, inverter manufacturers will have to provide daily cumulative generation data through an API to the national portal, mapped to the device’s serial number. The guidelines also require applications, monitoring and control servers and cloud-hosted data linked to inverter systems to be located in India.The data could help govt assess how much electricity rooftop systems are actually generating and identify under-performing installations. It could also allow generation to be analysed across states and power distribution companies (discoms), providing a clearer picture of the energy benefits being delivered by the scheme.A govt-appointed Expert Committee on Energy Statistics also flagged the absence of comprehensive data on electricity generated and consumed by decentralised renewable energy systems in a recent report.
Currently, more than 44 lakh RTS systems have been installed under the PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana (PMSGMBY), benefiting over 52 lakh households and adding 15.6 GW of solar capacity.The committee noted that electricity generated by rooftop solar systems is often consumed at the premises and does not pass through the grid, leaving it outside conventional electricity supply statistics. It said generation, export and self-consumption data from rooftop systems are not uniformly recorded or aggregated by discoms and recommended mandatory collection and reporting of such data to improve the accuracy of India’s electricity statistics.“Electricity generated from many of these systems is already metered. However, these meter readings are either not visible to the discoms or, even if they are visible, the readings are not recorded systematically and reported,” the committee said.Alekhya Datta, director, electricity and renewables division, TERI, said national-level centralised monitoring of electricity generation from rooftop solar systems would have multiple benefits. “If electricity distribution companies have data on electricity generated by rooftop solar plants (behind the meter) in their respective areas and the units consumed by consumers, they will be able to plan their power purchases accordingly,” Datta said.
“The amount of electricity generated by RTS plants will also give an indication of the quality of the system, and this attribute can be used in a vendor rating system as well as help improve operations and maintenance. Consumers, too, will get a sense of satisfaction from knowing their contribution to the environment.”Though the ministry has asked all inverter companies to share daily generation data, Datta said only around 15 per cent of inverters currently have the capability to share it through APIs. The govt is also yet to create an integrated dashboard where the data can be collated.
Atul Mathur is a Senior Assistant Editor at The Times of India with over 27 years of experience in journalism. Based in Delhi, he has spent much of his career reporting on governance, public policy and politics, churning out researched, data-driven stories that impact daily lives. Atul is known for investigative depth and strong human-interest narratives as he strives to bring clarity and context to complex issues. He currently tracks the energy sector, writing on power, renewable energy, coal and mines.

Households in Great Britain ‘could owe energy suppliers £7bn by end of year’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
15:40:33 UTC
00:40:33 KST

Households in Great Britain could owe their energy suppliers as much as £7bn by the end of the year after higher gas and electricity prices forecast for the winter kick in, an industry group is warning.
Domestic energy debt and arrears climbed by about £500m over the past year to a record £6bn at the end of June as the Middle East conflict continued to stoke rising gas market prices.
The amount of energy debt left unpaid for longer than 30 days is likely to accelerate to £7bn by the end of the year, according to the trade association Energy UK, as the government’s cap on gas and electricity prices is expected to climb to a three-year high.
The regulator is expected to confirm later this week a 4% increase on the energy price cap for millions of households from October as “too many households continue to feel the strain of high energy bills”, the group’s chief executive, Dhara Vyas, said.
She urged Andy Burnham’s government last week to consider a “targeted and more permanent” solution to the rise in energy bills – including a social discount tariff – rather than rely on “stopgap, ad hoc or emergency measures”.
The increase will more than wipe out the impact of the new prime minister’s promise to cut VAT from household electricity bills from October, which aimed to give voters “some breathing space” by shrinking bills by an average of about £45 a year.
“The current arrangements fail to provide the help needed and work out more costly,” Vyas said. “A social discount will address the fuel poverty gap and provide the right amount of support to the right households at the right time – reflecting that needs vary across different customers.”
  The forecast energy price cap rise means that over the final three months of 2026 the typical household faces a gas and electricity bill equivalent to £1,729 a year, forecasters at Cornwall Insight predict.
The consultancy expects electricity rates to rise from 26.11p a kilowatt hour to 26.57p, and gas charges will rise from 7.33p to 7.90p for households that pay via direct debit. However, the actual bill for a household will depend on how much each consumes.
The average bill under the price cap was calculated assuming lower annual energy use than in previous years, because the high cost of energy has forced many households to use less gas and electricity as debt levels rise. Using the previous methodology, the price cap would be forecast to rise to £1,940.69 from October – the highest level since the summer of 2023.
Ahead of the new cap, Energy UK told journalists that the rising cost of sourcing gas from the global wholesale market was the single largest contributing factor to the expected rise, although the expense of upgrading Great Britain’s energy networks was also playing a larger role in setting energy costs.
The trade group’s debt estimates are about £1bn higher than the official figures reported by Ofgem, which counts unpaid bills only once they are 90 days overdue. Although it uses a lower debt figure publicly, it spreads the cost of unpaid bills across all consumers using the higher estimates. This currently adds about £50 a year, or about 3% extra, to a typical annual bill.

Nearly half of Germans see AfD candidate Siegmund as threat to democracy: Poll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
15:40:24 UTC
00:40:24 KST

Ayhan Şimşek
24 August 2026•Update: 24 August 2026
Nearly half of Germans view the Alternative for Germany’s leading candidate in Saxony-Anhalt as a threat to democracy, according to a new nationwide poll, even as the far-right party holds a wide lead ahead of a key state election next month.
The INSA survey for Bild found that 47% of respondents consider Ulrich Siegmund a threat to democracy, while 35% disagreed. The poll also reflected broader unease about the party, with 53% of those surveyed describing the AfD as “right-wing extremist” and 37% rejecting that label.
Siegmund, 35, is leading opinion polls in the eastern state, where the AfD is drawing about 43% support ahead of the Sept. 6 election. A result near that level would mark a major breakthrough and the closest the party has come to assuming power in one of Germany’s states.
The nationwide poll also found widespread concern about potential economic consequences if the AfD led a state government. 49% of respondents said they expected an AfD-led administration to deter foreign investors, while 55% said it would discourage foreign skilled workers. 36% expected the broader economy in Saxony-Anhalt to worsen under AfD leadership.
The party’s strength comes despite repeated warnings from mainstream politicians and security authorities about its extremist tendencies. Germany’s domestic intelligence agency BfV has classified the AfD’s regional branches as proven right-wing extremist organizations. The agency has said parts of the party promote a racist and ethnic understanding of national identity that is incompatible with Germany’s democratic constitutional order.
Although the AfD leads in the polls in Saxony-Anhalt, it is not assured a majority in the state parliament. The outcome will depend in part on whether smaller parties clear the 5% threshold required to enter the legislature, which could significantly affect the distribution of seats.
According to the latest survey by Pollytix, the AfD stands at 43%, followed by Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) at 23%, the Left Party at 13% and the Social Democratic Party (SPD) at 7%. The Greens are hovering at the 5% mark, while the left-wing populist BSW is projected at 4%, below the threshold.
All major democratic parties have ruled out forming a coalition with the AfD because of its far-right positions, leaving uncertainty over how a government could be formed after the election.

Explainer-What are Iran's options to escalate further in face of US economic threats?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
15:38:37 UTC
00:38:37 KST

Explainer-What are Iran's options to escalate further in face of US economic threats?
LONDON, Aug 24 - U.S. threats to impose "the toughest sanctions in history" to force Iran to buckle to its demands after nearly six months of war have raised the prospect of a new round of escalation in the Gulf.
How could Iran respond to the economic pressure?
CAN IRAN STOP MORE OIL GETTING OUT OF THE MIDDLE EAST?
Mohsen Rezaei, the former Revolutionary Guards chief and secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, has already threatened to shut down oil exports — one of Tehran's main strategic approaches since the war began on February 28.
"If the economic war continues, not a single drop of oil will be exported, neither through the Strait of Hormuz nor from anywhere in the Persian Gulf," he said.
Iranian attacks and threats to shipping have already stopped most traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, largely shutting down a waterway that carried around a fifth of global energy before the conflict.
Although some oil tankers have been moving through the strait in recent weeks, volumes remain very low and on Sunday Iran blacklisted 45 tankers it says failed to comply with the rules it wants to impose on Hormuz shipping.
Missile, drone or speedboat attacks on tankers trying to leave the Gulf have repeatedly pushed up oil prices during the six months of the conflict.
Meanwhile, Tehran's Houthi allies have restricted Red Sea shipping with attacks and threats to blockade all Saudi Arabian shipping, which carries crude to Asia through the Bab el-Mandeb strait past the group's Yemeni stronghold.
While the attacks initially only stopped some vessels, with more than half still getting through in mid-August, the situation is difficult for shippers with Chinese shipping companies now rerouting away from Bab el-Mandeb, according to industry sources.
Further attacks, such as the one that targeted a vessel off the main Saudi Red Sea oil terminal at Yanbu on Monday or a drone strike near the Suez Canal in early August, could raise oil market anxiety levels and crude oil prices.
ARE GULF STATES STILL AT RISK OF IRANIAN ATTACK?
Iran has threatened to retaliate against any neighbours who take part in U.S. efforts to strangle the country's economy with "earthquake" force.
It has targeted Gulf states and Jordan repeatedly during the war, mostly focusing on U.S. bases but also hitting energy infrastructure and other targets.
Any intensified attacks that targeted upstream oil or gas facilities could further drive up energy prices in ways that inflict political damage on the Trump administration and could be harder to reverse than attacks on shipping.
Targeting power and water desalination plants in the hot, parched region would also pose a major risk to U.S.-aligned Gulf monarchies that function as significant financial hubs for the global economy.
CAN IRAN ATTACK WESTERN COUNTRIES DIRECTLY?
While Western countries are beyond the range of Iran's main munitions, the Revolutionary Guards have historically been willing to find alternative ways of attack.
On Monday, Britain said Iran-linked hackers had shut down a small electricity station while U.S. officials have said Tehran was likely behind cyber attacks on water plants in Minnesota. Iran has not commented on those allegations.
Western security services have also accused Iran of recruiting local people to stage attacks or attempt assassinations in the West. Iran has denied that. REUTERS

Tensions in the Alps after antisemitic video
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
15:38:32 UTC
00:38:32 KST

Each summer for decades, Orthodox Jewish communities have sought the calm of the Alps, but their presence and strict lifestyle can irritate locals and other tourists.
Usually peaceful, the Deux Alpes resort found itself at the centre of controversy a few days ago after a video went viral on social media in which a shopkeeper, leaning on the counter of her refreshment stall, can be heard telling an Orthodox Jewish man: "The Jewish community, there are too many of you. At some point it gets on people's nerves."
An investigation has been opened following the incident. But it has cast a chill over the resort, which every summer, for decades, has welcomed Orthodox Jewish families.
"Let's say it has created a bad atmosphere in the resort; Orthodox Jewish tourists don't cooperate at all, they don't take part in anything, not the restaurants, not the bars, not the activities – well, only the children's activities, the games, that's all," explains Danièle, a regular visitor to the resort.
The case has also got people talking and highlighted tensions that can arise in Alpine resorts between local residents and holidaymakers.
"There are other people who, even when we walk down the street with the children, speak badly to them because they are wearing kippot. That shows that people are frustrated that there are children around, that there are a lot of Jews, so in the end this is not an isolated situation," says Hannah Lasry, a Jewish tourist.
The director of the Alpe d'Huez tourist office, Sébastien Merignargues, says: "When I was in Tignes, there were issues, for example with the swimming pool, about bathing – men, women – the lifeguards had to be the same sex as the swimmers, small things like that, and it's true that these are ways of operating that we don't have, so they can, I don't know if 'conflict' is the right word, but in any case there is a need for adjustment and sometimes they are simply sticking points."
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez was quick to condemn the antisemitic remarks. After hearings, the investigation was passed "for review" to the Grenoble public prosecutor's office, the latter said at the start of the week.
For several years now, Deux Alpes has hosted the Beth Loubavitch summer seminar (part of the ultra-Orthodox Hasidic movement Chabad-Lubavitch), a major gathering for French-speaking Judaism that consistently attracts hundreds of people over three weeks. Created in the late 1960s, when hundreds of thousands of Jews from North Africa were arriving in mainland France, the seminar has since moved from resort to resort in the Alps.

Election Observers Say Kazakh President's Party Had 'Undue Advantage' As It Grabs 70 Percent Of Vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
15:36:46 UTC
00:36:46 KST

Four months ago, the Adilet party did not exist.
Today, it dominates Kazakhstan’s political landscape, following an election in which it gained 71.17 percent of the vote according to results announced on August 24.
The vote marks a further tightening of President Qasym-Zhomart Toqaev's grip on power -- and was roundly criticized by international election observers from the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).
“The 23 August early parliamentary elections, while technically well prepared, took place in an environment lacking political pluralism. Political choice was reduced by the lack of distinct political alternatives, with all contesting parties supporting the incumbent President’s policies,” an OSCE statement said.
In the August 24 statement, issued a day after the vote itself, the OSCE reported misuse of public resources, including public-sector employees being mobilized to attend campaign events, and concluded that Adilet had "an undue advantage that blurred the line between state and party.”
The OSCE noted that independent candidates had been excluded from the election, a factor which “limited political participation and electoral competitiveness.”
Observers also cast doubt on the results themselves, stating that discrepancies between what they saw at polling stations and official turnout data “raised questions about the integrity of the voter turnout reporting and the counting process.”
OSCE missions have made similar criticisms of all previous elections held in Kazakhstan since it became independent after the fall of the Soviet Union in 1991, noting a lack of genuine political competition in an authoritarian country dominated for decades by presidents Nursultan Nazarbaev (1991-2019) and his successor, Toqaev.
When Adilet was formed, in April, it absorbed the ruling party that had dominated Kazakhstan during and since the Nazarbaev era.
Its stated aim is to implement Toqaev's policies and it will now comfortably control Kazakhstan's new unicameral parliament, the Kurultai. Adilet’s vote share was more than eleven times that of its nearest rival.
The election was the first since constitutional changes rammed through by Toqaev earlier this year to switch from a previous bicameral structure.
Media Pressure Before the Vote
The election took place amid reports of pressure on independent activists and media.
Almaty-based civil activist Asset Abishev said police blocked access to his home on August 23, which he described as interference with his right to vote.
Another activist, Nurbol Arterkhan, who is under probation and subject to electronic monitoring, said he was repeatedly required to report to probation officials on election day and that police later visited his home.
According to the Committee to Protect Journalists, five prominent journalists have been jailed or convicted since mid-July, while criminal cases have been opened against two others. Several have also been barred from practicing journalism.
Media freedom was another major concern in the OSCE assessment.
“Long-standing concerns about arrests and pressure on independent journalists generate pervasive self-censorship,” it noted in its statement.
Sevilay Celenk, who headed a team of observers from the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE), also raised the issue.
“Without an inclusive, credible, and pluralistic media environment, political participation and representation are fundamentally limited, especially during elections,” Celenk said.

Coalition of the Willing reiterates Ukraine’s 'clear and inherent right' to defend itself against Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
15:34:24 UTC
00:34:24 KST

Burak Bir
24 August 2026•Update: 24 August 2026
 Marking the 35th anniversary of Ukraine's independence, the Coalition of the Willing countries on Monday reaffirmed Kyiv's "clear and inherent right" to defend itself against Russia.
"They were united in their continued support of Ukraine’s fight to defend its sovereignty, freedom and territorial integrity," a joint statement said after the leaders of the Coalition of the Willing convened in the capital Kyiv and by video conference to commemorate the 35th anniversary of the restoration of Ukraine’s independence, as the Soviet Union’s collapse was imminent.
The leaders condemned Russia’s "systematic and escalating" strikes on Ukraine’s cities, critical infrastructure, and civilians during the meeting co-chaired by UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, French President Emmanuel Macron, and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
"Leaders reiterated Ukraine’s clear and inherent right to defend itself against the Russian war of aggression, in full compliance with international law and Article 51 of the UN Charter," said the statement.
They said they would not be deterred from their support for Ukraine by what they called "irresponsible Russian threats."
The statement also condemned Russia’s attacks on Ukraine’s cultural heritage sites, which form an integral part of Ukraine’s national identity, including the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra, a historic monastery.
"The Coalition would continue to prepare the Multinational-Force Ukraine to deploy once a credible cessation of hostilities was in place, as part of a wider set of robust politically and legally binding security guarantees to ensure Ukraine’s future security and prosperity once a ceasefire enters into force," it added.
The leaders also agreed on the urgency of providing "immediate assistance" for Ukraine’s energy sector ahead of the coming winter, including through the Ukraine Energy Support Fund and providing specialist equipment.

Border Police discover Second Temple-period burial cave during operations in east Jerusalem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
15:33:00 UTC
00:33:00 KST

An ancient burial cave was discovered beneath a building by Border Police officers operating in the Silwan neighborhood of eastern Jerusalem, Israel Police announced on Monday.
Police called the find into the Israel Antiquities Authority (IAA), which sent over personnel to properly survey the site.
Preliminary investigations by the IAA indicate that the burials date back to the Second Temple period, between 516 BCE to 70 CE. Other archaeological artifacts were also found within the cave.
Israel and Border Police are securing the area in coordination with the IAA, in order to continue studying the findings as required.
The discovery came as part of police’s ongoing investigations into the violent clash between two feuding families in Silwan that occurred over the weekend and led to the deaths of three people.
One person was killed in the incident, while two others were shot by police after posing as “active threats” to the responding officers.
According to police, the two were wielding blunt instruments, blades, and Molotov cocktails.
'Bodies piling up at police station'
National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir on Sunday said that when he told the media that the public was quick to count those shot during police activity as deaths that occurred as part of Arab sector violence in Israel, "the media was quick to shout: Fake!"
"So here it is: All night long the left-wing media reported on 'three murdered,' cried about 'bodies piling up at the police station,' and asked, 'Where are the police?' And the truth? Two of them threw stones and Molotov cocktails and were shot by our heroic police officers during the incident! This is exactly the mind games I was talking about," he said.

Organ harvesting, dog rape: Contested claims of a Palestinian Feminist org. report - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
15:32:15 UTC
00:32:15 KST

A new report by the Palestinian Feminist Collective (PFC), supported by Progressive International (PI), argues that Israel has a documented history of systematic sexualized and gendered violence against Palestinians “across detention centers, homes, military operations, and systems of surveillance, from the Nakba of 1948 to the present.”
Among other things, the 187-page report, “A Predatory State: Israeli Systemic Sexualized and Gendered Violence Against Palestinians,” advances as fact the claim that Israel trains dogs to rape Palestinians. It adds that this is “an essential indicator of Israel’s operationalized intent to dominate and destroy Palestinian life and the Palestinian right and will to resist.”
The dog rape claim was published in a May 2026 New York Times opinion column by Nicholas Kristof and sparked global condemnation, accusations of modern-day blood libel from groups such as the American Jewish Committee (AJC), and a threatened lawsuit from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
“Sexualized violence, including rape and sexual enslavement, has been used by Zionist militias during the 1948 Nakba and later by the Israeli state as a method of displacement and domination over Palestinians. After 1967, such violence intensified against prisoners and detainees, laying the groundwork for the systematic sexual torture documented since October 2023,” the PFC report says.
It also pays particular attention to Israel’s purported “preponderance of attacks targeting Palestinian men, particularly their sexual and reproductive organs.”
CODEPINK’s Feminists: Stand with Palestine campaign has subsequently called on the Center for Reproductive Rights to share the reports in its networks and “uplift the findings regarding maternity health and sexual violence as it affects Palestinian women and families.”
The PFC is a US-based anti-Israel collective of Palestinian and Arab feminists that describes its work as advancing Palestinian social and political liberation through an anti-colonial and feminist framework.
On October 7, 2023, PFC posted on X/Twitter: “We affirm the right to resist settler-colonial dispossession, militarization, and occupation.”
PI is an international anti-Israel political network that seeks to organize progressive movements around a vision it describes as democratic, decolonized, egalitarian, anti-capitalist, and anti-imperialist. CODEPINK is a US-based, women-led grassroots anti-war and anti-Israel organization that supports Palestinian rights.
Report based on alleged testimonies framed as fact
The report is based on alleged testimonies that purportedly serve as evidence that sexualized violence took place at distinct times over the last two years, across multiple sites. The assaults were allegedly enacted by the “Israel Occupying Forces,” affiliated with multiple agencies, including soldiers, prison guards, police, and intelligence officers.
“Patterns of the documented sexualized violence include, but are not limited to the following: sexual slurs, forced nudity, forced stripping, forced witnessing of sexual acts, threats of sexual assault, sexualized comments or touch meant to degrade; physical torture that is sexualized in character or targets sexual or reproductive organs, including groping, squeezing, punching, and applying pressure to the genitals, forced oral sex, or being sexually abused while in stress positions; and cases of rape, including simulated rape, rape by IOF personnel, rape with a range of objects such as batons, phones, metal rods, sticks, or other objects, and rape by trained dogs.”
The patterns and methods used in the assaults reveal, “beyond a reasonable doubt, that sexualized violence is a systemic Israeli practice, which has accelerated in frequency and degree of brutality alongside the acceleration of genocide since 2023,” the report adds.
This alleged sexualized and gendered violence is framed throughout the report as a “colonial mechanism” deployed to destroy the “indigenous” Palestinian people.
It is also presented as an indisputable fact that “sexualized violence, rape, and sexual enslavement were methods purposefully used by Zionist extra-state forces during the 1948 Nakba and by the Israeli state following the Nakba to expedite the displacement of Palestinians from their land.”
The language used in the report, especially in Part 2 [“Israel’s Systemic Gendered Violence”] is highly polemical and pseudo-academic in its framing. While presented as fact, it is mostly activist language rooted in settler-colonial and feminist theory.
For example, one part reads, “The womb is an intimate site where past, present, and future converge in the gendered body. To theorize the Palestinian womb as a site of futurity is to recognize that Israel’s settler-colonial project against Palestinians is fundamentally a war against time: against the possibility that Palestinians will persist, continuing to create life, transmitting identity, memory, and relationship to land across generations.”
The report also persistently venerates “Palestinian martyrs.”
Report perpetuates conspiracy theories about organ harvesting
In “Case Study 2: Desecration of Martyred Bodies,” the report says, “The martyr, in this framework, is not released from political life at the moment of death; rather, it enters a new phase of state custody and juridical negotiation that affects martyrs’ bodies based on their gender, especially against Palestinian men.”
This interprets documented practices of holding on to the bodies of terrorists as a systematic form of Israeli necropower, further claiming that this power is gendered, without including any discussion of the reason for such a practice.
It also ventures into blood libel territory in this case study, when it discusses “organ stealing” as a practice it says Israel has carried out since the First Intifada in 1987. For this claim, it cites Palestinian Dr. Hatem Abu Ghazaleh who “noticed martyrs’ bodies, after being returned, were missing eyes and kidneys.”
“Abusing martyrs’ bodies in this fashion, by stealing their body parts and then desecrating their bodies to hide the theft, demonstrates how the Palestinian martyr is gendered in a way to deny their dignity, especially of young men resistance fighters.”
The problematic description of terrorists as “resistance fighters” aside, there has been no evidence of Israeli authorities systematically stealing organs from Palestinian bodies.
This is a misquotation of the quote Abu Ghazaleh provided to a 1990 article by Mary Barrett in the Washington Report on Middle East Affairs magazine. Barrett asked Abu Ghazaleh about widespread anxiety in Gaza and the West Bank concerning alleged organ theft after the Intifada began, to which he replied that there were “indications that for one reason or another, organs, especially eyes and kidneys, were removed from the bodies during the first year or year and a half.”
These indications were based on reports from what he defined as “credible people.” He did not examine the alleged corpses himself.
A 2001 report by Israeli journalist Ronen Bergman on practices at the Abu Kabir Institute of Forensic Medicine (Israel’s only facility authorized to conduct autopsies in case of unnatural death) uncovered a medical malpractice scandal: During 1988-2000, tissue and body parts, including skin and corneas, were removed from deceased Israeli soldiers, Israeli civilians, both Jewish and Arab, and Palestinians without relatives’ permission.
Discussion of organ harvesting as a broader and systemic practice is not based in documented fact and appears more connected to longer-term established antisemitic conspiracy theories.
Later on, in Case Study 6, the report claims that Israel’s use of artificial intelligence to decide which Palestinian buildings to target is a form of gendered violence, as it prevents Palestinian couples from having sexual intimacy.
“By assaulting the intimate, gendered spaces where bodily integrity, reproductive capacity, family and society building, and nurturing happen, militarized tracking through AI extends the reach and force of the predatory state by targeting the heart of reproductive and intimate life: the home. By displacing or killing as many Palestinians in a home as possible, AI-generated programs disrupt the conditions and spaces for pleasure, sexual intimacy, caregiving, and generational continuity.”
Once more, theoretical arguments are presented as empirical evidence.
Perhaps the most heinous part of the report is the final section, “Colonial Constructions of Palestinian Men.”
This argues that Israel fabricated all claims of sexual violence against Jews and Israelis on and after October 7 as a means of demonizing and racializing Palestinian and Arab men.
The report says that “racialized constructions of Palestinian, Arab, and Muslim men as other, violent, aggressive, and sexually deviant mirror the colonial histories and patterns across colonial projects where Indigenous and Black men have been imagined as threats, primarily to white women.”
It calls the graphic accounts of the rape of Israeli women on October 7, 2023, “fabricated” and intended to “construct Palestinians as barbaric and depraved.”
“For decades, the international community and Israel have remained silent about the rape of Palestinian women. Yet, after October 7, Israeli settler women have been positioned as the ultimate victims.”
It then goes on to say that “allegations that Hamas engaged in systematic rape on October 7 are rooted in the long-standing racialized colonial demonization of Palestinian, Arab, and Muslim men” and that there is “no credible forensic evidence, nor victim testimony, corroborating the October 7 mass rape allegations.”
“When Israel uses falsified allegations of sexualized violence supposedly perpetrated by Palestinians to establish moral justification for genocide, it is reversing the realities of power, repositioning Israeli settlers as victims and Indigenous Palestinians as perpetrators,” it concludes.
Sources cited in report largely disputed
It is worth noting that the majority of the sources on which the paper relies are controversial or have been the subject of controversy.
The report relies heavily on [anti-Israel New Historian] Ilan Pappé, [Palestinian writer and activist] Susan Abulhawa, [former convicted terrorist] Rasmea Yousef Odeh, B’Tselem, the Palestinian Centre for Human Rights, [US-sanctioned] Francesca Albanese, [Australian Muslim sociologist and lawyer] Randa Abdel-Fattah, and Al Jazeera [media blocked by the US, Israel, Pakistan, and at times by the PA].
Abulhawa, for example, described the October 7 attacks as a “spectacular moment that shocked the world,” called the Israel-Hamas War a “Jewish supremacist slaughter,” and said that “these sons of Satan will taste what they meted [out] to us.”
Yousef Odeh was a member of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP) convicted by Israeli military courts for involvement in a 1969 Jerusalem supermarket bombing, that killed two young civilians.

How can we stop destroying the prospects of a generation? Scrapping compulsory GCSE resits will be a start | Polly Toynbee
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
15:31:56 UTC
00:31:56 KST

GCSE results day was marked with the usual front pages filled with pictures of beaming students. What you didn’t see was the invisible third of 16-year-olds in England who failed their maths and English GCSEs, the obstacle to their future.
That’s 360,000 failed in a system designed by Michael Gove as education minister to mark out winners from losers. It’s a cast of mind shared by many in his party who still yearn for the 11-plus, which consigned a random number of children to failure before they’d hardly begun. A few councils still do it.
Once failed, this one-third must resit English and maths to do any other course: colleges cannot provide them with a blessed start from failed schooling, as they are refused funds for any student not taking repeated resits. Only about 17% of the wretched resitters ever pass. Quite apart from the despair, David Hughes, head of the Association of Colleges, points to the waste: of the far-too-few 16 teaching hours a week for students on post-16 study courses, resitters must be taught seven hours of hated English and maths that most of them will fail. That leaves just nine hours for the vocational courses they choose. No wonder UCL research shows the damage done: self-confidence is lost, many drop out altogether. That doesn’t happen in Wales and Northern Ireland, where resits are not mandatory for continuing study.
Labour gets it. Both the previous education secretary, Bridget Phillipson, and the current, Lucy Powell, well understand the damage done by this Gove-devised torment: finally compulsory resits will end in 2028. Instead, those who fail can take a new “stepping stone” qualification in functional maths and English, proving adequate literacy and numeracy skills.
But an ideological dispute remains among Powell’s advisers. They will still make every 16-year-old take English and maths GCSE in the first place, even if they will probably fail. Many only need the stepping-stone qualification anyway. This doesn’t sit well with Andy Burnham spreading his successful Greater Manchester baccalaureate (MBacc) nationally, a scheme that offers vocational courses suited to local employers alongside academic subjects from age 14, to keep them engaged and avoiding Neet status: not in education, employment or training.
But ideological purists think dividing them early between GCSE groups and stepping-stone groups sets up a two-tier discrimination, downgrading some who might have passed a full GCSE. But with a million Neets, the key priority must be making school encouraging, not rejecting.
Gove sticks to his Gradgrind resits. He calls Burnham’s approach “bring back stupid”, anti-intellectual and hostile to ambition. But had he invested in nursery education, where destinies are most surely set, there might be fewer 16-year-olds with failing grades to bully now. New research reported by the Institute for Fiscal Studies shows how entering childcare one year earlier gives an average 10% improved maths score by age 14 to 15, and a 28% higher score for those with a mother without qualifications.
The good news is that Labour’s emphasis on skills has been infectious, with a surge in applications to technical courses, well beyond the current demographic bulge, while university applications still rise by 3%. Alan Milburn’s commission to solve the crisis of 1 million Neets has real policy steam behind it to urge more skills training.
But further education (FE) has a lot of catching up to do. There are many ways England has not just neglected but discriminated against non-academic education. Despite recent extra funding for colleges, this still doesn’t cover the entire cost of any extra student accepted, an additional 25,000 are expected to enrol this autumn, and colleges lack space and staff after colossal cuts in the Tory years: over-19s adult education fell from £5bn in 2002 to £1.5bn in 2025.
Recent extra money for pay “only stopped the gap getting wider”, Hughes says, when FE staff are paid £10,500 less than school teachers, and are in short supply when construction and engineering jobs pay so much more. Why, he asks, do colleges pay VAT costing £200m, while schools are reimbursed?
The spur of Labour’s new growth and skills levy is incentivising employers to take on beginners with short courses. But as applications quadrupled for degree apprenticeships, more sought-after than Oxbridge places for earning while learning, places have halved.
Why do university students get maintenance loans, but FE students can’t? “Because too many will never earn enough to pay them back,” says Hughes bluntly. Worse still, Neets on benefits are barred from full-time courses, which is perverse.
Needless barriers need fixing. Neets who need driving licences for jobs and apprenticeships, essential from care to plumbing, find the waiting time for a driving test is 21 weeks or more.
Burnham’s eloquence on valuing “the hard hat as much as the academic cap” earns Gove’s contempt, but it has raised FE spirits. Talking to college heads, they see that Labour knows what to do. As ever, the problem is overcoming Britain’s forever low esteem for technical education. It will take heavy lifting to shift mentalities towards encouraging that third of 16-year-olds instead of tormenting them.
- 
  Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

France to press ahead with high school phone ban from next month
The ban is expected to take effect from the start of the new school year, which begins in September
The French government said on Monday it would press ahead with a ban on mobile phones in high schools from next month, but trade unions warned that the measure might be hard to implement quickly.
In July, France’s parliament approved legislation banning both social media access for children under 15 and mobile phone use in high schools.
It is part of a push by President Emmanuel Macron for children to spend less time in front of screens, which the government fears is arresting their development.
But earlier this month, the country’s top court struck down the social media provision, dealing a blow to Macron.
However the Constitutional Council did not rule on the separate provision banning mobile phone use in high schools.
On Monday, government spokeswoman Maud Bregeon said Macron “has decided to promulgate the law” containing the ban on phones, despite the Constitutional Council striking down its flagship provision.

Snakes on a plate: Could reptile consumption have freed us to settle down?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
15:28:25 UTC
00:28:25 KST

The snake slithered frantically into the underbrush, but it was too slow. It had been spotted and its fate was sealed. It had become a statistic.
Marks of stone tools on bones of reptiles unearthed at the el-Wad Cave on Israel's Mount Carmel show that the hunter-gatherer Natufians living there 12,000 to 15,000 years ago routinely ate snakes and legless lizards. This was the conclusion in a paper published last week in PNAS by University of Haifa researchers Ma'ayan Lev, Mina Weinstein-Evron and Reuven Yeshurun.
The question underlying the research had been the degree prehistoric peoples exploited such squamates for food. Reptile and tortoise remains have been identified in various archaeological circumstances, but the scale of the phenomenon was unclear.
Latter-day hunter-gatherer societies consume reptiles in desert climes and the American and Asian tropics. It's a bit niche, but in Florida, people hunt down and eat invasive Burmese pythons, though experts warn that one may want to analyze the dearly departed for heavy metal contamination before chowing down.
In other words, reptile is routinely eaten among peoples who are either crazed by TikTok or whose choices are severely constrained. Snake reportedly tastes like chicken, but where modern people have their druthers, they don't go there.
But how did ancient peoples in eras before animal husbandry view the scaly set?
Similarly to today: somewhat askance, perhaps. The evidence suggests that snakes and the like were not a favored food, not for the Natufians nor for anybody else. The degree of reptile consumption seems to depend on what else the people could catch. But the Natufians' reptile consumption was significant, almost a third of their animal intake in the Early Natufian stage at el-Wad.
In fact, squamate on the plate may exhibit not only their dietary flexibility. It may have even contributed to their settling down, the researchers suggest. How is that?
See snakes, can settle
The Natufian culture in the Levant predated agriculture. These hunter-gatherers broke the paradigm that farming must have emerged before permanent settlement. Evidently, it didn't. Thousands of years before the first wheat seed was deliberately planted or the first herbivore was domesticated, Natufian hunter-gatherers had left the cave life behind and settled down.
At el-Wad, in the Nahal Me'arot Nature Reserve, the evidence shows three phases of Early Natufian settlement: pre-architectural, architectural and post-architectural.
In other words, these folks didn't stride out of the cave, matted heads held high, and start to build stone houses. How did they live outside at el-Wad, for instance, before they built houses? "Maybe in tents," Yeshurun speculates over the phone with Haaretz. Or in simple huts, like separate work detected at Ohalo by the Sea of Galilee from more than 20,000 years ago.
But live there they did, and they continued to forage and hunt, as their ancestors had done before, possibly with the help of tame dogs, which we know they had. Hunting was how they gained their protein; they didn't have domesticated goats or cows. What did they hunt?
Some degree of reptile acquisition could have been predicted. Unrelated work at Tel Aviv University has demonstrated that over the last 1.5 million years, the average body mass of animals in the southern Levant shrank by more than 98 percent. Where once our species and ancestors preyed on megafauna, by the time of the Natufians, the biggest game left in town was gazelles and deer.
Archaeology of the Natufians has shown that this is exactly what they preferred to eat; gazelles comprised anywhere from 40 percent to 80 percent of the animals they consumed, going by bone finds. Now we learn that the Natufians did not shrink from snake.
In fact, they ate reptiles to a degree suggesting that this practice enabled their very settlement, freeing them of the need to roam far in search for more attractive protein, like gazelle. They could stay in their houses all year; the climate was gorgeous and the nutrition was right there for the taking. But would they have eaten the snakes if they had other options?
At the initial settlement stage, one finds some reptile consumption. Exploitation of reptiles increased during the architectural phase, to as much of 40 percent of the acquired animals. Then reptile consumption receded again, the researchers concluded after analyzing thousands of reptile bones throughout the 20-layer archaeological sequence at el-Wad Terrace, all of which date to the Natufians.
Actually, to what degree does el-Wad represent all Natufians, a culture that lasted around 3,000 years and was dispersed throughout the Levant? In terms of reptile finds and a few other aspects, el-Wad is the most detailed case study we have of this culture, Yeshurun explains.
He adds that not only did the Natufians destroy the paradigm of agriculture before settlement; in their voraciousness, they also disrupted the natural distribution of snakes, frogs and so on. Before them, squamate and amphibian distribution was dictated solely by geography. But Natufian sites are consistently dominated by large squamates; a Natufian site on the Carmel is like one at the Hula Valley to the north, for example, despite the geographical distance.
So yes, el-Wad can be taken as representative and it has the best record of cut marks and manipulation of reptile remains in the Epipaleolithic. Lev, who led the research, identified marks on 82 vertebrae, in roughly the same location on the bone, suggesting culinary attention. Note that a cut mark on snake bones refers to lesions on vertebrae because snakes don't have bones below the neck.
Okay. El-Wad represents Natufian culture. The reptiles the el-Wadders targeted were the biggest and slowest, the researchers found: the European glass lizard (which is legless and looks like a snake), the large whip snake (which is a snake), and the eastern Montpellier snake (also a snake).
The legless lizard appears in all the Natufian layers but the others appear mainly in the architectural phase.
Seeking to explain why the legless lizard was found in all layers, while other equally edible squamates were confined to the most intensely occupied layer, Yeshurun consulted a herpetologist (a reptile and amphibian expert). Could the legless lizard might have been attracted to human habitation? But commensal relationships aren't a thing with reptiles, the expert said, which brings us back to options.
Reptiles may have been part of the total Natufian subsistence package, but the intensification of their consumption after the Natufians settled down and built homes suggests that the other options had run out. Or away.
Note that to this day northern Israel is thronged with wild boars, some of which are bold enough to live in modern cities. Nor have gazelles and deer gone extinct. (Though a host of other decently sized animals such as the hartebeest and hippopotamus most definitely have gone extinct locally – and much later than many assume. They only disappeared forever more as wars raged over the land during the biblical period.)
So why didn't the Natufians eat many boars? Why resort to snakes, which may taste like chicken but hardly have any of the fatty layers that humans crave?
Slow snakes are relatively easy to acquire, while swine (and even deer) are smart enough to learn to avoid areas with permanent, hungry human habitation. Note that the boars living in Haifa and other Israeli cities are not subject to predation pressure, because we have supermarkets and can't be bothered to chase and kill them, so they don't need to learn to avoid us.
But back at el-Wad, the longer the Natufians stayed there, the more they had to rely on the animals that didn't have the smarts to hoof it.
The Malthusian Natufian
In the post-architectural phase of the Natufian culture, the people seem to have reverted to seasonal occupation of el-Wad. It isn't that they necessarily reverted to total nomadism, Yeshurun notes, but they did abandon the permanent settlement. "I think it was a very local thing," he says. "At el-Wad, we attribute it to the demographic cycle."
The model of a settlement is that it starts small; a few people in a great environment surrounded by food. After a few generations, the settlement reaches the maximum population that the environment can sustain, the population advance stops as food grows scarce and conflicts develop, and then some folks move away, some kill each other and, long story short, we have abandonment.
At el-Wad that cycle took several centuries at most, Yeshurun says, after which Natufians continued to live sporadically at the site for another 2,000 years.
We don't know why the architectural phase collapsed, but plausibly, even without the local serpent population imploding or fleeing, the environment couldn't sustain enough food for a growing sedentary population. Large animals hadn't gone entirely extinct but may have come under regional hunting pressure. It wouldn't pay for a sedentary Natufian to trek far away to hunt down a hartebeest and lug the cadaver home.
Peak snake consumption was during the middle phase, the architectural one. All this supports the thesis that the Natufians chose to settle in a lush environment that became progressively less so and ate prolifically of the legless lizards, the snakes, and other small animals like hares when they had no choice. Yeshurun adds that the snakes they targeted were not only slow and large but nonvenomous – there isn't evidence that they doted on viper.
After the Natufians and the collapse of their settlement endeavor, what happened? Agriculture started to emerge. In the pre-pottery Neolithic, we find the first stabs at orderly grain cultivation and animal husbandry, while people continued to hunt. But as cows, goat, wheat lentils and the like joined the menu, nobody needed to resort to snake anymore.

Europol Warns of Violent Shift in European Museum Heists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
15:28:00 UTC
00:28:00 KST

Reported by
Europol is warning of an alarming shift in museum heists across Europe, as criminal networks abandon traditional stealth in favor of brute force and extreme violence, according to a report published Monday.
The European Union’s law enforcement agency said perpetrators are increasingly ditching the traditional “deception and discreet execution” of art theft, historically viewed as a “non-violent form of organized property crime,” in favor of direct and confrontational methods.
Instead of niche experts, Europol’s report—”Changing Tactics, Changing Targets: The Evolving Nature of Museum Heists”—found that these new heists are often carried out by decentralized groups of opportunistic criminals recruited via social media on a “crime-as-a-service” basis. These new criminal profiles are increasingly armed with sledgehammers, axes, crowbars, and explosives and firearms to breach premises, smash display cases and intimidate or assault staff in broad daylight.
Recent high-profile incidents illustrate this violent shift. In November 2024, four suspects armed with baseball bats and axes stormed the Cognacq-Jay art museum in France during opening hours, smashing a display case to steal seven gold and diamond items before escaping on scooters.
In January 2025, thieves detonated explosives to blow off the doors of the Drents Museum in Assen, the Netherlands, to steal a 2,500-year-old Dacian gold helmet and three gold bracelets. Dutch police, with the help of an art detective, successfully recovered the helmet and two of the bracelets in April 2026 after a lengthy investigation.
A similar violent attack occurred at the Louvre Museum in Paris in October 2025, where thieves broke a window using a mechanical ladder, threatened guards and visitors, and smashed display cases in the Apollo Gallery to steal nine items of jewelry worth an estimated 88 million euros ($102.69 million).
Alongside the changing tactics, Europol noted that organized crime groups are shifting their focus away from traditional art and toward raw materials, increasingly targeting gold, silver, and gemstone-laden jewelry due to their rising market value.
Precious metals can be easily melted down to erase trace evidence for law enforcement and facilitate illicit sales during the fencing process, the agency explained, adding that precious stones can be easily removed and resold.
While the October 2025 heist at the Louvre Museum made headlines around the world, that jewelry theft was actually part of an accelerating trend across France. A month earlier, a Chinese national—already known to police—stole 7 kilograms of gold nuggets valued at 1.5 million euros ($1.75 million) from the National Museum of Natural History in Paris. French media outlets reported that she was arrested a few days later at Barcelona airport carrying a kilogram of melted gold and was placed under formal investigation for “theft as part of an organized gang.”
This summer, France saw a spate of other high-profile museum thefts. First, on July 1, an archaeological center was targeted in a robbery where approximately 40 Roman gold coins valued at 120,000 euros ($139,994) were stolen. Only four days later, sledgehammer-armed robbers broke into the Lalique Museum and fled with 27 jewelry items valued at 4.5 million euros ($5.25 million), while on July 24, a priceless, 2,500-year-old Celtic gold collar was stolen in broad daylight from the Musée du Pays Châtillonnais.

Ukraine faces €23B defense funding hole as Western cash lags
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
15:27:38 UTC
00:27:38 KST

Volodymyr Zelenskyy welcomes international leaders upon their arrival for a coalition of the willing meeting in Kyiv on Aug. 24, 2026. | Pool photo by Henry Nicholls via AFP/Getty Images
KYIV — Ukraine faces a €23 billion hole in its defense budget this year, leaving Kyiv scrambling for cash to fight Russia even as Western leaders gathered in the capital to mark the country's independence day and pledge ongoing support.
The money is needed not only for weapons and air defense, but also to pay soldiers, support the families of those killed and ensure Ukraine has the supplies it needs to start 2027.
“We are not asking [you] to fight for us. Give Ukraine everything to stop this war, to stop it faster than Putin can start the next one,” President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a speech Monday.
Advertisement
U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham was in Kyiv Monday for a meeting of the so-called coalition of the willing.
European Council President António Costa, Luxembourgish Prime Minister Luc Frieden, Moldovan President Maia Sandu, Estonian President Alar Karis, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and other Nordic and Baltic leaders also attended in person, while French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz joined remotely.
“Ukrainian people deserve not just continued support but our gratitude ... I am determined we [the coalition of the willing] will work together to deliver the support you need,” Burnham said in a statement.
The funding gap originated after the defense ministry brought forward spending originally planned for the second half of the year, while the EU’s €90 billion loan was delayed by roadblocks from Hungary.
“At the beginning of the year, decisions were made at the ministry to use in the first half of the year funds that were intended to be disbursed in the second half," Zelenskyy said during a meeting with reporters on Saturday. The shortfall comes on top of €30 billion in funding Europe has already pledged to Ukraine this year as part of the €90 billion loan.
Purchases made included "fiber-optic drones, middle-strike drones, interceptors,” former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov told POLITICO in June.
Advertisement
"Now, in the second half of the year, those funds need to be compensated for and supplemented,” Zelenskyy added.
The European Commission offered some relief Monday, approving €6.1 billion in new defense procurement for Ukraine. This latest disbursement from the EU’s €90 billion loan package will fund air-defense missiles and ammunition, as well as radars — among Kyiv’s most urgent needs. But the money falls far short of what Ukraine says it requires.
Ukraine needs about €6.8 billion to €8.5 billion to ensure a “normal start” to next year, the Ukrainian leader said. That money is effectively needed in advance to pay for weapons and other supplies for January 2027. Around €17 billion more is needed for military salaries, payments to the families of fallen soldiers and other expenses.
“A lot of money is needed,” he added.
But domestic politics are also creating obstacles to international funding. Zelenskyy admitted that Ukrainian lawmakers are stalling the implementation of reforms on which some international aid is conditional.
Overall, parliament is currently delaying 24 reform bills tied to Western funding disbursement. While not all the funds are tied to defense spending, getting EU money would free up Ukraine's scarce resources for other urgent defense needs.
Advertisement
Last week, the Ukrainian parliament’s law enforcement committee removed five government and judicial reform bills from consideration because they are no longer relevant, Ukrainian MP Anastasiya Radina said last week.
Maksym Buzhanskiy, a lawmaker from Zelenskyy's party, defended the committee's decision to remove the bills, claiming they do not correspond to Ukraine commitments needed for EU funding.
Zelenskyy is planning to ask for disbursement of EU funds ahead of schedule.
“I am working on this with the French and the Germans. Practically, we need to bring forward the second portion of the European funds allocated for Ukraine, and this is an extremely difficult task,” Zelenskyy said.

West turns Ukraine into 'frontier country' making money on war — economist

2026-08-24
15:26:30 UTC
00:26:30 KST

MOSCOW, August 24. /TASS/. The West has transformed Ukraine into a "frontier nation," whose sole purpose appears to be waging war while relying heavily on foreign aid, according to Oleg Pendzin, executive director of the Ukrainian Economic Discussion Club, who was speaking in an interview with the UNIAN news agency.
"From day one of the conflict, we've been fighting on borrowed money," Pendzin stated. "The socio-political climate surrounding us is causing significant concerns among our European partners regarding their own futures. Essentially, they are buying off Ukrainian blood."
Pendzin pointed out that Europe seems intent on shifting the entire burden of the conflict onto Ukrainian shoulders by funneling money and weapons into the country. He described Ukraine as a "frontier country" that exists solely through financial injections, aid, mercenaries, and weaponry - serving as a shield rather than an independent nation.
"Ukraine cannot survive solely on its own resources at this point," he emphasized. "Imagine if we didn't have access to the recent 90 billion euros from the EU lending program - our entire social system would collapse instantly. There would be no social assistance, no salaries for public sector workers, no aid for the impoverished, no pensions."
For several years, Ukraine's budget has been plagued by a record deficit. Domestic revenues no longer fully cover even military expenses, with Western aid filling the gap for most other expenditures. Kiev openly admits that its own financial resources are exhausted, and securing additional funding is increasingly challenging. Meanwhile, Western partners, including the IMF, are urging Ukrainian authorities to explore new avenues of self-financing, such as tightening tax policies. As former Ukrainian Prime Minister Nikolay Azarov (2010-2014) warned, without continued Western lending, Ukraine risks ceasing to exist as a functioning state.

Ex-Pussy Riot Member Says She Helped the FSB Spy on Kremlin Critics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
15:23:05 UTC
00:23:05 KST

Former Pussy Riot member Rita Flores has revealed that she was coerced into working as an informant for Russia’s FSB security service, saying that she gathered information on anti-war activists and was involved in a failed assassination plot against an exiled Kremlin critic.
Flores said FSB officers coerced her into signing a cooperation agreement following a February 2023 raid on her Moscow apartment, threatening her with criminal prosecution over social media posts about alleged Russian war crimes in Ukraine alongside death threats against her relatives.
“They began recruiting me with all kinds of threats and abuse [including] threats to murder my family and that I’d never be able to prove who killed my mother,” she told the exiled news outlet Port in a video interview.
Operating under the codename “Harley,” Flores said she was assigned to build detailed profiles on Russian artists and political dissidents. Between early 2024 and June, she received monthly payments of 50,000 rubles ($600) from her security service handlers after an initial disbursement of 30,000 rubles ($360).
Flores detailed how she deliberately sabotaged her FSB assignments for over two years, faking personal feuds with targets like artists Philippenzo and Pavel Krisevich to delay their arrest by law enforcement authorities.
In mid-2025, Flores said she was ordered to lure her ex-boyfriend and former Pussy Riot member Pyotr Verzilov into a cafe in Serbia where undercover FSB agents planned to kidnap and kill him. The activist said she was offered 3 million rubles ($36,000) for her role in that assassination plot.
“That was the point of no return. Before, I thought I just needed to wait to get my passport back and flee. But then I realized how far they were willing to go,” Flores said in the interview with Port.
Refusing to help carry out the assassination plot against Verzilov, Flores stalled her handlers and sought help from human rights lawyer Dmitry Zakhvatov. Exiled businessman Leonid Nevzlin subsequently helped her flee Russia earlier this month.
The Moscow Times could not independently verify any of the claims made by Flores.

Dae’Quan Wright is heading to LSU if he clears waivers after Browns released him
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
15:23:03 UTC
00:23:03 KST

After a stop in the NFL, Dae’Quan Wright could be heading back to LSU thanks to court order
BATON ROUGE, La. (AP) — After a stop in the NFL, former Mississippi tight end Dae’Quan Wright could be heading to LSU thanks to a court order that is creating havoc throughout college sports by allowing Wright and others an unexpected fifth year of eligibility.
Wright’s agent, Drew Rosenhaus, told The Associated Press on Monday that the tight end had been waived by the Cleveland Browns and, if he clears waivers, will join Lane Kiffin’s roster at No. 11 LSU.
If he joins the Tigers, Wright would be the first known player to return to college after playing in the NFL. He may not be the last.
At a news conference Monday, Kiffin declined to discuss any specific players, but he did say of the players in the lawsuit: “They’re available to recruit. So, ourselves, like many places around the country, are recruiting them.”
Not doing so, Kiffin said, could lead to a situation where “we may end up playing against them.”
Wright signed with the Philadelphia Eagles as an undrafted rookie following the draft. After Philly released him on Aug. 11, the Browns signed him. Wright didn’t play in Cleveland’s two preseason games. Wright played two seasons for Kiffin at Ole Miss. Last year, he caught 39 passes for 635 yards and five touchdowns for the Rebels.
Wright was among a group of players who sued in a Louisiana court, saying a new NCAA rule granting five years of eligibility to most athletes should apply to him and others who were not “grandfathered” into the rule, which did not include those who graduated high school in 2022.
In a statement released Monday evening, the Southeastern Conference said it firmly opposes professional athletes returning to play college sports.
“College athletes, not professional athletes, have been at the heart of the Southeastern Conference,” the statement said. “Individuals who choose to leave college athletics, sign professional playing contracts, and compete professionally should not then be permitted to return to college competition. Allowing that to occur will blur the line between college and professional sports, create significant competitive equity concerns and reduce opportunities for high school and current college athletes.”
The SEC concluded its statement by calling on Congress to pass a bill regulating college sports.
Wright and two others who played for Kiffin at Ole Miss — former New Orleans Saints defensive tackle Zxavian Harris and Arizona Cardinals safety Wydett Williams — were among those granted a temporary restraining order last week. Former LSU and current Tampa Bay Buccaneers linebacker Jack Pyburn also was among the plaintiffs.
The players can regain their college eligibility if they terminate their pro contracts and repay any pro earnings. Pyburn’s deal with the Bucs guaranteed him $115,000, including a $15,000 signing bonus.
“I’m just trying to maximize myself as a player and as a person and play my best football, wherever that is,” Pyburn told The Athletic last week.
A preliminary injunction hearing is scheduled for Aug. 31 in East Baton Rouge, Louisiana.
The SEC has its own rule barring transfers inside the conference beyond a designated window in January. Commissioner Greg Sankey sent the schools a reminder about that rule earlier this month, though there’s no certainty on how it would play into Wright’s move to LSU in the wake of the court order.
The judge in Louisiana allowed for the fifth year and also ordered the football transfer portal, normally open only in January, to reopen for a week for the players in the lawsuit.
“In my opinion, knowing the information, it’s really wrong to be critical of these kids,” said Kiffin, whose move from Ole Miss to LSU last season also created tension between the SEC schools. “They were granted a fifth year by a judge, saying they were wronged by the NCAA. … It’s simply that a judge decided they should have a fifth year, like everyone moving forward will have.”
Kiffin suggested that the current recruiting by colleges of NFL rookies is a “totally unique circumstance that came about because of the five-for-five (ruling), and players feeling like they should have known about it before, and because of all the cases around the country. I don’t think we’ll have this (situation) again.”
Other coaches, though, have been less supportive.
“I think there’s a lot of negatives that are involved around this,” Oregon coach Dan Lanning said. “Once you go to the NFL, to me, you’re in the NFL. You don’t get the opportunity to come back.”
Added Florida coach Jon Sumrall: “What I really struggle with is the rules are changing so daily based upon a court ruling, or what happens in a court in Colorado, or a court here, a court in Louisiana. We need to have some continuity and some consistency across the board.”
Tennessee coach Josh Heupel also made his feelings known Monday when asked to compare the two-game suspension given to Volunteers linebacker Arion Carter over a $427 plane ticket for a trip to an NFL training facility during the pre-draft process before he returned to college.
“You guys certainly have a clear picture of how I feel about that entire situation to begin with, even before some of the madness that is college football and rosters,” Heupel said.
___
Maaddi reported from Tampa, Florida.

Music Review: Mike D 5D’s debut solo album ‘Thank You’ offers glitchy, post-Beastie Boy fun
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
15:23:02 UTC
00:23:02 KST

Music Review: Mike D 5D’s debut solo album ‘Thank You’ offers glitchy, post-Beastie Boy fun
ATLANTA (AP) — Mike D 5D, a new project from former Beastie Boy Michael Diamond, will release “Thank You” on Friday — the debut solo album from the MC and the first new music from the Beastie Boys’ camp since the 2012 death of Adam “MCA” Yauch.
“Thank You” is a debut album unafraid to traverse new sonic ground — and suffers only the occasional misfire.
Joined by his band — his sons Skyler and Davis Diamond as well as Eddie Ruscha, Will Graefe and Milo Ruscha — Mike D’s album bristles with stuttering drum and bass breaks and distressed vocals on the opening tracks “Switch Up” and “What We Got,” both of which sound as if they were pushed through an overdrive pedal. Somehow it works and is fitting with Mike D 5D’s high-volume and energetic style.
Less necessary are meandering and repetitive songs such as “Secrets Pt. II,” in which Mike D discusses his discomfort. “I got secrets,” the rapper implores, repeatedly — no, seriously, a lot — while failing to reveal one. The rapper has a musical idea, but not much of a lyrical one.
Much of the album plays out like a man in a bedroom with a vintage synth, a half dozen beered-up friends and a laptop stuffed with aging drum software. Such is true of the track “Crypto,” which purports to cast a cautious eye at greed, but lurches melodically. Ultimately, it relents to a frenetic and fuzzy declaration from Mike D of “All these people in your ear, they’re in your ear / All these people talking in your ear, in your ear” — which apparently means something to him.
But overwhelmingly, “Thank You” is messy, noisy glitch-rap fun. Consider “I Don’t Care,” one of the top tracks. It holds a down-tempo pace and finds Mike D weighing the balance of responsibilities and their emotional returns: “We all have a role / I didn’t see mine,” he sings. “Start with a goal get lost in the deadline.” The track excels thanks to wonderful Mini Korg synth work from Hubert Blanc-Fracard, formerly one half of the French music duo Cassius.
Despite a dash of low lights, “Thank You” is refreshingly inventive. That in itself is an accomplishment. To have the aim and drive to create something this new and far afield deserves applause. He’s reaching beyond the low rung recreations of Beastie Boy flavor he could have easily leaned into. But that’s easy and accessible and where’s the fun in that?
Credit is due here for exploration and commitment. He’s Mike D and he gets respect.
___
“Thank You,” by Mike D 5D
Three stars out of five
On repeat: “I Don’t Care”
Skip it: “Crypto”
For fans of: A distressed “Paul’s Boutique”

Deportees who refused to exit a US flight in Liberia are sent to Equatorial Guinea

Deportees who refused to exit a US flight in Liberia are sent to Equatorial Guinea
DAKAR, Senegal (AP) — Six people who were deported by the United States to Liberia last week resisted getting off the plane and instead were sent to Equatorial Guinea, another African nation that signed a third-country deportation agreement with the Trump administration, a person on the plane and a lawyer in contact with the six said Monday.
Under a series of often secret agreements, the Trump administration has deported thousands of people to two dozen countries that aren’t their own as it pushes ahead with its immigration crackdown, advocates say. Immigration lawyers say the practice is being used as a legal loophole to indirectly return some asylum seekers to countries they fled.
The group who refused to get off the plane in Liberia on Thursday include four Cuban men, a Brazilian man and a Cameroonian woman, the person and lawyer said.
A Honduran deportee aboard the flight said the group refused to disembark, saying Liberia was “not their country” and that they would face danger there. They were then separated from the others, he said. He spoke on condition of anonymity out of fear of reprisals.
He said the other passengers got off in Liberia because they feared officers would force them.
Meredyth Yoon, litigation director for Asian Americans Advancing Justice-Atlanta, said the deportees who resisted leaving the plane in Liberia were told they would be returned to the United States but instead were flown to Malabo city in Equatorial Guinea.
“It was a really heartbreaking and chaotic scene when they arrived in Malabo on Thursday,” Yoon said.
Some arrived in chains and in extreme distress, she said, including the Cameroonian woman and one of the Cuban men, who Yoon said has a large abdominal growth and uses a colostomy bag that must be drained regularly.
There is no medical staff at the hotel in Equatorial Guinea where the six are being held, alongside around 40 other deported migrants, she added.
Conditions at the hotel have worsened in recent months, Yoon said, with food sometimes withheld and guards accused of threatening, beating and choking some of the migrants.
Equatorial Guinea’s government did not immediately respond to a request seeking comment.
Under an opaque $7.5 million deal with the Trump administration, Equatorial Guinea’s all-powerful president, Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo, has turned the hotel owned by his family into a prison for asylum seekers deported from the U.S.
